items.title: [good-first-issue] tests: make flaky vllm_bench throughput comparisons reproducible
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
Parent tracker: #5313 · Onboarding: #3372

## Confirmed flaky behavior

`k3-multiprocess-test / vllm / vllm_bench / zmq` changes its throughput verdict without a source update:

| Build #5340, September 29, 2026 (UTC) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| [Original job](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eab1-a517-4a38-8163-b0ec7cfaff63) | LMCache throughput **7.34% slower** than baseline; fails the 5% limit |
| [Retry](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eaba-4671-4f79-a910-4a02cfa0cadf) | LMCache throughput **0.62% faster** than baseline; passes |

Both are `dev` builds of **`9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125`**, with no PR-base merge, vLLM **`0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676`**, and torch **`2.13.0+cu130`**. Both baseline and LMCache completed all 50 requests with 500400 input tokens. This is an intermittent benchmark verdict, not an installation failure.

The inputs are not reproducible across those attempts: the original uses seed `1790644335`, the retry `1790645482`. Each attempt uses the same seed for its own baseline/LMCache pair, but the default `RANDOM_SEED` comes from `date +%s`. The seed change is a confirmed confounder; it is **not proven to be the sole cause** of the throughput fluctuation.

## Bounded good-first task

Make this benchmark's inputs reproducible across retries, and make the comparison auditable. This is the first test-harness improvement for the confirmed flake, not a production performance optimization.

1. Replace the clock-derived default seed with a documented stable default; continue honoring an explicit `RANDOM_SEED` override.
2. Save a small comparison manifest next to `baseline.json` and `lmcache.json`: effective seed, model, request count and lengths, actual checkout SHA, installed vLLM/torch versions, and the two throughput values/verdict. Keep any new diagnostics local to this workload.
3. Preserve separate attempt results when used in CI. Follow the existing result-directory/cleanup conventions, and ensure the manifest is accessible in the job log or a public Buildkite artifact rather than merely naming a container-local file.
4. Add focused CPU-only regression coverage using stub benchmark commands: default seed is repeatable, both sides receive it, an override is honored, and success/failure summaries retain the actual numbers.

Keep the 5% throughput limit, request/token checks, and cache-retrieval validation. Do not add blanket retries, remove assertions, or present a fixed seed as proof of a resolved performance issue. #5227 already added retry mitigation; this task addresses reproducibility within the workload.

Starting points, checked at `42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052`:

- [Workload seed and result comparison](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/workloads/vllm/vllm-bench.sh).
- [Result cleanup/copying](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/cleanup.sh).
- [Buildkite step and existing retry policy](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/pipeline.yml).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Default inputs are identical across attempts; explicit overrides still work.
- [ ] A reviewer can recover both results, the effective inputs, versions, and verdict from public job output/artifacts.
- [ ] Stubbed CPU coverage exercises default/override and passing/failing results.
- [ ] GPU validation reports first-attempt results with a fixed seed; remaining fluctuation is reported as unresolved rather than hidden.
- [ ] Existing behavioral assertions and thresholds remain effective.

## Reproduce the CI workload

The evidence below comes from CI; this issue does not claim a local GPU reproduction. Use a dedicated Linux x86_64 GPU test host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit, two available CUDA GPUs capable of running separate `Qwen/Qwen3-14B` servers, sufficient host RAM for the default 80 GiB LMCache buffer (plus the mock L2 storage for the L2 case), and disk/network access for the image, wheels, and model. CI uses CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12, and a 1 GiB `/dev/shm`. A maintainer can run the GPU validation for a contributor who only has a CPU machine.

These commands build the public CI image recipe, explicitly start Bash, and pin the historical LMCache and vLLM revisions. They are a reproduction recipe, not a fully locked copy of every historical dependency or GPU scheduling condition. Run from a fresh directory; make the actual PR against current `dev`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache.git
cd LMCache
git checkout 9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125
docker build -t lmcache-flake-ci \
  -f .buildkite/k3_harness/ci-base.Dockerfile .
docker run --rm --gpus '"device=0,1"' --shm-size=1g \
  --entrypoint bash \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace/LMCache" -w /workspace/LMCache \
  -e MAX_JOBS=1 \
  -e INFERENCE_ENGINE=vllm \
  -e LMCACHE_REQUEST_TRANSPORT=zmq \
  -e LMCACHE_PR_BASE_MERGE=never \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_VERSION=0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676 \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_ARCHIVE_INDEX_URL=https://wheels.vllm.ai/0da126676e38f5dc1b02b2c4f48dc85f90f5a79f/cu130 \
  lmcache-flake-ci -c '
    set -e
    source /opt/venv/bin/activate
    command -v git uv python3 nvcc gcc g++
    nvidia-smi
    git config --global --add safe.directory /workspace/LMCache
    .buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/run.sh vllm_bench
  '
```

Use the linked failed and passed jobs as the initial reproduction pair. For subsequent GPU runs, record the actual checkout SHA, installed package versions, GPU model, input settings, and first-attempt result. A green retry alone does not show that the underlying fluctuation was fixed.

## Claim and contribution rules

This is primarily for a new contributor. Claim **one active sub-issue at a time** by commenting `/claim` here; check existing comments and ass

items.author: DangerousANEN
items.body_excerpt:
## llm-vram-calc

A zero-dependency Python CLI that answers the #1 question in local inference: **"will this quantization fit in my VRAM?"** — before the 40GB download.

```bash
pip install https://github.com/DangerousANEN/llm-vram-calculator/releases/download/v1.1.0/llm_vram_calculator-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl
llm-vram-calc
```

### What it does
- 10+ model presets (Qwen 2.5/3, Llama 3.x, DeepSeek R1/V3, Phi-3, Gemma 2, Mistral)
- Quantizations from q2_k to f16 with per-model bit-precision maps
- Q8_0 auto-detection with llama.cpp fallback defaults
- Batch comparison across multiple configs
- **Offload layers calculator**: how many GPU layers fit when VRAM is short and system RAM picks up the rest
- **KV-cache estimator**: max context length for a given VRAM budget
- Verdict output: `fits` / `OOM` with exact MB breakdown (weights / KV-cache / overhead)

### Live interactive web version
https://ai.zxc1x1.ru/tools/vram/

### Russian-language deep-dives on the math behind VRAM estimation
Telegram: @llm_hubs — weekly LLM digest, benchmarks, no hype.

**Source code:** https://github.com/DangerousANEN/llm-vram-calculator
**Release (wheel + sdist):** https://github.com/DangerousANEN/llm-vram-calculator/releases/tag/v1.1.0

items.title: [Bug] HiCacheFile scans the whole store directory on every existence check, so the scheduler stalls as the store grows
items.author: Yunzez
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

With `--hicache-storage-backend file`, every prefix-existence check walks the **entire** store directory:

```python
# python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/hicache_storage.py:590
        if self.metadata_cache is None:
            existing_files = set()
            with os.scandir(self.file_path) as entries:     # O(files in the store)
                for entry in entries:
                    if entry.is_file() and entry.name in target_files:
                        existing_files.add(entry.name)
            return existing_files
```

`target_files` holds a handful of names. The branch below it does the right thing — `os.path.exists` per target key, O(len(keys)) — but it is only taken when `metadata_cache` is not None, and

```python
# python/sglang/srt/environ.py:723
    SGLANG_HICACHE_FILE_BACKEND_ENABLE_METADATA_CACHE = EnvBool(False)
```

so **a stock file-backend server takes the scanning branch**.

Every block is one file in one flat directory (`os.path.join(self.file_path, f"{key}.bin")`, no sharding), and the store grows continuously while serving. Under `--hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete` the lookup is synchronous on the request path, so as the store grows the scheduler stalls: the waiting queue stays non-empty while nothing is running.


Ask claude to measure if this is a real issue: 

It ran SGLang 0.5.19, `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`, one RTX 4090, 40-minute cells, identical seed, identical workload and the same single contract. The only difference is the L3 file tier:

| arm | server flags | iterations | scheduler stalls | latency spikes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| file tier | `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 2.0 --hicache-write-policy write_through --hicache-storage-backend file --hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete --hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"prefetch_threshold":64}' --max-total-tokens 8192` | 96 | **10** | 9 |
| host tier only (control) | the same **without** the three `--hicache-storage-*` flags, ratio 8.0 | **353** | **0** | **0** |

The control did **3.7x** the work -- 353 iterations and 7,663 requests against 96 and 1,884 -- and stalled zero times, with zero latency spikes and zero KV-leak rows. Its single contract was also judged 45 times against 2 on the file arm, because a lookup that returns promptly leaves room to judge. A stall is "the waiting queue was non-empty continuously for ≥3 s after the running queue drained to zero"; p99 TTFT on the file arm reached 36,975 ms at concurrency 3.

**Dose-response**, which is what points at the directory scan rather than at slow storage in general, same cell, same budget, differing only in how full the store was at the start:

| store at start | first stall | stalls in the run |
|---|---|---|
| 43 GB / 398,543 files (grown by a previous run) | iteration **13** | 17 |
| empty | iteration **37** | 10 |

The store reaches ~1.2 GB/min while serving; the two runs left 43 GB and 48 GB behind.


## Suggested fix
Either:

1. **Default `SGLANG_HICACHE_FILE_BACKEND_ENABLE_METADATA_CACHE` to true.** The correct code path already exists and is already tested; only the default keeps it out of reach.
2. Drop the scanning branch entirely and always use the per-key `os.path.exists` path. `os.scandir` over the whole store to find ≤ `len(keys)` names is never the better plan, it is strictly more work than stat-ing the names you are looking for.
3. Shard the store into subdirectories by key prefix, so no single directory grows without bound. Worth doing regardless of 1 and 2, since the directory is also enumerated elsewhere (`_scan_existing_files_to_metadata_cache`, the clear path).

### Reproduction

[repro_sglang_hicache_file_scandir.py](https://gist.github.com/Yunzez/b3de5dd240a2588cc515c2778bd3c5c9#file-repro_sglang_hicache_file_scandir-py)

### Environment

Python: 3.12.8 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Dec 11 2024, 16:31:09) [GCC 11.2.0]
CUDA available: True
GPU 0,1: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090

items.title: [good-first-issue] distributed: convert Bigtable L2 adapter logging to %-format
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
Follow-up for #5118 after #5125.

#5125 enabled Ruff `G004` repo-wide and added temporary `per-file-ignores` for files that still build logging messages with f-strings. This issue is one file from that cleanup queue.

Claiming: please comment `/claim` and wait for assignment so we avoid duplicate PRs.

## Scope

Convert only the logging f-strings in:

- `lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/bigtable_l2_adapter.py` (5 G004 findings)

The count above was measured on `dev` at `3ae0d9d` with `ruff check --isolated --select G004`.

## Expected change

- Replace logging f-strings with lazy `%`-style logging arguments, for example `logger.info("loaded %s tokens", num_tokens)`.
- Preserve the rendered log text and behavior, including numeric formatting such as `.2f`.
- Do not change non-logging f-strings or unrelated control flow.
- Remove the matching G004 ignore entry from `pyproject.toml` once the file is clean:
  - `"lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/bigtable_l2_adapter.py" = ["G004"]`

## Verification

```bash
ruff check --isolated --select G004 lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/bigtable_l2_adapter.py
ruff check --select G004 lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/bigtable_l2_adapter.py pyproject.toml
pre-commit run --all-files
```

The first command should report zero findings after the cleanup. The second verifies that the repo configuration still passes after removing the ignore entry.

Refs #3372

items.title: [Feature Request][MP] Concurrent multi-turn benchmark for memory-budget-aware KV offload and retrieval
items.author: shivankur-code
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**
new feature; multiprocess mode / benchmarking, if applicable.

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

I'd like to help evaluate memory-budget-aware KV offloading and retrieval for concurrent, multi-turn conversations. Before changing any policy, I'd like to agree on a small workload and the specific limitation it should test.

The concrete starting point is MP prefetch admission: the current controller limits in-flight requests by count, while their L1 footprints can differ a lot. Eight short-prefix loads and eight long-prefix loads are very different memory and transfer workloads. The existing [controller design](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/dev/docs/design/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/overall.md#max-in-flight-limiting) already calls out memory-based admission as a possible improvement.

I found #4529, which addresses this directly with byte-aware admission and aging, so I'm not proposing another implementation of that queue. What I'd like to check is how the existing approach behaves when conversations grow over successive turns, compete with one another, and overlap stores with retrievals under a fixed budget. I haven't run this experiment yet, and I'm not reporting a reproduced serving failure or claiming this coverage is absent everywhere.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Start with a focused benchmark/test extension using the existing engine-bench infrastructure from #5489, rather than a new scheduler. Initial scope would be one serving engine (vLLM), MP mode, one GPU and DRAM L1 plus local filesystem L2. No P2P or distributed placement changes.

The workload would:

- Interleave short and long conversations. Each conversation keeps its exact previous token prefix and appends subsequent turns, including generated output. Turns within one conversation remain ordered; different conversations run concurrently, with configurable think time.
- Use a deterministic seed and a working set large enough to produce actual tier pressure. Verify useful prefix hits and actual L2 reads, rather than assuming a large prompt exercises off-GPU retrieval.
- Sweep concurrency and context lengths at fixed GPU and host-cache budgets. Include an ample-capacity control and separate cold-start from warmed measurements.
- Compare no external offload, eager offload, and existing eviction-aware lazy offload. Evaluate #4529 separately on a pinned compatible revision, with its author's agreement. Deadline/fallback interactions from #5255 would be a follow-up, not a requirement to merge all pending work together.

The first deliverable would be a reproducible workload, a documented run matrix, and a report showing:

- p50/p95/p99 time to first token, inter-token latency, and requests meeting agreed latency targets;
- per-conversation queueing time and whether long conversations repeatedly lose admission;
- useful hit tokens, actual transfer bytes, allocation failures/fallbacks, and evictions;
- separate GPU KV-pool usage, GPU temporary/pinned-for-transfer usage, and host L1 allocated/staging bytes, identifying any unavailable measurements rather than estimating them as results.

If this exposes a reproducible problem that existing work doesn't cover, I'd bring back a narrowly scoped fix with regression tests. Fewer transferred bytes alone would not count as success if response latency or useful reuse gets worse. Any cancellation/timeout tests must keep buffers charged and protected until transfer completion or confirmed abort; returning a fallback result doesn't make outstanding I/O safe to forget.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Just lower the current in-flight request count or increase L1 capacity. Both are useful controls, but neither tells us how mixed-size conversations behave at equal resource budgets.
- Contribute tests directly to #4529 instead of adding a benchmark workload. I'm happy to do this if that is the more useful boundary.
- Build a new global scheduler or cost model. I'd rather avoid that before there is evidence of a gap in the existing policies.
- Compress L2 storage. That's a separate experiment: smaller serialized objects don't automatically reduce the engine's GPU-resident KV pool, since data may be reconstructed on load. Copying KV off GPU also isn't proof that its GPU blocks have been reclaimed.

**Additional context**

Related work I want to coordinate with:

- #4847: merged eviction-aware lazy offload.
- #4529: byte-aware MP prefetch admission, including small-load ordering and aging.
- #5255: optional prefetch deadline and recompute fallback.
- #5837 / #5838: L1 allocated-byte eviction accounting.
- #5489: merged tier-pressure benchmark.
- #5780, particularly #5782 / #5783: cost-aware admission and serving qualification. This request should complement those experiments, not duplicate them.
- #4557: earlier shared-L2 QoS proposal, including in-flight byte limits; closed, but relevant prior discussion.

Would this mixed-size, growing-prefix workload be useful as a separate benchmark contribution, or should it live under one of the existing threads? In particular, I'd appreciate guidance from the prefetch/benchmark maintainers and the authors of #4529 and #5780 on the scope before starting implementation. The first step is agreeing on that boundary, not changing defaults or claiming a new policy.

items.title: [RFC / Feature] SPICY-KV: 28.6x–50x Pre-RoPE Algebraic Multigrid KV Compression for RadixAttention & Long-CoT (91.7%–100% RULER Recall & 100% Shared-Prefix Multi-Query Reuse)
items.author: Yuge-Y
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [ ] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

### Motivation: Compressing `RadixAttention` Shared Prefixes & Long-CoT (`<think>`) Traces by 28.6x–50x

Hi `SGLang` team! We evaluated our newly released Pre-RoPE Algebraic Multigrid KV compression framework (**SPICY-KV**: *SPectral Invariant Coarse-graining with dYadic KV renormalization*) across both the **NVIDIA `RULER` benchmark suite** (`28.6x` / `3.5%` KV and `50.0x` / `2.0%` KV on `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B` & `1.5B`) and **4-Turn Shared-Prefix Multi-Query Reuse** (compressing a shared prefix once and answering 4 distinct sequential user queries without re-prefilling, directly mirroring `SGLang`'s **`RadixAttention`** tree nodes).

We wanted to share why existing eviction (`SnapKV`, `PyramidKV`, `H2O`, `StreamingLLM`) and post-RoPE token-merging (`KVMerger`, `CaM`) baselines break down on `RadixAttention` shared prefixes and extreme compression ratios, and discuss a 4-byte per-node kernel calibration hook for `FlashInfer` / `Triton` paged attention:

1. **Why Observation-Window Eviction (`SnapKV`, `H2O`) Fails on Shared `RadixAttention` Prefixes:** Eviction methods score prefix tokens using only the trailing observation window of the *first* prompt. When subsequent turns query different branches or facts in the cached prefix, evicted tokens are permanently gone (`62.5%` multi-query recall for `SnapKV`, `25.0%` for `PyramidKV`, `0.0%` for `H2O`).
2. **Why Post-RoPE Token Merging (`KVMerger`, `CaM`) Hits `0.0%` on `RULER`:** Linearly merging post-RoPE keys across positions $t_1 \neq t_2$ causes destructive trigonometric phase cancellation. `SPICY-KV` inverts RoPE ($R_{\Theta, t_i}^{-1}$, or taps pre-RoPE / MLA latent vectors $c_t^{KV}$) and applies **two-level moderated-step mean centering ($B_{\text{step}}=128$)** to strip `k_proj.bias` sink cones and cumulative causal drift.
3. **Hybrid Algebraic Multigrid ($C/F$) Splitting + 2nd-Order Subgrid Variance Closure:** Retains $C$-point landmarks (including cross-block bridge hubs and causally dilated bound-value spans) at exact $1\times$ resolution ($m_c=1, \sigma_c^2=0$) with exact positions $t_c$, coalesces $F$-point background bulk in unrotated space, and closes the **Softmax Jensen Inequality Gap** ($\mathbb{E}[e^{q^\top k}] > e^{q^\top \mathbb{E}[k]}$) by tracking intra-cluster subgrid key variance $\sigma_m^2$ via the Law of Total Variance:
   $$s_m = \frac{q_T^\top R_{\Theta, \bar{t}_m} \tilde{k}_m}{\sqrt{d_k}} + \log(m_m) + \frac{\lVert q_T \rVert_2^2 \sigma_m^2}{2 d_k}$$

---

### Headline Results: NVIDIA `RULER` (`7B` & `1.5B`) & 4-Turn Shared-Prefix Reuse

2. **`RadixAttention` Prefix Node Coarsening:** Compressing cold/shared `RadixCache` prefix blocks by $20\times\text{–}28.6\times$ via `SPICY-KV` single-pass hybrid $C/F$ restriction so `RadixCache` can hold $20\times+$ more concurrent prefix trees in GPU HBM without query-specific eviction blindness.

items.title: [Bug] FP8 block-quantized checkpoint on SM86 (FP8 Marlin) intermittently gives wrong tokens with the overlap scheduler; exact without it
items.author: DiaaAj
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
On an RTX 3090, SGLang 0.5.22 serves a 128×128 block-FP8 checkpoint through FP8 Marlin (weight-only; SM86 has
no FP8 tensor cores). In most runs of a 192-request workload, 1–5 requests produce wrong tokens, either
from their first token or from a later decode step. Rerunning gives different requests, and some runs are
clean. With `--disable-overlap-schedule` the same workload was exact in 5 of 5 runs.

The checkpoint's weights are exactly representable in FP8 with power-of-two block scales, and every output
token is known in advance, so these are not numerical differences:
- vLLM 0.31.0 is exact on the same checkpoint, also through FP8 Marlin;
- SGLang is exact on the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, with the same settings.

## Observed (probec probe twin of Qwen3-0.6B, 28 layers; greedy; 192 requests x 256 tokens)
| SGLang 0.5.22, RTX 3090, FP8 128×128 blocks | runs with wrong requests | wrong requests per run |
|---|---|---|
| default (FlashInfer attention, radix cache, overlap scheduler, CUDA graphs) | 5 of 7 | 0, 2, 0, 5, 1, 1 (+1 on another host) |
| `--attention-backend triton` | 1 of 1 | 3 |
| `--disable-radix-cache` | 1 of 5 | 1 |
| `--disable-cuda-graph` | 1 of 3 | 1 |
| **`--disable-overlap-schedule`** | **0 of 5** | 0 |
| bf16 checkpoint (control), default settings | 0 of 3 | 0 |

**What goes wrong.** In the probe, each layer looks one token up in the KV cache. A failing request's
output switches to the token the probe emits when a lookup finds nothing (the same token in every failing
request). So a layer's query, key or value for some tokens is wrong, or the attention read misses them.
Requests that share a prefix and were batched together fail at the same step, with the same tokens.

**The GEMM is exact in isolation.** [`tools/marlin_determinism.py`](https://github.com/DiaaAj/probec/blob/main/tools/marlin_determinism.py) calls SGLang's
`apply_fp8_marlin_linear` on the checkpoint's FP8 block weights (layers 0 and 27, all five projections). It
found no call that differed from the exact product:
- every M from 1 to 1024 plus nine larger sizes (10,330 calls);
- 20 repeats each of 12 sizes (no nondeterminism);
- two streams sharing a layer's lock workspace;
- input production, GEMM and readback on one side stream, as the overlap scheduler's forward stream does.

So the failure needs the engine, the overlap scheduler in particular.

## Repro
```
pip install "probec @ git+https://github.com/DiaaAj/probec" "sglang[all]==0.5.22"
probec compile --like Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --no-scale-check -o dense
probec quantize dense --format fp8-block --device cuda -o dense-fp8-block
probec run dense-fp8-block --engine sglang --matrix quick --only flashinfer/default --out results.jsonl   # repeat a few times
probec report results.jsonl
```

## Environment
SGLang 0.5.22 (pip), RTX 3090 (SM86), driver 595.84, CUDA 13.0 image; two hosts.

items.title: [Feature] Unified JIT / Precompilation Cache Directory
items.author: whybeyoung
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [ ] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation


## Summary

**Request:** Unify all JIT and precompilation cache paths under a single configurable root so that users and operators can manage cache location, size, and persistence in one place. The current situation is fragmented across multiple env vars and default paths (including `/tmp`), which makes it hard to reason about where compiled artifacts live and to reuse caches across runs or machines.

## Current State (Fragmented)

### 1. Triton JIT cache

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| Direct `@triton.jit` (e.g. allocator, MoE kernels) | `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` (Triton runtime) | Triton default: `~/.triton/cache`; often overwritten by Inductor to a path under `/tmp/torchinductor_*` |
| SGLang override | `SGLANG_TRITON_CACHE_DIR` (if implemented) | e.g. `~/.triton/cache` or `~/.cache/triton` |

- Set only in some entry paths (engine, gRPC launcher, scheduler process); custom/PD launchers may not set it.
- When PyTorch Inductor runs first, it can set `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` to its own subdir, so later Triton JIT (including allocator) writes under `/tmp`.

### 2. PyTorch Inductor (torch.compile)

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| Inductor cache | `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` (PyTorch) | `/tmp/torchinductor_<user>` (or similar) |
| SGLang override | `SGLANG_TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` (if implemented) | e.g. `~/.cache/sglang/inductor` |

- Default lives in `/tmp`, so cache is often non-persistent and can conflict with other users on shared nodes.

### 3. DeepGEMM JIT cache

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| DeepGEMM cache | `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR` / `DG_JIT_CACHE_DIR` | `~/.cache/deep_gemm` |

- Set in `layers/deep_gemm_wrapper/compile_utils.py`; separate from Triton/Inductor.
- 
## Problems

1. **No single root:** Triton, Inductor, SGLang torch_compile, and DeepGEMM each have their own env or default; some write to `/tmp`, others to `~/.cache/...`.

## Proposal

### 1. Introduce a single JIT cache root

- **New env var:** `SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT` (or `SGLANG_CACHE_ROOT` if we want to align with existing `SGLANG_CACHE_ROOT` in custom_all_reduce_utils).
- **Default:** `~/.cache/sglang` (or `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/sglang` when set).
- **Semantics:** All JIT/precompilation caches that SGLang controls should live under this root in fixed subdirs.

### 2. Standard layout under the root

Suggested subdirs (all under `SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT`):

| Subdir | Purpose | Maps from |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| `triton/` | Triton JIT (direct `@triton.jit` and, when possible, Triton used by Inductor) | `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` |
| `inductor/` | PyTorch Inductor (torch.compile) | `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` |
| `torch_compile/` | SGLang torch.compile cache (hash-based, when using SGLangBackend) | `SGLANG_CACHE_DIR` + `torch_compile_cache` |
| `deep_gemm/` | DeepGEMM JIT | `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR` / `DG_JIT_CACHE_DIR` |

- If we keep backward compatibility, existing env vars (`SGLANG_TRITON_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR`) could override the default subdir path when set; otherwise they are derived as `{SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT}/{subdir}`.

items.title: [Perf] HiCache PP-sync drain makes the PP prefill scheduler lock-step across ranks
items.author: xiaguan
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With HiCache enabled on a pipeline-parallel prefill server, every scheduler round on PP rank `r` blocks until PP rank `r+1` has received the previous round's HiCache PP-sync message. PP0's loop therefore cannot run more than one round ahead of PP1's. PP1 is held back by PP2 in the same way, and so on down the pipeline. `--pp-async-batch-depth` is meant to let PP0 run ahead, and this backpressure cancels much of that. PP0's GPU then sits idle while runnable work is queued.

## Mechanism

1. [`check_hicache_events`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/78185f4b3f565cbe0fec20d71bb5deb372428e80/python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py#L3609) calls `_drain_async_work()` at the start of every round.
2. [`_drain_async_work`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/78185f4b3f565cbe0fec20d71bb5deb372428e80/python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py#L354-L364) then `wait()`s on every `isend` from the previous round.
3. Those sends come from [`_pp_sync`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/78185f4b3f565cbe0fec20d71bb5deb372428e80/python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py#L379-L400): PP0 sends its ready counts down the pipeline with tag `HICACHE_PP_SYNC`. Each rank `r > 0` posts a blocking `recv` for them from its own `check_hicache_events`.
4. Each send is a CPU tensor on the PP group, so it uses gloo. It completes only once the receiver has posted the matching `recv`. As a result, round `k+1` on PP0 waits until PP1 reaches the HiCache step of its round `k`. Getting there includes PP1's whole tail of round `k-1` (`d2h_wait`, result processing, its own PP receives).

The single-round drain was added in #28916 to fix unbounded `work_list` growth: about 12 GB/h, with PP0 spinning idle rounds faster than the downstream ranks consumed them. That fix bounds the backlog to one round, which also makes the PP-sync channel lock-step.

## Evidence

Setup:
- Model: Kimi-K3, 1.5T, MXFP4 MoE, P/D disaggregation.
- Prefill: PP8 × TP1 over two 4-GPU GB300 nodes, eager prefill, `--chunked-prefill-size 16384`, `--pp-async-batch-depth 4`, `SGLANG_PP_COMM_OVERLAP=1`.
- HiCache: `--hicache-host-memory-mode cache --hicache-write-policy write_through --hicache-size 60`, no storage backend.
- Image: nightly at `ab580b2e0`, which includes #38959.
- Load: open-loop and below saturation. Unique 2048-token prompts, `max_new_tokens=1`, sent through the P/D router.

**py-spy on the PP0 / PP1 scheduler processes** (`--idle`, 200 Hz, 20 s, 16k tok/s offered), as a share of the PD prefill event loop's wall time:

| | in `_process_hicache_events` | of which `_drain_async_work` | `_pp_sync` recv | `writing_check` → `synchronize` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PP0 | 19.6% | 19.5% | 0.1% | 0.0% |
| PP1 | 12.7% | 12.2% | 0.4% | 0.1% |

Almost all of the HiCache step's time is the wait for the previous round's send. The count exchange and the D2H write acks themselves cost almost nothing.

**CPU time spent in the HiCache step**, per rank, over a 181 s window at 8k tok/s:

| PP rank | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| total (s) | 50.3 | 34.5 | 34.4 | 21.5 | 7.6 | 1.0 | 0.7 | 0.5 |
| p99 per round (ms) | 88 | 82 | 81 | 71 | 33 | 1.2 | 0.9 | 1.5 |

The time falls off rank by rank down the pipeline, as expected if each rank waits on the next one.

**GPU impact on PP0**, from CUDA events on the forward stream joined with per-step CPU timestamps. This is the share of wall time in which PP0's GPU was idle and PP0 had runnable work (an admitted request with tokens left to launch), and its loop was blocked in the HiCache step:

| offered load | PP0 GPU busy | idle, nothing to run | idle with work ready, blocked in HiCache step |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8k tok/s | 20.7% | 70.8% | 5.4% |
| 16k tok/s | 37.0% | 49.8% | 8.2% |

## Possible directions

1. **Bounded window instead of a single-round drain.** Keep up to `K` outstanding PP-sync sends, with `K` on the order of `pp_size + pp_async_batch_depth`. Block only when the window is full, and reap completed sends without blocking. This keeps the leak fix from #28916, and since the receivers consume the per-round increments in FIFO order, the semantics stay the same. It is a small, local change.
2. **Fold the HiCache ready counts into the PP consensus.** Since #38959, PD prefill already gathers rank-local status at PP0 (`PPConsensusStore`) and broadcasts PP0's decision once per round. Ready counts only increase, so a MIN over each rank's latest reported count is safe even when stale. That would remove the separate `HICACHE_PP_SYNC` channel and its backpressure. It would also fix the case described in #42433, where every rank consumes PP0's local count even though rank-local queues can diverge. #42433 takes this approach, but it builds on the two-pass bootstrap ring that #38959 replaced.

Related: #28916, #38959, #42433, #45085.

items.title: [Kernel] Optimize triton decoding kernels for long context
items.author: merrymercy
items.body_excerpt:
We noticed the current triton decoding kernel is very slow on long context. This is due to a missing flash decoding like optimization.

## Reproduce
We test the decoding speed with a context length of 200 and 2,000.

triton backend: The decoding speed drops from 147.64 token/s to 126.41 token/s
```
$ python3 -m sglang.bench_offline_throughput --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --dataset-name random --num-prompt 1 --random-input 128 --random-output 2048 --random-range 1 --attention-backend triton

[2024-11-30 05:10:04 TP0] Decode batch. #running-req: 1, #token: 234, token usage: 0.00, gen throughput (token/s): 147.64, #queue-req: 0
... 
[2024-11-30 05:10:18 TP0] Decode batch. #running-req: 1, #token: 2154, token usage: 0.00, gen throughput (token/s): 126.41, #queue-req: 0
```

flashinfer backend: The decoding speed only drops from 144.17 token/s to 143.35 token/s
```
$ python3 -m sglang.bench_offline_throughput --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --dataset-name random --num-prompt 1 --random-input 128 --random-output 2048 --random-range 1

[2024-11-30 05:11:40 TP0] Decode batch. #running-req: 1, #token: 234, token usage: 0.00, gen throughput (token/s): 144.17, #queue-req: 0
...
[2024-11-30 05:11:54 TP0] Decode batch. #running-req: 1, #token: 2154, token usage: 0.00, gen throughput (token/s): 143.35, #queue-req: 0
```

## Possible solutions
We can learn from the flash decoding triton kernel from lightllm and improve the [current triton decoding kernel](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/triton_ops/decode_attention.py). Related links:
- https://github.com/ModelTC/lightllm/blob/main/lightllm/models/llama/triton_kernel/gqa_flash_decoding.py
- https://pytorch.org/blog/flash-decoding/
- https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.01282

items.title: [Bug] Client-declared mm_hashes controls multimodal prefix-cache identity: wrong-image KV reuse and cross-tenant image disclosure
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

On multimodal deployments, the native `/generate` endpoint accepts a `mm_hashes` field: one hex string per image item, declared by the caller. In `tokenizer_manager.py` the caller value is applied directly to the item (`item.set_hash(int(hex_hash, 16))`), which short-circuits the internal content-based `hash_feature()` recompute. The comment there explains the intent: let an external KV router's routing decision agree with sglang's prefix-cache key for the same image.

In `schedule_batch.py`, `MultimodalDataItem.hash` determines the item's `pad_value`, and the image region of the token sequence is that pad value repeated. So the declared hash is the prefix-cache identity of the image segment: two requests whose items carry the same `mm_hashes` value produce matching token sequences for the image region, and the second request hits the first one's cached KV regardless of the actual image bytes.

The observable bug: a request that sends image B but declares a hash that was previously used for image A gets A's cached KV, and the model answers based on A. B's actual pixels are ignored. The response is a normal completion — no warning, no error, `finish_reason` is a regular stop. In our runs the third request below returned the first image's text with `cached_tokens` jumping from 15 to 193 (the 162-token image region served from cache), and completed faster than the uncached baselines.

Two notes on scope: the field has no flag gating or allowlist, and the OpenAI-compatible endpoints do not expose it, so this is native `/generate` only. Also, the Kimi embedding path already treats this as something to prevent — it rejects caller `mm_hashes` from redirecting cache identity (PR #34411) — while the generic path applies the caller value unconditionally.

### Reproduction

Tested with Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct. Prepare two same-size images (512x256): image A, white background with black text `IMAGE-A-SECRET-7f3a9c`; image B, black background with white text `IMAGE-B-DISTRACT-2c1b4d`. The prompt text must be byte-identical across the three calls and must place the vision placeholder inside the model's chat template (`<|vision_start|><|image_pad|><|vision_end|>` for Qwen2.5-VL).

```python
import base64, requests

def gen(path, mm_hash):
    img = base64.b64encode(open(path, "rb").read()).decode()
    r = requests.post("http://<host>:8200/generate", json={
        "text": "<|im_start|>user\n<|vision_start|><|image_pad|><|vision_end|>\n"
                "describe the image and transcribe all text in it<|im_end|>\n"
                "<|im_start|>assistant\n",
        "image_data": [img],
        "mm_hashes": [mm_hash],
        "sampling_params": {"max_new_tokens": 64, "temperature": 0},
    }, timeout=60)
    j = r.json()
    return j["text"], j["meta_info"]["cached_tokens"]

print(gen("A.png", "deadbeef00000001"))  # "IMAGE-A-SECRET-7f3a9c ...", cached_tokens 15
print(gen("B.png", "aaaa0000bbbb0002"))  # "IMAGE-B-DISTRACT-2c1b4d ...", cached_tokens 15
print(gen("B.png", "deadbeef00000001"))  # "IMAGE-A-SECRET-7f3a9c ...", cached_tokens 193
```

The third request sends image B but transcribes `IMAGE-A-SECRET-7f3a9c`, the content of the image cached under the declared hash. Swapping the roles (cache B first, then send A with the same hash) returns B's content the same way. Reproduced on 3/3 cold restarts.

The radix cache is shared across clients, so the aliasing is not limited to one connection: in a two-host check, a second client sending a plain gray image with the same declared hash received the first client's image content in the response (`cached_tokens` 190).

### Environment

SGLang at commit `b8a6adadfe8c292fbb673291dbd2a5d23232f500`, unmodified
Model: Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct, single RTX 4090
Launch: `python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path <model> --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8200 --disable-cuda-graph -attention-backend triton --mm-attention-backend triton_attn`
Linux, Python 3.10

items.title: [Feature] Prepare registered radix cache backends before worker graph initialization
items.author: feichai0017
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation

A registered radix-cache backend can need worker-owned layer-transfer events/counters to be installed before CUDA Graph capture. Today the scheduler initializes model workers, pools, attention backends and graphs before building the tree cache. Consequently, the backend factory cannot install dependencies that must appear in the initial captured graph. The existing public radix-cache registration API exposes construction, but no preparation callback at this earlier boundary.

At main `4fc86f73c2243e042c55a55d08afb07827d5096e`, see [worker initialization](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/4fc86f73c2243e042c55a55d08afb07827d5096e/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py#L1100), [runner graph initialization](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/4fc86f73c2243e042c55a55d08afb07827d5096e/python/sglang/srt/managers/tp_worker.py#L426), and [backend registration](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/4fc86f73c2243e042c55a55d08afb07827d5096e/python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/registry.py#L58).

### Proposed interface

Allow `register_radix_cache_backend(name, factory, *, prepare_worker=None)`. Invoke the selected backend's optional callback as `prepare_worker(tp_worker, capture_decode_cuda_graph)` once at the beginning of each `TpModelWorker.init_cuda_graphs` call, before any runner. Existing two-argument registrations and default cache selection remain unchanged. Resolve the backend from the published runtime configuration; registration itself must neither read that configuration nor invoke preparation. Reject invalid registrations before insertion, and propagate preparation errors before any runner initializes graphs.

This deliberately covers this worker method boundary, including `capture_decode_cuda_graph=False`. It does not add a general lifecycle manager, teardown/drain protocol, pending-query admission API, or coverage for direct runner recapture / `ensure_decode_cuda_graphs`. The backend owns idempotence and any resources it retains.

### Related resources and validation

The dynamic linker factory in #40595 addresses later construction, and whole-process checkpoint/restore in #44523 is a different boundary. I did not find an equivalent worker-preparation proposal in the searched issues/PRs.

A minimal implementation has real CPU registry and worker-method ordering tests. GPU capture/replay and model inference are not validated by those unit tests; the implementation will be proposed as a draft for interface discussion.

items.title: [Bug]: Persistent KV offload cache is not namespaced by model revision
items.author: mindungil
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The relevant output of python vllm/collect_env.py ```text ============================== System Info ============================== OS : Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (x86_64) GCC version : (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 CMake version : version 3.28.3 Libc version : glibc-2.39 ============================== PyTorch Info ============================== PyTorch version : 2.11.0+cu130 CUDA used to build PyTorch : 13.0 ============================== Python Environment ============================== Python version : 3.12.3 Python platform : Linux-6.8.0-136-generic-x86_64-with-glibc2.39 ============================== CUDA / GPU Info ============================== Is CUDA available : True GPU models and configuration : GPU 0: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU 1: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU 2: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU 3: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition Nvidia driver version : 580.126.09 cuDNN version : 9.18.1 ============================== Versions of relevant libraries ============================== flashinfer-python==0.6.14 numpy==2.3.5 nvidia-cuda-runtime==13.0.96 nvidia-cudnn-cu13==9.19.0.56 nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.28.9 torch==2.11.0 transformers==5.13.1 triton==3.6.0 ============================== vLLM Info ============================== vLLM Version : 0.23.1rc1.dev1312+g97a668152 git sha : 97a668152 ```
This issue concerns deterministic cache-path construction and is independent of the GPU architecture. ### 🐛 Describe the bug Persistent native KV offloading tiers derive their cache namespace from `FileMapper.fields`. The fingerprint includes the model name, KV dtype, cache geometry, and parallelism, but not the model revision. Two deployments using the same model repository name and persistent offload root, but different model revisions, therefore produce the same `FileMapper.base_path`. Block keys are derived from token content rather than model weights, so the newer deployment can report a filesystem or object-tier hit and load KV produced by the older weights. This can silently change model output after a model update. The problem is specific to persistent secondary tiers and survives engine restarts. #### Minimal reproduction On current `main` (`97a668152`): ```python from vllm.v1.kv_offload.file_mapper import FileMapper common = dict( root_dir="/tmp/cache", model_name="org/model", tokens_per_hash=16, blocks_per_file=1, tp_size=1, pp_size=1, pcp_size=1, dcp_size=1, rank=0, dtype="float16", ) # There is currently no model-revision input to distinguish these deployments. revision_a = FileMapper(**common) revision_b = FileMapper(**common) assert revision_a.base_path == revision_b.base_path ``` The revision cannot currently be represented by `OffloadingModelConfig` or passed through `FileMapper.from_offloading_spec`. vLLM already has an immutable resolved commit for Hugging Face models, even when the user does not explicitly pass `--revision`. For the locally cached `facebook/opt-125m` used to verify this: ```text ModelConfig.revision = None ModelConfig.hf_config._commit_hash = "27dcfa74d334bc871f3234de431e71c6eeba5dd6" ``` #### Observed behavior Persistent cache paths are identical for different revisions of the same model repository when the remaining cache configuration is unchanged. Existing KV files can consequently be treated as valid after deploying different weights. #### Expected behavior Different resolved model revisions should use different persistent cache namespaces. Deployments using the same resolved revision should continue to share a namespace. A possible fix is to: 1. add the resolved model revision to the normalized offloading model config; 2. prefer the Hugging Face config's resolved commit hash and fall back to the requested revision; and 3. include the revision in the `FileMapper` fingerprint when available. For local models without revision information, omitting the field can preserve the existing cache path. #### Affected components - `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/config.py` - `vllm/v1/kv_offload/config.py` - `vllm/v1/kv_offload/file_mapper.py` - filesystem and object secondary tiers that use `FileMapper` #### Duplicate check I searched open and closed issues and pull requests for combinations of `FileMapper`, model revision, fingerprint, stale KV, filesystem tier, and offloading. I did not find an existing report or change covering model-revision namespacing. I have a focused fix and regression tests ready and plan to submit a PR. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug][ROCm]: ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN gives wrong output on gfx950 when a layer's KV cache is 2–4 GiB
items.author: zhentaocc
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

MI355X (gfx950), image `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-rocm100-0cbac6cd1` (vLLM 0.30.1rc1.dev558, aiter 0.1.23). The aiter versions that vLLM pins today (v0.1.25, and also v0.1.26) have the same code.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` gives wrong attention output on gfx950 when a layer's KV cache is 2–4 GiB. No error is raised.

**Cause.** On gfx950, aiter's `unified_attention` runs `_unified_attention_gfx950`. That kernel uses 32-bit buffer loads when `k.nelement() * k.element_size() <= 2**31 - 1`. vLLM passes K and V as strided views of one cache that packs K and V together. Each view has half of the cache's elements but spans the whole cache. So for a 2–4 GiB cache the check passes, and the offsets of blocks past 2 GiB overflow. With Qwen3-32B or Qwen3-8B shapes (8 KV heads, head size 128, bf16) and the block size 64 that vLLM sets for this backend, that is every block id ≥ 8192. A request whose KV sits in those blocks gets attention output that has nothing to do with its context. One greedy prompt on Qwen3-8B gives normal text in low blocks and `’    CORPORATIONtoa  Equation Impossible藁 Royals p犊/bower…` in blocks past 2 GiB.

**When it triggers.** It needs requests that get blocks past 2 GiB. With prefix caching on (the default), the allocator walks through the whole KV pool. So once a server has allocated about 2 GiB per layer of KV in total, later requests start to get those blocks, even at low concurrency. For Qwen3-32B or Qwen3-8B that is about 524k tokens, since K and V take 4 KiB per token per layer. With `--no-enable-prefix-caching`, our runs kept reusing low blocks, and GSM8K and MRCR showed no change.

**Accuracy without spec decode.** GSM8K is 5-shot over all 1319 questions. MRCR is `tests/evals/mrcr/mrcr_eval.py` with 30 samples of 16k–33k tokens and 2, 4 or 8 needles. Both use temperature 0. There is one fresh server per backend.

Qwen3-32B with default settings: prefix caching on, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.85`, `--max-model-len 131072` with YaRN. The KV pool has about 700k tokens, about 2.7 GiB per layer. The first GSM8K run uses only low blocks. MRCR then moves the allocator through the whole pool, so MRCR and the second GSM8K run get blocks past 2 GiB.

| | `ROCM_ATTN` | `TRITON_ATTN` | unified attention | unified attention + aiter fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GSM8K, first run | 0.736 | 0.744 | 0.749 | 0.751 |
| MRCR | 0.498 | 0.478 | **0.327** | 0.502 |
| GSM8K, second run | 0.741 | 0.738 | **0.633** | 0.733 |

Qwen3-8B, worst case: the KV pool has 1,040,000 tokens (`--num-gpu-blocks-override`), about 3.97 GiB per layer. Filler requests with 525k distinct tokens move the allocator past 2 GiB first, so GSM8K runs on blocks past 2 GiB. MRCR follows.

| | `TRITON_ATTN` | unified attention | unified attention + aiter fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GSM8K | 0.859 | **0.002** | 0.863 |
| MRCR | 0.538 | **0.178** | 0.523 |

**Accuracy with spec decode (Qwen3-32B + EAGLE3).** The KV pool has 657,472 tokens, about 2.5 GiB per layer.

- Kernel check against an fp32 reference: max error 0.49. `TRITON_ATTN` gives 0.009. With a 1.6M-token pool (6.2 GiB per layer), the same batches pass.
- End to end, EAGLE3 acceptance length is lower than with `ROCM_ATTN` or `TRITON_ATTN` (OSL 1k, temperature 0; the range is over three runs):

| input, concurrency | `ROCM_ATTN` | `TRITON_ATTN` | unified attention | unified attention + aiter fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1k, 64 | 2.30 | 2.30 | 1.64–1.72 | 2.30 |
| 8k, 16 | 2.10 | 2.11 | 1.66–1.71 | 2.09 |

**Affected.** Any run that uses `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` on gfx950 with a per-layer KV cache of 2–4 GiB, once requests get blocks past 2 GiB. Whether a layer's cache is 2–4 GiB depends on the model, TP size, and `--gpu-memory-utilization`. On main, gfx950 auto-selects unified attention for KV connector runs.

### Tasks

The fix reaches vLLM only after an aiter release and a pin bump, because vLLM pins aiter to a release tag (`AITER_BRANCH` in `docker/Dockerfile.rocm_base`, currently v0.1.25).

- [ ] ROCm/aiter#6661: gate the buffer loads on the byte span of k and v, with a unit test.
- [ ] An aiter release that contains ROCm/aiter#6661, and an `AITER_BRANCH` bump in `docker/Dockerfile.rocm_base`.
- [ ] #62813 (interim, no dependencies): rank `TRITON_ATTN` above `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` on gfx950 for every model.
- [ ] #61433 (after the pin bump): rank `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` above `TRITON_ATTN` again. On MI355X, unified attention was 1.05–1.32× faster than `TRITON_ATTN` end to end on Qwen3-32B + EAGLE3 at 1k–8k input, and about 1.4–2.8× faster from 64k input on Qwen3-Next.

Related: #62828 is a separate accuracy bug in `ROCM_ATTN`'s sliding-window kernels.

cc @simondanielsson

items.title: MP mode: remaining unbounded request-state retention in vLLM client and sidecar prefetch bookkeeping
items.author: wuwanxu
items.body_excerpt:
## Deployment

We run a production **3P1D** deployment with vLLM and `LMCacheMPConnector`. Each serving node has a per-node LMCache sidecar; LMCache uses `fs_native` as the L2 adapter backed by local SSD. P2P, CacheBlend, and engine-driven transfer are not enabled.

The previous client-side MQ no-response leak is tracked separately in #5270. During a follow-up audit of upstream `dev` (checked at `05fc77a`, 2026-09-24), we found the two request-state retention paths below. This issue only reports the observed behavior and asks maintainers to determine the intended lifecycle and remediation.

## 1. vLLM client: `_returned_finished` grows for the worker lifetime

`LMCacheMPWorkerAdapter` creates:

```python
self._returned_finished: set[str] = set()
```

`_process_finished_stores()` uses this set to prevent a request ID from being reported repeatedly through `finished_sending`, then records returned IDs with:

```python
self._returned_finished.update(ret_stores)
```

We could not find a `discard`, `clear`, TTL, or capacity-based removal path. Therefore every request ID once returned as `finished_sending` remains resident until the vLLM worker exits. This path is exercised by normal successful requests as well as failure paths.

The set appears to be needed for async-scheduling deduplication after neighboring tracking sets are drained, but it also produces monotonic process-lifetime growth. With UUID-like Python request IDs, the retained footprint is roughly 150-200 bytes per request before allocator overhead; at sustained high QPS this can become material in a long-lived worker.

Relevant code:
- `lmcache/integration/vllm/vllm_multi_process_adapter.py` (`_returned_finished`, `_process_finished_stores`)

### Questions for maintainers

1. Is process-lifetime retention of every completed `finished_sending` request ID required by the vLLM connector contract?
2. What lifecycle or retention semantics should this deduplication state have in a long-running worker?

## 2. sidecar: abandoned prefetch jobs and completion Bitmaps are never reclaimed

`LookupModule` registers every lookup in:

```python
self._prefetch_jobs: dict[str, _PrefetchJob] = {}
```

The job is removed when `QUERY_PREFETCH_STATUS` or `WAIT_PREFETCH_STATUS` obtains a non-`None` completion result. If a client aborts or disconnects after LOOKUP, or stops polling after an RPC timeout/unhealthy transition, the job is not consumed by that path.

The corresponding `PrefetchController` completion state has the same consumer-driven ownership:

```python
self._completed_lookups: dict[PrefetchRequestId, int] = {}
self._completed_results: dict[PrefetchRequestId, Bitmap] = {}
```

`query_prefetch_result()` pops both the Bitmap and the lookup result. The source comment notes that failing to consume the prefetch result leaks memory. `Bitmap` is native/C++ memory, so its growth may not be visible in Python GC or tracemalloc. `END_SESSION` removes the session and touches L1 keys but does not remove the prefetch job or controller completion state.

In production we also see frequent `Session ... not found, skipping touch` warnings (roughly 378-953 over two hours), consistent with request-lifecycle skew and making normal client polling an unreliable sole ownership mechanism.

Relevant code:
- `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/lookup.py` (`_prefetch_jobs`, `query_prefetch_status`, `end_session`)
- `lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py` (`_completed_lookups`, `_completed_results`, `query_prefetch_result`)

### Questions for maintainers

1. What is the intended owner of a prefetch job and its completion result after the original client has abandoned the request?
2. Is there an existing cancellation or reclamation lifecycle that this MP path should use?
3. What cleanup ordering is required for an in-flight prefetch so that late completion cannot expose invalid L1 data or retain completion state?

## Expected behavior

For healthy-sidecar and abort/error paths alike, client and server request bookkeeping should have a defined bounded lifecycle. Abandoned request state should be reclaimable without requiring a vLLM worker or sidecar restart, while preserving correctness for normal in-flight requests.

## Reproduction direction

1. Run vLLM + `LMCacheMPConnector` + sidecar with an SSD-backed `fs_native` L2.
2. Send sustained requests and observe the vLLM worker: `_returned_finished` grows monotonically.
3. Submit LOOKUPs, then abort/disconnect before prefetch polling completes, or induce a prefetch-status timeout.
4. Observe `lmcache_mp.active_prefetch_jobs` and `PrefetchController.report_status()["completed_results_count"]`; entries can remain after the client has abandoned the request.

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4 + HiCache write_through: TP ranks deadlock under concurrent long prefills (scheduler and detokenizer go silent, /health 503)
items.author: divyvasal
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

DeepSeek-V4 with `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-write-policy write_through` deadlocks across TP ranks under a burst of long one-shot prompts. The same config without HiCache does not.

When it hangs:
- The scheduler stops and the detokenizer heartbeat goes quiet.
- `/health` returns 503 (`Server couldn't get a response from detokenizer`) indefinitely.
- All 4 GPUs of the replica sit at **100% utilization at ~260 W**, which on B300 means spin-waiting.
- Nothing is logged: no traceback, no watchdog fire within 5+ minutes.

It reproduced 3 times out of 3 on two replicas:
- 48 concurrent prompts of ~540K tokens: hung after ~14 min in the first run and ~1 min in the second.
- 8 concurrent: hung after ~1.5 min.

The same burst with the same flags minus `--enable-hierarchical-cache` processed 5.9M (48 in flight) and 8.3M (8 in flight) input tokens, about 11 and 15 completed ~540K prompts, with no stall.

In all three hangs, the last prefill batch logged before the stall is one in which **a long prompt finishes prefill while the next begins** (`#new-seq: 2`, `swa token usage` jumps from 0.00 to 0.09). In the two short runs it was the first such batch. Example from the 48-concurrent run that hung after ~1 min:

```
[06:35:47 TP0 EP0] Prefill batch, #new-seq: 1, #new-token: 8192, #cached-token: 0, full token usage: 0.03, swa token usage: 0.00, #running-req: 0, #queue-req: 15, #pending-token: 7978739
[06:35:47 TP0 EP0] Prefill batch, #new-seq: 2, #new-token: 8107, #cached-token: 0, full token usage: 0.03, swa token usage: 0.09, #running-req: 0, #queue-req: 14, #pending-token: 7970632
<no further batches; health 503 from 06:36 on; last_heartbeat 06:35:54>
```

That is the point where the first ~540K-token prefix is inserted and written through to host while other long prefills are still being chunked.

py-spy, taken 3 times over 3 minutes, is identical each time. The TP ranks are one step apart:

```
TP0, TP1, TP2  MainThread:
    _prepare_engram_history (model_runner_components/ngram_embedding_manager.py:203)   # torch.tensor(..., device=cuda) H2D copy = stream sync
    prepare_for_forward (model_runner_components/ngram_embedding_manager.py:117)
    get_next_batch_to_run (scheduler.py:3759)
    event_loop_overlap (scheduler.py:1970)
TP3  MainThread:
    forward (engram.py:312)
    _forward_layers_hc_pre_from_prev (deepseek_v4.py:4424)
    forward (deepseek_v4.py:4755)
    forward (deepseek_v4.py:5110)
    _execute_extend (runner/eager_runner.py:372)
detokenizer: idle in recv_pyobj
```

TP3 has launched the next forward, presumably waiting in a collective, while TP0-2 are blocked on a stream sync before theirs. This looks like the ranks scheduled different batches at that step. One guess is that the write-through backup's completion, or the prefix-match state it changes, is observed at different times on different ranks. We haven't confirmed which state diverges.

### Reproduction

- **sglang:** nightly at `4cbf290f`
- **Model:** DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (MXFP4), 4x B300 per replica
- **Flags:** `--tp-size 4 --ep-size 4 --mem-fraction-static 0.60 --context-length 1048576 --max-running-requests 128 --chunked-prefill-size 8192 --max-prefill-tokens 8192 --schedule-policy shortest-prefill-first --prefill-decode-interval 4 --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 128 --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 2 --hicache-write-policy write_through`

Steps:
1. Send N unique prompts of ~540K tokens each (random words and numbers) at the same time, `max_tokens 4`, with N = 8 or 48.
2. Within ~1-1.5 min the replica stops; it hangs every time.
3. The identical burst without `--enable-hierarchical-cache` completes.

An earlier load did not hang in two 15-18 minute runs: 48 threads of growing ~540K-token multi-turn conversations, started 6 s apart.

### Environment

8x B300 (2 replicas of TP4/EP4 on one node), CUDA image from the nightly above. Happy to collect more: py-spy `--native`, NCCL debug, or a run with `--disable-overlap-schedule`.

items.title: [Onboarding 2026] Good second issues — next step after your first PR
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
👋 Welcome back! If you've already completed a good first issue (see #3372) and sent your first PR to LMCache, this is your next step: **good second issues**.

These are small, well-scoped tasks — bug fixes, cleanups, docs/test improvements, tiny refactors — where the approach is usually clear and the diff stays small. They're a great way to go a bit deeper into the codebase before tackling bigger work.

## 0. Before you start
Same workflow as #3372:
- Base branch is `dev` — open PRs against `dev`, not `main`.
- Sign off your commits (`git commit -s`); DCO is required.
- Line length is **88** (`ruff format` / `ruff check`).
- PR title format:
  ```
  [good-second-issue] <area>: <imperative summary> (#<issue-number>)
  ```
- One issue = one PR; write `Closes #<issue-number>` and `Refs #<this umbrella>` in the PR description.

## 1. How to claim a task
1. Pick **one** issue below that has no assignee and no `🔒 claimed` comment.
2. Comment exactly: `/claim` (or `I'd like to work on this 🙋`).
   A maintainer will assign it to you within ~2 business days.(You can join the LMCache slack and feel free to ping one of the maintainer, it will help us avoid missing your claim request.) And you can also submit a PR and link it to the related issue.
3. If you go silent for 7 days we'll un-assign so others can pick it up — totally fine, just leave a comment if you need more time.

## 2. Available tasks
Pick an unassigned issue below, read it, then `/claim`:

- [ ] #5022 — [BUG][TURBOQUANT] FP9 key store kernel fails on A100 (SM80) with bfloat16 models
- [ ] #4981 — [Bug][CLI] bench engine includes reporting time in throughput and exports inconsistent final metrics
- [ ] #4646 — [Bug][CLI] query engine retries the chat endpoint after request failures
- [ ] #4591 — [Bug][SDK] LMCacheRequestStream.output_tokens includes prompt tokens
- [ ] #4597 — cannot cache function 'rolling_hash_windows_numba': no locator available
- [ ] #4698 — NixlStoreL2Adapter reports negative pool usage for multi-page backing files
- [ ] #4950 — [Bug] Operator deletes unrelated same-named ServiceMonitors when monitoring is disabled
- [ ] #4476 — cacheblend out of date
- [ ] #4416 — [Bug][CLI] trace replay percentiles are one sample too high at whole ranks
- [ ] #4204 — [Bug] server CLI crashes on startup via bigtable adapter protobuf TypeError
- [ ] #3889 — TRT-LLM connector: _TRTLLM_KERNEL_BATCH_SIZE (32) exceeds c_ops kernel's 4-object cap

**Maintainers**: please update this checklist as issues are claimed or closed. If an issue turns out to be bigger than it looks, uncheck it and pick a replacement.

Stuck? Drop a message in the `#contributors` channel of our [Slack](https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-4d1c2uk6t-55YZVvOQnJFNeAJK32U~Gg) or comment here. We're happy to help. 🙌

## Description

This RFC tracks the current state and planned improvements for Prefill-Decode (P/D) Disaggregation using the NixlConnector, which enables high-performance KV cache transfer between prefill and decode instances using the NIXL library.

  Core Infrastructure

  - [x] NIXL Integration - Core P/D disaggregation framework (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/17751)

  - [x] Fully asynchronous KV cache transfers
    - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/33377 - Bugfix for async scheduling + request abort + async KV transfer
    - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/28327 - Simplify async KV output aggregation
    - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/27648 - Async scheduling support
    - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/31583 - Fix resuming preempted requests after async load

items.title: [RFC] L2 Adapter-Level Trace Recording and Causal Replay
items.author: daegyu94
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

This RFC proposes an L2 trace level that records actual L2 adapter task
submissions and completions, then replays those operations directly against a
target adapter. The goal is to compare L2 backends with the same observed L2
workload.

Replay does not reconstruct source L1 state or copy original KV payloads. It
uses recorded keys, object sizes, timestamps, and minimal causal dependencies.
Source/target outcome differences are comparison metrics, not replay failures.

```text
source process                   target process

StorageManager/L1               replay driver
       |                              |
       v                              v
async controller -> L2 adapter   target L2 adapter
                      |                |
                      v                v
                  L2 trace       replay statistics
```

## Motivation

Storage-level replay re-executes `StorageManager` APIs. This is useful for
testing L1 reservation, locking, eviction, store, and prefetch semantics, but
replay-side L1 state may differ from the source and generate different L2 I/O.
It therefore cannot guarantee the same operation sequence, keys, object sizes,
submission intervals, or request lifecycle when comparing L2 backends.

This RFC moves the replay boundary immediately before the L2 adapter so L1
state is excluded from the backend comparison.

```text
vLLM -> StorageManager/L1 -> async controller -> L2 adapter -> backend
                                             ^ record/replay boundary
```

## Goals

- Record the actual L2 adapter workload.
- Submit recorded operations directly to one target L2 adapter.
- Preserve required causal order while retaining source concurrency.
- Expose saturation through schedule lag, dependency wait, buffer wait, and
  drain time.
- Report source/target outcome differences with performance results.
- Reject incomplete traces before replay.

## Proposed CLI

### Record

```bash
lmcache server --trace-level l2 --trace-output l2.lct
```

### Replay

```bash
lmcache trace replay l2.lct \
  --l2-adapter '{...}' \
  --prepare-l2 \
  --speedup 4
```

- `--speedup 4` replays submission intervals four times faster without
  scaling adapter I/O latency.
- `--trace-percent 10` selects the first 10% of L2 submissions.
- `--prepare-l2` prepopulates objects inferred to have existed before the
  trace, using synthetic payloads.

## Trace contract

### Events

Submission events are recorded for store, lookup-and-lock, load, unlock, and
delete. Completion events are recorded for store, lookup-and-lock, and load.
Unlock and delete have submission events only because their adapter APIs do
not expose separate completion results.

### Metadata

The trace records:

- monotonic submission and completion timestamps relative to trace start;
- adapter index and task ID where available;
- request ID for lookup/load/unlock correlation;
- complete `ObjectKey` identity, including `cache_salt`;
- key lists, object byte sizes, and lookup layout metadata;
- aggregate store `succeeded_count`, `failed_count`, and `bytes_transferred`;
- lookup `hit_indices`; and
- load `success_indices`.

`cache_salt` is part of each `ObjectKey`, not trace-wide metadata. A legacy
payload without this field decodes to `""`, but its original salt cannot be
recovered.

### Completeness marker

The final record contains recorder and EventBus drop counts. Replay is rejected
when the marker is missing or duplicated, either drop count is non-zero, the
header level is not `l2`, source store/lookup/load tasks use more than one
adapter, or the target does not contain exactly one adapter.

## Initial read-object preparation

Preparing every lookup key would turn source misses into target hits. Replay
therefore prepares only objects whose first source lookup indicates that they
already existed when tracing began.

```text
Was the first source lookup a hit?
        |
       no ─────> do not prepare
        |
       yes
        v
Was there a successful store completion before lookup completion?
        |
       yes ────> do not prepare
        |         (a replayed store or source overlap explains the hit)
       no
        v
Treat the object as pre-existing and prepare a synthetic object
```

The synthetic object uses the same key and byte size but not the original KV
payload. Preparation completes before measured replay and is excluded from
replay statistics.

Store completion currently records only batch-level counts. If
`succeeded_count > 0`, every key in that task is treated as a possible success.
The trace cannot recover exact object-level state for a partially successful
batch.

## Causal replay

Replay does not add a global barrier after every task. It derives only the
dependencies required to preserve source order, while unrelated tasks continue
on their timestamp schedule.

### Store completed before lookup submission

```text
Source
time ─────────────────────────────────────────────────>
      store(A) submit ── complete ── lookup(A) submit ── hit

Replay
      store(A) submit ── complete ── lookup(A) submit
                                  ^ dependency
```

For a source lookup hit, replay finds successful stores that completed before
lookup completion. If any also completed before lookup submission, the latest
one becomes a dependency. Replay waits for target store completion, not target
store success.

### Store and lookup overlapped

```text
Source
time ─────────────────────────────────────────────────>
      store(A) submit ── lookup(A) submit ── store complete ── lookup hit
                         <------- overlap ------->

Replay
      store(A) submit ── lookup(A) submit
                         ^ does not wait for store completion
```

If store completion occurred after lookup submission but before lookup
completion, replay adds no dependency. This preserves source overlap.

### Request lifecycle

```text
lookup completion -> load completion -> unlock submission
        |
        +-------

items.title: [Bug][MP/P2P] L2 attach timeouts leave untracked adapters after retries and peer removal
items.author: JasperChan929
items.body_excerpt:
## Maintainer scope check before a PR

Before preparing a patch, is a focused fix for timed-out L2 attachment in the current MP/P2P registration path welcome, and what addition-failure contract should it preserve? I have only prepared the reproduction below. Please let me know if this path is being replaced or if a fix is already assigned.

## Describe the bug

`StorageManager.add_l2_adapter()` publishes an adapter into its registry before the store and prefetch controllers acknowledge attachment. Both controller calls have a bounded wait and can raise `RuntimeError`, but their queued `AddAdapterOp` is not cancelled when that wait expires. The manager also retains the adapter and its resources.

The production P2P caller catches this error and returns `False` without recording the assigned adapter id. A later reconciliation therefore adds another adapter for the same peer. When the peer disappears, only the recorded retry is removed; the first, untracked adapter remains in the storage manager and controllers.

## Affected revision

Reproduced on LMCache `dev` at `b9a5ce0213618cc6e6a1e8eee20c4a3a696ad58f`. On 2026-10-13 I also checked current `dev` `240506edf5146613b015e9e2e51189f1fc099b76`: all four affected production files are byte-identical to the reproduction source. This is a source comparison, not a claim of a complete latest-base serving test.

- [Registration order](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/b9a5ce0213618cc6e6a1e8eee20c4a3a696ad58f/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_manager.py#L1161)
- [Store acknowledgement timeout](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/b9a5ce0213618cc6e6a1e8eee20c4a3a696ad58f/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/store_controller.py#L343)
- [Prefetch acknowledgement timeout](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/b9a5ce0213618cc6e6a1e8eee20c4a3a696ad58f/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py#L756)
- [P2P failure handling and peer bookkeeping](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/b9a5ce0213618cc6e6a1e8eee20c4a3a696ad58f/lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/p2p_controller.py#L578)

## Controlled reproduction

1. Create an empty host-backed `StorageManager` and a real native-filesystem L2 config. Both background controller threads run normally.
2. Use a threading event gate to delay processing of attachment operations on one real controller thread. Keep the original `add_adapter()` implementation, operation queue, wait duration, and backend unchanged.
3. Call `add_l2_adapter(config)`. After approximately 5.5 seconds, the original method raises the acknowledgement timeout.
4. Read `l2_adapters()` and `report_status()`, then release the event gate.
5. Write a small object through `reserve_write()` and `finish_write()`. The adapter from the failed addition still receives a real native-filesystem write.
6. Retry the same configuration. A second id is assigned while the first adapter remains.

Observed counts are `registered / store / prefetch`:

```text
normal addition:                    returned id 0, 1 / 1 / 1
invalid affinity control:           ValueError,    0 / 0 / 0
store acknowledgement timeout:      RuntimeError,  1 / 0 / 0
after delayed operation completes:                 1 / 1 / 0
after retry:                        returned id 1, 2 / 2 / 1

prefetch acknowledgement timeout:   RuntimeError,  1 / 1 / 0
after delayed operation completes:                 1 / 1 / 1
after retry:                        returned id 1, 2 / 2 / 2
```

A separate CPU probe uses real `P2PL2Adapter` instances and two NIXL/UCX host contexts with a loopback handshake. Synthetic discovery snapshots are passed directly to the production reconciliation method; this probe does not start coordinator HTTP, automatic polling, or a model server. The P2P controller is created with orchestration disabled so the scheduling is controlled explicitly.

```text
first reconcile after timeout:      peer count 0, storage ids [0]
after delayed attach and retry:     peer count 1, storage ids [0, 1]
after four peer-absent cycles:      peer count 0, storage ids [0]
                                   store adapters 1, prefetch adapters 1
                                   native transfer clients 0
```

## Expected behavior / contract question

A failed addition needs a recoverable outcome that the P2P caller can track. Options include coordinated cancellation/cleanup of the pending operation, or a retained operation/id that can be reconciled without allocating a second adapter. Simply closing the adapter on the exception is unsafe while a queued operation can still attach it later.

Peer disappearance should leave no adapter created for that peer after draining its work.

## Impact and scope

In the native filesystem probe, a failed addition retained four file descriptors and two OS threads and still wrote a 64-byte object. Retrying added another backend instance. Explicit manager cleanup released the resources; this is not a claim of leakage after process shutdown or of duplicate physical payload bytes.

The failure condition is an attachment acknowledgement exceeding the existing timeout. The probe deliberately forces that scheduling window; it does not establish its natural serving frequency. No GPU transfer, inference-output, or throughput claim is made.

## Related work

- #4369 retains peer bookkeeping when **removal** fails. Its inspected patch does not change `_add_adapter`, the registration queue, or `StorageManager.add_l2_adapter`, so it cannot identify the adapter lost during the failed first addition.
- #4334 addresses periodic-notifier creation/shutdown ownership. The P2P probe explicitly removes remaining adapters before manager shutdown to keep that separate defect out of this result.

Environment: Linux x86_64, Python 3.12.13, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130 with CUDA devices hidden, CPU-only LMCache common extensions built from this revision, NIXL 1.3.2 for the host handshake.
