items.title: [Roadmap] Prefill-Decode Disaggregation Roadmap (2026 Q4)
items.author: ShangmingCai
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation
Prefill-Decode Disaggregation is now the default way people run SGLang at scale, and over the last two quarters we have made it work with almost every model family, every parallel strategy (TP/PP/CP/DCP/DP-attention), HiCache, and speculative decoding (see the Q2 roadmap https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/21703 for the history).

The cost of that is visible in the code: three transfer backends that each carry their own copy of the protocol, a KVCache lifecycle that is only correct because of a long list of patches, and a decode side that still reserves every destination slot in HBM up front. So for Q4 the theme is less "support one more combination" and more "make the thing we already have correct, memory-efficient, and better coordinated with the router":

1. One protocol layer, per-backend transport (https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/34510).
2. KVCache liveness as an invariant, not a patch series.
3. Pre-allocate decode KV slots in HiCache / host memory instead of VRAM, and move the KV into VRAM once the transfer is done.
4. Router/engine coordination for agentic prefix reuse.

## Shared-protocol unification
Tracker: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/34510, RFC: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/33861 @jambow0320 @livingshade 

Mooncake / NIXL / Mori each implement bootstrap, room lifecycle, chunk orchestration, timeout, heartbeat, abort, and failure handling in their own `conn.py`. Every change has to be written up to three times: the liveness fixes below, every new model's KV layout, and every new parallelism combination. The target is one `KVManager / KVSender / KVReceiver / KVBootstrapServer` and a `BaseTransport` that only names remote memory and moves `(src, dst, len)`.

- [x] Step 0 / Step 1: behavior audit and low-risk alignment of the three backends (bootstrap timeout, heartbeat, ABORT delivery, stale-work skip, shared failure notification) https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37077
- [ ] Step 2: per-backend transport extraction (`MooncakeTransport` / `NixlTransport` / `MoriTransport`), starting from the sender/receiver consolidation https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41140 @jambow0320
- [x] Step 3: completion/failure delivery channel (transport notifications vs the ZMQ status channel), abort/quiescence (ABORT_ACK means "drained", not "received"), room generation / tombstones https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/44186
- [ ] Step 4: common protocol classes, `get_kv_class` → `make_transport`, and the Fake backend becomes `NullTransport` so the whole protocol runs in CPU-only CI
- [ ] Explicit request role and a canonical per-component `TransferPlan`, so layouts are validated before transport submission instead of inferred from payload shape https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/37765 @IvanShan177
- [ ] Wire version + rolling-upgrade story: a version frame and a dual-parse window before Step 4 changes the frames
- [ ] New backends land as a `Transport`, not as a fourth `conn.py` (UniFlow https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43437 @yexiangd)

## KVCache liveness and transfer correctness
A KV slot is not free when the allocator says so; it is free when every remote writer has finished. This year we closed a whole family of silent cross-request corruption bugs that came from freeing decode slots while RDMA writes were still landing (first reported by Z.ai, reproduced and audited by @kflansburg in https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38961). As of v0.5.21 the hold is on by default on Mooncake and NIXL for every failure kind, and Mori joined on main.

- [x] Deferred decode-side KV release until per-rank drain ACK or timeout, default-on https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/35049 https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41023
- [x] Generation-tagged ABORT/ABORT_ACK in the common layer, every failure kind defers, Mori under the hold https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37077 https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41404 @livingshade
- [x] Sibling races closed: intake-rejected requests never reach a handoff, HiCache retraction waits for the offload, decode restore outcome is TP-consistent, router cancels the paired decode on prefill failure https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38935 https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43562 https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41612
- [x] Opt-in KV transfer checksums and deferred-release metrics https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39500 https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41128 @cctry

## HiCache integration: pre-allocate in host memory, decode in VRAM
Today decode reserves a request's whole destination range in HBM at bootstrap, so a slow or long prefill occupies decode capacity that running requests need. The direction is: pre-allocate the destination slots in HiCache / CPU memory, receive the transfer there, and move the KV into VRAM once the transfer is done and the request is admitted to the decode phase.

- [x] Decode host receive: at a device-usage threshold, incoming KV lands in the pinned host pool and is restored on admission https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40238 @cctry
- [x] Unified-memory decode host pools https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39478 @ZYHowell
- [x] `--disaggregation-decode-allocation-policy prefill_complete`: reserve destination KV only once the final prefill result is accepted https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40703 @ekrim
- [ ] Pre-allocate decode destination slots in CPU memory by default for long-context decode, with HBM allocated at admission time. Host receive is the mechanism, but no in-tree backend sets `supports_host_destination` yet. What is missing: host destinations for Mooncake / NIXL / Mori, reconciling host receive with deferred-release accounting, and measuring the restore cost against the extra concurrency.
- [ ] L2-only decode radix cache: keep the decode prefix tree in host memory and stage into HBM per batch https://github.com/sgl-projec

items.title: [RFC] pd: Prefill short requests on the decode worker that caches their prefix (PPD)
items.author: alphabetc1
items.body_excerpt:
## TL;DR

In agentic and multi-turn traffic, the decode worker that served the previous turn already holds almost all of the next prompt in its radix cache: the previous prompt plus the tokens it decoded. Today the next turn still goes prefill -> KV transfer -> decode, even when only a few hundred tokens are new. This RFC lets the router send such a request **only to the decode worker**, which prefills the uncached suffix itself (chunked prefill), then decodes it. We call this **PPD** (prefill on the decode worker, for short prefills). Requests the router does not mark keep the normal PD path, so one decode worker serves both.

## Why

- **The prefill worker's cache is the wrong one.** It caches turn N's prompt but not turn N's output, which was generated on the decode worker. So turn N+1 misses on prefill at the first output token, while the decode worker's radix cache (`--disaggregation-decode-enable-radix-cache`) holds prompt N plus output N.
- **The PD path has a fixed cost that a short prefill cannot hide:** a bootstrap handshake, the prefill worker's queue, the KV transfer, and the decode worker's preallocation and polling. With HiCache, cache hit rates of 90%+ are common for agentic sessions, so the computed part is often a few hundred tokens, and the fixed cost dominates TTFT.
- The prefill worker spends compute and network bandwidth on work the decode worker can do in one or two short extend steps.

## Flow

Red blocks are new; everything else exists today.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant R as sgl-router
    participant P as Prefill worker
    participant D as Decode worker

    C->>R: request (turn N+1)
    R->>R: prefix lookup in the KV-event index (prefill and decode workers)

    rect rgb(255, 224, 224)
        Note over R,D: NEW: decode worker holds the prefix, uncached suffix is short
        R->>D: request + disagg_local_prefill=true (no bootstrap fields)
        D->>D: match decode radix tree, chunked prefill of the suffix
        D->>D: decode in the same running batch as PD requests
        D-->>R: stream tokens
    end

    Note over R,D: otherwise, unchanged PD path
    R->>P: request + bootstrap fields
    R->>D: request + bootstrap fields
    P->>D: KV transfer
    D-->>R: stream tokens
    R-->>C: response
```

## Who does what

| | Today | New |
|---|---|---|
| **sgl-router** (`experimental/sgl-router`) | `select_workers` (`src/server/routes/chat.rs`) looks up prefix matches, picks a prefill worker, then a decode peer with `DecodePolicyKind::{PowerOfTwo, LegacyHostAffinity}`; `dispatch` (`routes/chat/forward.rs`) sends both legs with one bootstrap room | Before picking a prefill worker, look up the decode workers' cached prefix in the same KV-event index. If a decode worker's uncached suffix is at most a threshold and its load allows, dispatch to that decode worker only, with `disagg_local_prefill: true`. Credit the decode worker, not a prefill worker, with the prefix (`record_prefill_route`). Pick decode workers with session or prefix affinity, so a conversation returns to the decode worker that holds it. |
| **Decode worker** | Admits only transferred requests: prealloc queue -> transfer queue -> waiting queue -> prebuilt batch | `--disaggregation-decode-enable-local-prefill`: a marked request enters `waiting_queue` and runs through the aggregated scheduler (radix match, chunked prefill, optional mixed chunk). Transferred requests move to a separate `disagg_decode_prebuilt_queue`. |
| **Prefill worker** | Prefills and transfers every PD request | No change; it just sees fewer short requests. |
| **Request API** | `bootstrap_host/port/room`, `disagg_prefill_dp_rank` | `disagg_local_prefill: bool` on `/generate`, `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/completions`, `/v1/responses`. A decode worker without the flag rejects it with 400. |

## Engine design (phase 1)

The decode worker becomes "an aggregated scheduler with a second source of requests that skip prefill":

1. **Queues.** With the flag on, `waiting_queue` holds only requests prefilled on this worker, so the aggregated code paths (prefill admission, priority, abort, timeouts, load reporting) keep their meaning. Transferred requests wait in `disagg_decode_prebuilt_queue`. With the flag off, nothing moves.
2. **Scheduling.** Each step first merges newly transferred requests into the running batch, as today, then calls the aggregated `get_next_batch_to_run`, which merges the last prefill batch, runs the next prefill chunk if any, and otherwise decodes. `--chunked-prefill-size` bounds a local prefill step and so the decode stall it causes; `--enable-mixed-chunk` lets running requests decode in the same step.
3. **Memory.** Preallocation for transferred requests reserves the remaining chunks of the in-flight local prefill, so remote admissions cannot starve it. Local admission uses the aggregated `PrefillAdder` budget, and decode retraction covers over-commit, as in aggregated serving.
4. **Retraction and pause.** A locally prefilled request has no prefill peer, so it is never rebootstrapped. When it is retracted, the worker skips the host backup and prefills it again locally, as an aggregated server does.
5. **Cache.** Phase 1 builds on the decode radix tree, not decode HiCache. Decode-side L2/L3 will come through the linker, so a local prefill can later hit KV that the decode worker offloaded.

Phase 1 rejects pipeline parallelism, DP attention, MoE all-to-all backends (their buffers are sized for decode batches), HiSparse, and decode host KV buffering.

## Phases

1. **Engine** (#45423): the flag, the request field, the scheduling and memory changes above, docs, unit tests, and an e2e test.
2. **sgl-router**: the decode-side prefix lookup and the local-prefill decision, `--pd-local-prefill-max-uncached-tokens`, decode affinity, and metrics for local versus PD routes.
3. **Engine**: DP attention and DeepEP decode. All-to-all buffers must fit a prefill chunk, and

### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with TP1/PP2 and NEXTN can produce different greedy output token IDs for the same input under dynamic concurrent arrivals, despite `--enable-deterministic-inference` and a fixed random seed.

This was reproduced on a single host with two H20 GPUs at the upstream commit listed above. The PP/speculative path is enabled through `SGLANG_ENABLE_PP_SPEC=1`.

**Expected:** with deterministic inference enabled and `temperature=0`, the same input should produce the same greedy tokens across repeated runs with the same cache warmup history. If this gated PP/NEXTN combination is outside the determinism guarantee, please clarify the limitation and consider warning or rejecting this configuration.

**Observed:** after flushing the cache and replaying the same warmup requests, one 1,024-token input produced two distinct 64-token sequences. They first differ at output index 19 (the 20th generated token). Both executions report 896 cached tokens and zero retractions.

| Field | Sequence A | Sequence B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Token at output index 19 | 318 | 321 |
| Completion tokens | 64 | 64 |
| Cached tokens | 896 | 896 |
| Acceptance length, including bonus token | 2.909090909090909 | 3.0476190476190474 |
| Verify count | 22 | 21 |
| Correct / proposed drafts | 42 / 66 | 43 / 63 |
| Correct-drafts histogram | `[5, 3, 3, 11]` | `[4, 2, 4, 11]` |

The observed upstream run was:

```text
cycle0-threads: first long input A; second long input A
cycle0-batch4:  first long input A; second long input A
cycle1-threads: first long input B; second long input A
cycle1-batch4:  first long input A; second long input A
```

The first long input has 896 cached tokens; the second has 960. A/B classification compares all 64 output IDs, not just the first differing position. The full A/B sequences are embedded in the client below, which saves complete responses from each reproduction run.

The mismatch occurred in one of the two concurrent-request rounds and neither of the two API-batch rounds shown above. This limited observation suggests sensitivity to request arrival or batching; it does not establish a failure rate or a reliable workaround. An API batch does not imply a fixed internal scheduler microbatch.

**Scope of the finding:** I have not isolated the responsible operator or state transition, and cannot yet distinguish batch-dependent numerical behavior from a PP/NEXTN recurrent-state/cache/scheduling issue. Matching cache-hit lengths do not prove identical recurrent state. This report does not establish an accuracy regression or identify the first bad commit. I have not isolated whether PP or NEXTN is individually necessary by removing one at a time.

Related reports reviewed: [#20509](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/20509) discusses Qwen3.5 determinism with FP8/TP8, a different configuration; [#39634](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/39634) tracks PP/speculative integration. I have not established that

### 🐛 Describe the bug

From Nick:
```
I think the problem is that each DP worker finds/assigns free ports dynamically/independently.. so there is a race condtion. I'm not sure of an immediate workaround apart from just re-attempt to start things when this happens. We'll have to look at how to catch and re-find a port if possible (though I have a memory this might be nontrivial).
```

From Reporter:
```
Received init message: EngineHandshakeMetadata(addresses=EngineZmqAddresses(inputs=['tcp://slurm-h200-207-083:60613'], outputs=['tcp://slurm-h200-207-083:36865'], coordinator_input='tcp://slurm-h200-207-083:34575', coordinator_output='tcp://slurm-h200-207-083:48025', frontend_stats_publish_address='ipc:///tmp/88ec875f-3de9-46ec-9947-6d1d6573b910'), parallel_config={'data_parallel_master_ip': 'slurm-h200-207-083', 'data_parallel_master_port': 41917, '_data_parallel_master_port_list': [60545, 36835, 47971, 37001], 'data_parallel_size': 32})
```

I'm looking at the code and I see that all code paths for getting ports eventually to go to _get_open_port, and that in _get_open_port there is basically no defence against choosing the same port twice. Can you please confirm my understanding?

_get_open_port in main is here: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/utils/network_utils.py#L177

UPD: I imagine the assumption here is that once a code path gets a port, that code path will use it immediately, and thus the port will be come busy. It doesn't seem to hold though.


Even where all sockets that vLLM chose for itself are unique, I get the stack trace below.
I have the following explanation in mind:

- vLLM chooses zmq ports before launching the engines
- launching the engines takes ~5 mins
- by the time the engines are launched, something can listen on this port, like for example Ray
- **It looks the right solution is to hold on to then chosen ports immediately are they are chosen.**

### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Describe the bug

  The V1 engine core silently deadlocks under concurrent load using default configuration. The API server remains healthy (/health returns 200, /metrics responds), but zero tokens are generated. Requests stay in "running" state indefinitely and
   the engine never recovers without a pod restart.

  vLLM serve command:
```
  vllm serve "$MODEL_DIR" \
      --tokenizer Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B \
      --dtype bfloat16 \
      --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \
      --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 \
      --max-model-len 16384 \
      --max-num-seqs 128 \
      --quantization fp8 \
      --trust-remote-code \
      --enable-prefix-caching \
      --async-scheduling \
      --default-chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking": false}'
```

  How to reproduce:

  1. Deploy vLLM with the configuration above
  2. Send concurrent requests (8-64 concurrency) — works fine initially
  3. Under sustained load or after a brief spike, the engine freezes
  4. No specific error triggers it — no OOM, no CUDA error, no validation error

  Engine log sequence showing the deadlock:
```
  13:57:45  Avg prompt throughput: 2598.6 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 1684.2 tokens/s, Running: 2 reqs, Waiting: 0 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 0.3%, Prefix cache hit rate: 96.9%
  13:57:55  Avg prompt throughput: 83.6 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 1.8 tokens/s, Running: 11 reqs, Waiting: 0 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 1.3%, Prefix cache hit rate: 96.9%
  13:58:05  Avg prompt throughput: 0.0 tokens/s, Avg generation throughput: 0.0 tokens/s, Running: 11 reqs, Waiting: 0 reqs, GPU KV cache usage: 1.3%, Prefix cache hit rate: 96.9%
```
  After 13:58:05, throughput stays at 0.0 permanently. Running count stays at 11. KV cache stays at 1.3%. The engine never recovers.

### Key observations:

  - Not resource exhaustion: Only 11/128 request slots used, 1.3% KV cache
  - API server alive: /health returns 200, /metrics responds
  - Engine core frozen: Zero tokens generated, forward pass never executes
  - Affects arbitrary request counts: Seen with 11, 124, and other counts
  - Does not self-recover: Requires pod restart
  - --request-timeout does not help: Engine core is frozen, can't enforce timeouts

  Investigation — deadlock tied to CUDA graph code paths:

  Systematic testing to isolate the trigger:
```
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              Config              │               Result               │
  ├──────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Default V1 + async-scheduling    │ DEADLOCK                           │
  ├──────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Default V1 + no async-scheduling │ DEADLOCK                           │
  ├──────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Default V1 + --enforce-eager     │ Didn't run enough but ~8x slower (not viable) │
  └──────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┘
```

  Incident 1 (nightly build): During a production spike, autoscaler scaled from 6→20→6 replicas. Two surviving replicas entered deadlock with 123-124 running requests each, stayed frozen 4+ hours until manual restart.

  Incident 2 (v0.17.1 stable): Same deadlock reproduced within minutes of a load test. Single replica, low concurrency (8→16 ramp). Froze at 11 running requests. No autoscaling involved.

  Current workaround: --enforce-eager prevents the deadlock but with ~8x throughput regression, making it unviable for production. Restarting affected replicas is the only practical mitigation.

items.title: [Feature]: Per-request prefix-cache miss attribution (prompt divergence vs. eviction)
items.author: sachinworks
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Automatic prefix caching is one of the biggest cost and latency wins for RAG and agent workloads, where every request re-sends a long, mostly identical scaffold (system prompt, tool schemas, few-shot examples).

vLLM already reports per-request cached tokens (`num_cached_tokens`, `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`), so you can tell roughly *where* the cache hit ended. What you can't tell is what happened to the first block after the hit. Users typically care about two common causes, which need very different fixes:

- **The prompt changed.** A timestamp or request ID in the system prompt, tool definitions serialized in a different order, a user name injected near the top. Each one invalidates every block after it. The fix is in the application.
- **The block was evicted.** The prefix was cached earlier but got pushed out under memory pressure. The fix is capacity, routing or cache offload, not the prompt.

vLLM can't infer the cause. The diagnostic below reports what it observed and leaves the interpretation to the user. Today both look identical from the outside: a short cache hit. Telling them apart means diffing tokenized prompts by hand and guessing about eviction.

**Proposal:** optional per-request diagnostics, disabled by default:

- a **miss reason** for the first uncached block after the longest hit: `evicted` (its hash was cached and evicted recently: with the flag on, hashes dropped in `BlockPool._maybe_evict_cached_block` are also recorded as `BlockHashWithGroupId` in a fixed-size LRU, e.g. sized to `num_gpu_blocks`, roughly one cache turnover; a hit there is definite) or `no_match` (not seen within that window: a changed prompt, a never-seen prompt, or an eviction older than the window; ambiguous by design). `no_match` covers both changed prompt tokens and changed extra keys mixed into the block hash (`cache_salt`, LoRA adapter, multimodal inputs), so on its own it is not proof that the text changed.
- a third outcome, `lookup_limit`, when the hit length reached the lookup cap (`num_tokens - 1`, rounded down to a full block). vLLM always recomputes the last prompt token for logits, so that next block is never probed; it is recomputed by design, not missed, and gets no miss reason
- the **kinds of extra keys** included in that block's hash (e.g. `cache_salt`, `lora`, `mm`), names only and never values, so users can rule out salt or adapter differences first
- optionally, an opt-in **comparison against a reference request** that returns a short decoded snippet around the first differing token, off by default for privacy

_Updated after discussion below: renamed `not_cached` to `no_match` and added extra-key kinds (`cache_salt` edge case), and added `lookup_limit` so fully cached prompts at a block boundary are not reported as misses. Test controls: 16/17/32/33-token prompts with block size 16. Later reworded so the labels state observations rather than inferred causes, and specified the eviction hook._

Scope: full-attention groups first, reported per KV-cache group; hybrid groups later if the approach holds up. Cost when enabled: one set lookup per request plus a bounded set; nothing when off.

These could be surfaced in debug-level logs and/or request-level metrics.

**Why it helps:** teams could catch cache-hostile prompt construction in CI or staging, and tie TTFT regressions to the right cause: a prompt change versus cache pressure in the serving stack.

### Alternatives

- Diffing tokenized prompts by hand against a known-good request. Works for divergence, but is slow, needs the exact tokenized input, and says nothing about eviction.
- Correlating with KV cache events (block stored / removed) externally. Possible, but requires running an event consumer and joining block hashes to requests outside vLLM.
- Re-hashing prompts client-side. This duplicates vLLM's block-hashing logic and drifts whenever that changes (block size, hash function, multimodal or LoRA extra keys).

### Additional context

Related: #43711 proposed a lower-level debug event at the lookup point (`KVCacheManager.get_computed_blocks`, right after `find_longest_cache_hit`). It was closed for inactivity without maintainer feedback. That lookup point looks like the natural place to compute the miss reason above.

Happy to work on a PR if maintainers agree on the approach.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Onboarding 2026] Good first issues — start contributing to LMCache in one PR
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
👋 Welcome to join lmcache slack channel. https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-4d1c2uk6t-55YZVvOQnJFNeAJK32U~Gg 

👋 Welcome to LMCache! This umbrella issue is the **single entry point** for first-time
contributors. If you've never sent a PR to LMCache before, start here.

> If you're looking for the older onboarding thread, see #627. This 2026 version
> focuses on smaller, well-scoped tasks with a friendly step-by-step PR workflow.

---

## 0. Before you start

- Read [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](../blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md). The most important parts:
  - Base branch is `dev`. Open PRs against `dev`, not `main`.
  - Every Python file starts with `# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0`.
  - Imports are grouped as `# Standard / # Third Party / # First Party / # Local`.
  - Line length is **88**, formatter is `ruff format`, lint is `ruff check`.
  - Never access `_private` members of other classes (SLF rule).
  - Public functions/methods need **type hints** + **docstring**.
- Set up the environment:
  ```bash
  uv venv --python 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate
  uv pip install -e . --no-build-isolation
  uv pip install -r requirements/test.txt
  pre-commit install
  ```

## 1. How to claim a task

These tasks are mainly for new contributors to learn the LMCache issue-to-PR workflow. Please claim **only one good-first issue at a time**. If you already have an assigned good-first issue or an open good-first PR, finish that work before taking another one, and leave the remaining tasks for other newcomers.

1. Pick **one** sub-issue below that has no assignee and no `🔒 claimed` comment.
2. Comment exactly: `/claim` (or `I'd like to work on this 🙋`).
   A maintainer will assign it to you within ~2 business days.
3. If you go silent for 7 days we'll un-assign so others can pick it up — totally fine,
   just leave a comment if you need more time.

## 2. Branch & commit

```bash
git checkout dev && git pull
git checkout -b gfi/<issue-number>-short-slug
# ... do the work ...
git commit -s -m "short imperative summary"   # -s is required (DCO)
```

- **Sign-off is required** (`-s`). PRs without DCO sign-off cannot be merged.
- Keep the PR small: one issue = one PR.

## 3. Local checks (must pass before pushing)

```bash
pre-commit run --all-files
pytest -xvs tests/<the_file_you_touched>.py    # if applicable
```

## 4. Open the PR

**PR title format** (please follow):

```
[good-first-issue] <area>: <imperative summary>  (#<sub-issue-number>)
```

Examples:
- `[good-first-issue] docs: fix broken link in quickstart (#1801)`
- `[good-first-issue] tests: add unit test for FooBar.flush (#1802)`
- `[good-first-issue] lint: add SPDX header to scripts/foo.py (#1803)`

**PR description** — please use this template (the repo's PR template already
gives you the skeleton; just fill it in):

```markdown
**What this PR does / why we need it**:
Closes #<sub-issue-number>
Refs #<this umbrella issue number>

<one or two sentences describing the change>

**Special notes for your reviewers**:
- This is my first PR to LMCache 🙇 please be gentle.
- I ran `pre-commit run --all-files` locally — all green.
- I ran `pytest -xvs tests/...` — all green.

**If applicable**:
- [ ] this PR contains user facing changes - docs added
- [ ] this PR contains unit tests
```

> Tip: writing `Closes #1234` in the description auto-closes the sub-issue when the
> PR is merged. Keep `Refs #<umbrella>` so the umbrella stays linked.

## 5. Finding a reviewer

You don't need to find one yourself — `.github/CODEOWNERS` will auto-request
the right people based on the files you changed. If the PR sits idle for **3 working
days**, leave a polite comment like:

> Friendly ping — PTAL when you have a moment 🙏 cc @<one CODEOWNER from the file you changed>

If you really can't tell who to ping, default to:
- Tests / CI / packaging → @hickeyma @sammshen @ApostaC @deng451e
- Docs / examples → @sammshen @deng451e
- Storage backends → @maobaolong @sammshen @chunxiaozheng
- Core engine / memory → @ApostaC @YaoJiayi @sammshen
- Multiprocess → @ApostaC @OasisGit @hlin99

(See [`.github/CODEOWNERS`](../blob/dev/.github/CODEOWNERS) for the full map.)

## 6. Responding to review comments

This is the part most newcomers miss — please follow it, it makes everyone happier:

1. **Address every comment.** For each thread:
   - If you agree → push a fix and reply `Done in <commit-sha>`.
   - If you disagree → explain politely, propose an alternative.
   - If you don't understand → ask! Reviewers expect questions.
2. **Don't force-push** during review (it loses inline-comment context). Just add
   commits; we'll squash on merge.
3. **Re-request review explicitly** once all threads are resolved:
   > Addressed all comments, PTAL again 🙏 @reviewer1 @reviewer2

   `PTAL` = "Please Take Another Look". Tag every reviewer who left comments.
4. If CI is red, fix it before pinging — reviewers will skip red PRs.


---

## 7. How to create and claim a sub-issues

- You can extend the new cli commend line tools, ref to https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3719 and https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3678

Stuck? Drop a message in the `#contributors` channel of our

items.title: Support KV cache events in MP mode (for Dynamo KV-aware routing)
items.author: glbyktjys
items.body_excerpt:
### Background

In non-MP mode, LMCache emits a [CacheStoreEvent](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/dev/lmcache/v1/cache_engine.py#L507) on each chunk store. vLLM pulls these event through the connector's [take_events() ](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/base.py)and publishes them as [BlockStored events](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_events.py) (--kv-events-config) for consumers like Dynamo's KV-aware router. 

See docs/source/production/kv_cache_events.rst.

### Problem

In MP mode, the cache engine runs in the LMCache server process rather than alongside the inference engine. As a result, cache store events are not propagated to the upstream engine.

### Goal

In MP mode, chunks stored by the LMCache server produce KV cache events published directly from the LMCache server to Dynamo's KV-aware router through Dynamo's KvEventPublisher, carrying the same information as non-MP BlockStored events. This bypasses vLLM's event path entirely.

###  Task (not limited to the following)

1. Write a design doc for the event path. Good reference: https://docs.nvidia.com/dynamo/v1.1.1/integrations/kv-events-for-custom-engines
2. Event creation in the MP server when a chunk is stored.
3. Integrate Dynamo's KvEventPublisher with the MP server.

items.title: [Bug] Shutdown and L1 TTL expiry can reclaim a buffer an L2 adapter is still loading into
items.author: JulianZJN
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

`L2AdapterInterface` makes the *caller* responsible for keeping a load buffer
valid "until the load task is completed", but gives the caller no way to find out
that a load it is no longer waiting for has stopped touching that buffer.
`PrefetchController.stop()` therefore frees L1 write reservations that an adapter
still owns, and, independently, the L1 write lock guarding such a reservation
is a TTL lock that expires after 600 s by default, after which the object becomes
readable by other requests and evictable by the eviction controller.

Both are reproducible on `dev` with in-tree components only.

## Affected version

`dev` at `dd35168c801fec49889b34b083a12204d3c02a2a` (reproduced there).

## Background: the contract gap

`lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/base.py:321-328` (`submit_load_task`):

> The caller is responsible for managing the lifecycle of the memory objects, and
> should make sure that the memory buffer is valid until the load task is
> completed.

`base.py:93-96`: *"The L2 adapter is not supposed to manage the lifecycle of the
memory objects."* But "completed" is defined only as `query_load_result`
returning non-`None` (`base.py:335-353`), and `close()`, `base.py:587-593`, says
nothing at all about in-flight loads. There is no `drain`, `join`, `quiesce`,
`wait_for_idle` or `num_inflight` anywhere in `L2AdapterInterface`.

From reading each adapter's `close()`, they do not agree on this. Some wait for their workers (`dax`, `raw_block`, `valkey`), several cancel their tasks and tear down, and at least two do neither for work that is already running:

* `p2p` (`p2p_l2_adapter.py:353-368`) unregisters its fds and removes the transfer-channel client without cancelling or joining posted reads.
* `fs` cancels a coroutine whose actual read runs on the default executor (`run_in_executor(None, self._read_with_odirect, ...)`, `fs_l2_adapter.py:707-718`), which cancellation cannot stop and `close()` never shuts down.

`serde_wrapper.py:350-355` already documents the hazard and asserts the guarantee
it needs, *"Both close() calls block until their in-flight reads / writes against
the temp MemoryObjs finish"*, which does not hold for the second and third
groups above.

## Repro 1, shutdown frees a buffer a pending load still owns

The test below (drop it in as `tests/v1/distributed/test_shutdown_ownership_repro.py`) drives the real `PrefetchController` and
`L1Manager` with a mock adapter whose gate sits before the copy into the
caller's buffers, so at the moment of shutdown the adapter has written nothing
and still holds the `MemoryObj`s it was handed. It asserts the safety contract
and is therefore RED:

```
E  AssertionError: shutdown reclaimed 4 of 4 L1 buffers that a pending L2 load
   still owns and has not written; PrefetchController.stop() joins only its own
   loop thread and no in-tree L2 adapter exposes a quiescence guarantee for
   in-flight loads (L2AdapterInterface.close() says nothing about them)
```

Mechanism, `storage_manager.py:1113-1127`:

```
    self._prefetch_controller.stop()     # joins its own thread, then frees
    ...
    for adapter in self._l2_adapters.values():
        adapter.close()                  # adapters consulted only afterwards
    self._l1_manager.close()
```

`PrefetchController.stop()` (`prefetch_controller.py:600-611` on dev) calls
`_cleanup_in_flight_requests()` (`prefetch_controller.py:1474-1491` on dev),
which does

```
    if request.phase == PrefetchPhase.PLAN_AND_LOAD:
        if request.write_reserved_keys:
            l1_mgr.finish_write_and_delete(request.write_reserved_keys)
```

`L1Manager.close()` (`l1_manager.py:902-909`) then frees everything else
unconditionally, with no lock check, so any adapter in the "cancel" or "neither"
group that returned from `close()` with work still in flight lands on freed
memory.

Swapping the two `close()` calls is not a fix by itself, since not every adapter's `close()` waits for in-flight loads.

## Repro 2, L1 write-lock TTL expiry, with `write_ttl_seconds=1`

The L1 read/write locks are `TTLLock` (`csrc/lmcache_native/ttl_lock.{h,cpp}`)
and the entire rule is `ttl_lock.cpp:74`:

```cpp
  return (counter_ > 0) && (current_time < expiration);
```

No TTL is ever refreshed for the duration of an operation: `write_lock.lock()` is
called once at `reserve_write` (`l1_manager.py:486`, `:522`), and neither
`unsafe_read` (`l1_manager.py:306-310`) nor `touch_keys`
(`l1_manager.py:782-796`) touches it. So the default 600 s
(`config.py:213-217`) is a hard wall-clock cap on how long an L2 load may hold a
reserved L1 buffer, unrelated to any L2 timeout.

Against the real `L1Manager` with `write_ttl_seconds=1` and `finish_write` never
called, exactly the state of a buffer a stalled load still owns:

```python
m.reserve_write([k], [False], layout)                     # SUCCESS
m.is_key_evictable(k), m.reserve_read([k])[k][0]          # False, KEY_NOT_READABLE
time.sleep(1.6)                                            # TTL expires
m.is_key_evictable(k), m.reserve_read([k])[k][0]          # True,  SUCCESS  <-- hands out the MemoryObj
m.delete([k])                                              # SUCCESS         <-- buffer returned to the allocator
m.finish_write([k])                                        # KEY_IN_WRONG_STATE
# WARNING L1Manager: finish write on non-write-locked key ...,
#         potential inconsistent data might be written
```

Consequences:

1. A second request reads a half-written buffer. `reserve_read` passes
   `available_for_read()` (`l1_manager.py:53-59`, "not write-locked") and returns
   `entry.memory_obj` (`l1_manager.py:288`).
2. Eviction frees it. `is_key_evictable` (`l1_manager.py:867-884`) returns
   True; the eviction controller passes it as the filter and calls plain
   `delete()` (`eviction_controller.py:184-198`); `delete`'s own "check again"
   safety net (`l1_manager.py:728-736`) uses the same expired `is_locked()`, so
   it does not help. The buffer goes back

items.title: [Bug] HiCache + hybrid (SSM/Mamba): failed cudaHostRegister on a secondary host pool aborts the whole instance, and the error path throws TypeError thereby hiding the real rc
items.author: flymysql
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On sglang `0.5.19` (torch `2.13.0+cu130`, CUDA 13.0, H20), starting a **hybrid SSM/Mamba** model
with `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-storage-backend dynamic` fails during
`attach_hybrid_pool_to_unified_cache` and **kills the entire instance**.

Two coupled defects:

1. **`cudaHostRegister` failure is treated as fatal.** `alloc_with_host_register` raises, which
   aborts scheduler init for all TP ranks. But the failure only means "this host pool is not
   zero-copy registered" — and sglang's own non-zero-copy path (`_generic_page_get/_set`) is
   fully functional without registration. A missing acceleration is escalated into a full outage.
2. **The error path destroys its own diagnostic.** Inside the `raise`, `cudart.cudaGetErrorString(rc)`
   is called with a **plain `int`**, which raises `TypeError` on this torch build — so the real
   `rc`/`offset`/`size` are swallowed. Operators only see a bare `TypeError`.

Additionally, the failure **leaves a sticky CUDA error**, which then surfaces later at an unrelated
call site (`_create_sync_groups` → `all_gather_object` → `torch.zeros`), which made this
considerably harder to root-cause.

### Environment

- sglang `0.5.19`
- torch `2.13.0+cu130`, CUDA 13.0
- 8 × H20 (96 GiB) / 8 × H20-3e (141 GiB), driver `535.161.08`
- Model: `Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8` (`Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration`, pool stack **KV + MAMBA**)
- Backend: `--hicache-storage-backend dynamic` with `interface_v1: 1` in the extra config
  (this selects the zero-copy page functions; the crash itself is in host-pool allocation and is
  not specific to any particular dynamic backend)
- Relevant flags: `--mamba-full-memory-ratio 0.37 --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer_lazy
  --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --hicache-mem-layout page_first_direct
  --hicache-io-backend direct --tp 8`

### Reproduction

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path <hybrid SSM/Mamba model, e.g. Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8> \
  --tp-size 8 --trust-remote-code \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.80 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 1.0 \
  --hicache-storage-backend dynamic \
  --hicache-mem-layout page_first_direct \
  --hicache-io-backend direct \
  --mamba-full-memory-ratio 0.37 \
  --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer_lazy \
  --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \

items.title: [RFC / HiCache] Same-node peer L2 sharing across DP ranks via /dev/shm
items.author: VNG-VMONITOR
items.body_excerpt:
# [RFC / HiCache] Same-node peer L2 sharing across DP ranks via `/dev/shm`

## Motivation

In deployments running multiple DP ranks on a **single node** (e.g. one host with 8 GPUs and `--dp-size 8`), each rank maintains a fully private L2 host KV cache. When two ranks receive requests with the same prefix — a common pattern for system prompts, few-shot examples, or shared document context — Rank B cannot see the KV pages that Rank A already produced, and must recompute the prefix from scratch.

Existing HiCache L3 backends (Mooncake, NIXL, AIBrix, 3FS, LMCache) do solve cross-instance sharing, but they all go through a networked / service-mediated data path. For **same-node** sharing that is common in single-box multi-DP deployments, the network round-trip is pure overhead — the ranks are all local processes with access to the same physical DRAM.

## Proposed design: `shm_peer_l2` HiCache storage backend

Two DP ranks on the same node map the same L2 host pool via named shared memory (`/dev/shm` tmpfs). Metadata (key → owner rank + slot address) is exchanged through a small direct-mapped index (also in `/dev/shm`). When Rank B misses in its own L1/L2, it looks up the index; on a hit, it performs one `memcpy` within the shared SHM to bring the peer's page into its own slot, then DMAs to GPU — no recompute.

Compared to a hypothetical "share via existing L3 file" approach (see `shm_cross_dp` below), the peer variant eliminates the L3 data copy: only a 288-byte pointer per page is written, giving:

- **Storage overhead**: ~55 MB total for a 475 GB L2 (vs. ~L2_size for a full mirror)
- **Read path**: 1 index lookup + 1 SHM memcpy + 1 DMA (vs. L3→CPU_buf→L2 + memcpy + DMA)
- **Write path**: 1 GPU→shared_L2 DMA + 1 index write (vs. + 1 memcpy to L3 file)

### Correctness

A per-page **generation counter** in shared memory prevents stale reads: when Rank A evicts and reallocates a slot, its generation counter increments. Rank B compares the stored generation against the current one; a mismatch is treated as a miss instead of copying whatever bytes now occupy the slot. The check is best-effort (no full memory barrier) — the tiny TOCTOU window between the generation read and the memcpy is accepted as per the "stale reads may be silently accepted" contract already present in HiCache read paths.

### Operational envelope

- `--dp-size >= 2`
- All DP ranks on the **same node** (`/dev/shm` is node-local tmpfs)
- `--hicache-write-policy write_through` required (`write_back` only flushes on eviction, so Rank B would not see data timely)
- Optionally with `--hicache-io-backend kernel` and `page_first`/`page_first_direct` layouts

Auto-computed capacity (`page_num × 4`, 25% load factor) at startup; explicit override via `--hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"peer_l2_capacity": N}'`.

Collision rate emitted every 10,000 writes; WARNING once it exceeds 10% (actionable — increase capacity).

## Existing prototype

A working implementation exists in a downstream fork. It shipped as two related backends registered through `backend_factory.py`:

- `shm_cross_dp` — shared L2 pool + full SHM L3 data file (simpler, more memory, extra copy)
- `shm_peer_l2` — shared L2 pool + tiny SHM index only (optimized; strict improvement)

Both reuse a common `ShmHostTensorAllocator` and named-SHM helpers added to `pool_host/common.py` and `storage/mmap/mmap_allocator.py`. Tests included: `test/registered/mem_cache/test_shared_l2_hicache.py` (CPU-only, `register_cpu_ci`), covering allocator wiring, slot partitioning, index CRUD, generation-counter stale-slot behavior, collision detection, auto-capacity, and a cross-process shared-L2 round-trip via subprocess.

The prototype hooks into:
- `HiRadixCache` — for `shm_name` derivation, `dp_rank/dp_size` forwarding to `MHATokenToKVPoolHost`
- `HostKVCache` (`pool_host/base.py`) — `clear()` partitions `free_slots` to `[slot_start, slot_start+local_size)`; `alloc()` fires registered callbacks; `slot_used` spans the full pool for cross-DP double-free detection
- `cache_controller` — `shm_peer_l2` added to the V1 interface allow-list

## The upstreaming question

We noticed [#40787](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40787) (merged 2026-09-22) removed `HiRadixCache` since [#35081](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/35081) migrated HiCache to `UnifiedRadixCache`. The prototype above was written against `HiRadixCache` and does **not** apply cleanly to current `main`.

Before we invest in porting to `UnifiedRadixCache`, we would like guidance from HiCache maintainers on a few design points:

1. **Integration point in UnifiedRadixCache** — where is the equivalent of `HiRadixCache.write_backup`, `_inc_hit_count`, and `prefetch_from_storage` in the unified architecture? Is there a documented extension surface for backends that need per-page alloc callbacks and slot-partitioned allocators?

2. **Shared L2 pool ownership** — is there interest in a first-class "shared host pool" concept inside `MHATokenToKVPoolHost` (dp_rank / dp_size / shm_name parameters)? The prototype adds them minimally, but a maintainer-blessed shape would be preferable.

3. **Scope split** — would you prefer:
   - (a) A single PR introducing the shared L2 pool infrastructure + one backend using it (either `shm_cross_dp` or `shm_peer_l2`), then a follow-up for the other, or
   - (b) The infrastructure alone first (no backend), then backends as separate PRs?

4. **Naming / positioning** — `shm_peer_l2` vs `shm_cross_dp` overlap significantly; would maintainers prefer we upstream only `shm_peer_l2` (the optimized variant) and drop `shm_cross_dp`, or keep both as complementary options?

5. **Alternative direction** — is there an existing or planned effort (Mooncake local mode, an internal HiCache broadcast, etc.) that already covers the same-node peer sharing use case and would make this redundant? We searched issues/PRs and did not find one but want to double-check.

Happy to open a draft PR against `main

items.title: [Bug] `/hicache/storage-backend/clear` returns "Hierarchical cache storage backend cleared." with a 400 when it did not clear anything
items.author: Yunzez
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Simply purely a reporting defect. 

Both the current endpoint and its deprecated alias build a **fixed** response body and vary only the status code, so the failure path returns a message that affirmatively claims the operation succeeded, and the reason it actually failed, which the handler is holding in `ret`, is discarded.

```python
# python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py:1072
@app.api_route("/hicache/storage-backend/clear", methods=["POST"])
@auth_level(AuthLevel.ADMIN_OPTIONAL)
async def clear_hicache_storage_backend():
    ret = await _global_state.tokenizer_manager.clear_hicache_storage()
    return Response(
        content="Hierarchical cache storage backend cleared.\n",     # <- always this
        status_code=200 if ret.success else HTTPStatus.BAD_REQUEST,
    )
```

The deprecated `/clear_hicache_storage_backend` (line ~1059) has the same shape, with the deprecation notice prepended to the same unconditional "cleared" sentence.

The body is `text/plain`, not JSON, so a client that reads the message, which is the natural thing to do for a plain-text endpoint, is told the cache was cleared when it was not.



### Reproduction

On a server with no hierarchical cache configured:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --port 30000
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30000/hicache/storage-backend/clear
```

```
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
...
Hierarchical cache storage backend cleared.
```

## Expected

The body should reflect the outcome and carry the reason the handler already has, e.g.

```
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
{"success": false, "message": "<whatever ret carries, e.g. no hierarchical cache storage backend is configured>"}
```

Status says the request failed; body says the work was done; neither says why.

items.title: [Bug] Hybrid attention models can fail to start with speculative decoding and --disable-radix-cache
items.author: rystewart-nvidia
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Adding `--disable-radix-cache` can make a hybrid model that works with speculative
decoding fail while setting up its caches. This happens when the target and draft
weights fit, but the default state-cache size exceeds the memory left for caches.
Hybrid models mix standard attention with layers such as Mamba or gated delta
networks, which also need memory to store their state.

I reproduced this on SGLang v0.5.21 with
`Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8` on a DGX Spark with one GB10.
It should also reproduce on any supported hardware with hybrid models that use
the same state-cache sizing code, if the target and draft weights fit but leave
too little memory for the saved state and temporary draft state of the default
48 requests.

The runs below show the failure when radix caching is disabled and the workaround
of setting a smaller request limit. Only the last run sets `--max-running-requests`:

| Mode | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Target model only, radix caching enabled | Server starts, health and model-list checks pass, and a test chat returns the correct answer. |
| Target model only, radix caching disabled | Server starts, health and model-list checks pass, and all eight test chats return the correct answers. |
| NEXTN, five steps, radix caching enabled | Server starts, health and model-list checks pass, and a test chat returns the correct answer. |
| Same NEXTN command, with only `--disable-radix-cache` added | Startup fails after both target and draft weights load. |
| Failing command plus `--max-running-requests 10` | Server starts, health and model-list checks pass, and all eight test chats return the correct answers. |

The target-only runs work with either radix setting. With speculative decoding
enabled and radix caching disabled, the server loads both the target and draft
weights successfully, then fails during cache sizing with the following error:

```text
ValueError: Loaded weights leave no GPU memory for the KV cache under --mem-fraction-static=0.82. Raise --mem-fraction-static above 0.686 (minimum viable = 1 - available/pre = 0.6853). If using speculative decoding, draft weights are now counted.
```

The suggested fix is confusing because the command already uses
`--mem-fraction-static 0.82`, above the suggested minimum of `0.686`. Both sets
of weights fit. The failure happens when SGLang then reserves too much memory
for the state cache, leaving none for the KV cache used by attention layers.

I would expect SGLang to choose a default state-cache size that fits the available
memory and leaves room for the KV cache, without needing an explicit request limit.

The cause appears to be in `KVCacheConfigurator._handle_max_mamba_cache`.
For these speculative runs, SGLang sets `--max-running-requests` to 48 when it
is omitted. With radix caching disabled, the cache planner treats that default
as a limit chosen by the user and sizes the state pool around it. For Qwen's
default FP32 state and six draft tokens, the saved state and temporary draft
state together need about 24.68 GiB.

Without speculative decoding, `--max-running-requests` stays unset, so the
planner fits the state cache to the available memory even with radix caching
disabled. There are also no draft weights or temporary draft states to reserve.
The target-only, radix-disabled run gets an effective limit of 114 requests;
that is calculated from the available memory, not a fixed default.

With speculative decoding and radix caching enabled, the planner fits the
state pool to the available memory. That Qwen run gets 41 state slots,
allows eight active requests, and serves successfully.

This has also been reproduced with other models that use the same state-cache
sizing code.

The GPU tests described here were run on a GB10.

Related reports:

- [#38846](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/38846) discusses showing
  the actual request limit after it is reduced to fit the state cache.
- [#24364](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/24364) reports running out
  of memory while allocating hybrid state on WSL2, including runs with explicit
  request limits. In this report, the failure occurs with the automatic limit.

### Reproduction

This reproduces on both v0.5.21 and main. I tested main at commit
`3a9cae27edec392ff8cc9f09d1164f557c653f42` with the dependencies required by that commit.

The following command reproduces the failure. I tested it on one GB10 using
the unmodified `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21` image:

```bash
sglang serve \
  --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8 \
  --revision c5f5f263bdd5cc134092897864e8905d8fe7b928 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.82 \
  --context-length 262144 \
  --speculative-algorithm NEXTN \
  --speculative-num-steps 5 \
  --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \
  --disable-radix-cache
```

Removing only `--disable-radix-cache` makes the command
work. Leave `--max-running-requests` unset in both cases. To try the workaround, keep
`--disable-radix-cache` and add `--max-running-requests 10`.

Removing the three `--speculative-*` options also makes the command work,
with radix caching still disabled and `--max-running-requests` still unset.

### Environment

The environment below is from the v0.5.21 image used for these tests.
I also reproduced the failure on main at the commit listed under Reproduction,
using PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130, sglang-kernel 0.4.9, Transformers 5.19.0, and
FlashInfer 0.7.1.

Recorded `check_env` output from v0.5.21:

```text
Python: 3.12.3 (main, Aug 31 2026

items.title: [Perf] HiCache Throughput Loss Analysis in Long-Context MLA Workloads
items.author: githlangub
items.body_excerpt:
---

## 1. Background

In our long-context MLA benchmarks, enabling HiCache L2 causes up to 44.6%–66.6% effective throughput loss at an 80% hit rate—revealing that hit-length-dependent overhead severely erodes the expected speedup of prefix caching.

Specifically, given a cache hit rate `r`, only `(1 - r)` of the tokens require new prefill computation (`extend` tokens). Ideally, if cache hits incurred zero overhead, the effective throughput of the uncached `extend` tokens would remain constant (equal to the 0%-hit baseline), and total throughput `ITPS` would scale by `1 / (1 - r)`. In practice, however, **the effective throughput of `extend` tokens degrades substantially as hit rate increases**—and this deviation widens sharply when L2 cache offloading is enabled.

This phenomenon indicates that cache hits introduce overhead proportional to the matched prefix length (e.g., attention computation over cached KV history, radix tree management, and L2<->L1 data transfers). To quantify this overhead, we evaluate cache performance internally using the following methodology:

We care deeply about actual compute efficiency under cache hits. Internally, we evaluate cache performance using the following methodology:


### 1.1. Defining Cache Performance via "Throughput Loss"
1. We measure pure Prefill throughput with Prefix Cache disabled (`--disable-radix-cache`) as the upper-bound throughput for computing newly extended (`extend`) tokens, denoted as `ITPS_baseline`.
2. With Prefix Cache enabled, the throughput of the `extend` tokens is `(1 - HitRate) * ITPS`, denoted as `ITPS_uncached` (written as `FTPS` in the result table below).
3. We define **Cache Loss** as:
   `Loss = 1 - (ITPS_uncached / ITPS_baseline)`

### 1.2. Why Define Loss This Way?
1. If cache hits were completely zero-cost, `ITPS_uncached` would equal `ITPS_baseline` under any hit rate (`Loss = 0%`).
2. Because cache hits incur non-trivial overhead in practice, `ITPS_uncached` drops below `ITPS_baseline`. We use the gap between the two as **Loss** to measure cache performance.

### 1.3. How We Measure Loss
1. We only benchmark **Prefill** instances. We use the fake bootstrap feature (`--disaggregation-transfer-backend fake`) to replace PD transfer with a no-op, and enable `--ep-dispatch-algorithm fake` to test the upper-bound Prefill throughput.
2. **0% Hit Rate Scenario:** Send 60K fixed-length requests directly to obtain `ITPS_baseline`.
3. **80% Hit Rate Scenario (taking L2 Cache as an example):**
   * **a.** First, send a batch of completely distinct 48K-token requests to populate the cache.
   * **b.** Clear the L1 Cache so that cached prefixes only reside in L2.
   * **c.** Append 12K new tokens to each of the previous requests (total 60K tokens, 80% hit rate) and run the benchmark to obtain `ITPS_uncached` (`FTPS`).

---

## 2. Benchmark Setup & Results

### 2.1. Environment Setup

| :--- | :--- |
| **CPU** | 2x Intel Xeon 6767P |
| **GPU** | 8x NVIDIA DGX B300 |
| **Docker Image** | `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.20-cu130` (`sha256:06e4f2ed21af...`) |
| **OS** | Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS |
| **CUDA** | Driver 580.126.09 / CUDA 13.0 |

**Server Launch Script (GLM-5.2-FP8, MLA + DSA, TP=8, CP=8, DeepEP):**

```bash

SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_BOOTSTRAP_TIMEOUT="90" \
SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_WAITING_TIMEOUT="90" \
SGLANG_LOG_MS="1" \
SGLANG_ENABLE_NVTX_SCHEDULER="1" \
SGLANG_ENABLE_NVTX_OPERATIONS="1" \
SGLANG_JIT_DEEPGEMM_PRECOMPILE="1" \
SGLANG_JIT_DEEPGEMM_FAST_WARMUP="1" \
SGLANG_DEEPEP_NUM_MAX_DISPATCH_TOKENS_PER_RANK="1024" \
SGLANG_TOOL_STRICT_LEVEL="1" \
nsys launch \
  --session-new="sglang-prefill" \
  --trace="cuda,nvtx,osrt" \
  --show-output="true" \
sglang serve \
  --host "0.0.0.0" \
  --port "30000" \
  --served-model-name "glm-5.2-fp8-offline" \
  --model-path "/path/to/glm-5.2-fp8-offline" \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --disaggregation-mode "prefill" \
  --disaggregation-transfer-backend "fake" \
  --disaggregation-bootstrap-port "8998" \
  --mem-fraction-static "0.835" \
  --max-total-tokens "2048000" \
  --max-prefill-tokens "196608" \

  --max-running-requests "256" \

  --dp-size "1" \
  --tp "8" \
  --attention-backend "dsa" \
  --enable-dp-attention \
  --enable-dp-lm-head \
  --disable-cuda-graph \
  --enable-prefill-cp \
  --attention-context-parallel-size "8" \
  --cp-strategy "interleave" \
  --moe-a2a-backend "deepep" \

items.title: [Bug] NGRAM speculative decoding corrupts radix-cached KV with the overlap scheduler when requests end on a stop token (0.5.22)
items.author: DiaaAj
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
With `speculative_algorithm="NGRAM"` and otherwise default settings, greedy (temperature 0) outputs of a
few concurrent requests are wrong. The radix cache, overlap scheduler and CUDA graphs are all on by
default; on 0.5.21, disabling any one of them made the outputs exact, and on 0.5.22 disabling the overlap
scheduler does. The trigger is requests that share prefixes, in a workload where requests end on a stop
token. Greedy speculative decoding should be lossless, so
this is silent corruption.

- **History:** in 0.5.21 it also showed with `ignore_eos` and `max_new_tokens` endings. A bisection of
  main pins its disappearance for those endings to #42720 ("Skip the decode for a request whose last
  token is already in flight"). #42720 skips the discarded trailing decode only for requests that finish
  by length.
- **0.5.22 still fails:** with stop-token endings, 3/192 requests are wrong, the same ones as on 0.5.21.
- **Same defect:** switching off only #42720's skip (one line) brings 0.5.22 back to 0.5.21's exact
  8/192 failure.
- **Probable mechanism:** the trailing NGRAM verify step that runs for a request whose last token is
  already in flight writes KV that ends up in, or over, radix-cached prefixes.
- **EOS endings:** they use the same finish check as stop tokens (`_check_token_based_finish`), so
  ordinary EOS-terminated traffic is most likely affected too. We did not measure EOS directly.

## How it was found
With probec: exact known-answer probe checkpoints, with synthetic weights whose correct outputs are known
exactly and are insensitive to floating-point reduction order, so any deviation is an engine error, not
numerics. The probe is a Qwen3ForCausalLM twin of Qwen3-0.6B (same shapes, synthetic weights).

## Environment
- **0.5.22:** pip, with torch 2.14.1, sglang-kernel 0.4.9 and flashinfer-python 0.7.1. RTX 3090 (SM86), driver 595.84.
- **0.5.21:** torch 2.13.0, sglang-kernel 0.4.7, flashinfer 0.6.18. It also reproduces on an H100 SXM.
- **Engine:** `sgl.Engine(model_path=probe, skip_tokenizer_init=True, dtype="bfloat16", random_seed=0,
  context_length=16512, mem_fraction_static=0.8, attention_backend="flashinfer",
  speculative_algorithm="NGRAM", speculative_num_draft_tokens=4)`.
- **Workload:** 192 requests submitted together. Prompts are 130–16,000 tokens, and about 30% share a long
  prefix with an earlier request. Up to 256 new tokens each, at temperature 0.
  - Stop-token endings: each request gets `stop_token_ids=[t]`, where t is its correct answer's token at a
    random position 8–240 that does not occur earlier; `ignore_eos=False`.
  - Length endings: `ignore_eos=True`.

## Results (deterministic; the run without speculation is exact in every row)
| Version | Endings | Variant | Wrong requests / 192 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5.22 | stop token | defaults | **3** (58, 109, 185) |
| 0.5.22 | stop token | `disable_overlap_schedule=True` | 0 |
| 0.5.22 | length | defaults | 0 |
| 0.5.22 | length | #42720's `self.enable_skip_finishing_decode = True` (in `event_loop_overlap`) changed to `False` | **8**, the same as 0.5.21 |
| 0.5.22 | length | `SGLANG_TEST_RETRACT=1` | 0 |
| 0.5.21 | stop token | defaults | 3, the same requests and verify counts as 0.5.22 |
| 0.5.21 | length | defaults | 8 (1,793 wrong tokens) |
| 0.5.21 | length | `attention_backend="triton"` | 8 |
| 0.5.21 | length | `speculative_num_draft_tokens=2` | 1 |
| 0.5.21 | length | `disable_radix_cache=True`, `disable_overlap_schedule=True`, `disable_cuda_graph=True`, `max_running_requests=1`, or no shared prefixes | 0 |
| 0.5.21 on an H100 | length | defaults | 6 (first failure identical to the RTX 3090's) |

### Which requests break
Each time, one request that owns a cached prefix goes wrong mid-generation, and the requests reusing its
cached prefix are wrong from their first reads:
- **Length endings:** request 15 (1,471-token prompt, no cache hit) diverges at generated token 151.
  Requests 48 and 100 reuse its cached prefix, 54 and 63 reuse 48's, and 67 reuses 63's; all are wrong
  from their first token. Request 116 (5,267 tokens) diverges at token 104, and 125 reuses its prefix.
- **Stop-token endings:** request 58 (3,408 tokens) diverges at token 137. Request 109 reuses 3,407 of its
  tokens and request 185 reuses 2,034 cached tokens of request 139's prompt; both are wrong from token 4.
  All three then miss their stop tokens.

### Bisection
- **Range:** main from bd78095 (v0.5.21 is a release-branch tag two cherry-picks past it) to d0a098b.
- **Method:** each commit was built from source with the Rust extensions.
- **Result:** the first clean commit for length endings is e14ef4b (#42720). Its parent 1fc6b89, a docs-only
  commit, fails the same 8 requests, and both were tested twice.
- **Dependencies ruled out:** the torch, sglang-kernel and FlashInfer upgrades all land at commits that
  still fail.

### Real model
On Qwen3-0.6B with real weights (greedy, 96 repetitive prompts), NGRAM and no-spec outputs diverge in
17/96 requests. But two no-spec runs, default and `--enable-deterministic-inference`, already diverge in
21/96. So real-model comparisons can't separate this bug from benign numerics; the probe's exact oracle
can.

## Related
- #23392 (shared-prefix load corrupts unrelated requests under NGRAM; involved cancellations; closed)
- #22819 (radix block-boundary corruption with deterministic inference; closed)
- #42720 (the change that hides it for length endings)

## Repro
```
git clone https://github.com/DiaaAj/probec && cd probec
pip install -e . "sglang[all]==0.5.22"
probec compile --like Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --no-scale-check -o twin
python tools/repro_sglang_ngram.py twin --finish stop
```
On 0.5.22 it prints "NGRAM vs no-spec: 3/192 requests differ; NGRAM vs exact oracle: 3 wrong". Without
`--finish stop` it prints 0/192 on 0.5.22 and 8/192 on 0.5.21.

[PR #26468](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/26468) moved vLLM config hashing toward an opt-out model so new compilation-relevant config fields are less likely to be accidentally omitted from torch.compile cache keys. 

This issue tracks the follow-ups and to-dos.

comments.body:
I can't reproduce this on stock v0.21.0, and after tracing the whole streaming path I don't think stock code can produce this exact signature. Writing up what I found.

**What the glyphs are**

`Ċ`, `åĹ¯`, `ï¼Į` are exactly what `tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens()` returns for those token ids (verified with a DeepSeek-R1 family tokenizer: 198 -> `Ċ`, 106287 -> `åĹ¯`, 3837 -> `ï¼Į`). So the reasoning stream is raw token strings that never went through the byte-level decode step.

**Why stock v0.21.0 shouldn't be able to emit that**

The streaming chain with `--reasoning-parser deepseek_r1` is:

1. The engine detokenizer produces `output.text` (already byte-decoded, incremental).
2. serving_chat sets `delta_text = output.text` and feeds it to the unified parser that `ParserManager.get_parser(reasoning_parser_name="deepseek_r1")` builds, which delegates to `DeepSeekR1ReasoningParser`.
3. That parser only slices `delta_text` around the `</think>` boundary. I audited every branch of `basic_parsers.py` and `deepseek_r1_reasoning_parser.py`: each return value is a substring of `delta_text`. There is no `convert_ids_to_tokens` anywhere in `vllm/entrypoints`, `vllm/parser`, or `vllm/reasoning` (the only hit is the unrelated `/tokenize` endpoint).

Your control experiments are the tell. Without the parser, the same `output.text` arrives as clean content, and non-streaming is clean too. So your detokenizer output is clean. The parser can only cut up what it receives; slicing clean text cannot turn one field back into raw token strings while the other stays clean. Something in your deployment is replacing the reasoning path with a token-string implementation between the detokenizer and the wire.

**Verification I ran**

In-process simulation of the exact serving chain (real tokenizer, CJK reasoning stream, token-at-a-time detokenization, then the same `_WrappedParser.parse_delta` the server uses):

- v0.21.0 tag + transformers 5.8.1 (your versions), fast detokenizer path: clean
- v0.21.0 tag + transformers 5.8.1, forced slow `detokenize_incrementally` path: clean
- current main + transformers 5.14.1, both paths: clean

One related landmine worth knowing about for this exact checkpoint: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B` declares `tokenizer_class: LlamaTokenizerFast` on the Hub while shipping a byte-level BPE `tokenizer.json`. items.title: [Performance]: Monolithic Triton top-k kernel falls back to full-vocab search on real logits (outlier gather misses)
items.author: abmfy
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

**Summary.** The top-k branch of `_topk_topp_kernel` (`vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py`) picks its gather pivot from a Gaussian fit to only the first 8192 logits of the row. On the MiMo-V2.6 logits we measured, that pivot is too high for 6-10% of rows at k=50-64 and for 43% of rows at k=200. The gather then returns `<= k` candidates, and the row falls back to a ternary search over the full vocabulary. On B300 (V=152576, top-k only, B=1), such rows take 256-473 us instead of 92-135 us. The grid has one program per row (for B up to the SM count), so the whole batch waits for the slowest row.

**How the top-k branch works today** (line numbers at [fa75d3456d](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa75d3456d60a5ffe923818c4b495295675b38e1/vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py)):

1. Zeroth pass ([L143-L171](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa75d3456d60a5ffe923818c4b495295675b38e1/vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py#L143-L171)) computes the mean and std of `offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)` only, i.e. token ids 0..8191 on CUDA. It sets `outlier_pivot = avg + std * sigma`, where `sigma` is `_PERCENTILE_TO_STD_TABLE[int(200 * k / V)]` lowered by 15% of its magnitude. For every k < V/200 (k <= 762 at V=152576), this is `avg + 2.19 * std`.
2. First pass ([L174-L197](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa75d3456d60a5ffe923818c4b495295675b38e1/vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py#L174-L197)) sweeps the full row once and gathers every logit above `outlier_pivot` into the per-program buffer.
3. If `num_outliers > k`, the ternary search runs over the buffer, usually a single 4096-entry tile per iteration. Otherwise ([L302-L383](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa75d3456d60a5ffe923818c4b495295675b38e1/vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py#L302-L383)) it runs over the full row: one full sweep per iteration, up to 18 iterations.
4. When top-p runs after top-k, a failed gather also forces one more full-row re-gather sweep ([L466-L510](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa75d3456d60a5ffe923818c4b495295675b38e1/vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py#L466-L510)).

**What happens on real logits.** We captured 1424 rows of MiMo-V2.6 decode logits (V=152576, bf16-valued, long-context code prompts) and emulated L143-L197 in PyTorch (same as `n_outliers` in the repro below):

| k | 20 | 50 | 64 | 200 | 500 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| rows whose gather fails | 0.07% | 6.4% | 9.7% | 43% | 86% |
| 16-row batches with >= 1 such row | 1.3% | 66% | 81% | 100% | ~100% |
| 64-row batches with >= 1 such row | 4.7% | 98.5% | 99.9% | 100% | ~100% |

Batch rates are over 4000 random batches drawn from the 1424 rows. The k=500 batch rates follow from the per-row rate.

Measured on B300 (CUDA graph, hot L2):
- B=1, top-k only, 24 real rows at k=50 and k=1000: rows that fall back take 256-473 us; rows whose gather succeeds take 92-135 us.
- B=1, monolithic kernel with top-p (p=0.95) after top-k: rows that fall back take another 76-126 us.
- 64 random real rows (4 / 7 / 24 of them fall back), top-k only: 383 / 426 / 426 us at k=50 / 64 / 200. Top-k+top-p: 555-557 us.
- Synthetic rows where every gather succeeds (repro below): 92-98 us top-k only, 115-166 us top-k+top-p.

**Two causes**, both visible in the MiMo rows:

1. **The first tile is not a random sample of the row.** Low ids carry systematically higher logits. The median tile mean drops from 3.2 in tile 0 to between -2 and -10 in the last seven tiles, and the argmax is in tile 0 for 74% of rows. The tile-0 mean sits above the row mean by a median of 4.7 logits on rows whose gather succeeds at k=50, and by 11.3 on rows that fail, so the pivot comes out too high. Taking the statistics from the whole row (or from a strided sample) lowers the emulated failure rate at k=200 / 500 from 43% / 86% to 12-13% / about 22%.
2. **The Gaussian z-score does not fit skewed rows.** `avg + 2.19 * std` assumes that 1.43% of entries lie above it. On the rows that fail at k=50, tile 0 is left-skewed (median skewness -0.81), its max is only 3.4 std above its mean, and only 0.35% of its entries lie above +2.19 std. On rows that succeed, these are 0.05, 4.8 std and 1.60%. Even with exact whole-row statistics, 4.8% / 6.3% of rows still fail at k=50 / 64.

**Ideas** (for discussion; not implemented):

- **Use an order statistic instead of `avg + z * std`.** Take a sample spread across the row and use its m-th largest value as the pivot. For example, with a strided sample of S entries, m = max(8, ceil(4 * k * S / V)).
  - In emulation on the same 1424 rows (S=8031), no row fails at any k we tried (20, 50, 64, 100, 200, 500, 1000).
  - The gathered set stays small (median 239 entries at k=64 and 790 at k=200, max 1110), so the buffer search still fits in one tile.
  - The margin matters: with 2 * k * S / V instead, 3.4% of rows still fail at k=64.
  - The m-th largest sample value could be found with a short in-register binary search, without extra global memory traffic. We have not implemented or timed this.
- **Make the fallback cheaper.** When `num_outliers <= k`, re-gather with a lower pivot instead of sweeping the full row on every ternary iteration. The per-program buffer already has room for V entries.
- **Measured sketch (not a fix): move the sample only.** We changed the top-k zeroth pass to `offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE) * NUM_TILES`. Results at B=64:
  - Sorted synthetic Zipf rows at k=200: 554 -> 100 us (top-k only) and 698 -> 129 us (top-k+top-p). This fixes the layout-only case.
  - "Two modes" rows: about 560-610 us on both, so the skewed case is not fixed.
  - Real 64-row batches still contain rows that fall back (k=64: 426 us on main, 428 us with the sketch).
  - Batches where no row falls back get 4-8 us slower (top-k only), presumably from the strided loads.
  - Top-k masks are identical to main's. Top-k+top-p masks differ from main's on 1-3 of 64 rows in some synthetic cases, including ca
