items.title: CPU-only lmcache server + CUDA vLLM worker: REGISTER_KV_CACHE fails with 'Device UUID not found' (examples/multi_process + docstring mismatch)
items.author: zhaotyer
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

When the `lmcache server` runs in a CPU-only container (no GPU visible → `StubCPUDevice`) and the vLLM worker has CUDA GPUs, the worker's `REGISTER_KV_CACHE` request fails at server side with:

```
RuntimeError: Device UUID f231cc14-0922-0ca9-5c57-efd8982e6c5e not found in the discovered devices. Please make sure the process can see all the accelerator devices
```

The `examples/multi_process/` k8s YAMLs describe exactly this topology (CPU-only DaemonSet + CUDA vLLM Deployment) but never set `lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode=engine_driven` on the client, so they appear to hit the same failure. Two related doc bugs make it hard to diagnose: the connector docstring describes `engine_driven` / `lmcache_driven` exactly opposite to what the factory code does.

## Reproduction

### Server (CPU-only container)

```bash
lmcache server \
    --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
    --l1-size-gb 20 --eviction-policy LRU --chunk-size 16
```

Startup log shows the server fell back to the CPU stub:

```
LMCache INFO:  torch_dev=StubCPUDevice(device_type=cpu), torch_device_type=cpu
...
LMCache INFO: Supported transfer mode: auto
LMCache INFO: LMCache ZMQ cache server is running on tcp://0.0.0.0:8000
```

### Client (vLLM with GPU, default `mp_transfer_mode=auto`)

```
vllm serve <model> --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheMPConnector", "kv_role":"kv_both", "kv_connector_extra_config": {"lmcache.mp.host": "tcp://<server>", "lmcache.mp.port": 8000}}'
```

### Error (server-side)

```
LMCache ERROR: Error handling request RequestType.REGISTER_KV_CACHE
...
  File ".../lmcache/v1/platform/cache_context.py", line 149, in _detect_device_type
    device_types = {w.to_tensor().device.type for w in kv_caches}
  File ".../lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py", line 145, in to_tensor
    device_index = self._get_device_index_from_uuid(self.device_uuid)
  File ".../lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py", line 79, in _get_device_index_from_uuid
    raise RuntimeError(
RuntimeError: Device UUID f231cc14-0922-0ca9-5c57-efd8982e6c5e not found in the discovered devices. Please make sure the process can see all the accelerator devices
```

## Root cause

1. Client-side default `mp_transfer_mode=auto` routes CUDA workers to `LMCacheDrivenTransferContext` (CUDA IPC path):
   ```python
   # lmcache/v1/multiprocess/transfer_context/worker_transfer.py:547-550
   # AUTO: dispatch by device type (CUDA -> handle path, else -> data path).
   if device_type == "cuda":
       return LMCacheDrivenTransferContext()
   return EngineDrivenTransferContext()
   ```
2. Worker wraps its KV tensors with `CudaIPCWrapper`, embedding the worker GPU's `device_uuid` (`lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py:135-136`).
3. On `REGISTER_KV_CACHE`, the server calls `create_cache_context()` → `_detect_device_type()` → `w.to_tensor()` → `_get_device_index_from_uuid()` (`cache_context.py:149`, `custom_types.py:145`).
4. `_discover_devices()` returns immediately when `torch_dev.is_available()` is `False` (`custom_types.py:56-57`), and `StubCPUDevice.is_available()` is always `False` (`lmcache/v1/platform/cpu/stub_cpu_device.py:214-220`). So `_discovered_device_mapping` stays empty and any UUID lookup raises.

Server-side `--supported-transfer-mode auto` loads both transfer modules (`lmcache/v1/multiprocess/server.py:198-200`), so it cannot rescue this — the failure happens earlier, in `REGISTER_KV_CACHE` routing on the client side.

## Expected behavior

One of:
- The `examples/multi_process/` YAMLs set `lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode=engine_driven` on the vLLM side (the documented escape hatch for this topology — see `docs/source/getting_started/quickstart.rst:452-455`).
- OR the server detects "CUDA worker IPC arrived but I have no GPU" and returns a clear error message at `REGISTER_KV_CACHE` time pointing the user at `engine_driven`, rather than a generic "Device UUID not found".
- OR `auto` on a CUDA worker falls back to `engine_driven` when the server is CPU-only (harder — needs a capability handshake).

## Environment

- LMCache: v0.5.0 (g389b9cfc)
- Server container: CPU-only (`torch_dev=StubCPUDevice`)
- vLLM worker: has CUDA GPUs
- Topology: same as `examples/multi_process/` (CPU-only lmcache DaemonSet + CUDA vLLM Deployment, co-located via `/dev/shm` hostPath)

## Workaround

Set `lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode=engine_driven` in `kv_connector_extra_config` on the vLLM side, or `export LMCACHE_MP_TRANSFER_MODE=engine_driven` in the vLLM container. This routes the worker through `EngineDrivenTransferContext` (worker-side gather/scatter copy), which does not require the server to open CUDA IPC handles.

## Doc bugs found while debugging

### 1. `examples/multi_process/` does not set `engine_driven`

`examples/multi_process/vllm-deployment.yaml` (line 39) only sets `lmcache.mp.host` / `lmcache.mp.port`, relying on the default `auto`. With a CPU-only server (`lmcache-daemonset.yaml` has no `nvidia.com/gpu` resource request) and a CUDA worker, this should hit the error above. Either the example needs `engine_driven` in `kv_connector_extra_config`, or the deployment doc (`docs/source/mp/deployment.rst`) should call out the topology assumption.

### 2. Connector docstring swaps `engine_driven` / `lmcache_driven` descriptions

`lmcache/integration/vllm/lmcache_mp_connector_0201.py:476-480`:

```python
- lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode: routing mode for the worker -> server
  transfer context. One of ``auto`` (default; CUDA -> engine_driven,
  others -> lmcache_driven), ``engine_driven`` (force IPC / SHM
  zero-copy), ``lmcache_driven`` (force worker-side gather/scatter
  copy). Overrides the ``LMCACHE_MP_TRANSFER_MODE`` env var when set.
```

This says `engine_driven` = "force IPC / SHM zero-copy" and `lmcache_driven` = "force worker-side gather/scatter copy". The factory code says the opposite:

```python
# lmcache/v1/multiprocess/transfer_context/worker_transfer.py:543-550
if resolved_mode is MPTransferMode.LMCACHE_DRIVEN:
    return _build_lmca

items.title: [Bug][MP] "full" prefetch drops columns that are partly in L1 when an L1 reservation fails
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

With `fetching_policy="full"`, if any L1 staging reservation fails, the prefetch controller trims the request to whole columns (Step 3.5 in `_transition_to_load_phase`, added in #5434). The trim only looks at `l1_reserved_keys`, so rows of a column that are already in L1 (`l1_locked_keys`) don't count. A column that is partly in L1 and partly loaded from L2 is never seen as whole, gets released, and turns into a miss.

`_finish_request` does count L1 rows when it picks the whole columns, so the same column is a hit when every reservation succeeds and a miss when some other column's reservation fails.

This affects the "full" callers: the blend sparse leg, warm prefetch and P2P. It shows up under L1 pressure, which is also when some rows of a chunk tend to get evicted.

**To Reproduce**

Three rows, two columns. Column 0 is in L1 for rows 0 and 2 and only in L2 for row 1. Column 1 is only in L2. L1 has room for three staging buffers, so the last row's reservation fails.

```python
rows = [make_group([make_object_key(i, gid=g) for i in range(2)], gid=g) for g in range(3)]
write_keys_to_l1(l1_manager, [rows[0].keys[0], rows[2].keys[0]], layout)
store_keys_in_l2(adapter, [rows[1].keys[0]] + [r.keys[1] for r in rows], layout)
# L1Manager sized for 5 objects
```

(helpers from `tests/v1/distributed/test_prefetch_controller.py`)

| case | hits |
| --- | --- |
| `full`, L1 big enough | `[[0, 1], [0, 1], [0, 1]]` |
| `full`, one reservation fails | `[[], [], []]` |
| `prefix`, one reservation fails | `[[0], [0], [0]]` |

**Expected behavior**

Column 0 is complete (two rows in L1, one loaded from L2), so the second case should return `[[0], [0], [0]]`.

**Additional context**

Seen on `dev` at 6448b447. Adding `l1_locked_keys` to the cells the trim checks fixes it.

items.title: [Bug][MP] A DAX L2 adapter can map a device L1 already uses when set at startup
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`StorageManager` doesn't check DAX device ownership when it builds the L2 adapters at startup. `add_l2_adapter` does, and `storage_manager.md` says duplicate device ownership is rejected, so this looks like a gap in the constructor.

The easiest way to hit it is a DEVDAX `--l1-manager` plus a DAX L2 adapter on the same device. With the old `--l1-devdax-path` flag that config was fine, because the matching device got moved out of L2 and used as L1 overflow. Since #5461 that only happens for the legacy single-L1 config. With the new JSON config both sides keep the device and both map it from offset 0, so L1 and L2 quietly overwrite each other's KV.

Two DAX L2 adapters on the same device get through too, and so does the same device under a different path (a hard link or symlink).

**To Reproduce**

```bash
--l1-manager '{"type":"DRAM","tag":"_default","size_gb":1}' \
--l1-manager '{"type":"DEVDAX","tag":"dax","size_gb":1,"path":"/dev/dax0.0"}' \
--l2-adapter '{"type":"dax","slot_bytes":4096,"devices":[{"device_path":"/dev/dax0.0","max_dax_size_gb":1}]}'
```

It starts without complaint. `_device_owner_names("/dev/dax0.0")` returns `['L1[dax]', 'dax']`, and bytes written through the L2 mapping show up in the L1 arena. Adding the same adapter with `add_l2_adapter` after startup fails with "already mapped", as it should.

**Expected behavior**

Startup should reject a DAX device that L1 or an earlier L2 adapter already maps, the same way `add_l2_adapter` does.

**Additional context**

Seen on `dev` at b9a5ce02. I reproduced it with regular files standing in for the device.

items.title: Storage manager: buffer references leak when a storage backend raises during a batched store
items.author: russfellows
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

When a storage backend raises synchronously while a batched store is being dispatched, the storage manager never releases its own references on the batch's buffers. This happens even when the backend that raised cleaned up everything it took itself.

## When it happens

A batched store is dispatched to one or more storage backends, and any backend raises during submission.

## Observed

Checked against current `dev`, using the manager's own batched-store logic with a backend that rejects the submission before taking any reference. After the exception, the manager-owned buffer reference was still 1 where 0 was expected. The release of the manager's references runs only after every backend submission has succeeded, so any exception skips all of them.

## Impact

Every failed batched store leaks the manager's references on all buffers in the batch. Under repeated backend errors this steadily drains the allocator.

## Expected

The manager should release the references it owns whether or not a backend raises, for example with try/finally around the dispatch. The exception should still propagate to the caller as it does today.

## Done when

- A backend that raises during batched submission leaves the manager's buffers at their expected reference counts.
- The success path is unchanged.
- Both are covered by a test.

Related: #5912 covers a reference leak and a stuck pending key inside the remote backend's own submission path. These are separate ownership boundaries, and fixing one does not fix the other.

items.title: RadixView: a live radix-tree view of SGLang KV-cache events
items.author: ClaudeLiang
items.body_excerpt:
Hey everyone,

We are working on an agent that already has active users. While reviewing its cache behavior, aggregate metrics such as hit rate were not enough—we wanted to see which prompts and tool definitions were actually shared, and where sessions started to branch.

That led us to build RadixView. It subscribes to SGLang's ZMQ KV-event stream and reconstructs a continuously updated radix-tree view of prefix sharing and eviction.

![RadixView showing shared prompts and session branches](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ClaudeLiang/RadixView/main/docs/images/page.png)

On our own traffic, the tree exposed branches much earlier than we expected. Following those branches back to their text helped us find several problems in the agent and tool design that were reducing prefix reuse.

Shared prefixes stay on the same path, sessions branch where their text differs, and the view updates as store and eviction events arrive. You can open any node to inspect its decoded text or search across the observed cache blocks.

RadixView is only a viewer. It does not proxy requests or read the cache in-process, and it can run on a different machine from the GPU server.

Install:

`pip install radixview`

<sub>Note: The synthetic demo is not included in the pip package. Clone the repository and run `python -m examples.demo` to try it without a GPU or model.</sub>

Source and setup instructions:

https://github.com/ClaudeLiang/RadixView

Feedback is welcome, especially from people working on agent or other prefix-heavy workloads.

items.title: [new feature]: Add lmcache-layerwise plugin
items.author: zxue2
items.body_excerpt:
Layer-wise retrieve lets the forward pass start as soon as the first layers' KV has arrived, instead of waiting for whole chunks. It was proposed in #4816 (draft, closed) and prototyped in #5689(draft). In #4816 we agreed that no layer-wise concept or code goes into the LMCache repository and the plugin repo should reuse the LMCache core existing path as much as possible.

This issue tracks the replacement plan:

- Layer-wise ships as an **external package** (working name `lmcache-layerwise-ext`) in its own repository under the LMCache org (proposed: `LMCache/LMCache-Layerwise`). The server side is loaded with `--server-module` (#5159); the vLLM side with `kv_connector_module_path`.
- The package keeps **only its layer-wise pieces** of native code: the pointer-array upload and the layer-major offset rule. The kernel, launcher, plan driver, staging copies, phase timing and plan types are **reused from core** through generic seams. Core gets no layer-wise native code.
- Core gets only **small, generic extension points**. None of them mentions layer-wise, and each is usable by any plugin that customizes the LMCache-driven transfer path.
- No core PR changes default behaviour.

## Core changes

| Core PR | What it adds |
|---|---|
| **Extension hooks** | `LMCacheDrivenTransferModule._create_cache_context`; `BaseCacheContext.transfer_object_group` (the copy seam); `GPUCacheContext._make_temp_buffer` (the staging layout); worker `_create_transfer_context`; connector `_worker_adapter_cls`. `_create_cache_context` also receives the registering `instance_id` (see "Model depths" below). A contract test pins the hook signatures. |
| **Extension calls** | `server_module_stream`: a server-streaming twin of `server_module_call`, built on the streaming RPCs from #5307. `server_module_affinity_call`: a unary call served on the caller's affinity worker. Both on ZMQ and gRPC, with no change to the core dispatch files. |
| **Native extension API** | Pure move of the device helpers, the kernel, its launcher and the plan driver from `mp_mem_kernels.cu` into a header, with two template parameters on the kernel and launcher: the **object-pointer source** (default: the by-value `MemoryObj4`) and the **object-side offset** (default: today's 2LTD formula). Core's own path uses the defaults, so its code does not change. Ship the public headers in the wheel with `lmcache.get_include()`. Export `lmcache_memcpy_async` and the phase-timing recorder from `cuda_ops` as a versioned C function table (PyCapsule), so out-of-tree launches use core's copies and show up in core's phase timing. In Python, `build_staging_copies` takes an optional byte range (`offset`, `nbytes`) and advances the pointer and the host offset together, for callers that stage part of an object. |
| **Transfer-module replacement** (RFC) | Reject duplicate RPC handlers at startup (today silently last-wins). Let one `--server-module` spec provide a `transfer_module_factory` that builds the `LMCacheDrivenTransferModule` subclass in place of the built-in one. |

Not needed in core any more (both were part of #5689):

- **Layer-major layout support** (`PageBufferShapeDesc.kv_interleaved` / `layer_stride_elems`, the L2TD offset branch, the pointer-array launch). These serve only the layer-major object layout, so they become the plugin's own offset policy and launch. The header split itself stays in core, as part of the native extension API. See Open question 1.
- **`EngineGroupInfo.model_depths`** (+ `common.proto` field 7 + `common_pb2.pyi`). The plugin can send depths itself. See Open question 2.

## What moves out of core

Everything layer-wise in #5689 moves into the plugin:

- Server: `modules/lmcache_driven_transfer_layerwise.py`, `modules/layer_major_plan.py`, `devices/cuda/cache_context_layerwise.py`, the layer-wise accessors added to `platform/base/cache_context.py`, `platform/base/event_pool.py`, the `--layerwise-batch` option and the module selection in `server.py` / `config.py`.
- Transport: `transport/base_layerwise.py`, `request_handler_layerwise.py`, `zmq_impl/{mq_streaming,client_layerwise,server_layerwise}.py`. They are replaced by the generic extension calls; `mq_streaming.py` duplicates what #5307 now provides.
- Worker / vLLM: `transfer_context/worker_transfer_layerwise.py`, `futures_layerwise.py`, `vllm_multi_process_adapter_layerwise.py`, `lmcache_mp_connector_layerwise.py`, and the layer-name → depth resolution in `kv_cache_groups.py` / `kv_layer_groups.py`.
- Native: `csrc/cuda/mp_mem_kernels_layerwise.{cu,cuh}` (kernel, pointer-array upload, launcher), the layer-major offset formula, the new `PageBufferShapeDesc` fields, their pybind exports, the torch fallback in `torch_ops/mp_mem_kernels.py` and the `build_profiles/cuda.py` source entry.

## Plugin design

**Server.** One `--server-module` entry:

```json
{"module_path": "lmcache_layerwise_ext.server",
 "transfer_module_factory": "build_lmcache_driven_transfer",
 "config": {"batch_layers": 8}}
```

The factory returns an `LMCacheDrivenTransferModule` subclass. Its `_create_cache_context` returns a cache context that overrides `transfer_object_group` and `_make_temp_buffer` together, so objects are staged in model-depth order and copied by the plugin's own kernels.

**Frames.** Each worker instance opens one long-lived `server_module_stream` at registration. Each retrieve is a `server_module_affinity_call` that pushes one frame per batch of layers into that instance's stream. The worker records the frame's CUDA event, and vLLM's `wait_for_layer_load` waits on it (vLLM side: vllm#56762).

**Model depths.** The staging buffer is built eagerly when the server handles `register_kv_cache`, so the layout must be known by then. The plugin's worker transfer context computes depths from the layer names in `kv_caches`. In its `register()` override it first sends `server_module_call("set_model_depths", instance_id, depths)` and waits for the reply, then calls the core `register()`. The server

items.title: [MP][ARC] Clarify ghost readmission semantics across L1 and L2
items.author: Mengmj
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

`discussion`, `mp_mode`.

**Summary**

ARC currently classifies a key returning from B1/B2 differently depending on the listener path: L1 reservation followed by admission leaves it in T1, while L2 storage completion puts it in T2. I would like to clarify whether this difference is intentional and add coverage for the agreed behavior. I am interested in taking ownership of the follow-up PR.

**Details**

Inspected revision: `dev` at `d66c61d9d08a78e6fd56d0d43eafb3e6fc52279f`.

For a key that is already in B1 or B2:

| Path | Policy callbacks | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| L1 write | `on_keys_reserved` followed by `on_keys_created` | T1 |
| L2 store | `on_keys_created` directly | T2 |

In the [L1 reservation handler](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/d66c61d9d08a78e6fd56d0d43eafb3e6fc52279f/lmcache/v1/distributed/eviction_policy/arc.py#L121-L154), ARC applies ghost feedback, removes the ghost entry, inserts the key into T1, and marks admission as pending. The subsequent creation notification consumes that pending marker without changing its classification.

The [L2 listener](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/d66c61d9d08a78e6fd56d0d43eafb3e6fc52279f/lmcache/v1/distributed/eviction.py#L233-L234) calls `on_keys_created` directly. Its [B1/B2 branches](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/d66c61d9d08a78e6fd56d0d43eafb3e6fc52279f/lmcache/v1/distributed/eviction_policy/arc.py#L98-L113) apply ghost feedback and insert the key into T2.

The reservation docstring describes keeping reservations in T1, but does not separately explain ghost readmission or the difference between L1 and L2.

**Steps / Reproduction**

At the policy/listener level, start each case from equivalent ghost state:

1. Create a key, optionally touch it to move it into T2, then select and confirm its eviction to produce a B1 or B2 entry.
2. For L1, call `on_l1_keys_reserved_write([key])`, then `on_l1_keys_write_finished([key])`.
3. In a separate equivalent case, call `on_l2_keys_stored([key], [size])`.
4. Compare `get_debug_state()`: the L1 case puts the key in T1; the L2 case puts it in T2.

This report is based on source and existing-test inspection. I have not run a full MP server or measured a performance regression for this issue.

**Expected Outcome / Goal**

Could maintainers clarify whether ghost readmission should intentionally differ between L1 and L2? If the paths should agree, which classification should they use?

I would like to take this on and prepare a focused PR once the intended behavior is confirmed. I can:

- Align the callbacks if the difference is unintended, or document the rationale if it is intentional.
- Add public-interface tests covering B1/B2 readmission through both listener paths, including repeated L1 reservations.
- Preserve coverage that cold writes stay in T1 and explicit accesses promote them to T2.

**Actual Outcome / Test Coverage**

The [L1 lifecycle test](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/d66c61d9d08a78e6fd56d0d43eafb3e6fc52279f/tests/v1/distributed/test_arc_eviction_policy.py#L203-L220) verifies cold admission and eviction into B1, but stops before readmission. The [existing ghost tests](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/d66c61d9d08a78e6fd56d0d43eafb3e6fc52279f/tests/v1/distributed/test_arc_eviction_policy.py#L108-L143) exercise `on_keys_created` directly and expect T2 behavior. I could not find a test covering ghost readmission through L1's reserve-then-admit sequence.

**Additional Context**

Related: #5347 and #5348 addressed duplicate notifications promoting cold L1 writes to T2; this question concerns keys returning from ghost history after eviction.

vLLM's CPU-offload ARC [explicitly documents insertion into T1 even for ghost entries](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/494663940b9b44f667c4f61c8c2407ba8e725ceb/vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/policies/arc.py#L30-L44). I am therefore asking about LMCache's intended contract before proposing a change based on classical ARC semantics.

items.title: [Roadmap] LMCache Roadmap 2026 Q4
items.author: ApostaC
items.body_excerpt:
# LMCache 2026 Q4 Roadmap

The main topic for Q4 is to make LMCache faster, safer, more stable, and more pluggable.


## 1. In-process mode deprecation and deletion

We don't list concrete tasks for the in-process mode deprecation because it will need a lot of ad hoc changes.
At a high level, we will separate in-process mode code to `lmcache/in_process` folder first, and then drop them together. (See #5831 and #5839 )



## 2. Security enhancements

As LMCache is continuously evolving, we noticed that some vulnerabilities have been introduced. Therefore, we will push more security enhancements into LMCache in Q4. 

- [ ] Deprecating the use of pickle
- [ ] Authentication to all user-facing HTTP APIs

## 3. Core improvements

In Q4, we are still going to keep making LMCache faster and better, with the following optimizations:

- [ ] Unfull-chunk persistence
- [ ] LMCache-native PD disaggregation
- [ ] Multi-tier L1 memory support (e.g., CXL, Remote RDMA memory server, and NIXL)
- [ ] GDS L2 storage adapters support
- [ ] General performance optimization (data copies, L2 adapter performance, and metadata management overheads).
- [ ] Centralized config source and support dynamic configuration



## 4. LMCache plugins and pluggable interfaces

We really appreciate the innovations in the community. To make sure that all the cool ideas can easily land in LMCache, we are going to introduce the LMCache plugin system. Once this is landed, everyone can add plugins and modify LMCache based on customized use cases and algorithms. 

- [ ] Standardize plugin interface and SDK
- [ ] Move out of tree of some L2 Adapters
- [ ] Move out of tree of some device backends
- [ ] Support out-of-tree GDS backend
- [ ] Extension module for layerwise transfers
- [ ] (Experimental) Token dropping outside inference engine
- [ ] (Experimental) Token dropping in inference engine

## 5. SGLang integration

For a long while, LMCache has had the most native integration with vLLM. In Q4, we want to improve and stabilize the SGLang integration with their latest interfaces. 

- [ ] Support SGLang external linker interface
- [ ] Improve SGLang integration tests
- [ ] Performance optimization with SGLang
- [ ] Stability enhancement


## 5. CI/CD and release pipeline

- [ ] Release `lmcache-client` package for a more lightweight integration with different inference engines (no extra dependencies is introduced)
- [ ] Performance dashboard and auto regression testing
- [ ] Better PyPI release with different hardware vendors and platforms

------

### For contributors

Since most of the items on the roadmap are pretty big topics, if you would like to participate in some of them, please directly reach out to the core team in the LMCache Slack workspace with the design docs so that we can discuss them. 
We generally don't accept big PRs without a discussed and converged design.

items.title: Eval bug: Qwen3.8-27B (qwen35 hybrid) llama-server crashes silently at ~520K prefill tokens with YaRN rope-scale 4 (just under 2x yarn-orig-ctx), b10434 CUDA
items.author: asaffulks
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

llama-server, build b10434 (commit range including #26623), Windows x64 CUDA 13.3 release binaries (`llama-b10434-bin-win-cuda-13.3-x64.zip`). Also reproduced on b10430.

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

1× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition (96GB, compute 12.0), driver-side CUDA 13.x, Windows 11.

### Models

`unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF` → `Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q8_K_XL.gguf` (arch `qwen35`, hybrid Gated DeltaNet + full-attention interval layers, native ctx 262144).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

With YaRN rope scaling ×4 to extend Qwen3.8-27B toward 1M context, **llama-server dies silently (no assert, no error output, process exits) at ~520K tokens of prefill** — suspiciously just under 2× the native training context (2×262144 = 524288).

Command:

```
llama-server.exe -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q8_K_XL.gguf -ngl 999 -c 1048576 --parallel 1 -fa on ^
  --rope-scaling yarn --rope-scale 4 --yarn-orig-ctx 262144 ^
  --override-kv qwen35.context_length=int:1048576 ^
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --port 8095
```

Then POST a single ~925K-token chat completion. Prefill proceeds normally (~900 t/s at that depth) until:

```
slot print_timing: id  0 | task 0 | prompt processing, n_tokens = 518144, progress = 0.56, t = 574.77 s / 901.48 tokens per second
slot print_timing: id  0 | task 0 | prompt processing, n_tokens = 520192, progress = 0.56, t = 578.98 s / 898.46 tokens per second
```

…then the process is gone. No further output on stdout/stderr. GPU memory is freed. VRAM was not exhausted (~69GB used of 96GB at time of death).

Data points that bracket it:

1. **Works:** native window, no YaRN, 224K-token prompt → completes, correct retrieval (6/6 planted needles), fa on, q8 KV. (Note: prompts >~90–100K crashed the same way on b10430 and were **fixed by b10434** — presumably #26623 `ggml: recurrent state rollback for ggml_ssm_scan`. This report is about a second, deeper boundary that remains.)
2. **Works:** YaRN ×2 (`--rope-scale 2 --override-kv qwen35.context_length=int:524288`, `-c 524288`), 444K-token prompt → completes, 6/6 retrieval.
3. **Crashes:** YaRN ×4 as above, dies at n_tokens ≈ 520192 (just under 524288 = 2× `yarn-orig-ctx`).
4. KV type doesn't matter (q8_0 and f16 both crash at the same place pre-b10434 for the first cliff; the ×4 crash above was with q8_0).

The "just under 2× orig ctx" position plus the silent death (reads like a segfault / device-side fault rather than a caught error) suggests a position/buffer boundary in the hybrid-attention or DeltaNet state path when positions exceed 2× the original training context under YaRN.

Happy to run diagnostic builds/flags if useful.

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

```
(see prefill tail above — process exits silently after n_tokens = 520192 with no error output)
```

items.title: Vulkan: deterministic GPU hang + SIGABRT on Intel Gen9.5 iGPU (UHD 630) with q8_0 KV cache — vk::Error escapes as std::terminate
items.author: NaustudentX18
items.body_excerpt:
**Title:** Vulkan: deterministic GPU hang + SIGABRT on Intel Gen9.5 iGPU (UHD 630) with q8_0 KV cache — vk::Error escapes as std::terminate

**Name and Version**

```
version: 0.4.0-dev (build 10809, commit 5266f24da7)
built with GNU 16.2.1 for Linux x86_64
```

(Arch Linux package `llama-cpp 0.4.0-1`.)

**Operating systems**

Arch Linux, kernel 7.2.5; Mesa 26.2.2 (ANV); kernel driver i915.

**GGML backends**

Vulkan (libggml-vulkan).

**Hardware**

CPU: Intel i5-9500T. GPU: Intel UHD Graphics 630 (CoffeeLake-S GT2, Gen9.5), Mesa ANV.

**Problem description & steps to reproduce**

```
llama-server --model Qwen3.8-2B-Q4_K_M.gguf --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --jinja \
  --ctx-size 16384 --threads 6 --parallel 1 --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking": false}'
```

Under sustained decode/prefill, three consecutive instances all failed within minutes:

1. Kernel logs repeated `Fence expiration time out i915-0000:00:02.0:llama-server[PID]` (compute batches exceeding the fence watchdog), then:
   ```
   i915 0000:00:02.0: [drm] Resetting rcs0 for preemption time out
   i915 0000:00:02.0: [drm] llama-server[PID] context reset due to GPU hang
   i915 0000:00:02.0: [drm] GPU HANG: ecode 9:1:8ed1fff2, in llama-server [PID]
   ```
2. One second later llama-server dies with SIGABRT. Reproduced 2/2 with the identical hang ecode (`9:1:8ed1fff2`), i.e. the same dispatch hangs deterministically. A third instance showed only fence expirations and was restarted before hanging.

**Stack trace** (systemd-coredump, symbolized via debuginfod for libc/libstdc++; ggml frames have no published debug symbols — both cores identical):

```
#0  __pthread_kill_implementation
#2  __GI_raise / __GI_abort
#3  __gnu_cxx::__verbose_terminate_handler
#4  ?? (libggml-base.so.0 + 0x2f1cb)          <- unresolved, in the rethrow path
#5  __cxxabiv1::__terminate
#6  std::terminate
#7  __cxxabiv1::__cxa_rethrow
#8  vk_queue_handle_unsynchronized::submit(vk::ArrayProxy<vk::SubmitInfo const>, vk::Fence)  (libggml-vulkan.so + 0x3372f6)
#9  ?? (libggml-vulkan.so + 0x2c52ef)
#10 ?? (libggml-vulkan.so + 0x2c53b0)
#11 ggml_backend_sched_synchronize (libggml-base.so.0)
#12 llama_context::synchronize() (libllama.so.0)
#13 ?? (libllama-server-impl.so + 0x13475e)
#14 server_queue::start_loop(long) (libllama-server-impl.so)
```

**Two distinct aspects**

1. The hang itself: the Vulkan backend (likely the q8_0 KV dequant/attention kernels on Gen9.5) wedges rcs0 hard enough that preemption times out and i915 resets the context. Related reports of the same failure class: #19327 (Arrow Lake iGPU), #17334 (Iris Xe), and the AMD gfx90c GPU-job-timeout device-lost reports.
2. The abort path: after the driver reports the reset, a `vk::Error` (device-lost class) thrown from `submit` is caught and rethrown inside the ggml Vulkan path and escapes through `ggml_backend_sched_synchronize` with no handler, reaching `std::terminate` → SIGABRT. Regardless of whether the trigger is a driver-level hang, a Vulkan error crossing the C API boundary should surface as a GGML log/status instead of terminating the host process.

**Workaround**

`--device none` (CPU-only) is stable on this host; no GPU hang, no abort. The fence expirations show the iGPU offered no speed benefit for this workload anyway.

items.title: [RFC]: Hot Standby Mode for Master Service Metadata High Availability
items.author: Libotry
items.body_excerpt: ## Introduction To address the issue where all metadata is lost after a master service failure and recovery, this solution proposes a **hot-standby synchronization mechanism** and a **hybrid approach** combining hot standby with snapshots, ensuring rapid data recovery following a master service failure. ## Motivation The current HA (High Availability) mode only supports rapid restart of the master service after a failure but cannot guarantee fast data recovery. The pain points of the current HA mode are as follows: | Issue | Impact | Severity | | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | | **Complete loss of metadata after Leader failure** | All KV cache location information is lost and must be rebuilt | 🔴 Critical | | **Follower lacks data pre-warming** | After successful election, the new Leader must start serving from scratch | 🟠 Medium | | **Long recovery time** | Relies on clients to re-register; may take several minutes to tens of minutes | 🟠 Medium | | **Service unavailability window** | Requests cannot be processed during Leader failover | 🟡 Low | ## Goals: 1. **Near-zero RPO**: Minimize the data loss window 2. **Fast failover**: Achieve second-level RTO (Recovery Time Objective) 3. **Data consistency guarantee**: Ensure correct synchronization between primary and standby 4. **Verifiability**: Include mechanisms to validate data integrity 5. **Low performance overhead**: Avoid impacting normal business operations ## Proposal ### 1. Core Design Approach **Use etcd as an intermediate reliability component to implement OpLog primary-standby synchronization**: - **OpLog Mechanism**: Primary Master records all state change operations to OpLog - **etcd Storage**: OpLog is written to etcd, leveraging etcd's strong consistency and persistence capabilities - **Watch Mechanism**: Standby Master receives OpLog in real-time through etcd Watch mechanism - **Ordering Guarantee**: Guarantee operation order through global sequence_id and key-level key_sequence_id ### 2. Architecture Design #### (1) Overall Architecture The overall architecture diagram shows the interaction relationships between Primary Master, etcd Cluster, and Standby Master: **Architecture Description**: - **Primary Master**: Handles client requests, records OpLog and writes to etcd - **etcd Cluster**: Acts as intermediate storage, providing strong consistency and Watch mechanism - **Standby Master**: Receives OpLog in real-time by watching etcd and applies to local metadata store #### (2) Data Flow Diagram The data flow diagram shows the complete flow from Client request to Standby synchronization: **Flow Description**: a. Client sends `PutEnd` request to Primary Master b. Primary Master records operation through `OpLogManager`, generating sequence_id c. `EtcdOpLogStore` writes OpLog to etcd d. etcd notifies Standby Master through Watch mechanism e. `OpLogWatcher` receives events and passes to `OpLogApplier` f. `OpLogApplier` checks order and applies to Standby's metadata store #### (3) Failover Sequence The failover sequence diagram shows the complete process from Primary failure to Standby promotion to Primary: **Flow Description**: a. **Normal Operation**: Primary maintains Lease, Standby continuously synchronizes OpLog through Watch b. **Primary Failure**: Primary's Lease expires, etcd notifies Standby c. **Standby Promotion**: Stop Standby service, initialize Lease, clean expired metadata, start leader election ### 3. Core Component Design #### (1) OpLogManager (Primary Side) **Responsibilities**: - Record all state change operations (PUT_END, PUT_REVOKE, REMOVE) - Generate global sequence_id and key-level key_sequence_id - Maintain memory buffer (for fast queries) **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogManager { uint64_t Append(OpType type, const std::string& key, const std::string& payload = ""); std::vector GetEntriesSince(uint64_t since_seq_id, size_t limit = 1000) const; uint64_t GetLastSequenceId() const; }; ``` #### (2) EtcdOpLogStore (Primary Side) **Responsibilities**: - Write OpLog to etcd - Update latest sequence_id - Record snapshot corresponding sequence_id - Clean up old OpLog **etcd Key Design**: - OpLog Entry: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/{sequence_id}` - Latest Sequence ID: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/latest` - Snapshot Sequence ID: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/snapshot/{snapshot_id}/sequence_id` #### (3) OpLogWatcher (Standby Side) **Responsibilities**: - Watch etcd OpLog changes - Read historical OpLog (for initial synchronization) - Process Watch events and pass to OpLogApplier **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogWatcher { void Start(); void Stop(); bool ReadOpLogSince(uint64_t start_seq_id, std::vector& entries); }; ``` #### (4) OpLogApplier (Standby Side) **Responsibilities**: - Apply OpLog Entry to local metadata store - Check global and key-level order - Handle sequence number discontinuities and out-of-order cases - Periodically clean up key_sequence_map_ (memory optimization) **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogApplier { bool ApplyOpLogEntry(const OpLogEntry& entry); bool CheckSequenceOrder(const OpLogEntry& entry); void CleanupStaleKey

comments.body: ### 1. Problem & Assumptions #### 1.1 Problem After a `Delete` (or eviction) on the primary master: - The primary frees a replica’s memory (returns buffer to allocator’s free list). - The `Delete` event is **not** replicated to the standby master. - The primary then crashes; the standby is promoted to new master. - The new master still believes that this replica exists, and returns its address to clients. - That buffer may already have been **reused by another object**, or may still contain **logically deleted data**. We must **never** return data that belongs to some other key/object/tenant due to buffer reuse, even if we allow some metadata loss. #### 1.2 Accepted Semantic Constraints We explicitly accept the following semantics: - **Metadata / delete operations may be lost across failover**: - A delete acknowledged by the old master may be “rolled back” after failover. - That is acceptable because the KV cache can be recomputed. - **Hard safety requirement**: - It is strictly forbidden to read data that **belongs to another key/object/tenant** as if it were the requested key. - In other words: buffer reuse must not cause **cross-key contamination**. Under these constraints, it is acceptable that: - A key that was “deleted” on the old master may reappear after failover (logical delete rolled back). - But it is **not** acceptable to read someone else’s data due to buffer reuse. --- ### 2. Idea We upgrade each replica from a “raw pointer” into a **versioned capability**: - In-memory layout of a replica buffer becomes: - The master generates a **64-bit version** for each successful `Put` of a key. - This `version` is stored: - In `ObjectMetadata` on the master. - In the `ReplicaDescriptor` returned to clients. - In the first 8 bytes of the actual buffer in the KV store. - On **Get**, the client always verifies: - Read the first 8 bytes of the buffer. - Compare with the expected version from `ReplicaDescriptor`. - If versions match → buffer still belongs to this key/epoch → safe to read payload. - If versions differ → buffer was reused by someone else → mark this replica invalid, do not use it. Thus, even if the physical address is reused for a different object, the client will detect it and reject the replica. --- ### 3. Data Model Changes #### 3.1 Version Type ```cpp using Version = uint64_t; ``` Version can be constructed as: - High bits: timestamp (e.g., microseconds since epoch). - Low bits: per-node monotonic sequence ID. Requirements: - For a single master process, each successful `Put` for a given key gets a **unique, monotonically increasing** version. - Version collisions are practically impossible within a process lifetime. #### 3.2 Replica Descriptor Extension Extend `Replica::Descriptor` (or equivalent) to carry version information: On `PutStart`, the master generates `version`, stores it in metadata, and includes it in each replica descriptor. --- ### 4. Write Path (Put) Design #### 4.1 Master: PutStart 1. Client invokes `Put(key, slices, config)`. 2. `MasterService::PutStart(key, slice_lengths, config)`: - Validates input. - Allocates replicas as it does today (segments, buffers, etc.). - Generates a new `Version version = MakeVersion()` for this key. - Stores `version` in `ObjectMetadata` for this key. - Fills `ReplicaDescriptor.version = version` for each allocated replica. - Returns the list of descriptors to the client. All replicas of the same key for this `Put` share the same version. #### 4.2 Client: Writing to Store We enhance `TransferWrite` to enforce the following **write order** per replica: 1. Write **8-byte version header** at `buffer_address`. 2. Write **payload** at `buffer_address + 8` for length `size`. comments.author: ykwd
comments.body:
Thanks for sharing the proposal. Unfortunately, this approach is not safe and does not actually guarantee the hard safety requirement you described, for two reasons:

First, RDMA reads and writes do not provide ordering and atomicity guarantees, which breaks the version-only validation scheme. In your design, correctness relies on the assumption that the first 8 bytes (the version) and the payload are written and observed atomically and in order. That assumption does not hold.

Second, the allocator does not guarantee alignment between successive allocations, which makes the embedded-version assumption invalid. Your scheme assumes that when a buffer is freed and later reused, the next allocation will reuse the same start address and layout, so that the version stored in the first 8 bytes corresponds exactly to the logical object boundary.

items.title: [RFC] Add CI Infrastructure for the SGLang MLU Backend
items.author: chenxb002
items.body_excerpt: ## 1. Motivation The SGLang MLU backend needs a CI mechanism to keep its functionality continuously usable. Changes to MLU-specific code, as well as changes to shared SGLang components used by the MLU backend, can introduce regressions. Relevant pull requests therefore need to trigger MLU tests so that functional correctness is validated before the changes are merged. The MLU hardware and its supporting execution environment are accessible only from Cambricon's internal network and cannot be attached directly to GitHub-hosted runners. This RFC proposes a CI architecture that connects the public SGLang GitHub workflows to the internal Jenkins and MLU cluster while preserving the internal network boundary. The resulting CI lane makes MLU validation visible to the SGLang community and helps maintain the backend's functional availability as the project evolves. ## 2. Summary This RFC proposes community-visible PR and Nightly CI infrastructure for the Cambricon MLU backend in SGLang. The integration connects GitHub Actions to an internally operated Jenkins and MLU cluster without exposing Jenkins or internal infrastructure to the public Internet. The corresponding implementation is tracked in [sgl-project/sglang#26898](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/26898). The proposed CI infrastructure has these properties: - Pull requests run only after the existing `run-ci` gate and the `run-ci-mlu` opt-in label pass. - During the initial observation period, the PR lane is a non-required check and does not block pull requests from being merged. - Test failures fail the GitHub job and remain visible as code-related failures. - Infrastructure failures and MLU resource queue timeouts are reported with a warning annotation, while the GitHub job concludes successfully because contributors cannot repair the private CI infrastructure. - Nightly and trusted manual/default-branch runs remain strict. - Results distinguish test failures, infrastructure failures, and timeouts. - Jenkins logs and structured result metadata are uploaded as GitHub artifacts when the GitHub job has started and reaches the upload step. - PR and Nightly jobs use separate labels in a dedicated runner group and run on one-job ephemeral self-hosted GitHub Actions runners on the VPS. - The PR workflow runs with `pull_request_target`, so its YAML and reusable gate come from the reviewed base branch. - The self-hosted runner never checks out or executes client code from the pull request. The proposal is intended to begin with an observation period. It does not ask SGLang maintainers to make the MLU lane required at initial rollout. ## 3. Proposed Architecture The architecture consists of four modules across three trust zones: public GitHub, the VPS, and the trusted internal network containing the controller, Jenkins, and MLU resources. ### 3.1 GitHub Community The SGLang-side integration includes PR and Nightly workflows, the existing `run-ci` gate and the `run-ci-mlu` opt-in label, and a reliability reporting workflow. GitHub Actions dispatches eligible MLU CI jobs and displays their status, annotations, logs, and artifacts to contributors. ### 3.2 VPS The VPS hosts: - a GitHub Actions runner provisioner; - one PR runner slot and one Nightly runner slot; - a task submission bridge and task/status store; - a trusted, preinstalled `sglang-mlu-ci` client. `sglang-mlu-ci` is an operator-installed command-line client invoked by the GitHub workflow. It submits validated task metadata, polls for progress, and publishes the final result without fetching or executing pull request code. ### 3.3 Internal Controller The internal controller retrieves pending tasks from the VPS, coordinates their execution in Jenkins, and returns status and logs. It also provides a runner broker that issues restricted JIT configurations for ephemeral runners. GitHub Actions has no direct access to Jenkins or MLU resources, and communication with internal services is initiated from within Cambricon's network. ### 3.4 Jenkins / MLU Cluster Jenkins receives the repository URL, immutable commit SHA, task ID, and trigger type. It checks out the exact SHA in an isolated MLU pod, prepares the MLU backend dependencies, and runs the registered PR or Nightly test suites. Execution status and logs are returned through the internal controller. ## 4. GitHub Workflow Policy ### 4.1 Trigger Policy The workflow uses `pull_request_target` so the workflow definition and reusable gate are loaded from the reviewed base branch. It never checks out the pull request or executes repository code on the self-hosted runner. The untrusted repository URL and immutable head SHA are passed only as data to the trusted client, and PR code is executed later in the isolated Jenkins MLU pod. The MLU PR job is entered only when: 1. the PR targets `main`; 2. the PR has the `run-ci-mlu` label, an explicit opt-in for the MLU lane; 3. the PR is not a draft; 4. the PR has the `run-ci` label; 5. the existing PR gate and rate-limit policy pass. The label check runs at gate time with a live fetch of the pull request's current labels, so a rerun after adding `run-ci-mlu` picks up the new label set; the workflow also re-fires when `run-ci` or `run-ci-mlu` is added. > [!IMPORTANT] > SGLang maintainers must review and merge the MLU workflow files into the default branch before the PR and Nightly lanes can run. GitHub loads `pull_request_target`, `schedule`, and `workflow_dispatch` definitions from the default branch. This bootstrap also prevents a pull request from replacing the commands executed on the self-hosted runner. ### 4.2 Lane Isolation The Organization runner group is named `mlu-ci` and is restricted to the SGLang repository. items.author: merrymercy
items.body_excerpt:
# SGLang Roadmap — 2026 Q4

*Contributions and feedback are welcome*. [Join Slack](https://slack.sglang.ai).

## Focus

- **Usability**: Simple launch commands for a single engine and large-scale deployments, easy to use cookbook and docker images for common models.
- **Agent-native development**: Auto review bot, Auto PR shepherd bot, modularization, full Rust rewrite.
- **Extreme performance**: Megakernel, low-latency kernel, and communication-computation overlap kernels, zero-overhead from CPU.
- **Feature compatibility**: Make all advanced features compatible with each other, such as hicache, speculative decoding, pd disaggregation.
- **Multi-hardware support**: Support flexible multi-hardware abstraction and out-of-tree development.

## Usability

- **Deployment and cookbook**  
  Slack: [#dev](https://sgl-fru7574.slack.com/archives/C07PEP77X6F)

items.title: [Bug] A silent DP rank leaves /flush_cache waiting without a deadline and blocks subsequent flush calls
items.author: Adeshen
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] Searched related issues and PRs; related work and limitations are noted below.
- [ ] Reproduced on the latest version. The service observations are from the pinned v0.5.17 image; current main was inspected as source only.
- [x] Included reproduction steps and the available environment information.
- [x] Report written in English.

### Describe the bug

In the pinned v0.5.17 deployment with DP=2, suspending one scheduler rank leaves `/flush_cache` without an HTTP response until the client times out. `FanOutCommunicator.queueing_call` waits for all expected replies while holding its queueing lock, without an internal wait deadline. Subsequent calls on the **same communicator** cannot dispatch until the active call finishes.

This is a worker-failure/deadline limitation of an existing all-rank collection contract. Related PRs already discuss the trade-off; this report adds a real-service reproduction and the observed health behavior, rather than claiming the mechanism was previously unknown.

### Reproduction

Use a dedicated test service in the image below with two NPUs:

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /models/qwen3-0.6b --served-model-name qwen3 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30130 \
  --device npu --attention-backend ascend --trust-remote-code \
  --context-length 4096 --mem-fraction-static 0.4 \
  --dp-size 2 --tp-size 1
```

1. After readiness, confirm `POST /flush_cache`, `GET /health` and a short generation request succeed.
2. In that test container's PID namespace, identify one scheduler rank with `ps -eo pid,stat,args`. Suspend that specific scheduler PID with `kill -STOP <scheduler-pid>`; keep the other rank and HTTP/tokenizer process running.
3. Run:

```bash
curl -sS --max-time 45 -X POST \
  -w '\nHTTP_CODE=%{http_code} TIME=%{time_total}\n' \
  http://127.0.0.1:30130/flush_cache
```

4. Resume the same PID with `kill -CONT <scheduler-pid>`, and check that a new flush succeeds. For the recovery observation, another flush was started while the rank was still stopped and allowed to remain pending across SIGCONT.

### Recorded results

These are measured real-service observations, not a model of the scheduler:

| Observation | Result |
|---|---|
| Baseline flush | HTTP 200, 0.006699 s |
| One rank stopped, flush | curl exit 28, HTTP code 000, 45.000981 s |
| Health probes during the quiet stopped-rank period | 503 / 200 / 503 |
| Four health probes with paced generation traffic during the same stopped-rank window | all 200 |
| Eight paced generation requests in that window | six HTTP 200 in under 0.1 s; two client timeouts |
| Flush started while stopped and spanning recovery | HTTP 200, total request time 41.384738 s |
| New flush after recovery | HTTP 200, 0.004737 s |

The 41.38 s figure includes waiting before SIGCONT; it is **not** a post-resume recovery latency. A second real-service variant stopped both ranks and also observed a 45 s flush timeout, with health checks returning 503.

A separate CPU integration test of the real communicator and control path supplied only one reply for fan-out 2: the first call stayed pending and a second caller did not dispatch (`dispatch_count=1`). Its transport/rank replies were declared fixtures. This is the direct measurement of same-communicator head-of-line blocking; no claim is made that every other control endpoint shares that lock.

### Code path and expected behavior

The relevant structure is:

```python
async with self._queueing_lock:
    # dispatch and initialize the per-call collector
    ...
    await self._result_event.wait()
    ...
```

The event is set when the expected reply count is reached. With a missing rank, the wait itself has no deadline. **Changing the count comparison from == to >= would not fix missing replies**; fewer than the expected count satisfies neither comparison.

On 2026-10-21, main at [`573b5716f5b4`](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/573b5716f5b47c77a5fb5f2c24ae9b0e596dc3d1/python/sglang/srt/managers/communicator.py#L41-L57) still has the bare event wait inside the lock. This is source inspection, not a fresh full-service reproduction.

Expected behavior to discuss: an explicit control-call deadline and a defined worker-failure/recovery outcome, rather than relying solely on the HTTP client's timeout. Any solution needs to preserve response ownership: simply releasing the lock after timeout can allow late replies to be consumed by a later call. Partial results must not be reported as successful all-rank completion.

### Related work and limits

- #30022 explicitly acknowledged that a scheduler which never replies can keep a control slot held.
- #30606 addresses FIFO serialization.
- #42694 addresses cancellation and late-reply ownership; its description explicitly states that it does not add worker-failure recovery or a drain timeout.
- #39562 concerns aggregating flush results; #40119 and #36152 concern exposing/forwarding the scheduler-side flush timeout. These are distinct from bounding the tokenizer-side reply wait when a rank cannot respond.

SIGSTOP is deliberate fault injection. No production frequency, irreversible deadlock, or permanent whole-service failure is claimed: resuming the rank allowed progress. Other control operations, real client-disconnect cancellation, and gateway behavior were not validated by this real-service run. Healthy responses occurred in the observed traffic window, not under all possible loads.

### Environment

Historical real-service runs were performed on 2026-10-11 with:
- SGLang v0.5.17, recorded commit `29481685462732237d80d86076d6563e1f658102`.
- Image: `quay.io/ascend/sglang:v0.5.17-cann9.0.0-910b`.
- Resolved image digest: `sha256:35852210819ac0d388bce69c24960189c0412a300dc3add13234b549ba00abda`.
- Ascend 910B3; Python 3.11.15; model: Qwen3-0.6B, mounted at `/models/qwen3-0.6b`.
- Full `python3 -m sglang.check_env` output was not captured in the historical archive; the information above is from the recorded i

items.title: [RFC][DSpark] Online latency correction for confidence-scheduled verification
items.author: SuperGoodGame
items.body_excerpt:
SGLang already has confidence-scheduled DSpark verification: estimated prefix survival probabilities and a profiled cost model determine the verification budget. This RFC proposes a focused extension: use completed serving observations to correct subsequent latency predictions when runtime conditions differ from profiling conditions.

I can take ownership of an initial opt-in implementation, add regression tests, and report controlled multi-GPU serving measurements. Implementation and benchmarking are starting locally; no speedup is claimed yet.

### Existing work and the gap

At inspected main [573b5716](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/commit/573b5716f5b47c77a5fb5f2c24ae9b0e596dc3d1):
- [The planner](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/573b5716f5b47c77a5fb5f2c24ae9b0e596dc3d1/python/sglang/srt/speculative/dspark_components/dspark_planner.py#L855) already evaluates expected output against an SPS or additive cost table.
- [Step observability](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/573b5716f5b47c77a5fb5f2c24ae9b0e596dc3d1/python/sglang/srt/speculative/dspark_components/dspark_observability.py#L335) records execution geometry and predicted/observed latency, and reports prediction error.
- I could not find feedback from these observations into the cost estimate used for subsequent budget decisions. Please point me to existing or in-flight work if I missed it.

The approach is inspired by [DeepInfer's runtime latency correction](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/8b16149741a4935e1dec8cea27853f273b374c5b/csrc/engine/mtp_varlen.hpp#L139): retain a profiled baseline and estimate a bounded correction from recent measurements. The attribution is intentional; the proposed contribution is adapting and validating this mechanism in SGLang.

### Proposed initial scope

Start with DSpark compact verification and a valid existing cost table:

```text
predicted_latency =
    profiled_latency(request_count, verification_budget)
    + correction_from_completed_runtime_observations
```

- Reuse the existing planner, cost lookup, and throughput objective; no main-model, draft-model, or confidence-head retraining.
- Consume completed, matched timing observations and actual executed graph/eager geometry. Use bounded robust statistics and fall back to the original estimate while observations are insufficient or invalid.
- Match the timing boundary of the profiled baseline. Draft, target verify, sampling, CPU iteration time, and full-step GPU time must not be added interchangeably or double-counted.
- Preserve causal confidence budgeting, target verification, and TP/DP rank-consistent layout/graph-tier selection. Reuse asynchronous timing where possible and account for any added synchronization overhead.
- Keep the feature opt-in and default behavior unchanged. Scope calibration state to the active execution configuration; do not change checkpoint formats.

This does not replace initial cost profiling or attempt to learn a missing acceptance-probability head.

### Validation plan

Compare static and corrected cost predictions using the same checkpoint, baseline table, request stream, and sampling settings. Exercise changing context lengths and concurrency, plus low-load and steady-load controls. Report prediction error, output throughput, TTFT/TPOT, verification-budget distribution, correctness checks, and instrumentation overhead. Any improvement claim will be backed by measurements and its tested hardware/topology.

CPU tests should cover cold start, observation eligibility, bounded history, invalid measurements, and a synthetic latency shift that changes the predicted best budget. Distributed/runtime tests should verify that updates cannot cause ranks to choose incompatible graph tiers.

### Related work

- #30261: merged DSpark confidence-scheduled verification.
- #35413: deriving an initial cost table during CUDA Graph capture; related bootstrap work, rather than runtime correction.
- #28045: cost-guided adaptive speculative steps; related policy work with a different integration path.
- #44866: online acceptance-probability estimation; addresses the probability side, not latency prediction.
- #30344: earlier roadmap mentioning online/adaptive cost modeling, later automatically closed for inactivity.

Is this runtime cost-feedback scope already owned by an existing effort? If useful, are there preferred timing and planner integration points maintainers would like the prototype to use?

items.title: [RFC]: Limit the use of envvars in vLLM
items.author: zhuohan123
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

vLLM's envvars are on the edge of getting out of control. There are many envvars should instead be configs. Like the attention backend, all2all kernel backend, and even there is a flag to control KV cache layout. envvars are evil because:

1. It is equivalent of using global variables everywhere in the code, which is a bad programming practice.
2. envvars have no advanced structure like, hierarchy, typechecks, etc. 

In summary, I think envvars are the kind of thing that is very easy to add so people tend to add envvars as the shortest path to implement their feature, but this can quickly becomes unmanageable and makes the project very hard to use. 

### Proposed Change.

I think we should:

1. Spend some effort on reviewing the current envvars and move many of them to configs.
2. Have very strict bar on what can be an envvar and question every new envvars in vllm.

items.title: [Docs] Document NIXL KV connector metrics aggregation semantics
items.author: NickLucche
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The NIXL KV connector logs transfer metrics periodically:

```
KV Transfer metrics: Num successful transfers=4, Avg xfer time (ms)=1.381, P90 xfer time (ms)=2.601, Avg post time (ms)=0.672, P90 post time (ms)=0.801, Avg MB per transfer=2.25, Throughput (MB/s)=1629.549, Avg number of descriptors=72.0
```

Currently there is no documentation explaining what these metrics represent, especially in the context of **multi-rank (TP > 1) deployments**. This has already caused confusion among users.

## Current behavior

All metrics are **aggregated across all TP ranks** before summary stats are computed:

1. Each TP rank independently records per-transfer telemetry (`transfer_duration`, `post_duration`, `bytes_transferred`, `num_descriptors`) via `NixlKVConnectorStats.record_transfer()` in [`stats.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py).
2. Stats from all ranks are concatenated via `aggregate()` (`list.extend()`).
3. `reduce()` computes averages, percentiles, and throughput over the **combined** pool of observations from all ranks.

This means:
- **"Num successful transfers"** is the total count across all ranks, not per-rank.
- **"Avg MB per transfer"** is the average over all individual rank-level transfers, not the total bytes moved for a single KV cache transfer operation.
- **"Throughput (MB/s)"** is `total_MB_all_ranks / total_time_all_ranks` — effectively an average per-rank throughput, not the aggregate system throughput.
- **Percentiles (P90)** are computed over the combined distribution of all ranks' transfer times.

This is unintuitive because users may expect metrics to reflect per-engine totals or aggregate system throughput.

## What needs to be documented

1. **Docstrings in `stats.py`**: Add clear documentation to `NixlKVConnectorStats` explaining that stats are aggregated across all TP ranks and what each metric represents in that context.
2. **Inline comments in `reduce()`**: Clarify the semantics of throughput and averages — that they are per-rank averages over the combined observation pool.
3. **Docstrings in `metrics.py`**: Document the `observe()` → `aggregate()` → `reduce()` → `log()` pipeline and the fact that stats arrive pre-aggregated across workers.
4. **(Optional) Docs page**: Add a section to the disaggregated serving documentation explaining how to interpret the KV Transfer metrics log line.

## Relevant files

- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py` — `NixlKVConnectorStats` (recording, aggregation, reduction)
- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/metrics.py` — `KVConnectorLogging` (observe/log pipeline), `KVConnectorStats` (base class)

## Context

See related discussion: metrics are aggregated across ranks rather than reported per-rank or per-engine. This is a deliberate design choice (fire-and-forget from workers), but it needs to be clearly documented so users can correctly interpret the numbers.

items.title: [Bug]: [ROCm] Qwen4Exp (AMD path): PLE n-gram IDs read a stale query_start_loc tail during PIECEWISE CUDA-graph replay
items.author: Eliovp
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- vLLM: ROCm build based on 0.29; `vllm/models/qwen4_exp/amd/model_state.py` sha1 81e31496 (identical to main e126687a9a); `ple_layer.py` path checked on main (e2414ec1db).
- GPUs: 2x AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201), ROCm 10.
- Model: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (quantized), MTP speculative decoding, CUDA graphs FULL_AND_PIECEWISE.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary**
- On the AMD backend, the PLE n-gram ID generation for Qwen4Exp (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) runs inside the PIECEWISE CUDA-graph pieces.
  - It binary-searches `query_start_loc` over `num_reqs` requests.
  - It reads `ngram_context[:num_reqs]`.
- PIECEWISE graphs are dispatched on the padded token count only, and were captured with dummy `num_reqs = min(num_tokens, max_num_seqs)` (`v1/worker/gpu/cudagraph_utils.py`, `create_forward_fn`). A replay with fewer requests therefore still reads `ple_query_start_loc[0:R_cap + 1]` and `ngram_context[0:R_cap]`.
- `Qwen4ExpModelState.prepare_inputs` only refreshes `ple_query_start_loc[:num_reqs_padded + 1]`, and for PIECEWISE, `num_reqs_padded == num_reqs`. The remaining entries keep values from earlier steps.
- When that stale tail is not monotonic, or is below the step's token count, real tokens are assigned to a stale request row and get wrong n-gram IDs. The output depends on the server's history. Example: after the V2 `warmup_kernels` sequence the buffer holds `[0, 1, 2, 12, 16, ..., 32]`, so an 8-token single-request step sees `[0, 8, 2, 12, ...]` and tokens 2..7 map to row 2.
- Affected steps: non-uniform batches of ≤ max capture size tokens, for example:
  - short prompts;
  - short final prefill chunks;
  - the small final step of the mamba-aligned prefix-caching split;
  - small mixed prefill and decode batches.
- FULL decode graphs are not affected, because they are captured with `num_reqs == num_reqs_padded`, which is exactly the refreshed range.

**Code (main)**
- `vllm/models/qwen4_exp/amd/model_state.py`: `prepare_inputs` copies `input_batch.query_start_loc[: num_reqs_padded + 1]`, and `_prepare_ngram_context` fills only `[:num_reqs_padded]`.
- `vllm/models/qwen4_exp/amd/ple_layer.py`: `qwen4_exp_amd_ple_ngram_ids` (#60021) launches the binary search with `num_reqs = query_start_loc.numel() - 1`. It is not a splitting op, so it is captured inside the pieces with the capture-time request count.
- By contrast, the NVIDIA path keeps request-count-dependent ID generation outside PIECEWISE graphs on purpose (splitting op `vllm::qwen4_exp_compute_ple_ngram_ids`).

**Suggested fix (minimal)**
- In `Qwen4ExpModelState.prepare_inputs`, after the `[:num_reqs_padded + 1]` copy, write `ple_query_start_loc[num_reqs_padded + 1:] = input_batch.num_tokens`. This is the same non-decreasing padding the runner applies to its own `query_start_loc`.
- In `_prepare_ngram_context`, fill every `ngram_context` row with EOS.
- This keeps the model kwarg shapes, adds at most one tiny fill per step, and leaves eager and FULL steps bitwise unchanged.
- Alternative: register the AMD n-gram ID op as a splitting op, as the NVIDIA path does.

**Evidence**
- CPU model of the stock methods: the V2 capture order and warmup sequence, PIECEWISE/FULL/eager read ranges, and n-gram IDs compared to an eager reference. Stock gave 94 real-token ID mismatches over 46 probe steps (tails, short prompts, final chunks), and also after a burst of concurrent requests; with the fix, 0.
- On 2x Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201), ROCm build with this exact `model_state.py` (byte-identical to main), tensor-parallel 1 and 2:
  - Prefix caching off: 10 probes (prompts of 3-32 tokens and short final chunks) gave different first tokens or logprobs before vs after one 8-way concurrent burst on a fresh server: **0/10 consistent**. With the fix: **10/10 consistent**. Long prompts and single-request decode were bitwise unchanged by the fix.
  - Prefix caching on (`--mamba-cache-mode align`, whose aligned split creates small final steps): cold-request results changed after a concurrent burst, **0/10 consistent**; with the fix **10/10**.
  - Throughput and TTFT were unchanged within run-to-run noise.

### Before submitting a new issue...

items.title: [Bug]: MoE LoRA accepts incompatible round-robin expert placement with EP
items.author: gc-fu
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

Reproduced on upstream main at `c2861f7f120d508dcb1be046d9fc659c93062508`

The distributed startup check used FP16, eager execution, TP2 with EP enabled and `all2all_backend="allgather_reducescatter"`. The metadata reproducer below does not download a model or adapter.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Fused MoE LoRA accepts an effective `round_robin` expert placement with EP even though its adapter loading assumes contiguous expert ownership.

For four global experts and EP size two:

| EP rank | Experts owned by round-robin routing | Experts selected by contiguous LoRA loading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0, 2 | 0, 1 |
| 1 | 1, 3 | 2, 3 |

The ownership sets disagree. A MoE adapter can therefore be loaded for experts different from those owned by routing, while initialization reports no compatibility error.

The [per-expert checkpoint filter](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c2861f7f120d508dcb1be046d9fc659c93062508/vllm/lora/lora_model.py#L40) and [fused adapter slicing](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c2861f7f120d508dcb1be046d9fc659c93062508/vllm/lora/model_manager.py#L971) use `ep_rank * local_num_experts`. The [LoRA EP compatibility check](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/c2861f7f120d508dcb1be046d9fc659c93062508/vllm/lora/layers/fused_moe.py#L234) checks the communication backend and sequence parallelism, but does not validate the resolved placement.

#### Minimal reproducer

Run this in a vLLM development environment. It uses the real placement resolver and checkpoint-key filter, then exercises the LoRA compatibility check without allocating model weights.

```python
from dataclasses import replace
from types import SimpleNamespace

import torch

from vllm.lora.layers.fused_moe import FusedMoEWithLoRA
from vllm.lora.lora_model import MoEEPLoadSpec, _is_remote_expert_key
from vllm.model_executor.layers.fused_moe.config import FusedMoEParallelConfig
from vllm.model_executor.layers.fused_moe.expert_map_manager import ExpertMapManager

parallel = replace(
    FusedMoEParallelConfig.make_no_parallel(), use_ep=True, ep_size=2
)
manager = ExpertMapManager(
    max_num_batched_tokens=16,
    top_k=2,
    global_num_experts=4,
    num_redundant_experts=0,
    num_expert_group=2,
    moe_parallel_config=parallel,
    placement_strategy="round_robin",
    enable_eplb=False,
)
spec = MoEEPLoadSpec(ep_rank=0, local_num_experts=2, global_num_experts=4)
routed = (manager.expert_map >= 0).nonzero().flatten().tolist()
loaded = [
    e for e in range(4)
    if not _is_remote_expert_key(f"model.layers.0.mlp.experts.{e}.gate_proj", spec)
]
assert manager.placement_strategy == "round_robin"
assert routed == [0, 2] and loaded == [0, 1]
print("Routing ownership:", routed)
print("LoRA load-time ownership:", loaded)

layer = FusedMoEWithLoRA.__new__(FusedMoEWithLoRA)
torch.nn.Module.__init__(layer)
layer.moe_config = SimpleNamespace(moe_parallel_config=parallel)
layer.base_layer = SimpleNamespace(expert_placement_strategy=manager.placement_strategy)
try:
    layer._ep_check()
except ValueError as exc:
    assert "requires linear expert placement" in str(exc)
    print("Rejected incompatible placement:", exc)
else:
    raise AssertionError("BUG: incompatible round-robin EP placement was accepted")
```

On the unmodified revision above, this prints:

```text
Routing ownership: [0, 2]
LoRA load-time ownership: [0, 1]
AssertionError: BUG: incompatible round-robin EP placement was accepted
```

#### Expected behavior

Until MoE LoRA loading supports non-contiguous ownership, reject a non-linear **resolved** placement with a clear error before allocating the adapter buffers. A request for round-robin that actually falls back to linear must remain valid, as must linear placement and configurations without EP.

#### Validation and related fix

Proposed fix: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62797

The reproducer fails on the unmodified revision and passes with that PR, reporting the explicit placement error. A two-worker randomly initialized DeepSeek-V2 fixture with two expert groups also starts with actual round-robin placement before the fix; both workers reject it after the fix. These checks establish the ownership mismatch and missing validation; they do not quantify trained-model accuracy loss.

### Duplicate search

Searched existing issues for LoRA expert placement, round-robin, `expert_placement_strategy`, `MoEEPLoadSpec` and the proposed error string; no equivalent report was found.

AI assistance was used to prepare this report and validate the reproducer.

items.title: [RFC] Expose allocator-issued KV block generations to asynchronous connectors
items.author: feichai0017
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation

Asynchronous KV connectors can retain a destination block while an external
DMA/RDMA operation is in flight. The connector APIs expose `KVCacheBlocks` at
`update_state_after_alloc`, but `KVCacheBlock` currently identifies a physical
slot only by `block_id`. The same object and ID are reused after the allocator
returns the slot to the free queue.

A late completion or release acknowledgement can therefore only be checked
against request/session metadata. Those identities do not prove that the
physical KV slot still belongs to the allocation that originally authorized
the transfer.

This matters even for connectors that correctly delay normal frees: fault
recovery eventually needs to distinguish the old allocation of block N from a
new allocation of block N without relying on timeout or process liveness as a
DMA termination proof.

### Requested contract

Please expose an allocator-issued generation for each writable KV block
allocation:

- `BlockPool` increments the generation whenever a physical block is handed
  out for a new writable allocation after reuse/eviction.
- `KVCacheBlocks` exposes `(block_id, allocation_generation)` to connectors at
  `update_state_after_alloc` and request-finish handoff.
- Cached read-only references retain the generation of the contents they
  reference; generation changes only when the slot becomes a new writable
  allocation.
- The value is monotonic for a slot within the owning process and never zero.

The allocator must issue the value. A connector-local counter keyed by block ID
cannot observe allocations made through other paths and would not be a valid
reuse fence.

This would not itself claim DMA cancellation or permit early free. It would let
connectors reject stale control completions after a separately proven physical
termination and make page-reuse tests deterministic.

### Relevant released interface

Observed on vLLM 0.31.0 commit `db9527a46873454610df6dbedf79a36d6bf1a7f6`:

- `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py::KVCacheBlock`
- `vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py::BlockPool.get_new_blocks`
- `KVConnectorBase_V1.update_state_after_alloc`
- `KVConnectorBase_V1.request_finished[_all_groups]`

I searched open and closed issues/PRs for KV-connector block reuse and allocation
generation and did not find a matching proposal. I can prepare a focused PR and
unit tests if maintainers agree with the API direction.
