items.title: [RFC] MP mode under-fills the per-step token budget when prefix-cache hits are high
items.author: larksudo
items.body_excerpt: ## Summary In-process mode (LMCache running inside the vLLM worker processes) fills vLLM's `max_num_batched_tokens` budget normally. In MP (multiprocess) mode with `lmcache_driven` transfer, the same budget is badly under-filled on the steps that admit cache-hit requests: the same tail-prefill work takes about twice as many engine steps, and because a step costs roughly the same whether it carries 1.5K or 4.6K tokens, MP ends up 15-30% worse on TPOT and ~10% worse end-to-end than in-process mode on the workload below. **Root cause**: retrieves complete asynchronously at staggered times. The scheduler can only admit requests whose retrieves happen to be ready at a step boundary, so a step typically carries one or two tails instead of filling the budget. Throughout, **tail** means the part of the prompt not covered by the cache hit — i.e. what the engine still has to prefill. ## Reproduction Benchmark setup (DeepSeek-V4-Flash w8a8, TP8, vLLM 0.23.0, vLLM-Ascend v0.23.0): ```bash vllm bench serve \ --model dsv4 \ --tokenizer /path/to/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-w8a8 \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8800 \ --dataset-name prefix_repetition \ --prefix-repetition-prefix-len 13824 \ --prefix-repetition-suffix-len 1536 \ --prefix-repetition-num-prefixes 50 \ --prefix-repetition-output-len 154 \ --num-prompts 500 \ --request-rate 2 \ --max-concurrency 16 \ --seed 48 \ --ignore-eos ``` vLLM config (plus the usual dsv4 tokenizer / tool-call / reasoning parser flags): ``` --max-model-len 133120 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 32 --tensor-parallel-size 8 --data-parallel-size 1 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --quantization ascend --no-enable-prefix-caching --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode": "FULL_DECODE_ONLY"}' --kv-transfer-config '{ "kv_connector": "LMCacheMPConnector", "kv_role": "kv_both", "kv_connector_extra_config": { "lmcache.mp.host": "127.0.0.1", "lmcache.mp.port": 5555, "lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode": "lmcache_driven" } }' ``` LMCache server (MP mode), running alongside the engine: ```bash lmcache server \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 5555 \ --chunk-size 4096 \ --l1-size-gb 50 \ --eviction-policy LRU \ --disable-metrics ``` The connector reaches this server through the `lmcache.mp.host` / `lmcache.mp.port` settings above, with the transfer mode given by `lmcache.mp.mp_transfer_mode`. In-process mode runs the same configuration and the same chunk size (4096), without the server: LMCache runs in the worker processes and is configured through `LMCACHE_CONFIG_FILE`. ## Observed behavior ### In-process mode (synchronous retrieve) ``` Step N: every retrieve that finished during the load window is visible at the same step boundary → 3 tails × 1536 = 4608 prefill + 28 decode → 4636 / 8192 ≈ 57% → ~50 tail-prefill steps in total ``` ### MP mode (asynchronous retrieve, current behavior) ``` Step N: only the tails whose retrieve finished by now are visible → 2 tails × 1536 = 3072 prefill + 28 decode → 3100 / 8192 ≈ 38% Step N+1: the next one or two tails → ~100 tail-prefill steps in total (2× in-process) ``` Both modes do the same total work, so MP spends roughly twice the engine time on tail prefill (65.0s vs 27.8s). A step does not get cheaper for carrying fewer tokens: its cost is dominated by fixed overhead — kernel launches, full-context attention, communication — not by token count. ### Trace evidence (step-level instrumentation) | Metric | In-process | MP (current) | |---|---|---| | Tail-prefill steps | 50 | 100 | | Avg tokens per tail step | 4608 | 3072 | | Avg step duration | 555ms | 650ms | | Total engine time on tail steps | 27.8s | 65.0s | ### Per-step prefill tokens (measured) Prefill tokens per engine step (decode excluded), same 8192-token budget. The SP-* runs are in-process at the labeled vLLM block size; MP 4096 is MP mode with chunk size 4096. - **SP 4096 / SP blk32**: bimodal — a dominant mode pinned at the 8192 ceiling (several tails admitted per step) and a secondary mode at ~3000-3500 (a single tail). - **MP 4096**: clustered at ~2900-3000 — one or two tails per step, rarely approaching the budget. Under the same budget, MP concentrates at ~3000 tokens/step (~38% utilization) while in-process routinely saturates 8192 — consistent with the trace table above. ## What we tried For this scenario we prototyped a worker-side hold in `get_finished()`: a completed retrieve is not reported to the scheduler until either a few others are also ready or a short timeout expires, so several tails land on one step boundary and the budget gets filled. In this workload it recovered most of the gap: | Metric | Without hold | With hold | Change | |---|---|---|---| | Mean TPOT | 79.9ms | 67.7ms | -15% | | TPOT P99 | 89.3ms | 75.9ms | -15% | | E2E duration | 449s | 401s | -11% | | Throughput | 171 tok/s | 192 tok/s | +12% | | Mean TTFT | 1850ms | 2183ms | +18% (the tradeoff) | ### Which scenarios can degrade - **Short reused prefix** — the tail is comparable to the whole budget, so a single request already fills the step and there is nothing to coalesce. - **Low concurrency / single stream** — no sibling retrieve arrives inside the window, so the hold has nothing to wait for. - **Deep request queues** — the hold stacks on top of an already backlogged queue and only adds latency. ## Where the decision actually belongs The worker is the wrong place to make this call, because it cannot see the signals that decide whether holding is worth it. Whether to hold depends on state that only the scheduler has: - how many requests are in the **running (decode) batch** — if decode already fills `max_num_batched_tokens`, holding buys nothing and only adds latency; - how deep the **waiting queue** is — if re

items.title: [RFC]: Parallelize long-running Mooncake Store unit tests
items.author: Aionw
items.body_excerpt:
## Status

Draft / implementation in review.

This RFC replaces the oversized prototype PR #2896 with six smaller draft PRs that have an explicit review and merge topology.

## Motivation

Several Mooncake Store unit-test executables contain many semantically unrelated cases and run for a long time as one scheduling unit. Splitting those cases by behavior gives CTest more useful parallel work and makes failures easier to locate, but creating one executable per source file increases compile/link overhead.

The proposal therefore separates two concerns:

1. Keep source files organized by semantic behavior.
2. Use a small CMake helper to combine compatible files into a bounded number of Unity-built test targets.

No hard-coded shard index or test-name routing table is introduced.

## Invariants

- Preserve all 296 source-defined GTest cases.
- Changes to test-only fixture behavior are acceptable when needed for isolation.
- Production behavior must not change.
- Each domain split must remain independently reviewable.
- The final target-balancing change must be isolated in its own commit/PR layer.

## PR topology

```text
                         +--> #2900 DummyClient + offload --------+
                         +--> #2901 SSD + snapshot SSD -----------+
RFC #2898 / main --------+--> #2902 promotion --------------------+--> #2905 Unity/target balance
                         +--> #2903 MasterService core -----------+
                         +--> #2904 snapshot MasterService -------+
```

The five domain PRs are all based directly on the same `main` commit and can be reviewed in parallel. #2905 contains those five commits plus one final CMake-only commit; review that final commit after the domain PRs, then let its diff shrink as #2900–#2904 merge.

## Tracking

| Order | PR | Scope | Source tests | Review dependency |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| 1 | #2900 | DummyClient + offload | 17 | RFC only |
| 2 | #2901 | SSD + snapshot SSD | 26 | RFC only |
| 3 | #2902 | Promotion | 40 | RFC only |
| 4 | #2903 | MasterService core | 144 | RFC only |
| 5 | #2904 | Snapshot MasterService | 69 | RFC only |
| 6 | #2905 | Unity build and target balancing | 296 total | #2900–#2904 |

## CMake design

`add_store_test()` remains the single registration primitive. The final PR adds `add_store_unity_test()`, which delegates to it and enables CMake `UNITY_BUILD` for compatible semantic source groups.

The result is:

- 30 independently registered targets in the five domain PRs, useful for isolated review and validation.
- 21 balanced targets in the final integrated layout.
- Semantic directories and filenames remain intact.
- No numeric shard constants or hard-coded test-case mapping in CMake.

## Validation

Five independent branches:

- All targeted builds passed.
- 30/30 CTest targets passed.
- Source-defined test count: 17 + 26 + 40 + 144 + 69 = 296.
- Four-way group wall times: 32.69s, 43.32s, 36.63s, 85.97s, and 89.85s.

Final integration branch:

- 21/21 targets built on current `main`.
- 21/21 CTest targets passed with `ctest -j4` in 204.53s.
- Isolated prototype measurement: 148.05s target build and 203.81s test time.
- A contended cold build measured 490.52s after four concurrent worktree builds; it is retained as a host-load datapoint and is not used as a regression comparison.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] 296 source-defined tests preserved.
- [x] Semantic source layout replaces the long monoliths.
- [x] Final test wall time is at most 210s at four-way concurrency.
- [x] Isolated changed-target build is at most 160s.
- [x] Combined isolated build + test time is at most 360s.
- [x] Domain PRs can be reviewed in parallel.
- [x] Target balancing is isolated for focused review.

## Rollout

1. Review #2900–#2904 in parallel.

4. Review the final CMake-only target-balancing commit.

items.title: [RFC]: [Store] Recoverable client liveness states and asynchronous offboarding
items.author: Doube-Suzerain
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Motivation

Mooncake Store currently treats one client heartbeat timeout as a permanent failure. Temporary network jitter, a client pause, or a delayed Master monitor loop can therefore irreversibly unmount recoverable resources and delete their metadata.

We propose adding a recovery window: after the first TTL expires, the Master retains the client's resources but stops routing new requests and work to them; a valid liveness signal makes them serving again. Terminal cleanup starts only if the client remains unavailable for a second TTL.

Resource availability checks are currently distributed across allocation, replica lookup, Copy/Move, task dispatch, drain, offload, and promotion. This proposal also centralizes that decision so the new liveness semantics are applied consistently.

## Changes proposed

- Introduce an **Active → Suspected → Offline** state machine for each client incarnation, with separate active and suspicion TTLs.
- Add a typed `ServingEligibility` seam for all client-owned resource routing, while retaining Suspected resources for possible recovery.
- Separate client liveness from remount readiness and segment lifecycle.
- Express terminal cleanup as a retryable `ClientOffboardingJob`; complete it synchronously first, then move the same job to an asynchronous executor.
- Preserve the existing Ping RPC schema and legacy TTL configuration.
- Rebuild process-local liveness records when restoring Master snapshots; keep NoF on its independent health model.

## Proposed design

### Client liveness

Each client incarnation has a `ClientLivenessRecord`:

```text
Active --active TTL--> Suspected --suspicion TTL--> Offline
   ^                       |
   +---- liveness signal --+
```

- **Active** resources may serve new requests.
- **Suspected** resources are retained but cannot receive new allocations, descriptors, or work. A valid liveness signal recovers the same incarnation.
- **Offline** is terminal for that incarnation and starts offboarding.

The suspicion TTL starts when the Master actually commits `Active -> Suspected`, so a delayed monitor does not shorten the recovery window. Ping and successful segment mounts are liveness signals; ordinary Put/Get traffic and task/offload/promotion heartbeats are not.

Ping remains wire-compatible: a ready Active client receives `OK`; an unknown or Offline client receives `NEED_REMOUNT`; Ping may recover a Suspected client before applying the existing remount-readiness check.

Client liveness, remount readiness (`ok_client_`), and segment lifecycle remain independent. In particular, `ok_client_` will no longer determine whether resources may serve or must be retained.

### `ServingEligibility`

Allocation, metadata reads, task routing, offload, promotion, and drain will use a small typed interface with the following common semantics:

```text
resource can serve
  = resource is intrinsically valid
  && segment lifecycle permits serving
  && owning ClientLivenessRecord is Active

ShouldRetainResources
  = ClientLivenessRecord is Active or Suspected
```

This supplements existing segment checks rather than replacing them. NoF resources continue to use their own probe and lifecycle rules.

While Suspected, the Master blocks new dependencies on the client, including allocations, descriptors, Copy/Move routing, task delivery, offload/promotion work, and drain selection. End, Revoke, failure, and completion callbacks for already-started work remain accepted so refcounts, quota, and task state can converge.

Memory allocator registrations and buffers retain the specific `ClientLivenessRecord` that created them, preventing a later incarnation from reactivating old memory resources.

### Offboarding

Terminal retirement uses one job interface:

```text
PrepareClientOffboarding(record) -> ClientOffboardingJob
CompleteClientOffboarding(job)
```

Prepare commits Offline and immediately isolates the incarnation. Complete performs the expensive work: metadata cleanup, memory segment unmount, LocalDisk/offload/promotion cleanup, quota convergence, and external metadata cleanup. The old record is removed only after all steps succeed; until then it acts as a Mount/ReMount barrier.

The first implementation calls Complete synchronously from the client monitor. A follow-up submits the same job to an asynchronous executor with batching, retry, shutdown draining, and queue observability. This keeps state and cleanup semantics unchanged when execution becomes asynchronous.

### HA restore and compatibility

After snapshot restore, each restored client starts as Active with a fresh active TTL, preserving the current recovery semantics. The Master rebuilds the liveness associations needed by restored resources, while readiness still follows the existing ReMount protocol.

Snapshot creation must not capture partially completed offboarding. The synchronous phase preserves the current exclusion behavior; asynchronous offboarding will add explicit snapshot/offboarding coordination.

New configuration:

```yaml
client_active_ttl_sec: 10
client_suspicion_ttl_sec: 20
```

`client_live_ttl_sec` and `--client_ttl` remain deprecated aliases for the active TTL. If an active/legacy TTL is explicitly configured but suspicion TTL is omitted, suspicion inherits the resolved active TTL. No RPC schema change is required.

LocalDisk and task metadata currently identify ownership by client ID. Initially, complete cleanup plus the Offline remount barrier prevents old resources from overlapping a new incarnation. An explicit incarnation token would provide stricter isolation for artificially reused client IDs, but requires a wire/schema change and is outside the initial scope.

## Development plan

1. Add `ClientLivenessRecord`, dual-TTL configuration, Ping/Mount integration, and the three-state monitor.
2. Introduce `ServingEligibility` across allocation, descriptors, Copy/Move, task/drain, LocalDisk/offload, and promotion.
3. Add synchronous `ClientO

items.title: [RFC]: Add GDS offload for mooncake-store based on existing TENT gds transport
items.author: tong1heng
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

Add opt-in GDS SSD offloading to mooncake store by reusing the existing TENT GDS transport.

The implementation adds:

1. A client-local, fixed-size GDS backing file exposed as a TENT `file://` segment and managed by an aligned extent allocator.
2. A first-class `ReplicaType::GDS` with storage identity, generation, offset, value size, and allocation size in store metadata and wire serialization.
3. Required dual-write behavior for enabled `BatchPut`: memory/NoF writes and GDS writes are submitted in parallel and waited on before finalization.
4. A GDS-only creation fallback when memory replica allocation fails because of capacity or tenant quota.
5. Memory-first `BatchGet` selection, followed by a local matching GDS replica, while retaining existing NoF, local-disk, and disk fallbacks.
6. TENT/Transfer Engine capability checks and GDS buffer-registration tracking needed for sub-slice cuFile requests.

The feature is enabled through environment variables and requires no changes to upstream vLLM, so existing deployments remain unchanged when it is disabled.

## Motivation

Mooncake store currently supports POSIX and `io_uring` file offloading. Its existing data path is as follows:

1. **Write path:** when memory usage in a global segment (CPU memory) reaches the configured eviction watermark, mooncake master selects objects for offloading and places them in the background offload queue. The client then reads the objects from the global segment and writes them to the configured file backend through POSIX or `io_uring`. After the file write completes, the master records the file-backed replica and may release the corresponding memory replica.
2. **Read path:** the client first queries the master for the object's replica metadata and prefers an available memory replica. If the object is no longer present in memory, the client loads it from the file backend through POSIX or `io_uring` and returns the data to the caller.

This data path becomes a bottleneck when host memory is constrained. GPU-to-CPU and CPU-to-SSD bandwidths are not matched: GPU data must first be copied into CPU memory and then written to SSD. **When GPU production outpaces this two-step pipeline, CPU memory and CPU-side file I/O cannot drain the global segment fast enough. Some KV cache is consequently discarded before it can be completely offloaded, preventing more valid KV cache from being offloaded to the SSD even when sufficient SSD capacity remains.**

GPUDirect Storage (GDS) addresses this mismatch by supporting GPU-to-SSD DMA, so the data can bypass the CPU staging path. The GDS transport has already been integrated into TENT, **but the data path between TENT and mooncake store has not yet been connected.** An earlier draft PR (#2731) attempted to add GDS offload at the mooncake store layer by introducing a separate GDS context. This approach would duplicate cuFile resource management and make mooncake store responsible for transport-specific details that already belong to TENT.

Therefore, the central design goal of this change is to preserve the existing separation of mooncake store and TENT while connecting the two components: TENT owns all GDS cuFile operations, transport selection, and buffer registration, while mooncake store owns only object and replica metadata, allocation/lifecycle decisions, and transfer-request submission. Mooncake store should reuse the existing Transfer Engine and TENT GDS transport instead of introducing another GDS/cuFile implementation. This keeps the GDS data path composable with store's replica semantics and avoids a second, divergent GDS context in mooncake store.

## Non-goals

- Replacing the existing `enable_ssd_offload`/`LOCAL_DISK` POSIX or `io_uring` path.
- Providing remote reads from another client's local GDS file. A remote GDS descriptor falls back to the existing memory, NoF, local-disk, or disk paths.
- Recovering a client's GDS index after restart or promising crash/durability semantics for the local file.

## Architecture

```text
RealClient (env opt-in)
  +-- client
      +-- GdsStorageManager
      |    +-- aligned extent allocator
      |    +-- file:// backing segment handle
      |    `-- storage_id + generation + read leases
      +-- TransferSubmitter::submitFile
      |    `-- TransferEngine / TENT GDS / cuFile
      `-- MasterClient RPCs
           `-- MasterService: GDS storage identities and replicas

BatchPut:
  reserve local extent
    +-- BatchPutStart -> MEMORY/NoF PROCESSING replicas
    +-- BatchAddGdsReplicaStart -> GDS PROCESSING replica
    `-- submit both write paths -> wait -> commit + BatchPutEnd

BatchGet:
  local MEMORY -> any MEMORY -> matching local GDS -> NoF/disk fallbacks
```

### Local GDS storage

`GdsStorageManager` creates/truncates and preallocates the configured backing file, opens it once through `openSegment("file://...")`, and allocates raw value extents aligned to 4 KiB. Reservations are move-only and automatically aborted unless committed or explicitly preserved after an uncertain RPC. A reference-counted read lease keeps an extent alive until all GDS read futures finish.

Each client registers a `storage_id` and `storage_generation` with the master. The generation changes when the file is recreated, preventing an old metadata descriptor from addressing the same offset in a new file.

### Store metadata and RPCs

`ReplicaType::GDS` is an independent replica type rather than an alias for `LOCAL_DISK`:

```text
GdsDescriptor {
  owner_client_id
  storage_id
  storage_generation
  value_offset
  value_size
  allocated_size
}
```

The master exposes storage registration/unregistration, `BatchAddGdsReplicaStart`, and `BatchCreateGdsOnlyObjects`. GDS replicas use the existing `PROCESSING` -> `COMPLETE` lifecycle, participate in `BatchPutEnd` / `BatchPutRevoke`, and are removed during stale-client cleanup. MessagePack serialization uses a stable explicit replica type value and validates the six-field G

comments.author: RuixiangMa
comments.body:
@tong1heng Great work! The design  is clean and well-motivated. A few points I'd like to understand better:
1. submitFile splits at 16 MiB and batches at 128 entries, but GdsTransport::submitTransferTasks already does the same splitting (kMaxSliceSize) and batch checking (io_batch_depth_, user-configurable). If a user sets io_batch_depth=32, submitFile still batches 128 — only 32 get accepted per TENT batch. Is this intentional double-protection, and if so, should the batch limit be read from TENT config rather than hardcoded?
2. Main has added some TENT infrastructure since this RFC was written. Transport::tracksLocalBuffer() seems like a natural fit for GDS's cuFileBufRegister (local-only, shouldn't be advertised via desc.transports). Transport::quiesce() could settle cuFile I/O before buffer deregister. And the all-or-nothing submitTransferTasks contract means partial failure needs rollback of pushed params. Would it make sense to reference these in the RFC?
3. Main recently refactored lease (shared_ptr<Lease>, group-shared) and group eviction (GroupDomain, all-or-none). How do GDS-only objects interact — do they get an independent or group-shared lease? Could UnregisterGdsStorage stale cleanup break all-or-none eviction by removing one GDS replica from a group?
4. Preserve creates finalized=false entries that are never auto-cleaned. If finalize RPCs fail repeatedly (network jitter, master restart), the backing file could be exhausted silently. The Roadmap mentions eviction policy as future work — should the gap be acknowledged in the main body with a short-term mitigation (metric, max count, or TTL)?
5. storage_generation algorithm and collision risk aren't specified. The PR uses steady_clock XOR client_id — steady_clock resets on reboot, so if client_id is reused (e.g. vLLM config), a timestamp collision (low but non-zero) could cause stale descriptors to be accepted. Would it be worth specifying the algorithm and confirming generation=0 as an invalid sentinel?

comments.author: tong1heng
comments.body:
Thanks for the thoughtful review! These points identify several implementation gaps and areas where the RFC needs clarification.

1. The two layers serve different purposes: `submitFile` bounds store-level submissions and manages their futures, while `GdsTransport::submitTransferTasks` enforces cuFile limits. However, the hardcoded batch limit of 128 is inconsistent with the configurable `io_batch_depth`. One clarification: an over-capacity submission returns `TooManyRequests`; it does not accept only the first 32 entries. We will expose the effective GDS batch depth through TENT and use it in `submitFile`, counting capacity in terms of entries after splitting. We will also align the splitting limits and add tests for different batch depths and submissions spanning multiple batches.

2. Agreed. We will reference these interfaces in the RFC and adapt the implementation accordingly. GDS will implement `tracksLocalBuffer()` using its local registration registry and stop advertising cuFile registrations through `desc.transports`. We will implement `quiesce()` to stop new submissions and settle outstanding I/O before teardown releases buffers and batch resources. For the all-or-nothing submission contract, we will validate all requests before modifying the sub-batch and restore appended state on failure. We will also verify cuFile’s submission-failure semantics to ensure potentially accepted I/O cannot be treated as a clean rejection and retried through another transport.

3. The PR currently uses the older group-registration path and needs to be adapted to main’s `shared_ptr<Lease>` and `GroupDomain` implementation. GDS-only objects should follow the same semantics as other objects: ungrouped objects have an independent lease, while grouped objects share the group’s lease. The local GDS `ReadLease` separately protects an extent during an in-flight read. `UnregisterGdsStorage` removes matching GDS replicas and deletes an object only when no valid replica remains. We will preserve group bookkeeping through the common metadata-removal path and add mixed MEMORY/GDS group tests. We will also clarify that invalid-storage cleanup is distinct from policy-driven eviction; current main tests permit safe members to be evicted while unsafe members remain, so strict all-or-none wording needs qualification.

4. Yes, we will acknowledge this limitation explicitly in the main body. `Preserve()` retains an allocation because an RPC failure does not establish whether the master applied the operation, but these uncertain entries currently have no reconciliation or automatic reclamation path. The issue also includes entries committed locally before a finalize RPC fails, so tracking only `finalized=false` is insufficient. As a short-term mitigation, we will track uncertain-entry counts, bytes, age, and allocation failures, and introduce a configurable admission limit. A TTL may trigger reconciliation, but it must not directly reclaim an extent without confirming that the master no longer references it and that local I/O has completed.

5. Agreed. `steady_clock` XOR the client ID does not provide a reliable cross-restart uniqueness guarantee when the client ID is reused. We will replace it with a fresh, randomly generated nonzero 64-bit storage-incarnation token whenever the backing file is recreated, preserving the current wire format. The RFC will specify the algorithm and its probabilistic collision properties. `generation=0` is already invalid: initialization avoids it, and `RegisterGdsStorage()` rejects it. We will document this invariant and add tests for zero-generation rejection and stale descriptors after storage recreation with a reused client ID.

items.title: Refactor: TRTLLMHAAttnBackend should not inherit from FlashInferAttnBackend when reuse is small
items.author: merrymercy
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`TRTLLMHAAttnBackend(FlashInferAttnBackend)` (in `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/trtllm_mha_backend.py`) inherits from `FlashInferAttnBackend`, but it reuses very little from the parent. Almost all attention-specific behavior is overridden, and some inherited setup is allocated-but-never-used. We should reconsider this inheritance: **if the reuse is small, we should not inherit from `FlashInferAttnBackend`** — inheriting directly from the base `AttentionBackend` (and pulling in only the small bits of plumbing that are actually shared) would be cleaner.

### What is actually reused

The only real reuse comes from `super().__init__(...)`:
- `req_to_token_pool`, `token_to_kv_pool`
- `max_context_len`, `skip_prefill`, `use_sliding_window_kv_pool`
- the `kv_indptr` / `kv_last_page_len` buffers (used by the companion `TRTLLMHAAttnMultiStepDraftBackend` draft steps)
- `forward()` dispatch — which actually comes from the base `AttentionBackend`, not from FlashInfer.

### What is overridden (not reused)

Essentially all the attention logic:
- `init_forward_metadata`, `init_cuda_graph_state`, `init_forward_metadata_out_graph`
- `forward_decode`, `forward_extend` (call `flashinfer.decode.trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache` / `flashinfer.prefill.trtllm_batch_context_with_kv_cache` directly)
- `get_cuda_graph_seq_len_fill_value`, `_resolve_swa_kv_pool`
- it uses its own `TRTLLMMHAMetadata` and its own page-table builder.

### Inherited-but-unused / redundant work

Because the TRTLLM kernels use a completely different API, part of the parent `__init__` is wasted:
- Parent builds `prefill_wrapper_ragged`, `prefill_wrappers_paged`, `decode_wrappers`, and the `FlashInferIndicesUpdater*` objects — TRTLLM-MHA never uses them.
- Parent sets `self.workspace_buffer` to the shared `global_workspace_buffer`, but the child **replaces** it with its own zero-init `global_zero_init_workspace_buffer`.
- `max_context_len` and `_swa_kv_pool` are set by the parent and then re-set by the child.

### Proposal

- Evaluate inheriting `TRTLLMHAAttnBackend` directly from `AttentionBackend` instead of `FlashInferAttnBackend`.
- Move the small amount of genuinely shared init plumbing into a thin shared helper/mixin (e.g. pool/buffer setup) rather than dragging in the full FlashInfer wrapper/indices-updater allocation.
- Avoid allocating FlashInfer wrappers and updaters that the TRTLLM path never uses.
- Apply the same review to `TRTLLMHAAttnMultiStepDraftBackend(FlashInferMultiStepDraftBackend)`.

As a general guideline: **do not inherit from `FlashInferAttnBackend` when the reuse is little** — prefer inheriting from the base `AttentionBackend` and sharing only what is actually common.

### Good first issue

This is a good first issue: it is well-scoped, localized to `trtllm_mha_backend.py` (plus the base classes), and mostly a refactor with clear before/after behavior to validate against existing tests.

items.title: [RFC] Orchestrator-facing Elastic EP lifecycle contract
items.author: julienmancuso
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

Dynamo is designing Kubernetes-managed Elastic EP in [Dynamo DEP #13121](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/issues/13121). SGLang's merged scale-up path is already close to what an external reconciler needs: it accepts an absolute EP target, distinguishes effective and pending size, lets joining cohorts wait for admission, and exposes asynchronous status.

To turn that into a reliable Kubernetes lifecycle, the orchestrator must be able to recover after a controller restart or request timeout, identify the joining or retiring cohort for one operation, and know when capacity is safe to delete. The goal is not to standardize SGLang's internal topology; it is to make the boundary used by an external process orchestrator explicit and queryable.

## Proposed orchestrator-facing contract

### Resize identity and status

- Accept an absolute target and associate it with an operation ID or generation.
- Treat a repeated request for the active or in-progress target as the same operation.
- Report a stable runtime instance ID, operation ID, effective size, pending target, documented phase, and operation-scoped error.
- Make it possible to distinguish an engine restart from an operation that is still progressing.

A conceptual status shape is:

```json
{
  "instance_id": "server-7",
  "operation_id": "resize-42",
  "effective_ep_size": 4,
  "pending_ep_size": 6,
  "phase": "waiting_for_cohort",
  "last_error": null
}
```

### Control-authority loss

The process that exposes Elastic EP status or coordinates a resize may fail independently of the workers. The external contract should document what happens when the tokenizer manager, primary, or other control authority restarts or disappears:

- whether the committed members can continue serving;
- whether an in-flight operation remains observable, can be resumed by a new authority, or becomes terminally `Unknown` or `NeedsRecreate`;
- whether the last committed topology remains authoritatively queryable;
- how the runtime instance ID changes and stale retries against the previous instance are rejected; and
- when the external orchestrator must recreate the complete engine group.

Transparent continuation is not required. A correlated, fail-closed terminal result that identifies the last authoritative topology—or states that topology is unknown—is sufficient for the orchestrator to retain capacity, fence traffic, and choose recreation safely.

### Joining-cohort identity

For scale-up, expose enough information to associate externally launched joiners with one operation:

- cohort or operation ID;
- expected rank range and ready-rank count;
- a topology/configuration fingerprint;
- explicit mismatch and timeout errors.

This prevents a stale joiner from a failed operation from being admitted into a later resize that happens to reuse the same rank offset.

### Bootstrap, committed membership, and serving readiness

The contract should distinguish three milestones:

- **Bootstrap/cohort progress:** participants have reached the native join or preparation barriers. A ready-rank count is not, by itself, proof of inference readiness.
- **Committed membership:** the engine has established the operation's resulting topology, correlated with its runtime instance and operation or topology generation.
- **Serving readiness:** that committed topology has passed the required engine/runtime serving checks. A retained completed operation is not a current health signal.

The required members and control components are those of the current committed topology, not necessarily the original startup topology. A supported survivor topology may become ready after recovery without waiting for a removed member to return.

The engine/runtime owns serving readiness and verification. Required warmup or inference verification must be able to finish without normal user traffic and without a controller acknowledgment or status write. This generalizes the separation between restored membership and `warming_up` described in the [fixed-slot recovery milestone](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/35376#issuecomment-5956887849).

The external orchestrator manages capacity and requests membership changes. The serving runtime follows engine readiness and its own prerequisites to register the appropriate endpoint(s); it does not need a second positive controller permission. Endpoint scope is backend-defined, not necessarily one endpoint per rank.

Outstanding withdrawal, drain, or retirement intent remains effective across restarts until explicitly resolved. The external traffic-lifecycle owner must preserve and enforce that intent; a healthy signal must not undo it. This does not require SGLang to interpret Dynamo-specific traffic policy, and readiness alone is not proof of drain completion or safe termination.

Launch ordering must follow the native protocol: resize preparation may need to start before joining processes launch. Document the bootstrap prerequisite separately from inference readiness, so an orchestrator neither waits for joiners to serve before starting the resize nor waits for a blocking resize to finish before launching participants it needs. Health and operation-status observation should remain reachable while inference is paused.

Conformance coverage should include bootstrap while inference is not yet ready, idle-world verification, and readiness becoming true after commit and required checks without controller acknowledgment. Serving-runtime integration should also verify that a restart does not undo outstanding withdrawal intent.

### Template-invariant initial formation and automatic append bootstrap

An orchestrator should be able to start every allocation of a new engine world from one immutable workload template. Initial formation should not be represented as a sequence of synthetic grow operations.

For the current TP1 automatic-bootstrap profile, let `W` be the number of accelerators visible to one allocation. SGLang should:

items.title: [Bug] Large HiCache UCX startup timeout on downstream build; not reproduced on v0.5.20
items.author: ByronHsu
items.body_excerpt:
### Result

**Not reproduced on the latest upstream image (v0.5.20).** A large HiCache pool triggered a UCX startup timeout on our earlier downstream build, but both HiCache and no-HiCache starts passed with the unmodified upstream image.

| Build | HiCache per rank | UCX initialization, all 8 ranks | Server ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Downstream `869abc0605`, NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21.0 | 234 GB | Six ranks explicitly timed out at 60s; none completed | No |
| Same downstream build, no HiCache | 0 | 3–4s | Yes |
| **Upstream v0.5.20, NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22.0** | **234 GB** | **~2s** | **234s after launch** |
| Same upstream image, no HiCache | 0 | ~2s | 62s after launch |

Each HiCache/control pair ran on the same eight-H200 node with fresh processes. The upstream pair used a different physical node from the downstream pair, and multiple software components changed: this does **not** identify a fix or prove the cause. Only startup was tested, with no inference requests. Both upstream runs registered all eight KV buffers, passed passive `/ready` checks for 30 seconds, and exited cleanly.

### Reproduction settings

8 H200s, approximately 2014 GiB host RAM; public `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite` real weights, revision `604d5664dddd88a0433dbae533b7fe9472482de0`.

Upstream image: `lmsysorg/sglang:latest` resolved to **v0.5.20**, source `94602c9c2b7cbdb8efd5c52802dac6a1c180089e`. Tested amd64 image digest:

```text
lmsysorg/sglang@sha256:b27fce60bc5494c118c4910702812bcfa8cee67abcdd1ff8b0902f21647552f4
```

No source overlay, serving patches, or dependency replacements. Download the model revision above into `$MODEL_DIR`, then run:

```bash
export SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_ENGINE_INIT_TIMEOUT=60
export SGLANG_NCCL_ALL_GATHER_IN_OVERLAP_SCHEDULER_SYNC_BATCH=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_STREAM_INTERVAL=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_CPU_IMAGE_PREPROCESSING=0

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path "$MODEL_DIR" --trust-remote-code \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000 \
  --tp-size 8 --dp-size 8 --ep-size 8 --enable-dp-attention \
  --disaggregation-mode prefill --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.7 --dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype bf16 \
  --page-size 64 --tokenizer-worker-num 4 \
  --context-length 150000 --max-running-requests 1024 \
  --skip-server-warmup --log-level debug --decode-attention-backend fa3 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 234 \
  --hicache-write-policy write_through \
  --hicache-mem-layout page_first --hicache-io-backend kernel
```

Remove the five HiCache options for the control. CUDA graphs stay enabled; NIXL is the PD transport, not L3 storage. Actual pool allocation: **234,001,612,800 bytes per rank**, about **1.872 TB total**. Size is per rank and requires sufficient host/cgroup headroom.

### Original failure

The downstream run failed **during UCX backend creation, before KV registration**:

```text
RuntimeError: NIXL create_backend('UCX', {'num_threads': '8'}) did not return within 60s
```

Five seconds before failure: **141.6 GiB host headroom**, **39.2–39.4 GiB free per GPU**, no host OOM-counter increase or CUDA OOM. Host memory pressure and compaction were high. No native stack inside UCX was captured. A later audit found rank 0 in a debugger tracing stop at 21:29:30 UTC, inside the 60-second UCX window, as well as earlier allocation-stage attachments. The retained samples do not establish total pause duration. Other ranks also timed out without a recorded tracing stop, but this run was not free of measurement interference. A telemetry gap further limits the evidence.

The upstream HiCache run kept at least **120 GiB host headroom**, logged no OOM, and completed UCX startup quickly. The underlying reason for the older failure remains unresolved.

<details>
<summary>Upstream runtime</summary>

Python 3.12.3; PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130; NIXL/nixl-cu13 1.4.1; bundled UCX 1.22.0; CUDA 13.0; driver 595.71.05; Linux 6.8.12; FlashInfer 0.6.18; Transformers 5.12.1. THP mode remains `madvise`. The 60-second UCX deadline and eight prefill backend threads were unchanged.

</details>

### Follow-up: the extra host memory is DC receive buffers

On one exclusive node, with the same upstream source/image and **232 GB/rank** HiCache, we compared fresh server processes:

| Native backend | DC interfaces | Receive-buffer chunks | Scheduler anonymous huge pages | UCX startup span |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22 | 0 | 288 | 12.498 GiB | 2s |
| NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21 | 288 | 576 | 23.188 GiB | 4s |
| Same 1.3.0 package, only `UCX_TLS=^dc_mlx5` added | 0 | 288 | 12.502 GiB | 3s |

All three initialized all eight ranks, registered KV buffers, and held passive readiness for 30 seconds. No compaction stalls, THP fallbacks, or OOM occurred. No inference or PD transfers were tested. The third case is a diagnostic intervention, **not a verified timeout fix**.

UCX debug logs and per-scheduler memory maps identify the difference: **8 ranks × 9 workers × 4 ports = 288 DC interfaces**, each eagerly allocating a **38 MiB** receive buffer through `rc_recv_desc`. Those extra buffers account for **10.6875 GiB** of huge pages. Excluding only DC on the old package removes them and matches the newer package. Actual loaded UCX versions were verified in server logs.

The old binary includes DC; the new wheel omits it. [NIXL PR 1708](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/nixl/pull/1708) disables DC in the manylinux build. The v1.3.0 source tag also contains that flag despite the tested wheel including DC, so we report observed binary features rather than infer build history from tags.

During the **original failing UCX initialization window**, kernel counters rose by **10,496 compaction attempts, 10,492 failures, 3,407 THP fallbacks, and 3,668 direct-reclaim stalls**. They were flat just before UCX started. The examined SGLang NIXL startup and host-pool files are byte-identical between the downstream and upstream revisions.

This supports a host-memory compact

items.title: [Bug] linker: Failed layer short-circuits the full completion barrier
items.author: feichai0017
items.body_excerpt:
## Describe the bug

`LayerWiseLoadCounter.finish()` promises to wait for every layer before dropping the batch entry, but `all(future.exception() is None for future in futures)` stops at the first failed Future. If a later layer is unresolved, `finish()` returns `False` and removes the entry without waiting for that layer.

This is a CPU completion-counter contract issue. It does not establish a GPU/RDMA use-after-free or physical transfer-termination failure. The normal success path already waits; the failed-prefix path should preserve the same completion barrier.

Confirmed against main `533020b500ba781bfafd1f5cbadabaf03d8986f7` and the same implementation in v0.5.22. I searched open/closed issues and PRs for `LayerWiseLoadCounter`, finish/pending counter and short-circuit layer loading. Related #40896 introduced the failure reporting, #44220 concerns graph replay waits, and #45106 changes Mooncake load grouping; none changes this `finish()` aggregation.

## Reproduction

No model or GPU is needed. With the SGLang Python package available:

```python
from sglang.srt.mem_cache.unified_cache.unified_cache_linker import LayerWiseLoadCounter

counter = LayerWiseLoadCounter(2)
index = counter.update_producer()
first, pending = counter.futures[index]
first.set_exception(RuntimeError("first layer failed"))

print(counter.finish(index))        # False: returns immediately
print(pending.done())               # False: later layer still unresolved
print(index in counter.futures)     # False: entry already removed
```

Expected: `finish(index)` must remain blocked, with the batch retained, until the pending layer resolves; then return `False` because the first layer failed. This example creates the intermediate Future state directly to make the premature return deterministic.

The proposed regression extends the existing `test_layer_counter_finish_waits_for_layers_still_loading` with success/failed-first-layer cases, uses a worker plus an event to check the wait, and always resolves the pending Future in `finally`. Against unmodified main: **1 failed, 2 passed** in the selected counter tests. Resolving every Future before aggregating errors: **3 passed**, process exit 0.

## Environment

- SGLang source: main `533020b500ba781bfafd1f5cbadabaf03d8986f7`
- Linux x86_64, Python 3.11.2
- CPU Future-only regression, no GPU/model execution
- Test: `python -m pytest -q test/registered/unit/mem_cache/test_unified_cache_linker.py -k layer_counter`

items.title: [RFC] Expose allocator-issued page generations to external linkers
items.author: feichai0017
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation

The UnifiedCache external-linker path hands an asynchronous linker physical
`device_indices`, but those indices can later be returned to the token/page
allocator and reused. Request IDs, tree node IDs, linker counters and process
epochs do not identify the allocation of the physical page slot.

For fault-safe external DMA/RDMA recovery, a delayed completion must be rejected
if the same page index now belongs to a newer allocation. A linker-local counter
is insufficient because it cannot observe allocations and frees performed by
other cache/scheduler paths.

### Requested contract

Please expose allocator-issued page generations to external linkers:

- The owning `BaseTokenToKVPoolAllocator` implementation issues a non-zero,
  monotonic generation when it allocates a physical page for new writable use.
- External-linker load/offload transfer descriptions carry the generation next
  to each page/device index.
- Reusing the same page ID after free produces a different generation.
- Linker completion can validate that the page allocation still matches before
  committing a result or releasing retained state.

This is a stale-control fence, not a DMA termination primitive: timeout,
cancellation or process liveness still must not authorize page reuse until the
transport supplies a physical completion/termination receipt.

### Relevant released interface

Observed on SGLang 0.5.22 commit
`baa9befa381511cd4d56f83980951e5a45fffc6d`:

- `BaseTokenToKVPoolAllocator` and `PagedTokenToKVPoolAllocator`
- `UnifiedCacheLinker` / `UnifiedCacheLinkerWrapper`
- external-linker `PoolTransfer.device_indices`
- `finish_layer_wise_loading` and offload completion

I searched open and closed issues/PRs for external-linker page reuse and
allocation generation and did not find a matching proposal. I can prepare a
focused allocator/linker PR and tests if maintainers agree with the contract.

items.title: [Feature]: Plan for enabling mypy in tests directory
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

**Goal:** Enable MyPy static checking in the `/tests` directory.

**Implementation:** Move `tests/**` from `--follow-imports skip` to `--follow-imports silent` in [`tools/pre_commit/mypy.py`](../../tools/pre_commit/mypy.py), one directory at a time, **with each PR enforcing the directories it fixed**.

Partial: #26533

/cc @hmellor @yewentao256

---

### Plan

**Note:** Errors below were measured with
`mypy --python-version 3.11 --follow-imports silent <dir>` — the target state for each directory.

---

#### Blocker: removing a directory from `SEPARATE_GROUPS` enforces nothing

`group_files()` iterates `SEPARATE_GROUPS` in **list order** and `break`s on the
first prefix match. `"tests"` is the first entry, so every `tests/**` file is
claimed by it:

```python
>>> group_files(['tests/config/test_multimodal_config.py',
...              'tests/v1/shutdown/test_processor_error.py'])
{'tests': [both files]}     # never lands in 'tests/config' or 'tests/v1/shutdown'
```

A file only gets `follow_imports=silent` by matching **no** entry at all and
falling through to the `""` group. Since `"tests"` matches everything under
`tests/`, no per-directory removal can ever take effect before `"tests"` itself
is removed — which is the very last step.

**Sorting `SEPARATE_GROUPS` by longest prefix does not fix this** (verified):
with `tests/config` removed, its files still match `tests` and still run with
`skip`. Sorting only changes which *skip* group a file lands in, which is
cosmetic today.

Consequence if the plan is executed as originally written: every PR from 1
through kv-C fixes real errors but enforces none of them, and all of that work is
free to regress until the final PR. **PR 0 below fixes the mechanism so that
stops being true.**

---

#### PR 0 — Make per-directory enforcement possible (prerequisite) (#49570) **DONE**

<details><summary>read more...</summary>

Add an allowlist of verified-clean directories, matched **before**
`SEPARATE_GROUPS`, that routes files into the `""` group (no `--follow-imports`
flag → pyproject's `silent`):

```python
# Directories verified clean under follow_imports=silent. Checked before
# SEPARATE_GROUPS; these files join the "" group and are enforced at silent.
# Moving a directory from SEPARATE_GROUPS to here is what makes a fix stick.
SILENT_GROUPS: list[str] = []
```

In `group_files()`, before the `SEPARATE_GROUPS` loop:

```python
if any(re.match(f"^{d}.*", changed_file) for d in SILENT_GROUPS):
    file_groups[""].append(changed_file)
    continue
```

Also sort the `SEPARATE_GROUPS` loop by descending path length so sub-directory
groups stop being shadowed by their parents. This is cosmetic today (all those
groups run at `skip`) but keeps the per-group log labels honest as directories
drain.

Verified behaviour with `SILENT_GROUPS = ["tests/config", "tests/v1/shutdown"]`:

```python
{'':                    ['tests/config/a.py', 'tests/v1/shutdown/b.py', 'vllm/x.py'],
 'tests/compile/passes': ['tests/compile/passes/d.py'],
 'tests/v1/core':        ['tests/v1/core/c.py']}
```

Clean dirs are enforced at `silent`; everything unfixed keeps its `skip` group;
`"tests"` can stay in `SEPARATE_GROUPS` until the very end.

**Bundle PR 0 into PR 1** rather than shipping it alone — AGENTS.md discourages
standalone mechanical PRs, and PR 1 gives it substantive work to ride along with.

</details>

---

#### Per-PR recipe (applies to PRs 1–9 and kv-A/B/C)

Every PR in this plan follows the same four steps. A PR that stops after step 1
is preparatory only and must say so in its description.

1. **Fix** the errors in the directories the PR owns.
2. **Move** each fixed directory from `SEPARATE_GROUPS` to `SILENT_GROUPS` in the
   *same* PR. This is the step that makes the fix stick.
3. **Verify** — both commands must pass:
   ```bash
   # the directory is genuinely clean at the strictness you are about to enforce
   .venv/bin/mypy --python-version 3.11 --follow-imports silent \
       --warn-unused-ignores <dirs owned by this PR>

   # the hook as CI runs it, with the new grouping in effect
   pre-commit run -a --hook-stage manual mypy-3.11
   ```
   `--warn-unused-ignores` is not on in CI, but run it locally — it catches
   `# type: ignore` comments that were never needed (PR 1 shipped one).
4. **Confirm the routing changed.** Cheap proof that step 2 took effect:
   ```bash
   .venv/bin/python -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'tools/pre_commit'); \
     import mypy; print([k for k,v in mypy.group_files(['<a/file/in/the/dir.py>']).items() if v])"
   # must print [''] — not the directory name, and not 'tests'
   ```

**Leaf-before-parent ordering is still required**, now for scoping rather than
mechanism: fixing `tests/compile/passes` before `tests/compile` means the parent
PR only deals with residual loose files in that directory, not the whole tree.

**Final step (end of PR 9):** once every sub-directory has moved to
`SILENT_GROUPS`, delete the `"tests"` entry from `SEPARATE_GROUPS`. At that point
`SILENT_GROUPS` has served its purpose and its `tests/**` entries can be dropped
in the same PR — everything under `tests/` falls through to `""` naturally.

---

#### Shared Error Patterns

These patterns account for the majority of errors across all directories.
Fixing the root cause once eliminates many errors simultaneously.

| Code | Total | Root cause | Fix |
|------|------:|-----------|-----|
| `[arg-type]` | ~1,000+ | Tests pass `list` where `tuple` is required, concrete mock/stub type where real type expected | Correct the literal (e.g. `list` → `tuple`, bare `str` → enum value), or type the fixture/stub class properly so it satisfies the declared interface |
| `[union-attr]` | ~700+ | Attribute access on `X \| None` without a `None` guard | Add `assert x is not None` before the access; one assert per test setup clears a cluster |
| `[method-assign]` | ~56 | Direct method replacement (`obj.method = MagicMock()`) — all instan

items.title: [Performance]:Skip gaps in sliding-window prefix-cache hit search
items.author: Ifelseer
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance


`SlidingWindowManager.find_longest_cache_hit` currently scans every block from right to left, costing up to `max_num_blocks` `BlockPool.get_cached_block` lookups even when the cache is cold. Sliding-window groups commonly run at a low hit rate, so a 128K-token request with a 4K window performs ~8192 lookups (block_size=16) although a hit only needs `cdiv(sliding_window - 1, block_size) = 256` contiguous blocks. The function already carries a TODO for this. Proposed change: probe every `stride = sliding_window_contiguous_blocks`-th block from the right. Every candidate run of `stride` cached blocks contains exactly one probe, so the lattice cannot skip a hit. On a probe hit, expand to the right (at most `stride - 1` blocks, since the next probe missed), verify only windows containing the probe, and after a miss at `idx` resume at the next aligned edge below `idx - 1`. Alignment retries advance by `alignment_tokens // gcd(alignment_tokens, block_size)` blocks, and the cached-prefix fallback is computed directly. Function-level measurements (`find_longest_cache_hit`, block_size=16, sliding_window=4096, 128K tokens, alignment=16, no EAGLE, single-thread CPU):

| pattern | main lookups | proposed lookups | main time | proposed time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| cold cache | 8192 | 33 | 4.49 ms | 0.021 ms |
| 1% random cached | 8192 | 33 | 4.61 ms | 0.021 ms |
| tail hit / full cache | 256 | 257 | 0.23 ms | 0.23 ms |
| adversary (cached blocks on the probe lattice) | 8192 | 128 | 4.63 ms | 0.11 ms |

The worst case remains O(max_num_blocks), but the common low-hit-rate case becomes O(max_num_blocks / stride), and the measured adversarial case is still well below the current full scan.



### Report of performance regression

_No response_

### Misc discussion on performance

### Relation to #53276 (not a duplicate)

#53276 targets the same TODO with a different, narrower approach: it checks `block_hashes[i - K + 1]` only when the current block misses and no run is being accumulated, and jumps by K only in that case. Every other path still advances one block at a time, alignment retries remain per-block, the cached-prefix fallback still comes from the full scan, and the PR adds no tests. This proposal is materially different:
- Every probe hit triggers right-expansion and verification bounded to windows containing the probe, so gaps are skipped regardless of which side the miss is on.
- Alignment retries jump by the alignment period, covering hybrid models where `alignment_tokens != block_size`.
- The cached-prefix fallback is computed directly.
- Correctness is backed by an offline exhaustive comparison with the previous implementation (all cached-block patterns up to 13 blocks over a grid of block sizes, windows, alignments, and EAGLE settings: 7,339,584 cases, 0 differences) plus a committed randomized test.

Happy to close this in favor of #53276 if maintainers prefer that direction.

  ### Additional robustness fix

`sliding_window=1` with EAGLE disabled makes `_contiguous_blocks_for_hit` return 0, which would leave the new probe loop's `i -= stride` at the same index. The implementation clamps the stride to 1, reproducing the previous behavior (one cached block is reusable) and terminating; a regression test is included.

  ### Misc discussion on performance

This is a scheduler-side CPU optimization; it does not change hit results, model output, or GPU execution. End-to-end serving numbers have not been collected yet.


### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

Python 3.12, torch 2.14.0+cu132, upstream main at ff01a6b14f, CPU unit-test harness. This is a scheduler-side CPU optimization and does not change hit results, model output, or GPU execution.

items.title: [Feature / Question]::  /v1/systemone rejects image inputs on standard multimodal VLMs with "this model does not take image inputs"
items.author: vishvaRam
items.body_excerpt:
### Problem Description

When using the `/v1/systemone` endpoint with multimodal inputs (`images`), the endpoint works seamlessly for dedicated decision models (e.g., `clef` / `clef-flash`), successfully resolving structured questions across both text and image context.

However, when serving standard Vision-Language Models (VLMs) (such as `Qwen` multimodal checkpoints or custom NVFP4 quantized variants):

* **Text-only state decisions work as expected** on `/v1/systemone`.
* **Multimodal decision requests fail immediately** with an HTTP 400 `BadRequestError: this model does not take image inputs`.

We tested this across both `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.32.0` and the latest `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` Docker images, observing identical behavior.

We would like to seek clarity on the intended architectural support for `/v1/systemone`:

1. Is `/v1/systemone` intended to support multimodal vision inputs only for dedicated classification/decision architectures (like Clef), or should standard autoregressive VLMs (that have multimodal processor support in `/v1/chat/completions`) also be able to ingest `images` here?
2. If standard VLMs are intended to be supported, what model configuration flags, task types (`--task`), or input structuring are required so that the model runner accepts image tokens under the System-One pooling handler?

---

### Reproduction Steps

1. **Serve a standard multimodal VLM using vLLM:**

```bash
vllm serve Vishva007/Qwen3.5-9B-NVFP4 \
    --host 0.0.0.0 \
    --port 8000 \
    --trust-remote-code \
    --limit-mm-per-prompt image=4

```

2. **Verify text decision works (Successful):**
Sending a text-only payload to `/v1/systemone` without the `images` key returns valid structured classification choices.
3. **Send a multimodal payload including `images` (Fails):**

```python
import base64
import httpx

RUNPOD_PROXY_URL = "https://<RUNPOD_ID>-8000.proxy.runpod.net/v1/systemone"
MODEL_ID = "Vishva007/Qwen3.5-9B-NVFP4"
IMAGE_PATH = "Decision-Models-vLLM/cats.jpg"


def to_data_uri(path: str) -> str:
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode("utf-8")
    return f"data:image/jpeg;base64,{b64}"


payload = {
    "model": MODEL_ID,
    "state": "Examine the image and check if it contains a cat.",
    "images": [to_data_uri(IMAGE_PATH)],
    "questions": {
        "is_cat": {
            "type": "choice",
            "instructions": "Determine if a cat is clearly visible in the image.",
            "criteria": {
                "yes": "A cat is present",
                "no": "No cat is visible",
            },
        }
    },
}

response = httpx.post(
    RUNPOD_PROXY_URL,
    json=payload,
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer EMPTY"},
    timeout=60.0,
)

print(response.status_code)
print(response.json())

```

---

### Actual Behavior

The server responds with HTTP 400:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "message": "this model does not take image inputs",
    "type": "BadRequestError",
    "param": null,
    "code": 400
  }
}

```

---

### Expected Behavior

Either:

* The VLM processes the vision embeddings alongside the prompt text under the `/v1/systemone` pooling/classification forward pass to evaluate the decision questions, **OR**
* The documentation / OpenAPI schema clarifies that the `images` input parameter in `/v1/systemone` requires models with a dedicated multimodal decision head / architecture (such as `ClefForConditionalGeneration`), while standard generative VLMs require standard chat completions.

---

### Environment Information

* **vLLM Endpoint:** `/v1/systemone`
* **Model Checkpoint:** `Vishva007/Qwen3.5-9B-NVFP4` (Multimodal VLM architecture)
* **Serving Environment:** RunPod Ubuntu container, NVIDIA GPU

items.title: [Bug]: ModelOpt Llama-4 Checkpoints Take 5+ minutes to load
items.author: robertgshaw2-redhat
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

In working on some MoE refactors, I discovered that L4 for ModelOpt takes 5+minutes to load weights even from CPU page cache. 
- https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8

The root cause is basically this hack logic to load the state dict that ModelOpt uses
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/models/llama4.py#L439-L523 [modelopt is the fused case] 

What happens is that the CPU tensor (loaded weight) that we are going to load into the GPU tensor (param) becomes non-contiguous due to this logic. As a result, when we eventually call `_copy()` from CPU->GPU we are calling this on a non-contiguous cpu tensor which takes 3-4s per weight.

To hack around this for local R&D, I simply immediately move the loaded_weight to the GPU. This makes the gather happen on the GPU which accelerates things a lot. This isn't reasonable as an actual solution though

We should investigate where the logic in the weight loader can avoid creating non-contiguous CPU tensors

comments.author: robertgshaw2-redhat
comments.body:
> [@robertgshaw2-redhat](https://github.com/robertgshaw2-redhat) tested on H200 with `nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8`:
> 
> Approach	Load Time

> **GPU-first** `.to('cuda').transpose()`	**37 sec (2.1x faster)**
> The GPU-first approach works well. You mentioned it's "not reasonable as an actual solution" - what are the specific concerns? Is it GPU memory during loading, or multi-GPU compatibility?
> 
> Happy to implement a different approach if preferred.

I thought it was a hack because we have:
- the param, which is loaded into gpu memory (empty tensor)
- the loaded_weight, which is coming from disk and is mapped into cpu memory

Right now, we have a simple trustworthy process where we never have a copy of `loaded_weight` in GPU ram. We simply call `._copy()` which copies the loaded wieight into the param. This guarantees that we do not have any straggling gpu memory from weight loading

If we move the loaded weight in to gpu memory, we have to be 100% certain that we put it back. This is kind of a can of worms IMO and I don't think we should do something like this to solve an edge case like a single model with a single quant framework (especially for a model that has limited usage like this)

So my preference would be to figure out if its possible to ensure that the cpu weights remain contiguous rather than moving them to the gpu unless we have a clean way to manage the lifecycle of the weight

comments.author: rohithputha
comments.body:
Hi, 
I have analyzed the possible causes for this issue. 
I have found some to be:
1. I believe there are two types of expert placement strategies: Linear and Round Robin. Linear is better for memory movement between CPU and GPU. I suspected that this problem might have been caused by the use of round-robin placement which causes multiple DMAs. But it turns out that the default is linear and mostly likely linear placement is being used.
2. One more root cause that I learnt might be that .transpose() in torch. PyTorch just Performs metadata remapping for transposing and hence this causes non contagious tensors and hence multiple DMA invokes.

These are some theories. I would like to test some solutions like performing indexing first, transferring to GPU and then performing transpose operations. 

I am new to contributing to vLLM and open source in general. If this approach works for you, I would like this to be assigned to me. Also, one note that I don't have Nvidia gpu to test and benchmark the changes. any leads or help or guidance regarding that would be appreciated.

comments.author: jadechip
comments.body:
Ran a few experiments against this issue and wanted to share the results in case they are useful.

- I was able to reproduce the slow post-warmup load: ~`495s` on 2x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell.
- The trace supports the issue hypothesis: the hot path is CPU -> GPU copies from non-contiguous CPU tensors in the Llama-4/ModelOpt MoE loader.
- Tried two fixes but did **not** help:

1. Make routed expert source tensors contiguous before copy:

```text
measured load: 532.63s
routed_experts.copy: 4080 ms
make_contiguous: 609790 ms
```

This made the copy cheap but made total load time worse -_-

2. Slice the local TP shard first, move only that shard to GPU, transpose on GPU, and skip the later TP narrow:

```text
measured load: 494.73s
routed_experts.copy: 0 measured events
local shard -> device: 465178 ms
```

This removed the `routed_experts.copy` hotspot, but did not improve wall-clock time.

I guess the expensive part is repeatedly consuming these non-contiguous CPU views. The simple fixes above mostly move the cost around. A better fix probably needs to avoid creating those views, or load/reshape the checkpoint tensors in an order closer to the final parameter layout?

comments.author: jadechip
comments.body:

I tried the “don’t fight the CPU view layout, use an existing GPU safetensors loader” path as well. This is not a real loader-side fix for the non-contiguous tensor issue, but it does seem like the best practical workaround I found so far.

Same model/setup as before:

- `nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8`

comments.author: ishrith-gowda
comments.body:
@guptapiyush16 @LeonxLJX heads up before you start, there are 3 open PRs against this issue already.

| PR | author | approach | file |
|---|---|---|---|
| #46766 | @pratheeknathani | `.contiguous()` before the copy | `models/llama4.py` |
| #50227 | @Dev-with-Mouzan | same, inline at the weight_loader call | `models/llama4.py` |
| #47580 | me | flip the strided side to the destination, no CPU gather | `layers/fused_moe/routed_experts.py` |

#46766 and #50227 are the same fix. `.contiguous()` is a no-op if already contiguous, so the conditional in #46766 and the unconditional call in #50227 do the same thing. #46766 was first, 2026-06-25.

That fix works but it makes the strided CPU gather explicit instead of removing it: `.contiguous()` still walks non-contiguous host memory element by element, then transfers the result densely. Same shape as #32081 (~68s to ~60s above), matches @jadechip's traces showing the cost moving, not disappearing.

#47580 removes the gather. Undoing the transpose recovers the contiguous on-disk slab for free, so the H2D transfer is dense with no CPU-side gather, and the layout change happens as a strided write on the device instead. No loaded weight ever sits in GPU memory, so it doesn't hit @robertgshaw2-redhat's lifecycle concern with GPU-first approaches. TP-narrowed slabs degrade to row-run memcpys instead of elementwise gathers.

Numbers: fp8 62.8ms to 4.0ms (15.8x), bf16 93.4ms to 7.5ms (12.4x) per copy on an A100-80G. End to end on a 24-layer truncation, 18.8s to 12.5s. @eric1932 then ran the full 48-layer model on 1x H200 with source-hash-verified builds and paired runs: 102.58s to 23.63s median, 4.34x, identical output tokens across all six runs. Thanks for that, it's exactly the full-model H200 datapoint this needed.

Two tradeoffs worth naming. It's in `routed_experts.py`, not `llama4.py`, so it covers any fused-MoE checkpoint that arrives transposed, not just Llama-4/ModelOpt. It's also bigger: +145/-3 vs +8/-0 and +5/-1, mostly a test file covering contiguous/transposed/TP-narrowed layouts across fp8/bf16/fp32; the fix itself is about 35 lines. If a maintainer wants the one-liner now and the general fix later, that's a fine call, I'd rather see this issue closed than fight for the merge.

Happy to rebase (it's ~2200 commits behind, still conflict-free) or split out the test file if that helps review.

items.title: [Bug]:  Streaming reasoning content misrouted to `content` when `stop` parameter is set (stop buffer desynchronizes `delta_text` from `delta_token_ids`
items.author: huanghuan3
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text Your output of `python collect_env.py` here ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug ## How you would like to use vLLM Using the OpenAI-compatible streaming API with a Qwen3 reasoning model, a `stop` parameter, and `include_stop_str_in_output=false` (the default). When the model's output crosses the `` boundary within a single batch of tokens (e.g. under MTP / speculative decoding / async output), the reasoning tail and `` marker leak into `content` instead of being correctly split between `reasoning_content` and `content`. ## The bug ### Summary When a streaming request carries a non-empty `stop` list and `include_stop_str_in_output=false`, the V1 detokenizer holds back up to `max(len(stop)) - 1` characters of visible text in a **stop buffer** to avoid prematurely emitting a stop string. However, the corresponding `delta_token_ids` are **not** buffered — they reflect all tokens generated in the current round. This creates a desynchronization between two inputs that the reasoning parser receives simultaneously: | Input | Source | Buffered? | |---|---|---| | `delta_text` | `detokenizer.get_next_output_text()` → `output.text` | **Yes** (stop buffer holds tail) | | `delta_token_ids` | `output.token_ids` (raw incremental token IDs) | **No** | The Qwen3 reasoning parser uses `delta_token_ids` to detect `` and `delta_text` to split the string. When the stop buffer delays the `` text but the token IDs already report it, the parser's state machine advances prematurely, and the subsequently released text is routed entirely to `content`. ### Concrete example Suppose the model generates in one batch: ```text 我已经想好了你好 ``` With `stop=["你好"]` and `include_stop_str_in_output=false`, `stop_buffer_length = len("你好") - 1 = 1`. **Round 1** — stop buffer holds back the last character(s): | | Value | |---|---| | `delta_text` (after stop buffer) | `我已经` | | `delta_token_ids` | tokens for `我已经想好了你好` | Parser (`qwen3_reasoning_parser.py:123`): `end_token_id in delta_token_ids` → **True**, but `delta_text.find("")` → **-1** (text not yet visible). Parser returns `None` (line 136). The reasoning text `想好了` is silently dropped. **Round 2** — stop buffer releases the remaining text: | | Value | |---|---| | `delta_text` | `想好了你好` | | `delta_token_ids` | `[]` (no new tokens) | Parser (line 142): `end_token_id in previous_token_ids` → **True** (it was in round 1's tokens). Parser returns `DeltaMessage(content="想好了你好")`. Everything — including `` — goes to `content`. **Result:** ```json { "reasoning_content": "我已经", "content": "想好了你好" } ``` **Expected:** ```json { "reasoning_content": "我已经想好了", "content": "你好" } ``` ### Why MTP / speculative decoding amplifies this MTP and async output make it more likely that a single returned batch spans the `reasoning tail → → content head` boundary. Combined with the stop buffer delaying `delta_text` by one or more rounds, the text window and the token window become misaligned precisely at the `` boundary — the worst possible place for the parser. ## Root cause analysis ### 1. Stop buffer in the detokenizer `vllm/v1/engine/detokenizer.py`: ```python # Line 86-89: stop buffer length if self.stop and not self.include_stop_str_in_output: self.stop_buffer_length = max(len(s) for s in self.stop) - 1 else: self.stop_buffer_length = 0 # Line 148-164: get_next_output_text holds back tail characters def get_next_output_text(self, finished: bool, delta: bool) -> str: buffer_length = 0 if finished else self.stop_buffer_length ... length = len(self.output_text) - buffer_length last_offset = self._last_output_text_offset if last_offset < length: self._last_output_text_offset = length return self.output_text[last_offset:length] return "" ``` When `finished=False` and `stop` is set, the last `stop_buffer_length` characters are withheld from `delta_text`. ### 2. Token IDs are NOT buffered `vllm/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/serving.py`: ```python # Line 755: delta_text comes from detokenizer (stop-buffered) delta_text = output.text # Line 776-780: current_token_ids from raw output.token_ids (NOT buffered) current_token_ids = previous_token_ids + as_list(output.token_ids) ``` `output.text` has passed through `get_next_output_text()` and is stop-buffered. `output.token_ids` is the raw incremental token IDs for this round — no buffering applied. ### 3. Qwen3 parser uses token IDs for state, text for splitting `vllm/reasoning/qwen3_reasoning_parser.py:95-147`: ```python def extract_reasoning_streaming(self, previous_text, current_text, delta_text, previous_token_ids, current_token_ids, delta_token_ids): ... if self.end_token_id in delta_token_ids: # line 123: token-based detection end_index = delta_text.find(self.end_token) # line 125: text-based split if end_index >= 0: reasoning = delta_text[:end_index] content = delta_text[end_index + len(self.end_token):] ... return DeltaMessage(reasoning=..., content=...) # line 136: end_token_id in IDs but not in text → return None ← BUG return None if not delta_text: return None elif self.end_token_id in previous_token_ids: # line 142: already ended return DeltaMessage(content=delta_text) # ← everything → content else: return DeltaMessage(reasoning=delta_text) ``` The desynchronization scenario: 1. **Round 1**: `end_token_id in delta_token_ids` is True (token is present), but `delta_text.find(end_token)` is -1 (text held by stop buffer).
