items.title: OTel tracing overhead cliffs at c=50 on TP=2 deployments — level/flush tuning has no effect
items.author: wangxf1987
items.body_excerpt:
## Title

OTel trace overhead benchmark on a production-style K8s deployment (TP=2, 2 replicas): throughput loss of 20-33% at c>=50, trace level and flush threshold have negligible effect

## Summary

We benchmarked `--enable-trace` overhead on a production-shaped K8s deployment (RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, not docker-compose), Qwen3.6-27B-CHO on sglang v0.5.18, TP=2 per replica x 2 replicas (4 GPUs total, not an exclusive full node). This complements the larger-scale results already discussed elsewhere for TP=8 exclusive-node setups, and shows the overhead shape is very different at smaller TP.

Full report (charts + tables): attached PDF (`report-en.pdf`). Raw data (`result.csv`, GPU/CPU logs) available on request.

## Environment

- sglang `v0.5.18` (community image), `SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC=1`
- Deployment: K8s RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, TP=2 per replica, 2 replicas, 4x H20 GPUs
- Trace path: sglang engine -> local OTel Agent (DaemonSet, node-local endpoint) -> Gateway -> backend, i.e. a two-hop agent-gw architecture, not a direct hardcoded Gateway connection
- 4 configs compared:
  | Group | trace level | async | flush threshold |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | G1 baseline | disabled | - | - |
  | G2 | 2 | 1 | default |
  | G3 | 3 | 1 | default |
  | G4 | 2 | 1 | 50 |
- Load generator: fixed-prompt benchmark client, concurrency swept across 1/10/50/100/200, 3 repeats per level (median)

## Findings

1. **Overhead is mild at low concurrency (c<=10)**: ttft_p99 +6~71%, throughput loss only 3~4%.
2. **c=50 is a clear inflection point**: ttft_p99 jumps 4.6x (172ms -> 965ms) going from G1 to G2 — roughly equivalent to the G1 baseline's own c=100 latency level being pulled forward to c=50. In other words, enabling trace shifts the whole latency-saturation curve left by one concurrency tier.
3. **From c>=50 onward, throughput loss is stable at 20~33%**, and grows with concurrency (-20.3% at c=50, up to -33.1% at c=200).
4. **Trace level 2 -> 3 produced no measurable incremental overhead** at c>=10 (all deltas within noise, ±2%).
5. **`SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC_FLUSH_THRESHOLD=50` vs. default also produced no measurable benefit** at c>=50 (within ±16%, mostly ±2%; one anomalous +132.9% ttft_p99 spike at c=10 looked like a transient one-off, not reproduced at other levels).
6. **Root cause for (4) and (5): CPU was never the bottleneck in this setup.** Host CPU utilization on the GPU node stayed at 2~3% across all 4 groups (vs. GPU sm% rising from 14.8% baseline to 16~19% with trace enabled). Both trace-level and flush-threshold tuning target CPU-side span processing cost — with only 2 TP ranks, span volume is low enough that CPU headroom is never exhausted, so those knobs have nothing to bite on at this scale.
7. This is a **much smaller overhead** than what we see at TP=8 on an exclusive full node (throughput loss there was 75~79%, itl_p99 spiking ~28x, with CPU pegged at 99% — happy to share that data too if useful). The magnitude gap tracks roughly linearly with TP rank count, since span generation scales with the number of ranks, and the TP=8 test used synchronous export while this one used async by default.

## Why we're filing this

- The community advice we've seen elsewhere ("lower `SGLANG_TRACE_LEVEL` to reduce overhead", "tune the async flush threshold") holds at high TP / high CPU pressure, but **doesn't transfer to smaller TP configs** — those knobs are simply inert until CPU saturates. Worth calling out in docs/guidance so users at TP<=2-4 don't spend time tuning a lever with no effect.
- The **c=50 inflection point** (throughput loss going from ~4% to ~20% within one concurrency step) suggests there may be a queueing/lock-contention effect on the trace export path that kicks in once concurrent in-flight spans cross some threshold, rather than a smooth linear cost per request. Might be worth profiling `trace_async.py`'s buffer/flush path under concurrent load to see if there's a lock or queue that serializes once request volume rises (in our TP=8 investigation, we found `trace_req_finish()`/`abort()` and `__getstate__` all trigger unconditional flushes regardless of the configured threshold, and `trace_req_start()`'s `tracer.start_span()` + `propagate.inject()` calls are synchronous OTel API calls on the request path — happy to dig further if maintainers think that's a productive direction).
- Production guidance: for small/mid TP deployments (TP<=2-4), default trace config (level=2, async on) is fine as-is. For TP=8-class deployments, overhead is materially higher and level-tuning is the effective lever — but this should probably be stated explicitly since it's not obvious from the trace docs which regime a given deployment falls into.

## Attachments

- `report-en.pdf` — full benchmark report with charts (ttft_p99 / itl_p99 / e2e_p50 / throughput vs. concurrency, delta% overview, GPU/CPU resource usage)
[Uploading report-en.pdf…]()

items.title: [Bug] GLM-5.3-Flash on SM120: fa4 attention backend crashes at CUDA-graph capture (hybrid extend reshape) — triton is the only working backend
items.author: Lei-010
items.body_excerpt:
# GLM-5.3-Flash on SM120 (RTX PRO 6000): attention backend matrix — fa4 crashes on hybrid extend, triton is the only working path

## Environment

- 8× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (SM120, 96 GB each), driver/CUDA as stock
- SGLang `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.20` docker image (built 2026-09-18)
- Model: `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` (official FP8 weights, TP8)
- Draft (for spec decoding legs): `incoai/GLM-5.3-Flash-DFlash2` (DFlash2DraftModel, sha256-verified)
- `--trust-remote-code`, `--context-length 131072`, `--mem-fraction-static 0.85`

## Summary

We systematically tested every attention backend that boots for Glm5Next on SM120. **Only `triton` works.** Both `flashinfer`-default (trtllm-gen fmha — already tracked in #40558) and `fa4` crash during engine init / CUDA-graph capture. The fa4 failure is a distinct bug: a shape reshape error in `forward_extend` that also reproduces **without** speculative decoding, i.e. it is not DFlash2-specific.

## Backend matrix (all TP8)

| Config | Result |
|---|---|
| default (trtllm-gen fmha) | ❌ `TllmGenFmhaRunner ... Unsupported architecture` (see #40558) |
| `--attention-backend fa4` + DFLASH | ❌ see below |
| `--attention-backend fa4`, no spec | ❌ same error — **reproduces without spec decoding** |
| `--prefill-attention-backend fa4 --attention-backend triton` + DFLASH | ❌ same error at decode capture |
| `--attention-backend triton` + DFLASH | ✅ healthy, accept len 2.73–3.90 |
| `--attention-backend triton`, no spec | ✅ healthy |

## fa4 failure signature

```python
RuntimeError: shape '[-1, 64, 8, 0]' is invalid for input of size 753975296
```

Stack (abridged):

```
sglang/srt/model_executor/runner/decode_cuda_graph_runner.py, line 464, in __init__ → self.capture()
  ... capture_one_shape → self.backend.capture_one
sglang/srt/layers/radix_attention.py, line 290, in forward
sglang/srt/layers/attention/hybrid_linear_attn_backend.py, line 1327, in forward → 1276, forward_extend
sglang/srt/layers/attention/flashattention_backend.py, line 1704, in forward_extend
RuntimeError: shape '[-1, 64, 8, 0]' is invalid for input of size 753975296
```

Observations:

1. The failing view has a trailing **0** dimension — with Glm5Next's hybrid layout (KDA linear-attention layers interleaved with full-attention layers) the fa4 `forward_extend` path receives a zero-length draft/extend token axis and `reshape` fails instead of short-circuiting.
2. `flash_attention_v4_sm120` (selected automatically when `device_capability[0] == 12`) handles decode `flash_attn_with_kvcache`, but the extend path reshaping assumes a non-empty second batch axis.
3. Repro is deterministic across ≥3 containers; failure occurs at first CUDA-graph capture (bs=48, ~90 s after weights load).

## Reproducer

```bash
docker run --gpus all --network host --ipc host \
  -v /path/GLM-5.3-Flash:/model:ro \
  --entrypoint python3 lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.20 \
  -m sglang.launch_server --model /model --tp 8 --trust-remote-code \
  --attention-backend fa4 --port 8000 --mem-fraction-static 0.85
# → RuntimeError: shape '[-1, 64, 8, 0]' is invalid ... at decode graph capture
```

## Working config (for anyone blocked on this)

```bash
... --attention-backend triton [--speculative-algorithm DFLASH --speculative-draft-model-path /draft]
```

With `triton`, GLM-5.3-Flash FP8 TP8 serves fine on SM120, and DFLASH spec decoding reaches accept len ~3.3 (block_size 8). Note prefill throughput with triton is low (~140 tok/s on an 8K prompt, single stream), which is why a working fa4/flashinfer path on SM120 matters.

Happy to provide full logs if useful.

items.title: [Feature]  Streamed restore: chunked materialization for oversized storage hits in buffer_only HiCache mode
items.author: R-omk
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation


`--hicache-host-memory-mode buffer_only` (PR #34798 + #36345) turned host RAM
into a pure staging buffer between L3 (disk) and L1 (VRAM), which fixed a
whole class of L2/L1 consistency problems. But it introduced a hard sizing
constraint: **a storage hit larger than the empty host arena is rejected
wholesale** (`_reject_oversized_prefetch` → *"declined: cannot fit in an
empty host arena"*), and the entire prompt is recomputed by prefill even
though every one of its pages exists on disk.

In practice this forces `--hicache-size` to be at least as large as the
longest conversation (host RAM ≈ max context), defeating the point of a
"transit buffer" for long-context agentic workloads:

- Qwen3.8-27B hybrid GDN, 524k context (YaRN), TP=4: `hicache-size 6`
  (~24 GiB of pinned host RAM across ranks) just to guarantee that a 500k
  restore never gets declined.
- Cold prefill of a 300k prompt: **~89 s** at ~3.4k tok/s. The same prompt
  is fully written to L3 via `write_through`, yet it is still re-prefilled
  from scratch whenever it exceeds the arena.

What buffer_only is missing is the ability to **stream an oversized hit
through a small arena in chunks**, the same way a download streams through
a bounded socket buffer — the arena should be a throughput knob, not a
capacity ceiling.



## Proposed approach

Split an oversized hit into arena-sized chunks and pipeline them:

1. **Trim** (`_trim_oversized_prefetch`): instead of rejecting, cut the hit
   to the largest page-aligned prefix that fits an *empty* arena
   (anti-livelock: a busy arena still defers the whole hit) and park the
   remainder in a `pending_stream_tails` registry.
2. **Materialize** (`_materialize_stream_chunk`): an intermediate chunk is
   published straight to the device tree as a **KV-only leaf** (evict →
   `cc.load` H2D → root-relative insert with the stock ownership
   choreography and a fail-stop post-insert check). The mamba state is
   not needed mid-span: the tree keeps FULL-only leaves valid, and the
   joint match excludes them until the endpoint checkpoint lands.
3. **Continue** (`_finish_stream_chunk` at the H2D ack): free the bounce,
   unpin the leaf, settle the chunk's share of the storage-hit accounting,
   and re-issue the parked tail as a fresh prefetch into the hit drain —
   which may trim again for 3+ chunk spans.
4. **Admit**: the *final* chunk rides the normal staged-admission path; by
   then the device tree holds every earlier chunk, `prepare_staged_prefetch`
   plans from the FULL match over the whole span, and the mamba endpoint
   checkpoint arrives with the tail's TRAILING_PAGES fetch.

The main invariants the implementation must preserve: the admission gate
has to hold the request across the whole chunk cycle (it spans scheduler
ticks where `ongoing_prefetch` is empty); each chunk's H2D needs an explicit
`start_loading()` (stock only submits loads during admission, which the
gate withholds) plus a `has_free_load_back_slot()` check; and the Rust
TreeCore currently expects a donated `mamba_value` on every insert
(`rust/sglang-radix-tree/src/components/mamba.rs`), so KV-only leaves today
require `SGLANG_UNIFIED_RADIX_TREE_CORE_BACKEND=python` or a Rust-side
change. The full lifecycle rules (anchor pins, stale-tail rebasing,
accounting) are documented in the patch header linked below.

## Measured results

TP=4 RTX 5090, Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 hybrid GDN, 298,567-token prompt, L3 on
PCIe Gen5 NVMe RAID0, sglang main `ed8c3139f1` (2026-10-16). `hicache-size`
is per-rank GiB (TP=4): size 6 ≈ 24 GiB total, size 2 ≈ 8 GiB total.

| Metric | Before (size 6, whole-hit-or-decline) | After (size 2, streamed) |
|---|---|---|
| Host staging RAM (TP=4 total) | 24 GiB (arena 647k > max ctx — streaming never triggers) | **8 GiB** (arena 216k) |
| Warm restore from disk (L1 empty) | n/a at size 2 — would decline & re-prefill **~89 s** | **15.5 s** (2 chunks: 215,680 + 82,880; 298,560/298,567 tokens from storage = 99.998%) |
| Repeat hit after restore | 0.4 s (L1) | 0.4 s (L1) |
| Decode / EAGLE over restored ctx | 144 tok/s, accept 0.68 | unchanged |

Server flags for the "After" column (full setup in the Gist):

```bash
--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-host-memory-mode buffer_only \
--hicache-size 2 --hicache-mem-layout page_first --hicache-io-backend kernel \
--hicache-write-policy write_through --hicache-storage-backend file \
--hicache-storage-prefetch-policy timeout --page-size 64 --tp 4
```

RAM cost drops 3× while keeping the zero-recompute guarantee for any
conversation length; `--hicache-size` becomes a throughput/parallelism knob
instead of a correctness constraint.



### Related resources


- **Working patch (Gist)**: [`streamed-restore.patch` ](https://gist.github.com/R-omk/5ea76d1317147af28393654f58ebd859) 
  against sgl-project/sglang@ed8c3139f1 (main, 2026-10-16), three files
  (`buffer_mode/pipeline.py`, `unified_radix_cache.py`,
  `unified_cache/components/mamba.py`), ~1,100 diff lines.
  Self-contained header documents scope: TP lockstep preserved, SWA models
  excluded (declined as before), PP prefetch excluded (asserted), requires
  the Python TreeCore today.
- The decline being removed: `_reject_oversized_prefetch` in
  `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/buffer_mode/pipeline.py`.
- Buffer-only mode foundation: #34798, #36345 (Mamba support).
- Adjacent open work the patch builds on: #41453 (in-flight storage prefetch
  retry helper — the tail re-issue reuses the same retry set),
  #44344 (write-backlog throttle — orthogonal, write side).

The patch has been exercised on single-request cold and warm restores,
modified-tail requests, and mid-cycle aborts, with correct decode output
over the restored context

items.title: [Bug] Startup OOM with 32 tokenizer workers and auto-selected CUDA VMM transport on multi-node GB300
items.author: Phoenix3334
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On a two-node GB300/MNNVL deployment of Kimi-K3 with SGLang v0.5.22, startup with `--tokenizer-worker-num 32` and automatically selected `cuda_vmm` multimodal feature transport fails with CUDA out-of-memory errors before any client request is sent.

The initial suspicion was eager tokenizer-side CUDA VMM pool initialization. Matched controls now show that this is only part of the startup cost: lazy initialization removes unnecessary eager VMM allocation for text-only / no-MM-warmup startup, but the default multimodal startup warmup still exceeds available memory. The broader OOM therefore remains open.

A standalone lifecycle/perf improvement is proposed in #45384: **[Perf] multimodal: Lazily initialize CUDA VMM feature transport**. It is related to this issue but intentionally does not `Fix` / `Close` it.

### Environment

- Kimi-K3, 2 nodes × 4 GB300 GPUs, TP8 / DCP8, DCP backend `fi_a2a`.
- SGLang v0.5.22, CUDA 13.0 / arm64 image.
- Non-PD serving (`disaggregation_mode="null"`) for correctness checks.
- Custom all-reduce disabled in the affected baseline.
- A local GPU-name detection patch recognizes the OEM-named GB300 devices and exposes the existing MNNVL-dependent auto-selection branch; no multimodal transport code was changed by that patch.
- Startup failures were reproduced at `mem_fraction_static=0.94` and `0.90`.

Observed startup messages include:

```text
Multimodal feature transport auto-resolved to cuda_vmm (multi-node GB200/GB300 MNNVL).
reserving up to 1024 MiB on base GPU 0 across 32 tokenizer worker(s)
CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY
```

### Source findings

1. Auto-selection is conditional, not a universal v0.5.22 default. It requires a multimodal CUDA model, non-PD mode, multiple nodes, MNNVL detection, an IMEX channel, and model support for CUDA VMM feature transport. The same branch already exists in the earlier v0.5.21 source `e00930c5`; this is not established as a v0.5.22 regression.

   [v0.5.22 serving_hook.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.22/python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/serving_hook.py)

2. `TokenizerManager.__init__` constructs `CudaVmmFeatureTransport`, whose constructor immediately constructs `CudaVmmMemoryPool` when the selected transport is `cuda_vmm`. This happens before a request needs multimodal feature transport.

   [tokenizer_manager.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.22/python/sglang/srt/managers/tokenizer_manager.py) · [cuda_vmm_transport_utils.py](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.22/python/sglang/srt/utils/cuda_vmm_transport_utils.py)

3. The configured feature-pool budget is split across workers:

   ```python
   return total_pool_size // tokenizer_worker_num
   ```

   At the default 1024 MiB budget, 32 workers receive approximately 32 MiB each rather than 32 separate 1 GiB pools. The worker-count effect is therefore not explained by multiplying the configured pool budget by 32. CUDA context/runtime overhead and multimodal warmup allocations remain relevant to the total pressure.

   [get_mm_feature_pool_size_per_worker](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.22/python/sglang/srt/multimodal/transport/cuda_ipc.py)

### Matched controls

Fresh starts were run on the same two nodes with the same model/source/dependencies and MF=0.90:

| Case | Tokenizer workers | MM feature transport | Result |
|---|---:|---|---|
| T1 | 1 | auto → `cuda_vmm` | READY; peak used ~260 GiB, ~23 GiB free |
| T2 | 32 | auto → `cuda_vmm` | OOM during default multimodal warmup |
| T3 | 32 | explicit `--mm-feature-transport cpu` | READY; real image request succeeds |

For T3, tokenizer workers hold 0 GPU memory on base GPU 0 for MM feature transport. This validates CPU feature transport as a practical workaround for this startup path.

### Lazy-initialization prototype

A prototype changed `CudaVmmFeatureTransport` so `CudaVmmMemoryPool` is created only on the first actual multimodal publication, from the existing single-thread publisher executor.

#### A. `--skip-server-warmup`, then first real image

Configuration: `cuda_vmm`, 32 tokenizer workers, MF=0.90.

- Startup: tokenizer workers hold 0 MiB on base GPU 0 for the VMM pool; server reaches READY.
- First real image: CUDA VMM allocation appears on demand; observed tokenizer-side aggregate allocation on GPU 0 reaches ~0.9 GiB.
- Request succeeds.
- Shutdown is clean.

This demonstrates that lazy initialization is useful for text-only startup / deployments where multimodal transport is not exercised during warmup.

#### B. Default 448×448 multimodal startup warmup

With the same lazy-init prototype and 32 tokenizer workers:

- Startup still OOMs during multimodal warmup.
- GPU free memory falls from approximately 24.1 GiB to 6.0 GiB before failure; the OOM reports about 0.32 GiB free.
- The failing path is `mm_processor.process_mm_data_async` inside `_execute_server_warmup`.
- The VMM transport allocation is only ~0.9 GiB aggregate on GPU 0, so the dominant pressure is the warmup's own multimodal compute / activations / temporary allocations rather than the transport pool itself.

Therefore lazy initialization does **not** fix this issue when startup itself performs multimodal warmup.

### Related PR

#45384 implements the lazy-init lifecycle change as a self-contained perf/lifecycle improvement:

- no `CudaVmmMemoryPool` allocation in `CudaVmmFeatureTransport.__init__`;
- first real multimodal publication creates the pool exactly once under a lock;
- pool budget is unchanged;
- cancellation and rollback paths are unchanged;
- shutdown prevents first-time allocation after closing begins while preserving the existing pool shutdown retry/idempotency contract;
- CPU-only unit coverage is added to the existing registered multimodal transport test file.

The PR is intentionally `Related to #45345`, not `Fixes #45345`.

### Current interpretation

The evidence now separates two effects:

1. **Eager VMM transport initialization is unnecessary for text-only/no-

items.title: [Performance]: FlashInfer NVFP4 KV cache causal prefill is ~1.7-1.8x slower than FP8 on SM120
items.author: lemonade1997
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On NVIDIA consumer Blackwell (SM120), FlashInfer attention with an NVFP4 KV cache shows a significant causal prefill regression compared with an FP8 KV cache.

In a matched profiler segment with the same 48 causal paged-prefill kernel calls, the NVFP4 path took about **145.8 ms**, while the FP8 path took about **84.0 ms**. This makes NVFP4 prefill approximately **1.74x slower** (about 1.7-1.8x across measurements).

The profiler indicates that the current SM120 path uses BF16 Q with packed NVFP4 KV:

```text
NVFP4:
BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel<
  ...,
  __nv_bfloat16,      # Q
  __nv_fp4x2_e2m1,    # KV
  __nv_bfloat16,      # output
  ...
>

FP8:
BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel<
  ...,
  __nv_bfloat16,      # Q
  __nv_fp8_e4m3,      # KV
  __nv_bfloat16,      # output
  ...
>
```

The regression appears to come from the existing SM120 NVFP4 software unpack/dequant path: packed FP4 KV values and their FP8 block scales must be unpacked, converted, and scaled before the BF16 QK/PV computation. Prefill is compute-heavy, so the KV bandwidth reduction does not compensate for this per-element conversion overhead.

### Environment

```text
GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell, compute capability 12.0 (SM120)
PyTorch: 2.10.0+cu129
CUDA: 12.9
FlashInfer: 0.6.15
Attention backend: FLASHINFER
KV cache layout: HND
Model dtype / Q dtype on this path: BF16
KV cache modes compared: nvfp4 and fp8_e4m3
```

The vLLM code includes the recently added NVFP4 KV cache path. The NVFP4 cache is represented as packed E2M1 data plus one FP8 block-scale value per 16 head-dimension elements.

### Kernel-level profile

A comparable trace segment was selected from each profile. Both segments contain exactly 48 causal prefill calls:

| Metric | NVFP4 KV | FP8 KV | NVFP4 / FP8 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Causal paged-prefill calls | 48 | 48 | 1.00x |
| Causal paged-prefill total | 145.81 ms | 84.03 ms | 1.74x |
| Mean per call | 3.04 ms | 1.75 ms | 1.74x |
| CUTLASS GEMM total in the same segment | 93.61 ms | 96.69 ms | 0.97x |
| All GPU kernels in the segment | 297.73 ms | 238.45 ms | 1.25x |

The similar CUTLASS GEMM time suggests that the model's weight/MoE kernels are not the primary source of this difference. Most of the additional GPU time is inside `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel`.

### Decode and KV append observations

The same profiles show that NVFP4 is beneficial for decode:

| Kernel | NVFP4 KV | FP8 KV |
|---|---:|---:|
| Single-token/decode paged attention | ~9.63 us/call | ~12.35 us/call |
| KV append/write | ~8.39 us/call | ~3.01 us/call |

NVFP4 decode is about 22% faster in this workload because decode is more bandwidth-bound. The NVFP4 append kernel is about 2.8x slower because it performs quantization, packing, block-scale generation, and slot mapping, but its cumulative cost is only around 7 ms and is not the end-to-end bottleneck.

### End-to-end capacity stress result

With 30 concurrent requests:

| KV dtype | Completed | Preemptions | Peak running | Peak cache | Wall time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NVFP4 | 30/30 | 0 | 30 | 68.6% | 102.3 s |
| FP8 | 30/30 | 6 | 24 | 97.6% | 65.4 s |

NVFP4 provides the expected capacity benefit and avoids preemption, but the causal-prefill regression dominates this particular workload.

### Expected behavior / proposal

On SM120, the packed NVFP4 KV representation matches the hardware block-scaled FP4 MMA layout well. An optimized path could:

1. quantize Q to per-16-block NVFP4 on the fly;
2. execute QK directly with SM120 block-scaled NVFP4 MMA;
3. avoid expanding K through the FP4 -> FP16/BF16 conversion chain before QK;
4. retain the existing dequantized P x V path where the V-scale axis does not match the MMA reduction axis.

This is similar to the A4Q approach demonstrated for SM120/SM121, where an opt-in FlashInfer kernel uses FP4 Q x FP4 K block-scaled MMA.

Would the vLLM maintainers be interested in tracking or integrating an optimized FlashInfer A4Q-style path for NVFP4 KV prefill on SM120? At minimum, it would be useful to document that the current NVFP4 KV path trades substantial prefill performance for capacity/decode benefits on this architecture.

### Additional notes

- The NVFP4 cache itself is correctly compact: packed FP4 data plus FP8 scales uses about 56.25% of FP8 KV storage, giving an expected capacity ratio of about 1.78x.
- The two profiler JSON files contain more than one non-contiguous capture interval, so the comparison above uses matched segments instead of comparing total trace file size or total event counts.
- Full profiler JSON files can be provided if useful.
- Related NVFP4 KV integration discussion: #49011 and #32220.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Searched existing and past issues for NVFP4/FP4 KV prefill performance and unpack/dequant regressions.

items.title: [Bug]: --attention-backend b12x cannot serve hybrid attention/mamba models on v0.32.0 — hybrid page alignment inflates the block size to 2176, B12X only supports (64, 128)
items.author: mike2307
items.body_excerpt:
> Drafted with AI assistance; every claim below was verified against the
> `v0.32.0` tag source (and `main`, checked 2026-10-18), the `b12x 1.5.1`
> wheel metadata, and a live deployment log.

## Describe the bug

On v0.32.0 (and current `main`), serving a **hybrid** model (full-attention
layers + GDN linear-attention ("mamba") layers — `Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration`,
Qwen3-Next family) with `--attention-backend b12x` fails at engine-core startup:

```
(EngineCore) INFO [interface.py:1096] Setting attention block size to 2176 tokens
    to ensure that attention page size is >= mamba page size.
(EngineCore) INFO [interface.py:1120] Padding mamba page size by 1.49% to ensure
    that mamba page size and attention page size are exactly equal.
(EngineCore) ERROR [core.py:1510] EngineCore failed to start.
...
ValueError: Aligned KV cache block size 2176 is not supported by attention backend(s): B12X.
RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed. See root cause above.
```

The b12x backend itself initialized fine right before (from
`vllm/v1/attention/backends/b12x.py`):

```
(EngineCore) INFO [b12x.py:717] Using b12x with q_heads=16 kv_heads=2 head_dim_qk=256
    head_dim_vo=256 window_left=-1 planned_page_sizes=(64, 128) verify_q_per_req=4
    extend_q_capacities=(128, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192) scratch=1666048 bytes.
```

## Repro

```sh
vllm serve <Qwen3_5Moe NVFP4 model> \
  --attention-backend b12x --linear-backend b12x \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 128 \
  --enable-prefix-caching --max-model-len 262144 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}' \
  --max-num-seqs 8 --tensor-parallel-size 1
```

**No `--block-size` combination works.** Phase 2 of
`Platform.update_block_size_for_backend()` (`vllm/platforms/interface.py`) runs
`_align_hybrid_block_size()` unconditionally for `model_config.is_hybrid`, and it
overrides the user setting:

```python
attn_block_size = kernel_block_alignment_size * cdiv(
    mamba_page_size, kernel_block_alignment_size * attn_page_size_1_token)
...
if cache_config.block_size < attn_block_size:
    cache_config.block_size = attn_block_size
```

For this model (2 KV heads × 256 head-dim, fp8 KV → 512 B/token/layer,
≈1 MiB GDN state page per layer) with `--block-size 128`:
`kernel_block_alignment_size = max(min(64, 128), 128) = 128` →
`attn_block_size = 128 * cdiv(~1 MiB, 128 * 512 B) = 128 * 17 = 2176`.

## Root cause

`B12xPagedAttentionBackend` (both v0.32.0 and `main`) hard-codes

```python
_B12X_SUPPORTED_PAGE_SIZES = (64, 128)
...
@classmethod
def supports_block_size(cls, block_size):
    return block_size is None or int(block_size) in _B12X_SUPPORTED_PAGE_SIZES
```

and the `b12x` package's paged planner pre-builds decode/verify/extend plans for
exactly those page sizes (the `planned_page_sizes=(64, 128)` log line above). It
cannot plan 2176, so the mandatory hybrid alignment produces a block size the
only SM12x-tuned attention backend in vLLM rejects.

Notes:

- The strict `ValueError` above comes from the check added in #58457
  (2026-10-04). Without it the same mismatch would still die in the b12x impl
  constructor (cf. #62265) — the hard failure predates the check; the check
  just moved it earlier.
- The `b12x 1.5.1` wheel (which vLLM 0.32.0's own `[b12x]` extra pins) exposes
  no configuration to widen the planned page-size set.
- The identical alignment is open for non-b12x backends in #54458 (GLM-5.3-Flash
  inflated to 7808 tokens — degrades prefix caching/concurrency rather than
  hard-failing, because those backends accept larger pages). The in-code
  `TODO(tdoublep)` notes the constraint can be relaxed by changing the mamba
  chunk layout.

## Worked on v0.31.0

The identical flag set runs fine on v0.31.0 + `b12x 1.3.0` in production —
`_align_hybrid_block_size` does not exist in v0.31.0's `platforms/interface.py`
(verified by diff). This regression blocks bumping our base image past 0.31.0
for any hybrid model on SM120/SM121 with the b12x backend.

## Ask

Either (or both):

1. Let the b12x backend participate in hybrid alignment — plan/compile paged
   kernels for the aligned page size (the planner would need to accept page
   sizes beyond `(64, 128)`, e.g. any multiple of 128), or
2. Relax the mandatory attention-page ≥ mamba-page alignment for backends that
   declare a bounded page-size set (per the in-code TODO), so hybrid models can
   keep backend-native block sizes.

Interim: the failure is correctly fail-fast; a pointer to #54458 (or this
issue) in the `ValueError` message would save hybrid+b12x users the
investigation.

## Environment

- vLLM 0.32.0 (`vllm-openai:v0.32.0` dev image; `main` checked 2026-10-18 — unchanged)
- b12x 1.5.1 (the pin in vLLM 0.32.0's `[b12x]` extra)
- torch 2.13.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0
- GPU: RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell SE (SM120), TP=1
- Model: NVFP4-quantized Qwen3_5Moe hybrid (attention + GDN linear attention),
  `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, prefix caching, MTP spec decode (3 tokens)

items.title: [Bug]: DeepSeek-V4.1: wrong output when the last chunk of a chunked prefill runs as a piecewise CUDA graph
items.author: DiaaAj
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
With DeepSeek-V4.1 (`DeepseekV41ForCausalLM`), vLLM 0.32.0 and main give wrong greedy outputs when the last
chunk of a chunked prefill runs as a PIECEWISE CUDA graph. One request is enough: an 8202-token prompt with
`max_num_batched_tokens=8192` (last chunk 10 tokens) is wrong from the first generated token, and the same
request with `enforce_eager=True` is exact.

| GPU | `max_num_batched_tokens` | prompt tokens | last chunk | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| H100, H200 | 8192 | 8202 | 10 | wrong from token 1 |
| H200 | 8192 | 8208 | 16 | wrong from token 1 |
| H200 | 8192 | 8227 | 35 | wrong from token 1 |
| H200, `cudagraph_decoder_replay=False` | 8192 | 8202 | 10 | wrong from token 1 |
| H100 | 2048 | 8202 | 10 | wrong from token 1 |
| H100 | 257 | 524, 1807, 1809, 1815 | 10, 8, 10, 16 | wrong from token 1 |
| H100 | 257 | 1800 | 1, ran as a FULL graph | exact |
| H100 | 257 | 1834 | 35, ran eagerly (above the largest captured size, 32) | exact |
| H100, H200, `enforce_eager=True` | 257, 8192 | 1809, 8202 | 10 | exact |

The H200 rows are the repro script below with default settings. The H100 rows come from our harness, which
sets `max_num_seqs=16`, so its captured sizes stop at 32. Every wrong run returns the same tokens,
`[2997, 2550, 2550, ...]`, on both GPUs and on reruns (for the 8202-token prompt the expected tokens are
`[3817, 2242, 3949, ...]`).

The CUDA-graph mode decides it. With six concurrent requests at `max_num_batched_tokens=257`, where one
request's prefill ends on a 10-token chunk:

| setting | wrong requests of 6 |
|---|---|
| default (`FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`) | 1 |
| `cudagraph_mode="PIECEWISE"` | 1 |
| `cudagraph_mode` `"FULL"`, `"FULL_DECODE_ONLY"` or `"NONE"` | 0 |
| `enable_prefix_caching=False` | 1 |
| `swa_bounded_replay=False` | 1 |

A per-step trace of the H100 runs (the scheduler's output and the V2 model runner's `CudaGraphManager.dispatch`)
shows that with graphs enabled, the exact and the wrong runs differ only in the last chunk. Every earlier
chunk ran eagerly and was followed by a 128-token `DecoderReplayCudaGraphManager` dispatch (also eager). The
last chunk was dispatched as PIECEWISE (10 tokens padded to 16) in the wrong runs, and eagerly (35 tokens) or
as a FULL graph (1 token) in the exact runs. With `enforce_eager=True` there are no replay dispatches.

## What goes wrong
The checkpoint is a probec probe twin of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: the released format and `quantization_config`
(FP8 32x32 with UE8M0 scales, MXFP4 experts) at production widths (hidden 5120, 64 heads x 512, q_lora 1280,
o_lora 1024 in 8 groups, sliding window 128, index top-k 512, candidate blocks 2048 x 8, hc_mult 4), 10 layers
with `compress_ratios [0,0,2,2,2,2,1,1,1,1]`, KV sources 2/4/6, index sources 2/4/6/8, candidate source 6, and
64 routed experts. Its weights make every greedy output known in advance and insensitive to reduction order.
DeepSeek's own reference (`inference/model.py` of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, run on a CPU) reproduces the
expected tokens, including on a prompt that fails in vLLM.

The twin follows a pointer through the KV cache: layer 0 reads the current token, and the layer pairs (2, 3),
(4, 5), (6, 7) and (8, 9) each move the pointer one hop. The wrong first token is the one the twin emits when
the last hop (layers 8 and 9) finds nothing, that is, when their attention returns zero for the last prompt
token. Layers 6-9 are the twin's decoder-replay layers (from `max(kv_source_layer_ids)` = 6 on), the
counterpart of layers 20-39 in the released model. Like those, they read compressed KV from the last KV source
and include a later index source (8 here; 24, 28, 32 and 36 in the released model). We did not trace inside the
layers, so we don't know which op goes wrong.

The first token of a request is computed in its last prefill chunk. So on the twin, a prompt starts with a
wrong token whenever its last chunk runs as a PIECEWISE graph. For a request on its own under the default
`FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, that is a last chunk of 2 to `max_cudagraph_capture_size` tokens. We did not test prompts
that fit in one chunk, or the released weights.

## Related
- #62651 (decoder replay can return incorrect target-token scores): the same replay machinery, but in eager
  mode, through prompt-logprob row trimming. Our eager runs are exact.
- #53257 (DeepSeek-V4-Flash output at temperature 0 changes with concurrency; root cause open): concurrency
  also moves where chunked prefills end. Not verified to be the same cause.

## Repro
```
git clone https://github.com/DiaaAj/probec && cd probec
pip install -e .            # into an environment with vllm 0.32.0
python tools/repro_vllm_v41_tail_chunk.py --budget 8192 --length 8202             # last chunk 10: WRONG
python tools/repro_vllm_v41_tail_chunk.py --budget 8192 --length 8202 --eager     # EXACT
```
On first use, the script builds the twin from the released `config.json` (about 6 GB, a few minutes,
deterministic). It then prints the expected and the generated token ids. `--length 8208` and `--length 8227`
(last chunks 16 and 35) are also wrong, and so is `--compilation-config '{"cudagraph_decoder_replay": false}'`.

## Environment
vLLM 0.32.0 (PyPI wheel, torch 2.13.0+cu130) on one H100 80GB HBM3 (driver 610.57.04) and one H200 NVL (driver
615.71.09). Also nightly 0.32.1rc1.dev183+g7e3d55956 (torch 2.14.0+cu130), with the six-request case, on the
H100. Offline `LLM(...)` with token-id prompts, TP=1, the default `FLASHMLA_SPARSE_DSV41` attention backend.

items.title: [Feature]: Qwen4Exp PLE cpu_offload without UVA (NVIDIA Confidential Computing)
items.author: yeighta
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

**Qwen4Exp PLE `cpu_offload` without UVA, so Qwen3.8-Flash-Next fits a single GPU under NVIDIA Confidential Computing**

`--engram-config.cpu_offload` (#54371, on by default) keeps the Qwen4Exp n-gram PLE table in pinned host memory, and a Triton kernel reads its rows through UVA. Under NVIDIA Confidential Computing (H100 CC on SEV-SNP), the device view of pinned host memory is not coherent. #59981 therefore turns `is_uva_available()` off when it detects CC, and model init then stops in `Qwen4ExpPLEPinnedHostEmbedding.__init__`:

```
RuntimeError: Engram CPU offload requires UVA support
```

Without offload, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next does not fit one GPU. With a W4A16 checkpoint the GPU-side weights are about 67 GiB, but the BF16 PLE table adds about 95 GiB more. So on CC there is currently no way to serve Flash-Next on a single H100.

**Proposal:** when `cpu_offload` is on and UVA is unavailable, gather the rows on the host and copy them to the device explicitly, instead of refusing to start. The table is only looked up, and Flash-Next has one PLE layer (`ple_layer_ids=[2]`), so each step moves about 5 KB per token (16 heads × 160 dims, BF16).

This is the same shape as the disk offload in #59958: before the forward, outside any CUDA graph, `Qwen4ExpModelState.prepare_inputs`

1. computes the n-gram ids on the GPU (existing `ple_ngram_ids` kernel) and reads them back,
2. gathers the rows from the host table with `torch.index_select`,
3. copies them with one H2D into a fixed device buffer.

The forward only reads that buffer, so FULL and PIECEWISE CUDA graphs replay unchanged. The only difference from #59958 is where the rows come from: ordinary host memory instead of the checkpoint files. If #59958 lands first, this could be a host-memory row source behind its staging path.

I have a working prototype on v0.32.0 + #59981 (about 200 lines in `vllm/models/qwen4_exp/{common,nvidia}/ngram_embedding.py` and `nvidia/model_state.py`) and can open a PR if this direction is acceptable.

### Results with the prototype

One H100 NVL 94 GB in CC mode (Azure `Standard_NCC40ads_H100_v5`, driver 580.95.05, CUDA 13.0), vLLM 0.32.0 + #59981 (`f37260ad`) + the prototype, V2 model runner, default `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, `VnimanieAI/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-W4A16`, `--max-model-len 65536 --max-num-seqs 64 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --moe-backend marlin --language-model-only`.

- Memory: 67.2 GiB weights + 14.8 GiB KV cache (514K tokens) on the GPU, table in host RAM.
- Cost of the three steps above (median of 20, same VM): 0.14 ms for 32 tokens, 12–19 ms for an 8192-token prefill chunk. The H2D runs at about 4.1 GB/s, the bounce-buffer limit under CC.
- `vllm bench serve`, random dataset, `--ignore-eos`, total output tok/s / mean TPOT ms:

| concurrency | input 1024 / output 1024 | input 4096 / output 512 |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 121.6 / 8.1 | 112.5 / 8.1 |
| 8 | 630.6 / 12.1 | 532.7 / 12.6 |
| 32 | 1289.9 / 23.5 | 855.7 / 31.4 |

- Correctness: per-token prompt logprobs over 30 fixed texts (5,756 tokens), compared against a naive reference that looks the rows up synchronously inside the forward (`--enforce-eager`). The prototype differs from the reference by a mean |Δlogprob| of 0.052, the same as two runs of the reference against each other (0.052). Leaving the staged rows at zero gives 0.395 and raises the mean NLL from 0.68 to 0.92, so the host table does reach the model.

The cost is a host stall each step: the ids depend on the tokens sampled by the previous step, so the read-back waits for that step to finish and removes some async-scheduling overlap. With no UVA baseline on CC I could not measure that part separately.

### Reproduce the error

```bash
# H100 in CC mode, vLLM 0.32.0 with #59981 applied, V2 model runner
VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 vllm serve VnimanieAI/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-W4A16 \
  --language-model-only --moe-backend marlin --max-model-len 65536
# -> RuntimeError: Engram CPU offload requires UVA support
```

Without #59981, UVA stays on under CC and the V2 runner produces wrong output (#57224).

### Alternatives

- Keep the table on the GPU: does not fit (about 162 GiB total).
- Disk offload (#59958): works without UVA, but in a confidential VM we keep model state off the disk, since storage I/O patterns are visible to the host.
- V1 model runner: `PLE inputs were not prepared`; the PLE inputs are only prepared by the V2 runner's `Qwen4ExpModelState`.

### Additional context

Two unrelated issues hit with this checkpoint on 0.32.0, worked around locally: the fused q/k/v + indexer projection (#59533) fails with `Found different quantization schemes` because the checkpoint keeps the indexer in BF16, and the MoE HUMMING conversion ran out of memory for its 6.25 GiB scratch on a 94 GB GPU (`--moe-backend marlin` avoids it). Happy to file these separately.

cc @ybgao-nvidia (#59981), @stecasta (#59958)

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [RFC] Support VMM Allocations in lmcache-driven
items.author: bluayer
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Serving processes may outlive their GPU allocations. A long-lived inference engine may release most of its HBM so another colocated workload can use it. When its KV remains reusable, LMCache can retain the logical KV in CPU or storage tiers and later restore it into a replacement GPU allocation. Colocated RL is one use of this pattern. Multi-model serving is another: an inactive engine can return HBM for another model server and later resume.

Engine-driven resolves the active GPU allocation in the inference worker for each transfer. lmcache-driven instead relies on an LMCache server registration of that allocation. That registration must be retired before the physical memory can be safely reclaimed and replaced before transfers resume. LMCache has no common lifecycle contract for this transition today, so choosing a virtual memory management (VMM) allocator can make lmcache-driven unavailable.

This RFC keeps both transfer modes available when an inference engine uses VMM allocations. It defines an engine-independent lifecycle contract that coordinates allocation replacement with LMCache registration retirement and re-registration. `vmm_fd` is the "experimental" registration transport to apply this contract to exportable same-node VMM allocations. `framework_ipc` remains the default, and engine-driven is unchanged.

## Terminology

- **Inference engine:** the vLLM or SGLang serving runtime, including its control components and execution workers. It coordinates scheduling and allocation-lifecycle transitions.
- **Inference worker:** an execution-side process or rank within the inference engine. It runs model execution, creates and holds its local active GPU KV allocation, and hosts the LMCache worker adapter.
- **LMCache server:** the separate LMCache MP process that manages cache storage and server-side transfer work.
- **Engine-driven:** the inference worker performs the GPU-side gather or scatter and exchanges CPU or shared-memory data with the LMCache server.
- **lmcache-driven:** the inference worker submits transfer metadata and synchronization events, while the LMCache server performs the GPU-side transfer against registered device memory.

The transfer-mode names identify where GPU-side KV movement runs. They do not identify allocation ownership. In both modes, each inference worker creates and holds its local active GPU KV allocation, while the inference engine coordinates the allocation lifecycle.

## Motivation

### Preserve transfer choice across GPU-memory handoff

An inference engine may return most of its HBM without exiting. In colocated RL, rollout yields memory to training. In multi-model serving, an inactive engine can yield memory to another model server and later resume. If KV from the same model version remains useful, LMCache can keep it in CPU or storage tiers until a replacement GPU allocation is ready.

Public inference-engine support for these allocation lifecycles is clearest today in colocated RL:

- The [vLLM Q3 2026 RL roadmap](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48314) models transitions between sleeping and awake, paused and running, old and new weights, and stale and fresh KV. Its [scheduler lifecycle RFC](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48311) covers drain, sleep, wake, weight update, and releasing only KV between rollout steps.
- [SGLang's RL integration](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/advanced_features/sglang_for_rl.md) exposes tagged release and resume operations for `kv_cache` and `weights`. Releasing `kv_cache` flushes its logical contents, so these operations define the engine-side memory lifecycle but do not preserve reusable KV outside the released allocation.

These interfaces define when the inference engine releases and restores an allocation. They do not define whether logical KV remains valid or where it is stored while the GPU allocation is absent. Engine-driven already works with these lifecycle interfaces because no imported engine allocation survives in the LMCache server. The remaining compatibility gap is lmcache-driven, whose cross-process registration must be retired before the inference worker releases the physical memory.

The lifecycle boundary may support broader reusable-KV policies in the future, but those policies are outside this RFC.

### VMM breaks the current direct-access registration

The current lmcache-driven registration format cannot represent arbitrary VMM allocations held by an inference worker.

VMM separates the virtual address from the lifetime of the physical memory:

```text
allocation lifetime #1: pointer X -> physical allocation A
release:                pointer X -> unmapped
allocation lifetime #2: pointer X -> physical allocation B
```

The pointer can remain `X`, but an IPC registration for allocation A must not be used for allocation B. Supporting only initial VMM import would therefore be unsafe; LMCache must also drain, retire, and replace registrations as part of the inference worker's allocation lifecycle.

### What this proposal changes

The required interface has two ordering points: retire the current registration before allocator mutation, then register the replacement before transfer resumes. It also needs a unique identity for each allocation lifetime so a reused virtual address cannot resolve stale work to new physical memory.

The contract is defined around allocation retirement and replacement. `vmm_fd` applies it to exportable same-node VMM allocations; `framework_ipc` remains the default and engine-driven is unchanged.

## Proposal

The proposal has two parts:

1. An engine-independent lifecycle contract for retiring and replacing an LMCache-visible GPU allocation.
2. `vmm_fd`, an experimental same-node transport for registering POSIX-FD-exportable VMM allocations under this lifecycle contract.

The lifecycle contract is transport-independent. `vmm_fd` uses POSIX FDs on Linux, but a future transport could use CUDA Fabric or another pla

items.title: [L2][fs_native] Failed stores stay visible to lookups — later retrieves serve corrupted KV (gibberish output)
items.author: stefanskiasan
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With the `fs_native` L2 adapter enabled, `Store task N to adapter 0 failed for
keys: [...]` warnings appear at a low but steady rate — and **every subsequent
retrieve that hits one of those keys returns corrupted KV**. The model answer
degenerates into gibberish, at temperature 0, reproducibly.

The failed store leaves the key visible to lookups. It is only a `WARNING`; no
exception is raised, and the key is not invalidated.

## Environment

- 8× MI355X (gfx950), ROCm 7.2.3, one server per 4-GPU replica
- vLLM with `glm_moe_dsa` (GLM-5.3, full model), TP4, MTP k=4,
  `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, `--block-size 16`, prefix caching on
- `LMCacheMPConnector`, `lmcache_driven` transfer mode, chunk-size 256
- Server: `--l1-size-gb 150 --separate-object-groups --eviction-policy LRU`
  `--l2-prefetch-policy retain`
  `--l2-adapter '{"type":"fs_native","base_path":"/l2","num_workers":8,"use_odirect":false}'`

## Reproduction

Two replicas, identical except for the L2 adapter:

| | replica A | replica B |
|---|---|---|
| `--l2-adapter fs_native` | yes | **no** |
| failed stores | 44 → 66 during eight requests | **0** in 25 049 stores |
| answers on a cache hit | **gibberish** | correct |

The cleanest probe is `cache_salt`, which changes only the cache key:

```
prompt without salt   (cache hit)   3.4 s   GARBAGE  '0.  district120 is0, the ...'
same prompt, new salt (cache miss)  5.0 s   CORRECT  '73605 The user has provided ...'
same prompt, new salt (cache miss)  5.0 s   CORRECT
prompt without salt   (cache hit)   3.4 s   GARBAGE  '1 district contains1.3,. ...'
```

Note the timing: the corrupted runs are **faster** than the correct ones —
they are served from the cache instead of being computed.

The corruption survives a full vLLM restart (the cache server outlives it) and
survives restarting the cache server itself, because new failures keep
occurring: 22 fresh failures during the eight requests above.

## Not the cause

- Disk: write test 4.9 GB/s into the L2 directory, inodes at 1 %, 459 GB free,
  ext4, no errors in the log and no traceback anywhere.
- vLLM side: with LMCache disabled entirely (prefix caching still on), all
  eight requests are correct.
- Recreating the same server **without** `--l2-adapter` makes the problem
  disappear completely: 0 failed stores, 8/8 correct, needle test 5/5 twice
  (the second run with a warm cache).

## Expected

A store that fails must not leave a lookup-visible key. Either the key is
rolled back on failure, or the retrieve path must validate that all object
groups for a key are actually present before serving it. Silently serving a
partially stored entry turns an I/O warning into a correctness bug that looks
like model failure — it cost us two and a half hours of debugging the model
before we suspected the cache.

Related: #4987 (IPC event churn on ROCm in the same connector).

items.title: [Bug] P2P load timeout can report terminal failure while the transfer is still active
items.author: 0andy
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`P2PL2Adapter.query_load_result()` returns a terminal all-zero `Bitmap` as soon as `load_timeout_s` expires, without querying or cancelling the underlying `TransferChannelClient` read ([p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336)). The read may still be in flight at that point, so the adapter reports "finished (failed)" for a load whose transfer has not reached a terminal state.

The existing test `test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure` asserts exactly this behaviour, so I am raising it as a contract question rather than a regression: is a terminal load result allowed to precede the end of the transfer?

**To Reproduce**

On `dev` @ 8d7d2c47, add this test to `tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py`:

```python
def test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight():
    keys = [_key(0)]
    now = [100.0]
    in_flight = TransferChannelReadResult(finished=False)
    with (
        _adapter(load_timeout_s=0.01) as (adapter, _mq, _tc_ctx, tc_client, _n),
        patch.object(p2p_mod.time, "monotonic", side_effect=lambda: now[0]),
    ):
        adapter._remote_addresses[keys[0]] = TransferChannelAddress(offset=100, size=10)
        tc_client.submit_read.return_value = 123
        tc_client.query_read_status.return_value = in_flight
        task_id = adapter.submit_load_task(
            keys, [MagicMock(shm_offset=0, shm_byte_length=10)]
        )
        now[0] = 100.02  # past the 0.01 s load deadline
        assert not in_flight.is_finished()
        assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
```

```
pytest -v tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py -k "deadline or not_finished"
```

Result (CPU-only build, transfer channel mocked):

```
>           assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
E           assert 0 is None
E            +  where 0 = query_load_result(0)

LMCache WARNING: P2P load task 0 timed out; treating as a failure (p2p_l2_adapter.py:335)

test_lookup_deadline_expired_yields_miss PASSED
test_load_not_finished_returns_none PASSED
test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure PASSED
test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight FAILED
1 failed, 3 passed
```

(`0` is the repr of a one-key, all-zero `Bitmap`, i.e. a terminal failure.)

This test only demonstrates the current behaviour; its assertion would need adjusting depending on which direction below is preferred.

**Expected behavior**

Either the adapter does not report a terminal load result while its transfer-channel read may still access the destination buffers, or the contract states explicitly that a terminal result does not imply the transfer has quiesced and callers handle that.

**Additional context**

To be clear about what is and is not shown:

*Reproduced (unit test above):* the read is modelled as unfinished, and after the deadline `query_load_result()` returns a terminal failure.

*Derived from reading the code, not reproduced:*
- On that result, `PrefetchController._poll_load_results()` calls `finish_write_and_delete()` for the failed keys and then `submit_unlock()` ([prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395)); for P2P, `submit_unlock()` sends `p2p_unlock_objects` to the peer ([#L277-L280](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L277-L280)). So both the destination staging buffer and the source-side lock are released.
- The NIXL transfer channel registers the whole L1 buffer once ([nixl_impl.py#L344](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L344)). This creates a window in which a late read may write into memory that has since been reassigned to another key.
- After the timeout the adapter no longer queries the read, so the `NixlTransferChannelClient._tasks` entry and its xfer handle are only released on `close()` ([#L178-L181](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L178-L181), [#L202-L206](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L202-L206)).

*Not reproduced:* actual stale or corrupted KV data end to end. I have not run a two-instance NIXL test for this.

**Possible directions** (not proposing a specific fix yet)

- **A. Stay pending until the transfer is terminal.** After the deadline, keep polling `query_read_status()` and only report once it finishes. Simple ownership model; a hung transfer would hold its buffers and locks indefinitely.
- **B. Add per-task cancellation to `TransferChannelClient`** ([abstract.py#L52-L88](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/abstract.py#L52-L88) has only `submit_read`, `query_read_status`, `close`), and report terminal only once the cancel is confirmed. For NIXL this would map to `releaseXferReq`, which the BackendGuide says "can return error, meaning it was not successful in aborting the request", so it still needs A as a fallback. The Mooncake wrapper has no cancel today; I have not checked the engine itself.
- **C. Drop the adapter-level load deadline** and rely on the controller-level deadline from #5255, which already keeps late loads' buffers and locks until the load result arrives.

The P2P adapter is the runtime caller of `submit_read()`; the transfer-channel benchmark also calls it directly, so an API change in B would touch both.

**Related**

- #5263 — same ownership family, on the shutdown / TTL paths rat
items.author_work_intent: If maintainers agree this is a contract gap, I'm happy to work on the fix. I'd especially appreciate guidance on whether the preferred direction is to keep timed-out reads pending until terminal, add a TransferChannel cancell

comments.author: holtwood
comments.body:
I checked another timeout case at [`1ca53a8`](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/1ca53a8aadca1d054f171fd67350be35797cfddc/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L326-L347) using the original query methods with mocked dependencies. I haven't run a real NIXL transfer.

Even when the transfer is already marked `DONE`, polling after the deadline returns a zero bitmap without calling `query_read_status`. The adapter removes its task, so later adapter polls return `None`. The client's `close()` still has a separate cleanup path.

This seems worth covering in the timeout tests, including cleanup of an already-completed transfer. I can help add that case if it's useful.

items.title: Unauthenticated fleet control plane on LMCache MP Coordinator (default 0.0.0.0:9300)
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

The LMCache MP Coordinator — the fleet-level cache control plane — starts by default on 0.0.0.0:9300 with no authentication on any endpoint. A network peer registers fake cache instances, deregisters real ones (removing them from scheduling), rewrites tenant quotas, injects fabricated cache events, and enumerates the fleet's key directory. Runtime-confirmed on lmcache 0.5.5 (latest PyPI release); the companion controller API server (`lmcache.v1.api_server`, default 0.0.0.0:9000) exposes the same unauthenticated /lookup, /clear and /pin surface. Suggested severity: High, CVSS 8.8.

### Details

`lmcache.v1.mp_coordinator.config` hardcodes `host: str = "0.0.0.0", port: int = 9300`. The coordinator's FastAPI app (`lmcache/v1/mp_coordinator/app.py`) mounts routers with no authentication middleware anywhere in the package (a full-source scan for api_key/auth/token primitives returns zero hits):

- `POST /instances` / `PUT /instances/{id}/heartbeat` / `DELETE /instances/{id}` — anyone registers, keeps alive, or removes fleet instances; deletion removes the instance's reported placements from scheduling.
- `PUT /quota/config` and `PUT /quota/{cache_salt}` — fleet and per-tenant quota tampering.
- `POST /cache/pins`, `DELETE /cache/pins`, `POST /events` — pin manipulation and fabricated cache events that feed the coordinator's placement/eviction views.
- `GET /directory/keys` (paged), `POST /directory/lookup`, `POST /directory/blend-lookup` — full key directory with token-id lists and per-instance placements.

The controller API server (`lmcache/v1/api_server/__main__.py`, `--host` default 0.0.0.0, port 9000) adds `POST /lookup` (token-to-placement layout), `POST /clear` and `POST /pin` for any instance_id, likewise with no authentication.

### PoC

Environment: Linux, `pip install lmcache==0.5.5`, `python -m lmcache.v1.mp_coordinator --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9300` (`ss -ltnp` confirms 0.0.0.0:9300). From any peer:

```bash
curl -s http://192.168.105.123:9300/healthz                       # 200
# register a fake instance (schemas read from the installed package's pydantic models)
curl -s -X POST http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @fake_instance.json   # 200/201
curl -s http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances                      # fake instance listed
curl -s -X PUT http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances/attacker-mp-aaa/heartbeat -d @hb.json      # 200
# remove an instance from the fleet
curl -s -X DELETE http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances/attacker-mp-bbb                          # 200
# quota tampering and event injection
curl -s -X PUT http://192.168.105.123:9300/quota/config -d @quota.json                           # 200
curl -s -X PUT http://192.168.105.123:9300/quota/default -d '{"...": 0}'                         # 200
curl -s -X POST http://192.168.105.123:9300/events -d @fake_events.json                          # 200
# fleet key directory
curl -s "http://192.168.105.123:9300/directory/keys?limit=100"                                   # keys+placements
```

Observed on 0.5.5: every call above succeeded without any credential; the fake instance appeared in `GET /instances`, the DELETE removed an instance, quota writes were accepted, `/events` accepted a fabricated batch, and `/directory/keys` returned the directory enumeration surface. The api_server on 0.0.0.0:9000 likewise answered unauthenticated `/lookup` (200 with layout structure) and accepted `/clear` and `/pin` requests. Expected secure behavior: a fleet control plane authenticates callers and authorizes instance/quota mutations.

### Impact

Any network peer that can reach the coordinator port (fixed, documented default 9300, bound on all interfaces) corrupts the fleet's shared cache state: deregistered workers disappear from placement (requests lose their cache or fail over), fake instances redirect placement decisions, quota tampering starves or floods tenants, injected events poison placement and eviction views, and the key directory discloses which prefixes (token id lists) are cached where across the fleet. Confidentiality (directory/placement disclosure), integrity (fleet membership, quotas, events), availability (instance removal, quota starvation). Suggested CVSS:3.1 vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:H (8.8), CWE-306. Affected: lmcache <= 0.5.5 (latest release), deployments running the MP coordinator / controller API server; no patched version yet.

items.title: Engine shutdown: per-step time limits do not let shutdown continue past a stuck step
items.author: russfellows
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The engine's shutdown applies time limits to some steps, such as closing components and destroying the engine, but those limits do not let shutdown move on. When a step's wait times out, the timeout is logged, and then shutdown still waits for that same step to finish before it goes to the next one. A step that never finishes therefore blocks shutdown forever, and every later step is skipped.

## When it happens

Any step under one of these time limits hangs or runs longer than its limit, for example a storage component that does not finish closing.

## Observed

Checked against current `dev` with a step that blocks. The timeout message for that step was logged after about five seconds, but shutdown did not reach the next step until the blocked step was released by hand. The same pattern is used both for closing components and for destroying the engine.

## Impact

- Shutdown is not bounded by the configured limits, and a single stuck component can hang it indefinitely.
- Under a process manager or an operator that sends a hard kill after a grace period, the later shutdown steps never run.

## Expected

After a step's time limit expires, shutdown should log the timeout and continue with the next step without waiting for the timed-out one. The stuck step can be left running in the background.

## Done when

- With a step that never finishes, shutdown passes that step after its limit and runs the remaining steps.
- The total shutdown time is about the sum of the configured limits.
- This is covered by a test.

items.title: [Bug] Isolated IPC: timeline-semaphore record/wait fail with CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_CONTEXT on threads without a current context
items.author: VikingDeng
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

With `--isolated-ipc`, the timeline-semaphore event backend fails when a thread that hasn't made any CUDA runtime call records or waits on an event:

```
RuntimeError: cuStreamWriteValue64 (record) failed: <CUresult.CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_CONTEXT: 201>
```

The driver calls are wrapped in `with torch.cuda.device(idx)`. If `idx` is already the thread's current device (e.g. 0 on a new thread), that doesn't call `cudaSetDevice`, so there's no current context. On an explicit stream the call still works, but on the default stream (handle 0) it fails. `WorkerTransfer.create_transfer_event` records on `current_stream()`, so any producer that records from a worker thread runs into this.

You can see it with `lmcache bench server`, which runs clients in threads when `--concurrency` > 1. With isolated IPC on both sides (server `--isolated-ipc`, and the bench client's policy set via `set_isolated_ipc(True)`, since the bench has no flag for it), c=1 works and c=4 / c=8 fail every time.

**To Reproduce**

```python
import threading, torch
from lmcache.v1.platform.devices.cuda.timeline_semaphore_event_ipc import TimelineSemaphoreEventIPCBackend

dev = torch.device("cuda", 0)
be = TimelineSemaphoreEventIPCBackend()
ev = be.create_event(dev); be.record_event(ev, torch.cuda.current_stream(dev))  # fine on the main thread

def worker():
    e = be.create_event(dev)
    be.record_event(e, torch.cuda.current_stream(dev))  # CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_CONTEXT

t = threading.Thread(target=worker); t.start(); t.join()
```

On the fresh thread, `current_stream()`, `default_stream()` and `stream=None` all fail. A stream created on the main thread works.

**Expected behavior**

Record and wait should work from any thread, the same as with the default event backend.

**Environment**

LMCache `dev` @ dbe22ef8, torch 2.13.0+cu130, cuda-python 13.4.4, driver 580.173.02, RTX 3090, Python 3.12.

Fix in #5929.

items.title: [MP] gRPC codec converts repeated int fields one item at a time
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
The gRPC codec handles `repeated int64` fields with a Python loop that calls `int()` on every item, both when encoding and when decoding (`proto_codec.py`). Every cache key carries its token IDs in one of these fields, so a lookup for an 8K-token prompt runs `int()` 8,192 times on the client and 8,192 more times on the server. The calls don't change anything, since protobuf already hands back Python ints and type-checks values in C.

They do cost a lot, though. For an 8K-token `IpcCacheServerKey`, the conversion takes about 450 µs in each direction, while protobuf itself parses the message in about 18 µs. Since the server mostly runs on one core because of the GIL, this alone limits gRPC lookups to about 1,100 req/s at 8K tokens and 375 req/s at 32K. KV event batches hit the same path through their token IDs.

Passing the whole sequence to protobuf in one call (`extend(value)` / `tuple(field)`) avoids the loop. I mentioned this in #5906 as something to look at separately, and I have a small PR for it.

items.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
items.author: catnanami
items.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

items.title: Misc. bug: Nemotron 3 / 3.5 GGUFs are tagged "pixtral" and get the wrong pre-tokenizer
items.author: tkran2
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

b11757-20-g839a572a4 (master 839a572a4), built from source, macOS, Apple M4 Pro

### Operating systems

Mac

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core library), Python/Bash scripts

### Command line

```shell
./build/bin/llama-tokenize -m NVIDIA-Nemotron3-Nano-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf -p "दी" --ids --log-disable --no-bos
./build/bin/test-tokenizer-0 ggml-vocab-nemotron-h.gguf
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

For the Nemotron 3/3.5 GGUFs, the Llama 3 pre-tokenizer regex is used by llama.cpp. This is because the converter's `chkhsh` for the Nemotron tokenizer is the same as Pixtral-12B's (`0e9433cb…`), therefore `tokenizer.ggml.pre = "pixtral"`. `llama-vocab.cpp` maps "pixtral" to LLAMA3. This is correct for Pixtral since its tokenizer.json utilizes the Llama 3 regex, but it is incorrect for Nemotron, whose tokenizer.json uses the Tekken regex. Additionally, Nemotron's `clean_up_tokenization_spaces` is false, however the LLAMA3 branch sets `clean_spaces` to be on.

The affected GGUFs include NVIDIA's `Nemotron-3-Nano-4B-GGUF` and `Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-24GB-GGUF`, ggml-org's `Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B` and `Super-VL-120B-A12B`, and GGUFs from Unsloth, bartowski and LM Studio, with over 500k downloads last month. It is also inconsistent between publishers: Unsloth's Bolt BF16 is tagged "tekken".

To reproduce, read `tokenizer.ggml.pre` from NVIDIA's Nano 4B Q4_K_M GGUF, which is `pixtral`. `llama-tokenize ... -p "दी" --no-bos` gives `[4894, 2063]`, while Hugging Face `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-4B-BF16` gives `[44213]` for the same text. A test vocab (update-script strings plus Hindi/Thai) has 2 failures on master. The exact commands and output are in the logs below.

The effect is different token counts for llama.cpp versus HF: for Hindi, 27 instead of 16, for Tamil 20 instead of 15, for Telugu 15 instead of 11, for Bengali 19 instead of 15, and for Thai 18 instead of 15. English is the same. In decode, it drops the space before punctuation, so `" !"` returns as `"!"`. With InferCheck (https://github.com/tkran2/infercheck) there are 1,175 encode + 564 decode mismatches out of 22,794 total strings.

The tests miss this bug because the converter's standard test strings tokenize the same under both regexes with this vocab, which is also the reason for the hash collision.

The fix is a load-time fix that I tested: if pre == "pixtral" and arch is `nemotron_h` / `nemotron_h_moe`, then use TEKKEN. This fixes the already published GGUFs, with Pixtral unchanged. With it, `test-tokenizer-0` passes 15/15 and mismatches go to 0. The alternative is to detect it in the converter, for new conversions only. Which method would be preferred, or both? I could open a PR and add a test vocab to ggml-org/vocabs. This is the same Tekken regex as #30845.

_No response_

pixtral
[4894, 2063]
[44213]
operator() : failed test:    'दी हिन्दी'

items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

b11769-14-g339f3242c

### Operating systems

Mac

libllama (core library)

### Command line

```shell
# harness: https://github.com/tkran2/infercheck/blob/main/harness/llama_tok/llamatok.cpp (llama_tokenize + llama_detokenize)
python - <<'EOF'
import subprocess
V='../llama.cpp/models/ggml-vocab-gemma-4.gguf'; T='harness/llama_tok/llamatok'
for s in ['if (x != y) {', 'x = a ? b : c', "It 's fine"]:

    dec=subprocess.run([T,V,'--decode'],input=ids+'\n',capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.split('\n')[0]
    print(repr(s), '->', repr(bytes.fromhex(dec).decode()))
EOF
'if (x != y) {' -> 'if (x!= y) {'
'x = a ? b : c' -> 'x = a? b : c'
"It 's fine" -> "It's fine"

python -c "from transformers import AutoTokenizer; t=AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('google/gemma-4-12b-it'); ids=t.encode('if (x != y) {', add_special_tokens=False); print(ids, repr(t.decode(ids)))"

```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

The spaces before . , ! ? and before 's 'm 're 've are deleted by common_detokenize as well as llama_detokenize. The text is unchanged by Hugging Face; clean_up_tokenization_spaces is not set or it is false for these models. The cause of this problem is that clean_spaces = true is set in llama-vocab.cpp for every one of the BPE vocabs and it is turned off for just some of the pretokenizers (qwen2, deepseek, qwen35, and command-r). The Hugging Face setting is not stored by the GGUF. The models which are affected are Gemma 4, GLM-4.x/5.x, LFM2, Mellum2, Nemotron (pixtral), Granite 4.1 (dbrx), and MiniCPM5. This can be seen by users in llama-mtmd-cli chat history, which is afterwards retokenized, the server's prompt field, and any app which calls llama_detokenize. Streamed output on the other hand is not affected. The scale of this issue is that it affects 71 of the 500 most downloaded GGUF repos, with 20.7 million downloads in only 30 days. A related PR is #28472, which just adds a way of reading the setting. A question I have: store the Hugging Face's setting in the GGUF or change the default? I would be happy to open the PR.

items.title: CPU backend: garbage output (repetition loops) for the qwen35 hybrid family (Qwen3.8-27B / Holo4), while the Vulkan backend serves the same binary and GGUF correctly
items.author: baustin27
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The **CPU backend** produces garbage for the qwen35 hybrid family (24 Gated DeltaNet + 4 gated full-attention layers), while the **Vulkan backend serves the same binary and the same GGUF correctly**.

Concretely, on this box:

* `llama.cpp` b11756, `Qwen3.8-27B-AD-IQ3_XXS.gguf` (the *base* model, a plain IQ3_XXS — **not** an imatrix/i1 quant), Intel Arc Pro B70:
  * `--device none` → every prompt degenerates into a repetition loop.
  * `--device Vulkan0` → correct answers.
* Same result with `Holo4-27B.i1-IQ4_XS.gguf` and with `Holo4-27B.i1-IQ3_M.gguf`.

This is the mirror image of #21888 (garbage on Vulkan Intel, correct on CPU), so it looks like a separate defect rather than a known one.

## What was measured

CPU (`--device none`):

```
"2+2"                ->  "+ + + + + + + + + …"
"capital of France"  ->  "capitale capitale capitale capitale …"
"… before writing his report …"  ->  "writingwritingwritingwritingwriting…"
"Paris is the capital of France. ×3 …"  ->  "])])])])])])])])])])])])])])"
```

Vulkan (`--device Vulkan0`), same binary, same GGUF:

```
"2+2"                ->  "4"
"capital of France"  ->  "Paris"
"Paris is the capital of France. ×3 …"  ->  "The first sentence is \"Paris is the capital of France.\""
```

The CPU output is not random noise: it is a **repetition loop whose repeated token is drawn from the prompt** ("writing", "capitale", "+"), which is the classic signature of a model that cannot use the context and falls back to the highest-probability continuation.

## Repro

```bash
# CPU (garbage)
./llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-AD-IQ3_XXS.gguf \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 18995 -c 32768 --device none -t 8 --jinja \
  --reasoning off --reasoning-format none \
  --chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":false}'
# then:
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18995/v1/chat/completions -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 2 + 2? Reply with just the number."}],
       "max_tokens":48,"temperature":0.2,"chat_template_kwargs":{"enable_thinking":false}}'
# -> content: " \"+ \"+ \"+ \"+ \"+ …"

# Vulkan (correct) — same binary, same GGUF
./llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-AD-IQ3_XXS.gguf \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 18992 -c 32768 -ngl 99 -fa on --device Vulkan0 --jinja \
  --reasoning off --reasoning-format none \
  --chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":false}'
# -> content: "4"
```

Environment: Intel Arc Pro B70 (Xe2 / Battlemage), Vulkan driver Mesa 26.2.5 (ANV), Level Zero 1.3+, oneAPI 2026.2, Ubuntu 24.04, tag b11756.

## Notes

* Not the quant: the base `IQ3_XXS` model fails identically, and so do all five `i1` Holo4 GGUFs. Nothing i1-specific is required.
* Not the chat template: `--jinja` is on in both runs above, and the rendered prompt is byte-identical between the CPU and Vulkan servers (`/apply-template` returns the same string).
* Not the KV cache dtype: the CPU failure is the same with `-ctk/-ctv f16` and `q4_0`.
* It is specific to this architecture family in a way that looks like the Gated DeltaNet path: the family is 24 GDN + 4 attention layers, and a state-carrying layer whose CPU implementation is wrong would produce exactly this — a model that cannot use the context.
* Related, possibly the same root cause on the GPU side: [#27756](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/27756) (silent instant-EOS beyond ~130k context for Qwen3.8-27B) and [#29493](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/29493) (`test-recurrent-state-rollback` failing deterministically for the qwen35 arch). If the CPU recurrent-state path and the GPU one share a code path, this may be the same bug seen from two angles.
