items.title: [Performance]: Nemotron-3.5-Lightning NVFP4 decode ~16% slower on DGX Spark (GB10/SM121) since v0.29.0
items.author: saveriospeziali
items.body_excerpt:
### Report of performance regression

Single-request decode of `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4` on DGX Spark (GB10, SM121) is **~16% slower from v0.29.0 onward** without speculative decoding, and ~8% slower with DSpark. v0.30.0 and current nightly do not recover it.

Same host, same command line, same weights, official images run back to back; only the image tag changes.

**Without speculative decoding** (decode tok/s, 1 request, 512 generated tokens, median of 5):

| image | greedy | temp 0.6 |
|---|---|---|
| v0.28.0 | **67.9** (67.7–68.0) | 67.1 |
| v0.29.0 | **57.2** (57.1–57.5) | 56.9 |

**With DSpark** (`num_speculative_tokens=3`), greedy, median of 5:

| image | decode tok/s | draft acceptance |
|---|---|---|
| v0.26.1rc1.dev994+gd626108b1 | 102.7 | 56% |
| v0.27.1 | 98.1 | 52% |
| v0.28.0 | **100.7** | 56% |
| v0.29.0 | **92.8** | 54% |
| v0.30.0 | 93.2 | 57% |
| v0.30.1rc1.dev558+g0cbac6cd1 (nightly) | 95.1 | 58% |

Draft acceptance is unchanged, so the drafter is not the cause; the per-step cost of the target went up.

**What I ruled out**

- **Model Runner V2**: v0.28.0 with `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1` gives 101.0 tok/s (DSpark, greedy), the same as default v0.28.0. (V1 cannot be tested on v0.29+: "Model Runner V1 does not support: dspark speculative decoding".)
- **Mamba SSU backend**: with `--mamba-backend=triton` instead of `flashinfer` the gap remains (DSpark, greedy: v0.28.0 102.7 → v0.29.0 95.2).
- **CUDA graphs**: both versions capture the same graphs (35 PIECEWISE, 17 FULL, 17 dspark FULL).
- **torch / CUDA / triton**: identical in both images (torch 2.13.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, triton 3.7.1).

What does differ between the two images: FlashInfer 0.6.16.post3 → 0.6.18 (#54313), fastsafetensors 0.3.3 → 0.4.0, and vLLM itself. Both versions select the same kernels in the log: `MARLIN` NvFp4 MoE backend, `MarlinNvFp4LinearKernel`, `FlashInferFP8ScaledMMLinearKernel`, `FLASH_ATTN` for the target. Possibly related, not verified: #54048 (cuBLAS out_dtype router GEMM on all archs including GB10) and #54427 (weight-only NVFP4 routed through W4A16), both in v0.29.0. #58624 is a different SM12x decode regression (DeepGEMM MoE); this model uses Marlin for the MoE.

### Command (without speculative decoding)

```bash
docker run --gpus all --shm-size 8g -p 8803:8000 \
  -v $HF_CACHE:/root/.cache/huggingface vllm/vllm-openai:v0.29.0 \
  --model=nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \
  --served-model-name=Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B \
  --tensor-parallel-size=1 --trust-remote-code \
  --gpu-memory-utilization=0.7 --max-model-len=262144 \
  --max-num-seqs=32 --max-num-batched-tokens=8192 \
  --kv-cache-dtype=bfloat16 --moe-backend=marlin \
  --mamba-backend=flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode=align \
  --enable-chunked-prefill --enable-prefix-caching \
  --load-format=fastsafetensors \
  --override-generation-config='{"temperature":0.6,"top_p":0.8,"top_k":20}' \
  --reasoning-parser=nemotron_v3 --tool-call-parser=qwen3_coder --enable-auto-tool-choice
```

For the DSpark numbers, add:
`--speculative-config='{"model":"nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4-DSpark","num_speculative_tokens":3}'`

### Measurement

Streaming `/v1/chat/completions`, `max_tokens=512`, a fresh UUID at the start of each prompt (no prefix-cache hits), one warmup request discarded. Decode rate = (completion_tokens − 1) / (time of last delta − time of first delta), counting both `content` and `reasoning` deltas. Draft acceptance from the `vllm:spec_decode_num_accepted_tokens_total` / `vllm:spec_decode_num_draft_tokens_total` deltas on `/metrics`.

### Environment

- NVIDIA DGX Spark, GB10 (SM121), 128 GB unified memory, driver 580.178.04
- Ubuntu 24.04.5, kernel 7.0.0-1019-nvidia, Docker 29.6.2
- `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.28.0` (`sha256:61fc8a896b0a…`) vs `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.29.0` (`sha256:c29147676055…`), linux/arm64

items.title: [Bug]: FlashInfer fp4_gemm autotune changes temperature-0 tokens on Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 (SM120)
items.author: jpvelasco
items.body_excerpt:
### Environment

`collect_env.py` was not captured from the container. The versions below are from the official image logs.

- Image: `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.32.0`
- Digest: `sha256:befccf0e7e4089aa23926bb6f887a85c0d46c2a99e6de5c5ffdf5cb7957c5b34`
- Engine: vLLM 0.32.0, V1
- FlashInfer: 0.7.0.post1 (autotune cache directory), arch folder `120f`
- GPU: 1x NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090, 32 GB, SM120
- Process env: `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True`
- Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4`
- Revision: `16b6615af3548b88e2d8e382457bc705b00479cf`
- Resolved architecture: `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, MTP `Qwen3_5MTP`
- `dtype=torch.bfloat16`, quantization `compressed-tensors`, `kv_cache_dtype=fp8`
- Startup log: `Using FlashInferCutlassNvFp4LinearKernel for NVFP4 GEMM`
- Startup log: `Using FlashInfer GDN prefill kernel (requested=auto, head_k_dim=128)`
- Attention log: FlashInfer, prefill and decode `torch.bfloat16`, decode backend `xqa`, KV `torch.float8_e4m3fn`, arch `sm120`

### Bug

`--enable-flashinfer-autotune` changes a temperature-0 completion on this build. The server stays up. The same prompt, seed, and flags produce different code, and that code fails a unit test that passes with `--no-enable-flashinfer-autotune`.

This is one pair of fresh processes of the same image. The only intentional difference is the autotune flag. Both boots logged `GPU KV cache size: 166,616 tokens`. Both set piecewise CUDA graphs with capture size `[1]`. The failing request was the first generation after startup, and it was text only.

### Shared serve flags

```text
vllm serve unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 \
  --revision 16b6615af3548b88e2d8e382457bc705b00479cf \
  --max-model-len 163840 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.98 \
  --max-num-seqs 1 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 2048 \
  --enable-chunked-prefill \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --async-scheduling \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image":2,"video":1}' \
  --media-io-kwargs '{"video":{"num_frames":16}}' \
  --mm-processor-cache-gb 0.5 \
  --generation-config vllm \
  --default-chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":true,"preserve_thinking":true}' \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder \
  --spec-method mtp \
  --spec-tokens 3 \
  --optimization-level 3 \
  --performance-mode interactivity \
  --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"PIECEWISE","cudagraph_capture_sizes":[1]}'
```

One process added `--no-enable-flashinfer-autotune`. The other added `--enable-flashinfer-autotune`.

### Request

`POST /v1/chat/completions` with `temperature=0`, `seed=12345`, `max_tokens=2048`, `stream=false`, and `reasoning_effort=none`.

System message: `You write correct, minimal Python modules that pass hidden tests.`

User message:

```text
Output a single Python module only. No markdown. No tests.

Implement class TTLCache with:
- __init__(self, maxsize: int, ttl: float, timer: Callable[[], float] | None = None)
- get(self, key, default=None)
- put(self, key, value) -> None
- delete(self, key) -> bool
- cleanup(self) -> int
- stats(self) -> dict[str, int]

Rules:
- maxsize must be positive, ttl must be non-negative.
- get returns default for missing or expired keys.
- get of a live key refreshes LRU recency but not expiry.
- put inserts or updates a key, refreshes recency, and resets its expiry.
- delete returns True only if a live key was removed.
- cleanup removes expired keys and returns the count removed.
- LRU eviction applies only among live entries after expired entries are cleaned.
- stats returns exactly these keys: size, maxsize, hits, misses, evictions, expired.
```

The check that fails does this: `put("a")`, `put("b")`, `get("a")`, then `put("c")` on a cache with `maxsize=2`. That last `put` is the eviction path.

### Observed

Autotune off: `finish_reason=stop`, 756 completion tokens. The module passed. Three other short coding prompts in that same process also passed (token bucket, topological sort, interval merge): 4/4.

Autotune on: startup stayed healthy. The log said `Running FlashInfer autotune with 2048 tokens` and listed buckets `1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 768, 1024, 1280, 1536, 1792, 2048`. It tuned `fp4_gemm` for 16 profiles, twice, then saved 32 configs (32 new, 0 previous). The same TTLCache request finished with `finish_reason=stop` and 736 completion tokens. The generated class defines `cleanup`, and `put` calls `self._cleanup()` once the new key would exceed `maxsize`:

```text
AttributeError: 'TTLCache' object has no attribute '_cleanup'. Did you mean: 'cleanup'?
```

The other three prompts still passed: 3/4.

Expected: autotune selects kernel configs and leaves greedy tokens unchanged for the same weights, seed, and prompt.

### Allocator warnings in the same autotune pass

These warnings did not stop tuning, and the server still served the request. They are included because they happened while `fp4_gemm` was being tuned.

`CUDACachingAllocator` reported that `expandable_segments` failed to map 20971520 bytes. Free memory in those warnings was 18350080 bytes, then 16252928 bytes. Total memory reported was 33670758400 bytes. The autotune log then said the process ended and the 32 configs were saved.

### Search

I looked through open vLLM issues for FlashInfer autotune changing greedy tokens on this NVFP4 checkpoint. The nearby reports are different: tensor-parallel NVFP4 padding, MoE autotune hangs, and FP8 KV backend selection.

items.title: Feature Request: Slow prompt processing when MoE experts are read from disk via mmap - an optimization using O_DIRECT
items.author: A233S
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

When a MoE model is larger than RAM, prompt processing with op offload (copying experts to the GPU) is much slower when the experts are read through mmap than when they are read with O_DIRECT.

### Motivation

With 12GB VRAM, 32GB RAM and a 106.6GB model, the speed of master vs the patch is:

```
GPU: RTX 5070 Ti Laptop 12GB, RAM: 32GB, CPU: i7-14650HX
Disk: ZHITAI TiPlus7100 2TB (PCIe 4.0 NVMe), xfs, Linux 7.0
Model: 106.6GB MoE GGUF (125B-A6B, 512 experts, 10 active), mmap
Base: 4fea119de
Args: -ngl 99 -ncmoe 45 -c 65536 -b 2048 -ub 2048 -t 16 -fa on
Page cache dropped before each run.

prompt tokens | master (t/s) | patched (t/s)
           80 |          4.6 |          16.3
          412 |         13.0 |          48.4
         1332 |         35.3 |         117.5
         3502 |         35.2 |         140.3

disk read during prompt processing: ~1.1 GB/s (master) vs ~4.1-4.9 GB/s (patched)
tg after long prompts: 11.7 t/s (master) vs 14.4 t/s (patched)
correctness: 1332-token prompt, top-3 token probs bit-identical to master over 14 runs
```

In addition, long prompts flush the page cache, which makes token generation slower afterwards.

### Possible Implementation

This is a patch made with Claude Opus 5 xhigh: https://gist.github.com/A233S/64d391631a1ca1341b306bd53aa042c4

When copying experts, the patch does not read them through mmap. It reads them directly with O_DIRECT, with multiple threads, into pinned memory, and uses double buffering to transfer them to the GPU. Experts that are already in the page cache are still read from the cache.
(See above for results.)

Drawbacks:
1. Linux only
2. The patch currently finds the file through /proc/self/maps. A better way would be for the model loader to pass it in.
3. The patch is currently controlled by environment variables, not by parameters.

Related:
- #18758: discusses direct-io at load time; the patch keeps mmap
- #25294: more complex; the patch is only a small change to the existing path

The patch was generated by Claude Opus 5 xhigh. The text was written by me in Chinese and translated to English with Claude.

items.title: [SYCL] Gated DeltaNet produces token soup on long prompts (greedy fails, dense models fine to 131K+)
items.author: baustin27
items.body_excerpt:
# Bug Report: llama.cpp DeltaNet SYCL kernel produces token soup on long prompts

## Environment
- **Hardware**: Intel Arc Pro B70 Graphics (32GB VRAM)
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04
- **llama.cpp**: upstream fb92b3c (also tested ik_llama fork)
- **Compute Runtime**: 26.35.39758.10
- **Models tested**: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B IQ4_XS, Qwen3.8-27B AD-Q4_K_M

## Description
When running Gated DeltaNet hybrid models (Qwen3.6, Qwen3.8) on llama.cpp with SYCL backend, short prompts work correctly but any prompt >~2K tokens produces incoherent "token soup" - repetitive garbage, empty outputs, or multilingual nonsense.

The bug occurs in **both** llama.cpp forks tested:
1. Upstream llama.cpp (commit fb92b3c, built with `-DGGML_SYCL=ON`)
2. ik_llama fork (same SYCL backend)

## Evidence
| Model | Prompt Length | Temp | Result |
|-------|---------------|------|--------|
| Qwen3.6 IQ4_XS | 8K | 0.6 | Token soup (multilingual garbage) |
| Qwen3.6 IQ4_XS | 8K | 0.0 (greedy) | Empty output |
| Qwen3.8 AD-Q4_K_M | 8K | 0.6 | `///` spiral repetition |
| Qwen3.8 AD-Q4_K_M | 8K | 0.0 (greedy) | Empty output |
| Nemotron 3.5 Q4_K_XL | 8K | 0.6 | Empty output |
| **Glimmer-30B Q4_K_XL** | **131K** | **1.0** | **COHERENT** |

**Key finding**: Dense attention models (Glimmer) work to 131K on same binary. Only DeltaNet hybrids fail.

## Minimal Repro
```bash
# Requires Qwen3.6 IQ4_XS GGUF
LLAMA_BIN=./build-sycl2/bin/llama-server \
MODEL_PATH=/models/.../Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf \
CHAT_TEMPLATE_FILE=/path/to/qwen3.6/template.jinja \
USE_JINJA=1 REASONING= REASONING_FORMAT= REASONING_BUDGET= \
CANDIDATE_ID=qwen36-greedy ANCHOR_KEY=QWEN36-RECALL-351 \
BENCH_TEMPERATURE=0.0 BENCH_TOP_P=1.0 BENCH_TOP_K=1 \
CONTEXTS='8192' KV_TYPES='q8_0' MAX_TOKENS=256 \
PROMPT_FILL_RATIO=0.50 REQUEST_TIMEOUT=3600 \
bash scripts/benchmark-iteration.sh .out/test-$(date -u +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
```

**Expected**: Greedy decode retrieves anchor key "QWEN36-RECALL-351" from 8K context.

**Actual**: Empty response, HTTP 200 but no tokens generated.

## Root Cause Hypothesis
The SYCL DeltaNet kernel (`ggml-sycl/gated_delta_net.cpp`) computes the recurrent state update:

```cpp
// Line 91: delta_col = (v_t[col] - g_val * kv_col) * beta_val;
// Line 99: s_shard[r] = g_val * s_shard[r] + k_t[i] * delta_col;
// Line 128: s_shard[r] = sycl::native::exp(g_t[i]) * s_shard[r] + k_t[i] * delta_col;
```

Issues:
1. **No fp32 accumulation** - all math in fp16, recurrent state `s_shard` accumulates error over sequence length
2. **`sycl::native::exp` precision** - may differ from CUDA/CPU implementation
3. **Warp reduction** - `warp_reduce_sum` may lose precision vs CPU sequential sum
4. **State slot management** - `keep_rs_t` template path may have off-by-one in snapshot indexing

The CPU reference in `ggml-cpu/ops.cpp` uses fp32 throughout and is correct.

## Comparison: Dense vs Hybrid
- **Glimmer (dense attention)**: Uses `mul_mat`/`flash_attn` → works to 131K
- **Qwen3.6 (DeltaNet)**: Uses `gated_delta_net` SYCL kernel → fails at 8K

## Fix Proposed
1. **Accumulate in fp32**: Change `s_shard` to `float` (or `double`) even when inputs are fp16
2. **Use precise math**: Replace `sycl::native::exp` with `sycl::exp` or manual fp32 exp
3. **Add fp32 kernel variant**: Template on `ACC_DTYPE` defaulting to float for recurrent state

## Files to Modify
- `ggml/src/ggml-sycl/gated_delta_net.cpp` - main kernel
- `ggml/src/ggml-sycl/ggml-sycl.cpp` - op registration (add fp32-only guard)

## Test Results After Fix
With fp32 accumulation patch (local build):
- Greedy decode at 8K: **anchor retrieved correctly** ✓
- Sampling at 8K: coherent output ✓
- 32K/128K/256K: needs validation

## Impact
- Blocks all DeltaNet hybrid models on Intel GPU via llama.cpp
- Only workaround: CPU offload (5+ min for 8K) or fp32 quantization (not available)

## Request
Review the fp32 accumulation patch for `gated_delta_net.cpp` and consider making fp32 the default for recurrent state in hybrid architectures.

items.title: Eval bug: SYCL F16: NaN output on dense Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_M since #29107 (IQ3 code reorder); fused GEMM off fixes it (Arc Pro B70)
items.author: killercatfish
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version
llama.cpp b11755 (704366d), built with IntelLLVM 2026.1.0, `-DGGML_SYCL=ON -DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON -DGGML_SYCL_DNN=OFF`

### Operating systems
Linux (Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0.0-38, xe driver)

### GGML backends
SYCL

### Hardware
Intel Arc Pro B70 (BMG-G31, 32 GB), Ryzen 5 7600X. Compute runtime 26.22.38646.6, IGC 2.36.3, Level Zero 1.28.6.

### Models
unsloth Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf (dense, hybrid Gated DeltaNet; weights Q4_K/Q5_K/Q6_K)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce
With `GGML_SYCL_F16=ON` (or `GGML_SYCL_DYNAMIC_PRECISION=F16/BF16`), every answer is one odd token followed by
`!!!!...` (token 0, i.e. NaN logits), at any prompt length, even 124 tokens. Turning off only the XMX fused
dequant-GEMM (`GGML_SYCL_XMX_GATHER_TYPES=0`) gives correct output. Bisected to #29107 (see Regression).

```
ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:0 ./llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 -fa on -sm none -c 32768 --jinja
# greedy, thinking off: ask it to repeat a code planted in the prompt
```

| Build / env | Output | Prompt tok/s (2K) |
|---|---|---|
| `GGML_SYCL_F16=OFF` (default) | correct to 14K tokens | ~270 |
| `GGML_SYCL_F16=ON` | `!!!!` garbage, every length | ~640 |
| F16=OFF + `GGML_SYCL_DYNAMIC_PRECISION=F16` | garbage | ~290 |
| F16=OFF + `GGML_SYCL_DYNAMIC_PRECISION=BF16` | garbage (so not f16 overflow) | ~290 |
| F16=ON + `GGML_SYCL_XMX_GATHER_TYPES=0` | **correct** | ~540-700 |
| F16=ON + `GGML_SYCL_DYNAMIC_PRECISION=F32` | correct | ~257 |

Also tried, no change: compute runtime 26.18.38308.1 + IGC 2.34.4 (the `.devops/intel.Dockerfile` pin), flash
attention off. `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT` passes 2273/2273 on the same build, so the test shapes don't reach this
path (they're small; the failing GEMMs here are K=5120, M up to 248320).

**Regression:** same model, same flags, `-DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON`, each tag built fresh:
| tag | result |
|---|---|
| b11491, b11493 (#29245 adds `fused-gemm.cpp`), b11497, b11540, b11565 | correct |
| **b11635** (parent of 529ac893) | **correct** |
| **b11636** (= 529ac893, #29107 "sycl: IQ3 code reorder") | **`!!!!` garbage** |
| b11684, b11685, b11755 | garbage |

#29107 adds "reorder-aware dequantization for subsequent prefill operations" and touches the mul_mat dispatch in
`ggml-sycl.cpp`. Our guess, not verified in the code: after it, the fused GEMM (#29245) reads Q4_K weights in the
reordered layout as if they were plain (or the reverse). Masking out only Q5_K or only Q6_K
(`GGML_SYCL_XMX_GATHER_TYPES`) still gave garbage; masking out only Q4_K was inconclusive (one run, which hit an
unrelated GPU fault on our chipset-slot card before answering).
Workaround until fixed: `GGML_SYCL_XMX_GATHER_TYPES=0`, or `GGML_SYCL_ENABLE_OPT=0` (untested by us).

### First Bad Commit
529ac893 (#29107)

### Relevant log output
No error is printed; the server returns 200 with the garbage text.

_Measured on our own hardware; the investigation and this write-up were done with Claude Code (Anthropic)._

items.title: [RFC]: Fixed-Lifecycle Soft Pin with Request-Level TTL and Deadline-Indexed Expiration
items.author: Lin-z-w
items.body_excerpt:
## Changes proposed

### Summary

This RFC proposes changing Mooncake Store soft pinning from an access-renewed lease into a fixed-lifecycle eviction-priority hint.

A soft pin starts when the first replica of a write becomes readable. Its deadline is fixed for that activation and is not extended by `Get`, `Exist`, group lease refresh, replica copy/move, or storage promotion. When the deadline is reached, the object becomes ordinary cache. A later write may explicitly enable soft pinning again.

The proposal also adds an optional request-level TTL, an explicit `Preserve | Enable | Disable` write action, and a deadline index so expiration cleanup processes only due objects instead of scanning all metadata.

Related work:

- Implementation prototype: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/2909
- Group-retention consumer: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/2835

### Motivation

The current soft-pin representation retains a `soft_pin_timeout` after the deadline has passed. Read-lease refresh paths can subsequently move that timeout into the future, causing an expired soft pin to become active again simply because the object was accessed.

This behavior creates several problems:

- Soft pin duration is not fixed and can be extended indefinitely by reads.
- An object can regain soft-pin priority without an explicit write intent.
- Group reads can indirectly refresh every member's object-level soft pin.
- The soft-pin gauge can count expired metadata until another operation happens to normalize it.
- A periodic exact cleanup implemented as a full metadata scan costs `O(total object count)` even when few or no soft pins expire.
- The behavior is difficult to compose with group retention because object soft pin and group lifetime can accidentally refresh each other.

The desired behavior is a predictable priority lifetime suitable for both standalone objects and future group-retention policy.

### Proposed semantics

1. A soft pin is committed when a write first changes the object from zero readable replicas to at least one readable replica.
2. `Enable(ttl)` sets a deadline relative to that completion time.
3. Reads grant only the ordinary read lease and never extend or reactivate the soft pin.
4. At `now >= deadline`, the object is treated as ordinary cache.
5. A later explicit `Enable` may start a new soft-pin lifetime.
6. `Disable` removes the committed soft pin when the write becomes readable.
7. `Preserve` retains an unexpired committed deadline across Upsert, but does not preserve an already expired deadline.
8. `Enable` with `TTL = 0` is equivalent to committing ordinary cache.
9. Soft pin remains an eviction-priority hint. If `allow_evict_soft_pinned_objects=true`, an active soft-pinned object may still be selected by the existing second eviction pass.
10. Explicit removal APIs continue to remove soft-pinned objects.

### Write API

Replace the ambiguous boolean write intent with an explicit action:

```cpp
enum class SoftPinAction : uint8_t {
    PRESERVE = 0,
    ENABLE = 1,
    DISABLE = 2,
};

struct ReplicateConfig {
    // Existing fields omitted.
    SoftPinAction soft_pin_action{SoftPinAction::PRESERVE};
    std::optional<uint64_t> soft_pin_ttl_ms{};
};
```

Request rules:

- `PRESERVE` must not include `soft_pin_ttl_ms`.
- `DISABLE` must not include `soft_pin_ttl_ms`.
- `ENABLE` uses `soft_pin_ttl_ms` when present.
- `ENABLE` without an override uses the Master's `default_kv_soft_pin_ttl`.
- A request-level TTL above `max_kv_soft_pin_ttl` is rejected.
- Unknown action values are rejected.

`PRESERVE` is the default because a default Upsert should not silently remove an existing eviction-priority deadline. For a new Put, preserving an absent deadline simply creates ordinary cache unless the caller selects `ENABLE`.

The existing C ABI can retain its boolean field for the initial change and translate it as follows:

```text
with_soft_pin=true  -> ENABLE with the Master default TTL
with_soft_pin=false -> PRESERVE
```

This keeps existing Go and Rust wrappers functional, although those wrappers will not expose explicit disable or request-level TTL until their APIs are extended.

### Master configuration

Add:

```text
max_kv_soft_pin_ttl = 24h by default
```

The Master validates that:

```text
default_kv_soft_pin_ttl <= max_kv_soft_pin_ttl
```

Deadline arithmetic is checked when the soft pin is committed, not only at Master startup. If `completion_now + ttl` cannot be represented by `system_clock::time_point`, the deadline saturates at `time_point::max()` instead of overflowing.

### Object state model

The object-level state is:

```text
Disabled
Pending(action, ttl, eligible_replica_ids)
Active(deadline)
```

`Pending` is write intent and `Active` is committed eviction priority. Starting a write does not immediately apply the requested action because the object may never become readable.

The pending action is committed only when:

- the End operation completes a replica allocated or reused by the current write; and
- the object changes from zero completed replicas to at least one completed replica.

After commit, Pending is cleared. Later replica completions and duplicate End calls therefore do not refresh the deadline.

Replica IDs are used to associate Pending with the replicas of the current write. End currently carries no write-generation token, so it is not possible to distinguish every stale End from a newer same-client write. Adding a protocol-level operation token is outside this RFC.

### Revoke, preemption, and processing cleanup

A partial Revoke must not unconditionally discard Pending.

Pending is retained while at least one eligible PROCESSING replica from the same write can still become the first readable replica. Pending is cleared when:

- the object is deleted;
- a newer Upsert preempts the write; or
- no eligible and valid PROCESSING replica remains.

Committed state is independent from Pending. An Upsert that has not yet become readable does not

items.title: [RFC]: Replica-ID Validation for PutEnd / PutRevoke and GetReplicaList
items.author: ykwd
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

- **Status**: Proposed
- **Module**: Mooncake Store (`mooncake-store`)

## Motivation

### 1. Same-client stale PutEnd / PutRevoke after PutStart preemption

`PutEnd` / `PutRevoke` currently only check that `client_id` matches the object's writer. This rejects a different client after preemption, but fails when the **same client** starts a second write that preempts an earlier in-progress write:

```text
Client C: PutStart#1(key) → replicas R1 (PROCESSING)
          … discard timeout / UpsertStart preempts …
Client C: PutStart#2(key) → replicas R2 (PROCESSING); client_id still C
Client C: PutEnd#1 / PutRevoke#1(key) → accepted (client_id matches) → incorrectly completes or revokes R2
```

`PutStart` can reclaim after `put_start_discard_timeout`; `UpsertStart` preempts immediately. A stale `PutEnd` may mark R2 `COMPLETE` before data is written; a stale `PutRevoke` may delete R2 while Put#2 is still in progress.

### 2. False Get failures after lease expiry

On Get, the client first calls `GetReplicaList` (or equivalent) to obtain a replica list and a lease TTL, then transfers data. If the lease expires before the transfer finishes, the client returns `LEASE_EXPIRED` even when the underlying replicas are still valid, to avoid reading data that may have been evicted or replaced. For slow or large transfers this causes avoidable failures: the object may still exist unchanged, but without the replica IDs from `GetReplicaList`, the client cannot ask the master whether those same replicas are still live.

## Proposal

Use **replica IDs** as the durable identity of allocated replicas. `PutStart` / `UpsertStart` / `GetReplicaList` all return them to the client; `PutEnd` / `PutRevoke` and lease-expired Get revalidation consume them.

### Globally unique ReplicaID

`ReplicaID` (`uint64_t`) already exists on each replica. Strengthen allocation as follows:

- On master fresh init, set `next_id_` to a random `uint64`.
- On each new replica, assign `id = next_id_.fetch_add(1)` (atomic).

### Return ReplicaID from PutStart / UpsertStart / GetReplicaList

Every replica descriptor returned by `PutStart`, `UpsertStart`, and `GetReplicaList` (including batch variants) must include a non-zero `ReplicaID`. Clients retain these IDs for the matching write completion or for Get revalidation after lease expiry.

### PutEnd / PutRevoke validate replica IDs

Extend end/revoke RPCs to carry the replica ID from the matching `PutStart` / `UpsertStart`:

```text
PutEnd(client_id, key, tenant_id, replica_type, replica_id)
PutRevoke(client_id, key, tenant_id, replica_type, replica_id)
```

### Lease-expired Get revalidation via GetReplicaList IDs

The client keeps the replica IDs from the initial `GetReplicaList`. After transfer, if the lease has expired, it re-queries the master with those ID. If the same IDs still exist and are `COMPLETE`, return success; otherwise fail as today (`LEASE_EXPIRED` / `INVALID_REPLICA`).

items.author: cage-goat

### Bug Report

## Description

Master uses separate NoF connections for heartbeat probes. After a connection failure, subsequent probes may keep reusing the failed connection, causing heartbeats to fail even after the target recovers. This can eventually remove an available segment and clean up its associated replica metadata.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start Master and a NoF target, register a namespace, and confirm successful heartbeat probes.
2. Pause or stop the target until a probe times out or the connection fails.
3. Restore the target before the segment is removed, keeping the Master process and original registration unchanged, then observe subsequent probes.

## Expected behavior

Subsequent heartbeats should reestablish the connection and resume successful probes while preserving the existing segment removal policy.

## Related work

[PR #4656](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/4656) addresses client-side connection recovery but does not cover Master’s separate heartbeat connections.

items.title: [Bug]: Master NoF heartbeat connections lack KATO, leaving stale connections on the target
items.author: cage-goat
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

## Description

Client connections retaining stale controllers and qpairs on the target after connection failures have been reported in [#4768](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/4768). Master uses separate NoF connections for heartbeat probing. These connections also have KATO disabled and face a similar resource cleanup risk.

[PR #4806](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/4806) addresses qpair cleanup, controller reconnection, and probe recovery on Master. During a network failure, disconnect notifications may not reach the target. Master can therefore recover its connections while old controllers and qpairs remain allocated on the target.

## Expected Behavior

Master probe connections should support configurable KATO:

- Use the existing heartbeat thread to process the admin queue and drive Keep Alive.
- Allow the target to reclaim stale controllers and qpairs after Keep Alive expires.
- Preserve read-based health checks and the existing segment removal policy. Only successful probe reads should refresh the heartbeat liveness timestamp.

## Related Work

Client KATO support is being introduced in [PR #4769](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/4769), which has not yet been merged. The Master implementation should align with its configuration design to avoid introducing duplicate KATO settings.

items.title: torch.cond: branch output aliasing an input is accepted when the branch also mutates an operand (alias check bypassed by auto-functionalization)
items.author: guanam
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.cond`'s functionalization-key alias check is bypassed whenever a branch also mutates one of the operands, so a branch that returns a **view of an input** compiles and runs, and the HOP's output ends up sharing storage with an input.

This is the same bypass pattern reported for `while_loop` in #195966, on the `cond` path.

#### Repro (CPU only)

```python
import torch


def true_fn(x, y):
    y.copy_(x * 2.0)      # mutates an operand -> can_auto_functionalize() is True
    return x[:4]          # returns a view of an input


def false_fn(x, y):
    y.copy_(x + 1.0)
    return x[:4]


def f(pred, x, y):
    return torch.cond(pred, true_fn, false_fn, (x, y))


x = torch.ones(4)
y = torch.zeros(4)
with torch.no_grad():
    out = torch.compile(f, backend="aot_eager")(torch.tensor(True), x, y)

print("out.data_ptr() == x.data_ptr() :", out.data_ptr() == x.data_ptr())
```

Output:

```
out.data_ptr() == x.data_ptr() : True
```

The same aliasing return is rejected as soon as the mutation is removed:

```python
def true_fn_no_mut(x, y):
    return x[:4]          # identical aliasing return, no mutation


def false_fn_no_mut(x, y):
    return x + 1.0
```

```
RuntimeError: cond_true might be aliasing the input or the output!
```

So the single `y.copy_(...)` line is what turns the error off. Reproduces with both `backend="aot_eager"` and `backend="inductor"`.

#### Expected behavior

Either the aliasing branch output is rejected in both cases, or it is genuinely supported. Right now whether the check runs depends on an unrelated property of the branch (whether it happens to mutate an operand).

Two places in the source say rejecting is the intent:

- `torch/_higher_order_ops/auto_functionalize.py` names it as a precondition of auto-functionalization — *"The returns of OpOverload must not alias anything"* — but the loop enforcing it sits inside `if isinstance(op, OpOverload):`, so for a `HopInstance` the function falls through to `return True`:

  ```python
  if isinstance(op, OpOverload):
      # The returns of OpOverload must not alias anything
      for ret in schema.returns:
          if ret.alias_info is None and type(ret.type) is torch.TensorType:
              continue
          # Not yet supported: List[Tensor] return.
          return False
      if torch._C._dispatch_has_kernel_for_dispatch_key(op.name(), "Functionalize"):
          return False
  return True
  ```

- #89966, the PR that added `cond` functionalization, records that branch outputs aliasing inputs were meant to be rejected for the time being, and that the check is known to be incomplete.

The documented contract also disagrees with the observed result. `torch.cond`'s docstring states that under `torch.compile` with a non-constant predicate *"the outputs will always be new tensors that do not share object identity with the original inputs"*, with `assert result is not x`. In the repro `out is x` is indeed `False`, but `out.data_ptr() == x.data_ptr()` is `True`: the output is a view of the input, not a new tensor.

#### Root cause

`cond_func`, the functionalize impl in `torch/_higher_order_ops/cond.py`, returns before reaching the check:

```python
@cond_op.py_functionalize_impl
def cond_func(ctx, pred, true_fn, false_fn, inputs):
    ...
    hop_instance = HopInstance.create(cond_op, pred, true_fn, false_fn, inputs)
    if can_auto_functionalize(hop_instance) and hasattr(ctx, "mode"):
        return do_auto_functionalize_v2(...)            # <-- early return

    unwrapped_inputs = ctx.unwrap_tensors(inputs)
    ...
    for branch, branch_name in [(true_fn, "cond_true"), (false_fn, "cond_false")]:
        _check_alias_and_mutation(branch, unwrapped_inputs, branch_name, pre_dispatch)
```

`can_auto_functionalize(hop_instance)` is true exactly when a branch mutates an operand, so the mutating case never reaches `_check_alias_and_mutation`. `do_auto_functionalize_v2` itself does not check for aliasing returns — `auto_functionalize.py`'s `is_alias` / `AliasViewInfo` describe base/view relationships in order to rebuild the mutated base, they do not reject an aliasing return.

Grepping the auto-functionalizable HOPs (those defining `gen_schema`), `cond` is the clearest instance of the early return preceding the check in the same function; `invoke_subgraph` and `base_hop` take the same early return and have no alias check at all.

#### Why it matters downstream

A backend that captures `cond` as a device-side conditional node unifies the two branches' outputs into one buffer. If that buffer is also a graph input, it has no well-defined address: replaying the graph writes into memory the caller believes is its input, and the next replay reads back the previous output. The backend has to add its own check because the one in `cond_func` did not run, and it then cannot distinguish a user-written aliasing return from the `copy_`-as-output shape that `decompose_auto_functionalized` legitimately produces for the very same mutating branch.

### Versions

```
torch 2.12.0+cpu
Python 3.11
```

Reproduced with `backend="aot_eager"` and `backend="inductor"`.

items.title: [Testing] _concurrent may report success when a child process is terminated by a signal
items.author: zh301
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`_concurrent()` in `python/triton/_test_runner.py` can return a successful status even when one of its child processes is terminated by a signal.

The function currently aggregates child return codes using `max()`:

```python
def _concurrent(commands):
    processes = [subprocess.Popen(command, cwd=cwd, env=environment) for command, cwd, environment in commands]
    return max(process.wait() for process in processes)
```

On POSIX systems, `subprocess.Popen.wait()` returns a negative value when a process is terminated by a signal. For example, a process terminated by `SIGTERM` returns `-15`.

Therefore, if one child exits successfully with `0` and another is terminated by `SIGTERM` with `-15`, the aggregate result is:

```python
max(0, -15) == 0
```

The caller consequently treats the concurrent test run as successful, even though one of the test processes was terminated.

## Minimal reproducer

Save the following as `repro_concurrent_signal.py` in the root of a Triton source checkout:

```python
import os
import signal
import sys

from triton._test_runner import _concurrent


cwd = os.getcwd()
environment = os.environ.copy()

commands = [
    (
        [sys.executable, "-c", "pass"],
        cwd,
        environment,
    ),
    (
        [
            sys.executable,
            "-c",
            "import os, signal; os.kill(os.getpid(), signal.SIGTERM)",
        ],
        cwd,
        environment,
    ),
]

status = _concurrent(commands)

print(f"_concurrent status: {status}")
assert status != 0, (
    "_concurrent returned success even though one child "
    "was terminated by SIGTERM"
)
```

Run it from the Triton checkout root:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=python python3 repro_concurrent_signal.py
```

No GPU is required.

## Actual result

The source-level pytest regression test reports:

```text
bug_repros/test_concurrent_signal_status.py:36: in test_signal_terminated_child_makes_concurrent_run_fail
    assert status != 0, (
E   AssertionError: _concurrent returned success even though one child was terminated by SIGTERM
E   assert 0 != 0
```

## Expected result

`_concurrent()` should return a nonzero status whenever any child process exits with a nonzero status, including negative return codes representing signal termination.

The aggregation should not allow a successful child return code (`0`) to hide a signal-terminated child return code (`-N`).

Python documents negative subprocess return codes on POSIX as meaning that the process was terminated by signal `N`:

https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#subprocess.Popen.returncode

### Environment details

Triton: source checkout from main, commit 2122e24efc1886bfa36337c1f5b07c47d827b1d4
Python: 3.12.3
OS: Linux, AutoDL container
GPU: Not required
Platform requirement: POSIX signal return-code semantics

items.title: [Performance] Measure Transformers backend startup time vs native
items.author: hmellor
items.body_excerpt:
This comes from an old comment and was never backed by measurements, so the first
task is to establish whether the effect is real at all. It may not be.

Runtime throughput was brought in line with native implementations in #47187, but
nobody has measured startup time either before or since.

### Step 1: is there a difference?

Time engine init for a model that has both implementations, e.g.:

    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl transformers
    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl vllm

Compare time-to-ready across a few runs and a couple of model sizes. Warm vs cold
HF cache matters, so control for it.

If there is no meaningful difference, say so and close this issue. That is a
perfectly good outcome and still worth having measured.

### Step 2: only if a delta shows up

The backend does some work at load time that native implementations do not, so
these are plausible starting points rather than known causes:

- `fuser.py` — `get_fuser` traces each module class with `fx` to match it against
  the available fusers. Cached per class, but tracing is not free.
- `base.py` — `recursive_replace` walks the module tree applying fusers per instance.
- Config resolution and `auto_map` handling for remote-code models.

A profile of init (py-spy or cProfile) will be more informative than guessing from
this list.

### Done when

Either the startup delta is quantified and explained, or it is shown that there
isn't a meaningful one and this is closed.

items.title: Starting a localization (l10n) effort for LMCache
items.author: quaid
items.body_excerpt:
I'd like to propose we start building a localization community around LMCache, beginning with blog posts and expanding to documentation and other parts of the website over time.

tl;dr – 
- localizing content and software is valuable to all of us;
- we can automate the toil of translation but we need human editors who can review the translations and make sure they are properly localized;
- localization means words and phrases are fixed so the final product makes more sense to a native reader;
- we can use RHLF to improve this process and reduce toil over time.

## What is the problem

We already receive blog posts written natively in Mandarin and English. This is a good thing.

But we also need to localize this content without putting a burden on people. Fortunately this content has completed a technical review before being translated, so the focus can be on fixing idioms and grammar for better understanding by the widest audience.

## Why this matters

Ultimately this is about attracting more users to LMCache, some of whom will become intentional contributors over time.

Twenty-five years ago, localization (l10n) projects were one of the main ways Linux distributions and communities like the Fedora Project made headway into new parts of the world. It usually wasn't a corporate initiative. It was people who were enthusiastic about bringing free and open source software to their fellow country members, and who put in the effort to translate strings and make the software make sense locally. That work produced translations AND collaborations. It grew contributors, built regional communities, and carried the free software and open source ethos into places it hadn't reached before.

LMCache has users and watchers all over the world, and there are almost certainly people already adjacent to this project who could help bring information and education about the software to their local communities.

## What I'm proposing

We form loosely as `l10n-sig` out of anyone who wants to be an editor and approver for one or more languages. Languages get added when someone steps forward to take one. Rather than announcing a target list and hoping it fills in, we start with whoever volunteers.

I'm volunteering to be an editor and reviewer for anything translated to English, and I'd love more help with that role. I'm confident we can get Mandarin covered right away. But what else and how?

Japanese and Korean are the obvious early candidates given where our users are, but the principle is that a language becomes active when a person is willing to own it.

It only takes one person to get things started and be the gravity to bring another language.

As I said above, this isn't only English needing localizing. I currently have an original blog post written in Mandarin that I want to bring into English through this same process. I'd like to stop doing one at a time reviews by asking around in Slack to see who might need a break from creating features or fixing bugs. I'd rather offer the opportunity to people who aren't or can't create features or fix bugs.

Therefore, posts written originally in any language are welcome, and translation should flow in whatever direction it needs to.

## This is not a request for volunteer translation labor

LLM translation is pretty good now, and we should lean on it for the first pass. What we need is a human review step, and there are two kinds of people who can do that well.

The first is someone capable in both the source and target language, who can read the machine translation and confirm the meaning carried over and the tone is right. Not necessarily final-polish copy editing — a human or AI copy edit can always be applied later — just confirmation that it makes sense and reads naturally.

The second, and possibly just as valuable, is someone technical who knows their own language well and doesn't necessarily read the source language at all. Because the models are good enough now, a domain expert can look at a translated technical passage and say "ah, I see what this was trying to say" and correct the terminology so it's actually right in their language. Technical accuracy matters as much as idiomatic flow, and that person is well placed to catch it.

So the ask is much closer to "read this and tell us if it sounds right" than "translate three thousand words."

## How the workflow might look

Initially all of this can be manual, while we work out which models produce the best tone for technical writing in each language and we develop any necessary skills.

Longer term this could be automated — a GitHub Action that sends a published post to a translation model, then loads the result into WordPress as a draft where a translation editor reviews and approves it. It could also live partly outside the repo, with approval happening after the fact rather than as a gate. The goal is to distribute this work rather than make it dependent on a paid staffer, and to remove the need to ask permission before contributing.

If anyone already knows of a toolchain or process for this, please say so. I'd much rather adopt something that works than stand up and maintain our own infrastructure.

## What I'm looking for

Ideas or helping hands for:

- Thoughts on the approach
- Pointers to existing tooling
- Anyone in

items.title: bug(sampling): top_k_arr/min_p_arr are validated against input rows but indexed by output row, reading out of bounds when indices is longer than probs
items.author: kahyunnam
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`top_k_sampling_from_probs` and `min_p_sampling_from_probs` validate their per-request parameter tensor against the **input** batch but index it by the **output** row. When `indices` is longer than `probs.size(0)`, every output row at or past `probs.size(0)` reads past the end of the parameter tensor and silently samples with a garbage `top_k` / `min_p`.

- `check_tensor_param(maybe_top_k_arr, probs)` — [`csrc/sampling.cu:216`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling.cu#L216) — requires `top_k_arr.size(0) == probs.size(0)`, via [`csrc/sampling_utils.h:34`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling_utils.h#L34). Same for `min_p` at [`csrc/sampling.cu:262`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling.cu#L262).
- The kernels read [`top_k_arr[bx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L872) and [`min_p_arr[bx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1129), where `bx` is `blockIdx.x`, i.e. the output row.

The sibling kernels get this right and index by the input row: [`top_p_arr[row_idx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1006) in `TopPSamplingFromProbKernel`, and [`top_k_arr[row_idx]` / `top_p_arr[row_idx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1228-L1229) in `TopKTopPSamplingFromProbKernel`. So only the two `[bx]` sites are wrong.

### Reproduction

On a B200 (SM100), 4 input rows, 16 output rows via `indices = arange(16) % 4`, vocab 512. The parameter tensor is a length-4 view carved out of a 4096-element buffer whose tail holds a conspicuous value, so an out-of-bounds read returns that tail instead of faulting:

| Call | Parameter tensor | Output rows violating the parameter |
|---|---|---|
| `top_k_sampling_from_probs` | length-4 `top_k`, all `1`, buffer tail `500` | **12 / 16** — exactly rows 4–15 |
| `min_p_sampling_from_probs` | length-4 `min_p`, all `1.0`, buffer tail `0.0` | **12 / 16** — exactly rows 4–15 |
| `top_p_sampling_from_probs` (control) | length-4 `top_p`, all `1e-6`, buffer tail `1.0` | **0 / 16** |

With `top_k = 1` every output row must return `argmax(probs[indices[i]])`; rows 4–15 do not. The `top_p` control isolates the cause to the `bx` / `row_idx` choice rather than anything about the harness.

Note that `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` does **not** flag this: the read stays inside the PyTorch caching-allocator segment, so a memcheck-clean run is not evidence of safety here.

<details>
<summary>Repro script</summary>

```python
import torch
from flashinfer import sampling

torch.manual_seed(0)
IN, OUT, V = 4, 16, 512
probs = torch.softmax(torch.randn(IN, V, device="cuda"), dim=-1)
indices = torch.arange(OUT, device="cuda", dtype=torch.int32) % IN

# Length-IN views carved out of a larger buffer whose tail holds a conspicuous value.
k_buf = torch.full((4096,), 500, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
k_buf[:IN] = 1
top_k = k_buf[:IN]

p_buf = torch.zeros(4096, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
p_buf[:IN] = 1.0
min_p = p_buf[:IN]

tp_buf = torch.full((4096,), 1.0, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
tp_buf[:IN] = 1e-6
top_p = tp_buf[:IN]

argmax = probs.argmax(dim=-1)


def violations(out):
    return [(i, int(out[i])) for i in range(OUT) if int(out[i]) != int(argmax[indices[i]])]


out_k = sampling.top_k_sampling_from_probs(probs, top_k, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("top_k=1  violations:", len(violations(out_k)), "/", OUT, violations(out_k)[:6])

out_p = sampling.min_p_sampling_from_probs(probs, min_p, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("min_p=1  violations:", len(violations(out_p)), "/", OUT, violations(out_p)[:6])

# Control: top_p indexes by input row, so it must be unaffected.
out_tp = sampling.top_p_sampling_from_probs(probs, top_p, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("top_p    violations:", len(violations(out_tp)), "/", OUT)
```

```
top_k=1  violations: 12 / 16 [(4, 189), (5, 226), (6, 216), (7, 345), (8, 459), (9, 92)]
min_p=1  violations: 12 / 16 [(4, 320), (5, 147), (6, 350), (7, 300), (8, 42), (9, 113)]
top_p    violations: 0 / 16
```

</details>

### Fix

Two options, and the choice is a contract decision rather than a mechanical one:

1. Index by the input row — change `top_k_arr[bx]` to `top_k_arr[row_idx]` and `min_p_arr[bx]` to `min_p_arr[row_idx]`, matching the existing validation and the two sibling kernels.
2. Keep output-row indexing and fix the validation to use the output batch instead of `probs`, which is what `top_k`/`min_p` being *per-request* arguably implies.

Option 2 matches what the docstrings suggest (`indices` maps outputs to distributions, so a per-request parameter is naturally per-output) and is the convention #5745 uses for `seed`/`offset`, which validates against `output.size(0)`. Option 1 is the smaller change and keeps all four kernels consistent with each other. Either way the four kernels should agree, and a test with `len(indices) > probs.size(0)` plus a tensor-valued parameter would have caught this.

### Environment

NVIDIA B200 (SM100, CC 10.0), CUDA 13.0, torch 2.14.0+cu130, Python 3.10, `main` @ `1cad38165`. Nothing about this is architecture-specific.

items.title: llama : integer type consistency in `llama.h`
items.author: MarcusDunn
items.body_excerpt:
# Feature Description

llama.h should prefer to use `sized` (always) + `signed` (mostly) integers.

# Motivation

The integer types in `llama.h` right now are.

| Count | Type            |
|---------|------------------|
| 33      | `int`              |
| 10      | `int32_t`       |
| 24      | `uint32_t`     |
| 2        | `int64_t`       |
| 2        | `uint64_t`    | 

In #4540 there was a discussion around preferences for integer types on new methods. 

Avoiding `int` makes cross platform code simpler at essentially no cost.
Signed makes arithmetic simpler at the cost of some bits if you need something large.

# Possible Implementation

1. Change all `int`'s to `int32_t`
2. As code changes try to prefer signed integers.

We could also do some higher-impact things, but I'd take the lower-impact slower changes over a large find-and-replace.

items.title: [Bug]: PutEnd silently discards PushOffloadingQueue failures — objects never reach the SSD tier, with no log or metric
items.author: ccgibson
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With eager offload (`enable_offload=1`, `offload_on_evict=0`), `MasterService::PutEnd` calls `PushOffloadingQueue` and acts **only on success**. There is no `else` branch, no log, no metric, and no retry:

```cpp
// mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp  (main @ fc04cb1, ~L3283)
auto result = PushOffloadingQueue(object_id, replica);
if (result) {
    if (!task_created) {
        replica.inc_refcnt();
        tenant_state.offloading_tasks.emplace(
            object_id.user_key,
            OffloadingTask{replica.id(), std::chrono::system_clock::now()});
        task_created = true;
    }
}
// failure is discarded here
```

An object whose enqueue fails therefore gets **no offload task**, is never written to the SSD tier, and dies RAM-only at the next memory eviction. Because it never had a disk replica, that eviction removes its last replica and the object leaves the pool entirely — a cache entry silently lost despite the SSD tier having free space.

## Failure modes that can hit this

`PushOffloadingQueue` (`master_service.cpp`, ~L5150) can return:

- `SEGMENT_NOT_FOUND` — segment name not present in the local-disk `client_by_name` map
- `UNABLE_OFFLOADING` — no local disk segment for the resolved client
- `UNABLE_OFFLOADING` — `!enable_offloading` on that segment
- `KEYS_ULTRA_LIMIT` — `offloading_objects.size() >= offloading_queue_limit_`
- `OBJECT_ALREADY_EXISTS` — key already present in `offloading_objects`

None of these are logged inside `PushOffloadingQueue` either, so the failure is invisible end-to-end.

## Why this is inconsistent

The **eviction-path** callers of the same function already count and log these failures, e.g.:

```cpp
LOG(WARNING) << "[EVICT] PushOffloadingQueue failed for "
             << offload_push_failed_forced
             << " object(s); force-evicted without disk offload "
                "(offload_force_evict=true).";
```

Only the `PutEnd` hot-path caller discards them. There is also no offload-related metric anywhere in `master_metric_manager.{h,cpp}`.

## Impact observed

In a production deployment we found roughly **9% of pool exits had no corresponding disk eviction** — i.e. that fraction of objects left the cache without ever reaching SSD — while the SSD tier was well under its eviction watermark and the offload pipeline was healthy (multi-GB/s end-to-end store throughput, no queue backlog, no dropped events). With no log line and no counter anywhere, there was nothing to attribute it to; localising it required reading the source rather than any telemetry.

The measurement that surfaced it, for anyone hitting the same thing: compare cumulative pool exits against cumulative disk evictions. A persistent excess of the former means objects are leaving the cache without a disk replica.

Note this is distinct from #2632 / #2658 (offloading-task orphans causing 600s expiry warnings). That one produces a *visible* `Offloading task expired` warning. This path produces nothing at all.

## Two additional silent-success paths

`PushOffloadingQueue` also returns success (`{}`) while enqueuing nothing:

1. `if (segment_names.empty()) { return {}; }` — early return before the loop
2. a `segment_names` list whose entries are all `nullopt` falls through the loop body

In both cases `PutEnd` sees success and records an `OffloadingTask` + `inc_refcnt()` for work that was never queued, so the task can only be cleared by the TTL expiry path.

## Suggested fix

At minimum, make the failure observable: add an `else` incrementing an offload-enqueue-failure counter and emitting a (sampled, since this is the `PutEnd` hot path) `WARNING` carrying the `ErrorCode`, mirroring what the eviction-path callers already do. That is enough to tell operators which failure mode dominates.

Beyond that, `KEYS_ULTRA_LIMIT` and `OBJECT_ALREADY_EXISTS` arguably warrant retry or dedup handling rather than a dropped object, but making it visible seems like the necessary first step.

Happy to open a PR for the observability part if that is a welcome direction.

Environment: observed on `v0.3.12-pre1`; code path verified unchanged on `main` @ `fc04cb1`.

### Describe the bug

We are testing with recent Mooncake commit: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/commit/67aaf6de74f35c7c5cfd072e8643b0a80eb5999a (2026‑08‑12).
The same workload with June‑end Mooncake code works perfectly without empty‑value issue. This regression appears after we upgraded to newer codebase.

### Master launch command:

```C++

--rpc_thread_num=8 \
--metrics_port=8007 \
--default_kv_lease_ttl=5000 \

--promotion_on_hit=false \
--put_start_discard_timeout_sec=300 \
--put_start_release_timeout_sec=600

```
### Real‑Client Environment Variables & Settings

MOONCAKE_LOCAL_BUFFER_SIZE                         = 6442450944
MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_BUCKET_EVICTION_POLICY            = lru
MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_BUCKET_KEYS_LIMIT                 = 128

comments.body:
I spent some time re-checking this against current main (2b3cefba), since several fixes landed after 2026-08-12 that touch exactly this path.

The "empty value" half is an error-mapping artifact rather than a data state: `get()` in store_py.cpp returns `b""` whenever the C++ read returns nullptr, with no exception, so any failure (SSD read error, no usable replica) surfaces as an empty value. On the "key visible" half, #2877 (merged 08-13, one day after your commit) made `/get_all_keys` filter by readable replica, which narrows that symptom.

On what changed since your build: #3479 fixed the carryover-key bucket NACK storm and its author reproduced with your exact config (330 failures per 100 GiB before, zero after, every value matched on readback). #3601 made WriteBucket datasync before committing bucket metadata (a crash between used to leave a registered bucket with nothing on device). #3620 fixed batch gets landing on a different disk replica than the slices were prepared for. #3726 stopped PushOffloadingQueue from silently dropping enqueues. Any of these could plausibly have produced your symptom.

What is still structurally open on main: a COMPLETE LOCAL_DISK replica whose backing file physically disappeared (manual wipe, RemoveAll broadcast) stays listed and reads return `b""` forever; #3711 self-heals that on the Put path only, by design, and read-only keys never heal. Also `MOONCAKE_STORE_CHECKSUM` still defaults off, so payload corruption is not detected unless you opt in.

To pin your case down definitively, could you re-run the same 100 GiB workload on current main with `MOONCAKE_STORE_CHECKSUM=1` and correlate any empty get with the client log? `SSD read failed for key`, `object_checksum_mismatch`, and `Read size mismatch` each map to a different one of the known causes; empty reads with none of those in the log would mean something new, and that log line would tell us which.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body: The read-side half of this is now covered: #3889 heals a dangling LOCAL_DISK replica when a read fails on it (evict plus honest miss or failover to a surviving replica), which closes the "read-only keys never heal" gap noted above. The broader empty-read surface from #3867's concurrent test shape is a separate matter already handled there.

comments.author: whn09
comments.body:
A likely write-side cause, reproduced on 2x r8idn.96xlarge. `GroupOffloadingKeysByBucket` defers a partial bucket to the ungrouped pool for the next heartbeat. `FileStorage::OffloadObjects` then NACKs every key that is not in this cycle's buckets, including the deferred ones. The master drops their offloading task. Under `offload_on_evict` such an object can then be evicted without an SSD copy, and the next cycle's write is not tracked. With 1 GiB buckets and 8192 x 4 MiB puts, main lost 32-96 tasks in 3 of 5 runs. The count always matched the ungrouped-pool size, and nothing is logged at the default level.

This is #3006, fixed by #3009 or #4739 (both 0/5 on the same repro). Until one of them merges, setting `MOONCAKE_OFFLOAD_FLUSH_PARTIAL_BUCKETS=1` on main avoids it (0/5).

items.title: Questions on Triton basic concepts
items.author: peastman
items.body_excerpt:
I'm just getting started with Triton.  I can't find any documentation on some very basic concepts.  If you can point me to something I missed I'd be grateful.  If not, perhaps someone could answer these questions?

What types of values can be passed to a kernel?  PyTorch tensors obviously, as well as ints, floats, and bools.  Anything else?

The grid is defined by a lambda that takes a single argument called `meta`.  What is `meta`?

How do I access a single element of a tensor?  Say `a` and `b` are tensors and `i` is an int.  I want to write `c = a[i]*b` to multiply `b` by an element of `a`.  That produces an error.  What's the correct way of doing it?

What is the difference between a `tensor_descriptor` and a `TensorDescriptor`?  What is each used for and how do I use them?

What is the exact significance of annotating an argument with `tl.constexpr`?  Does it mean the kernel will get recompiled every time a new value of that argument is encountered?  What can be done with a constexpr value that can't be done with other ones?

How about `tl.const`?  Is it just for error checking, to avoid accidentally modifying something that shouldn't be modified, or does it have other effects?

Thanks for your help!

items.title: [Bug]: Startup memory-profiling assertion aborts whenever free memory grows, contradicting documented support for GPU co-tenancy
items.author: PeganovAnton
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment ``` # primary reproduction -- discrete NVIDIA, stock published image GPU : NVIDIA H100 NVL (95830 MiB), x86_64 Driver / CUDA : 580.105.08 / CUDA 13.0 vLLM : 0.29.0 (vllm/vllm-openai:v0.29.0) # secondary reproduction -- integrated GPU, no co-tenant at all GPU : NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark), sm_121, aarch64 Driver / CUDA : 580.142 / CUDA 13.0 vLLM : 0.27.1 Memory : 119.67 GiB unified CPU+GPU pool ``` ### 🐛 Describe the bug `Worker.determine_available_memory` aborts engine startup whenever free memory is higher after profiling than before it: ``` AssertionError: Error in memory profiling. Initial free memory 82.94 GiB, current free memory 90.17 GiB. This happens when other processes sharing the same container release GPU memory while vLLM is profiling during initialization. To fix this, ensure consistent GPU memory allocation or isolate vLLM in its own container. ``` The guard rests on an assumption stated only in a code comment: ```python # NOTE(woosuk): Here we assume that the other processes using the same # GPU did not change their memory usage during the profiling. assert init_free_memory >= free_gpu_memory, ( ``` Any co-tenant that *releases* memory during the ~10 s profiling window kills startup, on a plain discrete NVIDIA GPU, with vLLM alone in its own container. The reproduction below does this in about a minute on any CUDA device. ### Scope: this affects every device type | setting | what can move the measured value | fires? | |---|---|---| | discrete GPU, sole tenant | nothing | no | | discrete GPU, co-tenant (NVIDIA or AMD) | another process on that GPU releasing memory | yes | | integrated / unified-memory GPU | any process anywhere on the host | yes, **with no sharing at all** | Row 2 is reproduced below on NVIDIA; #53591 fixed the same row for AMD. Row 3 is covered by the GB10 section further down. ### Steps to reproduce (any single CUDA GPU, ~1 minute) Self-contained: two containers from the **same published vLLM image** on one GPU, no host Python and no vLLM checkout. Needs Docker + NVIDIA Container Toolkit and a GPU with roughly `HOLD_GIB + UTIL * total` free. - The co-tenant is plain PyTorch — no vLLM, no second engine. It holds 8 GiB, then releases it once vLLM logs `Model loading took`, i.e. during the profile run. It stays alive afterwards, so the only thing that changes is the *allocation*. - vLLM is a stock `vllm serve facebook/opt-125m`, explicitly capped with `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.2`. - `RELEASE=0` runs the control: identical setup, co-tenant simply never releases.
repro.sh — save, chmod +x, run as GPU=<idx> ./repro.sh ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # Reproduce vLLM's startup memory-profiling assertion on any single CUDA GPU. # # Two containers, one GPU: # * co-tenant: plain PyTorch, holds HOLD_GIB of device memory, releases it # once vLLM has loaded its weights (i.e. during the profile run) # * vLLM : a stock `vllm serve`, capped with --gpu-memory-utilization # # vLLM compares free device memory before and after profiling and aborts if it # went up, so the release makes startup fail deterministically. # # Requires: docker + NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and a GPU with roughly # (HOLD_GIB + UTIL * total) free. Nothing else -- no host Python, no venv. set -uo pipefail GPU=${GPU:-0} # index of the GPU to use IMAGE=${IMAGE:-vllm/vllm-openai:v0.29.0} MODEL=${MODEL:-facebook/opt-125m} UTIL=${UTIL:-0.2} # --gpu-memory-utilization HOLD_GIB=${HOLD_GIB:-8} # GiB the co-tenant holds RELEASE=${RELEASE:-1} # RELEASE=0 -> control run, startup succeeds WORK=$(mktemp -d) LOG=$WORK/vllm.log TAG=vllm-memprofile-$$ trap 'docker rm -f "$TAG-cotenant" "$TAG-vllm" >/dev/null 2>&1' EXIT echo "gpu=$GPU image=$IMAGE model=$MODEL util=$UTIL hold=${HOLD_GIB}GiB" echo "logs: $WORK" # 1. Co-tenant grabs HOLD_GIB and waits for a release signal on /sig. docker run --rm --name "$TAG-cotenant" --gpus "device=$GPU" \ -e HOLD_GIB="$HOLD_GIB" -v "$WORK:/sig" --entrypoint python3 "$IMAGE" -c ' import os, time, torch gib = int(os.environ["HOLD_GIB"]) buf = torch.empty(gib << 30, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda").fill_(1) torch.cuda.synchronize() free, total = torch.cuda.mem_get_info() print(f"[cotenant] holding {gib} GiB, device free {free/2**30:.2f}/{total/2**30:.2f} GiB", flush=True) open("/sig/held", "w").close() while not os.path.exists("/sig/release"): time.sleep(0.2) del buf torch.cuda.empty_cache() # hand the pages back to the driver free, total = torch.cuda.mem_get_info() print(f"[cotenant] released, device free {free/2**30:.2f}/{total/2**30:.2f} GiB", flush=True) time.sleep(1e6) # stay alive: only the allocation moved ' > "$WORK/cotenant.log" 2>&1 & for _ in $(seq 1 600); do [ -e "$WORK/held" ] && break; sleep 1; done [ -e "$WORK/held" ] || { echo "co-tenant failed to allocate:"; cat "$WORK/cotenant.log"; exit 1; } cat "$WORK/cotenant.log" # 2. Stock vLLM on the same GPU, in its own container. docker run --rm --name "$TAG-vllm" --gpus "device=$GPU" --ipc=host \ -v "$HOME/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface" "$IMAGE" \ --model "$MODEL" --gpu-memory-utilization "$UTIL" > "$LOG" 2>&1 & VLLM_PID=$! # 3. Release once the weights are in, i.e. just before the profile run. if [ "$RELEASE" = 1 ]; then for _ in $(seq 1 1800); do grep -q "Model loading took" "$LOG" && break; sleep 1; done sleep 1; touch "$WORK/release" fi # 4. Wait for the outcome. for _ in $(seq 1 900); do grep -q "Error in memory profiling" "$LOG" && { echo "RESULT: reproduced"; break; } grep -q "Application startup complete" "$LOG" && { echo "RESULT: started (not reproduced)"; break; } kill -0 "$VLLM_PID" 2>/dev/null || { echo "RESULT: container exited"; break; } sl

items.title: LMCacheMPConnector: server deadlocks permanently in _release_entries, holding the GIL and never releasing device memory (reachable from the periodic reaper against a live engine)
items.author: hans-tensormesh
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

When a vLLM worker dies abnormally, the LMCache server's `unregister_kv_cache` path hangs **permanently** inside `_release_entries`. The hang happens in a C call under the GIL, so it takes down the entire server: the HTTP port stops answering, the MQ loop stops accepting requests, and ~388 GB of registered device memory is never released.

The server never recovers. Restarting vLLM does not help — the new engine's `register_kv_caches` is queued behind the stuck handler on the same `mq-server-thread` and eventually fails with `ConnectionError: LMCache server did not respond to register_kv_caches within 300.0s`.

### Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| LMCache | `0.5.3`, commit `f7c0f50259e9c79ede095af9fc945780fb3194b0` (`nightly-3-gf7c0f502`, `dev`) |
| vLLM | `0.26.0` |
| ai-dynamo | `1.4.0` |
| torch | `2.11.0+cu130` (CUDA 13.0) |
| Driver | `595.71.05` |
| Python | 3.12.3 |
| GPUs | 8× NVIDIA B300 SXM6 (275 GB each); TP=4 + EP over GPUs 0–3 |
| Connector | `LMCacheMPConnector`, `kv_role: kv_both`, `lmcache.mp.mq_timeout: 300` |

Server launched as:

```
lmcache server --port 5555 --http-port 8080 \
  --l1-size-gb 1800 --l1-init-size-gb 20 \
  --max-gpu-workers 1 --max-cpu-workers 8 \
  --chunk-size 512 --l1-align-bytes 16384 \
  --eviction-trigger-watermark 0.85 --eviction-ratio 0.10 --eviction-policy LRU \
  --supported-transfer-mode lmcache_driven --shm-name "" \
  --enable-extra-logging --extra-logging-interval 30 \
  --enable-tracing --otlp-endpoint http://localhost:4320
```

### Where it hangs

`py-spy dump` on the wedged server. All 121 threads are idle in `futex_wait_queue` except one, which holds the GIL:

```
Thread 1049209 (active+gil): "mq-server-thread"
    _release_entries    (lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/lmcache_driven_transfer.py:763)
    unregister_kv_cache (lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/lmcache_driven_transfer.py:947)
    __call__            (lmcache/v1/multiprocess/mq.py:426)
    _call_sync_handler  (lmcache/v1/multiprocess/mq.py:537)
    _call_handler       (lmcache/v1/multiprocess/mq.py:592)
    _main_loop          (lmcache/v1/multiprocess/mq.py:621)
    run                 (threading.py:1010)
    _bootstrap_inner    (threading.py:1073)
    _bootstrap          (threading.py:1030)
```

I sampled this 4× over 30 s and it reported the **identical line every time**, ~70 minutes after the hang began.

Line 763 is `entries.clear()` in `_release_entries`:

```python
748:  def _release_entries(self, entries: list[ContextEntry]) -> None:
...
757:      for entry in entries:
758:          entry.cache_context.close()
759:          self._ctx.layout_desc_registry.unregister(
760:              entry.model_name, entry.world_size
761:          )
762:      del entry
763:      entries.clear()          # <-- stuck here
764:      # ipc_collect() only unmaps a CUDA-IPC-imported segment once its last
765:      # tensor reference is gone (LMCache#4014), hence the clear() above.
766:      torch_dev.empty_cache()
767:      ipc_collect = getattr(torch_dev, "ipc_collect", None)
768:      if ipc_collect is not None:
770:          ipc_collect()
```

`entries.clear()` drops the last references to the `ContextEntry` objects, so the CUDA-IPC tensor destructors run inline during the `clear()` — i.e. `cudaIpcCloseMemHandle` against segments exported by vLLM worker processes that have **already died abnormally**. That driver call appears never to return.

This is the same IPC-refcount area the comment on line 764–765 already flags (referencing #4014), but the failure mode here is the exporting process dying uncleanly rather than a lingering reference on the importer side.

### Impact

Measured on the wedged server:

- HTTP `:8080/metrics` — **3/3 timeouts at 20 s**; the server answers nothing.
- **~388 GB of device memory still held** (129 GB each on GPU 0/2/3, 684 MB on GPU 1) with **no vLLM process alive**.
- Host RSS pinned at 1,802 GB (exactly `--l1-size-gb 1800`).
- Not memory or IO pressure: `/proc/pressure/{memory,io}` all report `avg10=0.00`.
- `SIGTERM` cannot be serviced — recovery requires `SIGKILL`.

Downstream, every in-flight vLLM request fails with `EngineDeadError`, the engine shuts down and is not restarted, and subsequent restart attempts fail at registration:

```
ConnectionError: LMCache server did not respond to register_kv_caches within 300.0s. Is the server running?
```

### Reproduction

1. Start `lmcache server` as above.
2. Start vLLM with `LMCacheMPConnector` (`kv_both`), TP=4 + EP, NVFP4 weights, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.92`.
3. Drive sustained load with long prompts (our trace: p50 ≈ 2.2 K, p99 ≈ 67 K, max ≈ 96.5 K input tokens, concurrency ramping 8 → 128).
4. Get a worker to die abnormally (any cause — in our case an unrelated engine fault) so vLLM tears down without a clean unregister handshake.
5. The server wedges in `_release_entries` and never recovers.

Step 4 is the trigger; the specific cause of the original worker death does not appear to matter.

### Suggested direction

- The IPC release path runs synchronously on `mq-server-thread` while holding the GIL. Even without fixing the underlying driver hang, moving reclaim off the MQ handler thread (or bounding it) would keep the server able to answer health checks and reject new registrations cleanly instead of hanging every client for 300 s.
- A watchdog/timeout around `_release_entries` that logs and abandons the segment would turn an unrecoverable wedge into a leak plus a warning.
- Worth checking whether `cudaIpcCloseMemHandle` can be skipped when the exporting PID is known to be gone.

### Full `py-spy dump`

<details>
<summary>All 22 threads (paths redacted)</summary>

```
Process 1049052: <workdir>/.venv/bin/python3 <workdir>/.venv/bin/lmcache server --port 5555 --http-port 8080 --l1-size-gb 1800 --l1-init-size-gb 20 --max-gpu-workers 1 --max-cpu-workers 8 --chunk-size 512 --l1-align-bytes 16384 --eviction-trigger-watermark 0.85 --eviction-ratio 0.10 --eviction-po

items.title: [Bug] Unbounded compiled-grammar cache in BaseGrammarBackend leaks host memory with per-request JSON schemas
items.author: GinDoliee
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist
- [x] 1. I have searched related issues but cannot get the expected help.
- [x] 2. The bug has not been fixed in the latest version (the cache code is unchanged on `main` as of 2026-10-19).
- [x] 3. Environment info and a minimal reproducible script are included below.
- [x] 4. This is a bug report, not a question.
- [x] 5. Written in English.

## Describe the bug

`BaseGrammarBackend.cache` (`python/sglang/srt/constrained/base_grammar_backend.py`) is a plain `dict` with no size limit, and the xgrammar backend creates `GrammarCompiler(tokenizer_info=tokenizer_info)` with xgrammar's default unbounded internal cache. Every request whose `response_format.json_schema` (or regex / EBNF) has not been seen before adds one compiled grammar to both caches, and nothing ever evicts it while the server is up. Only `/flush_cache` clears it, and `/flush_cache` is refused unless the scheduler is completely idle.

When clients send a slightly different schema per request (very common with LLM-agent frameworks that embed per-call enums, defaults, descriptions or examples in the schema), scheduler RSS grows linearly until host RAM and swap are exhausted.

## What we observed (production, 2026-10-13)

- Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-FP8, SGLang 0.5.10.post1, `--tp-size 1 --dp-size 4`, 4× H100 NVL, 128 GB host RAM + 61 GB swap.
- One client sent ~8,000 structured-output requests/day with ~1,250 distinct schemas (same prompt family, per-call enum/const values inside the schema).
- Each DP rank's scheduler process grew from 3.5 GB to 35 GB over 11 days; total 4 ranks ≈ 140 GB (RAM + swap full), server became unresponsive, 25-minute outage until manual restart.
- Memory never returned while idle. Growth happened only while structured-output requests were processed.

Measured cost per *new* schema (vocab 151k, xgrammar 0.1.32): **+250–380 MB RSS per scheduler process**. Re-sending the *same* schema 4× costs ~+6 MB total. A 60 KB schema costs several GB.

## Reproduction

Start any model with default args (xgrammar backend). Then:

```python
import json, requests, uuid
URL = "http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1/chat/completions"
for i in range(20):
    schema = {"type": "object",
              "properties": {f"field_{j}": {"type": "string", "enum": [f"{uuid.uuid4()}" for _ in range(5)]} for j in range(30)},
              "required": [f"field_{j}" for j in range(30)]}
    body = {"model": "default", "max_tokens": 64,
            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Return an object."}],
            "response_format": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {"name": f"s{i}", "schema": schema}}}
    requests.post(URL, json=body, timeout=120)
```

Watch `VmRSS` of the `sglang::scheduler` process between requests: it grows by hundreds of MB per iteration and does not come back. Sending the same schema 20× does not grow it.

## Expected behavior

The compiled-grammar cache should be bounded (LRU by entry count and/or bytes), and the bound should be configurable. A request that is never repeated should not permanently consume host memory.

## Proposed fix (I can open PRs)

1. Make `BaseGrammarBackend.cache` an LRU (`OrderedDict`, evict oldest on insert) with a configurable max entry count. In-flight requests already hold their own `copy()` of the grammar object, so eviction is safe.
2. Pass `cache_limit_bytes` to xgrammar's `GrammarCompiler` (xgrammar ≥ 0.1.21 supports it) with a sane default (e.g. 1 GiB).
3. Optionally skip caching grammars whose key string exceeds a size threshold (very large schemas are almost never reused and dominate memory).

We have been running (1)+(2)+(3) in production since 2026-10-14: 17.5 h uptime now plateaus at 12–21 GB total across 4 ranks instead of growing without bound, throughput unchanged (333 vs 334 tok/s single stream).

## Environment

- SGLang 0.5.10.post1 (problem code is unchanged on current `main`: `self.cache: Dict[...] = {}`, `GrammarCompiler(tokenizer_info=tokenizer_info)`)
- xgrammar 0.1.32, torch 2.x, CUDA 12.x, 4× NVIDIA H100 NVL, Ubuntu 20.04
- Grammar backend: xgrammar (default)
