items.title: [Bug]: etcd watch callback cancels discovery watch under asyncio debug mode
items.author: codebreaker77
items.body_excerpt:
On main `46d9966b54d9d11998b712e732fb20f64d4d35c0`, a real etcd notification can
cancel a live watch and leave its asyncio reader blocked when debug mode is
enabled. Re-requesting the same prefix returns the cached dead handle.

## Reproduction

With a dedicated etcd 3.5 server and a matching TensorRT-LLM Python environment:

```python
import asyncio
import uuid
from tensorrt_llm.serve.cluster_storage import Etcd3ClusterStorage

async def main():
    storage = Etcd3ClusterStorage("etcd://127.0.0.1:2379", "repro")
    prefix = "watch-repro/" + uuid.uuid4().hex + "/"
    watch = await storage.watch(prefix)
    pending = asyncio.create_task(watch.drain())
    await asyncio.sleep(0)  # reader waits before the SDK thread delivers
    assert await storage.set(prefix + "worker", "registered")
    print("key:", await storage.get(prefix + "worker"), flush=True)
    print(await pending, flush=True)

asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)
```

Run under an external process timeout: the failed wakeup can leave an orphaned
reader, so an asyncio timeout is not a sufficient whole-process safety bound.
Setting `debug=False` is the successful control.

## Observed

Three independent runs against real etcd all produced:

- Debug off: event delivered; SDK watch stays active.
- Debug on: logs `Non-thread-safe operation invoked on an event loop other than
  the current one`; no event delivered; key still readable; SDK watch removed.
- After recording failure and repairing the orphaned wakeup for test cleanup,
  disabling debug and calling `watch(prefix)` returns the same cached handle;
  a second etcd write produces no notification.

This could make a discovery consumer stop receiving worker changes. No router
state, model-serving traffic or GPU effects were measured. Production-mode
controls passed; the established runtime failure is under asyncio debug.

## Cause / proposed scope

`Etcd3WatchEventQueue.add_events_from_resp` mutates an asyncio queue directly on
the etcd SDK callback thread. Its later `call_soon_threadsafe(lambda: None)` is
too late to make that queue operation safe. The exception handler then cancels
the watch, while storage keeps its cached handle.

Capture the owning event loop and enqueue events on that loop using
`call_soon_threadsafe`, with focused threaded-delivery and pending-reader tests.
The unsafe pattern was already flagged in an old review:
https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/pull/8210#discussion_r2415560025
I found no dedicated issue or current fix through searches for etcd/thread,
debug, watch/reconnect and the queue class name. This report adds runtime
evidence rather than claiming the pattern was previously unknown.

## Validation boundary

Real etcd-sdk-python 0.0.7 with Docker etcd 3.5.21. Full unchanged storage/logger
source modules loaded while bypassing TensorRT/native package initialization.
Windows Python 3.10 client with real-server I/O; supplementary actual-thread and
SDK-event checks also reproduce on Linux Python 3.12. The normal-package snippet
above and model serving were not executed locally. This is separate from the
expired-lease failure in #20529.

## Proposed patch and follow-up validation

A focused fix is available on [my fork](https://github.com/codebreaker77/TensorRT-LLM/tree/fix/20684-etcd-watch-threading),
commit [819f5c8f](https://github.com/codebreaker77/TensorRT-LLM/commit/819f5c8f).
It captures the owning event loop and schedules queue insertion onto that loop,
removing the private queue-loop wakeup. It does not include the separate lease
recovery work from #20529.

The nine new CPU cases produce 5 failures / 4 passes on unchanged source and
9 passes with the fix. The full existing storage suite plus these cases passes
62 tests on Linux Python 3.12. Six real-etcd runs with the fix (three each with
debug on/off) deliver two successive notifications and keep the watch active.
The same native-bootstrap isolation described above applies; no full-package,
model-serving or GPU validation is claimed. Applicable formatting/lint checks
pass. The branch is prepared for issue triage; no upstream PR has been opened.

items.title: [BUG] Given boolean tgt_mask, TransformerDecoder produces wrong results with MPS backend
items.author: quanyi-li-oxa
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Two tokens are decoded in this example. Ideally, the output feature on the first token should be the same regardless of the sequence length as a square subsequent mask is applied. Here are two ways to generate the tgt mask. One is from the official example where a float mask is generated first but converted into a boolean mask later. Another way is to generate the boolean mask directly.

:heavy_check_mark: If running with `cpu` backend, the three printed values should be the same:
```
Token_1 (Ground Truth): [[[ 1.1367519  -0.7223548   0.81752294 -1.2319201 ]]]
Ground Truth: [ 1.136752  -0.7223549  0.8175233 -1.2319204]
Buggy Results: [ 1.136752  -0.7223549  0.8175233 -1.2319204]
``` 

❌  However, if we run it on `mps` backend, the directly generated boolean mask would result in the wrong decoded feature for the first token. The result looked like this:
```
Token_1 (Ground Truth): [[[ 1.4028326  -1.0564857  -0.8273474   0.48100036]]]
Ground Truth: [ 1.4028326  -1.0564857  -0.8273474   0.48100036]
Buggy Results: [ 1.3671896  -1.1002903  -0.79846895  0.5315697 ]
```

The bug can be reproduced by this minimal script:
```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# Define the parameters
dropout = 0.  # Dropout rate
d_model = 4
device = "mps"
# device = "cpu"
torch.manual_seed(0)
decoder_layer = nn.TransformerDecoderLayer(batch_first=True, d_model=d_model, nhead=1, dim_feedforward=32,
                                           dropout=dropout)
transformer_decoder = nn.TransformerDecoder(decoder_layer=decoder_layer, num_layers=1)
transformer_decoder = transformer_decoder.to(device)
for p in transformer_decoder.parameters():
    if p.dim() > 1:
        nn.init.xavier_uniform_(p)

# Dummy inputs
tgt = torch.rand(1, 2, d_model, device=device)  # [target sequence length, batch size, embedding size]
memory = torch.rand(1, 20, d_model, device=device)  # [source sequence length, batch size, embedding size]

# generate mask
def _mask_to_float(mask):
    return mask.float().masked_fill(mask == 0, float('-inf')).masked_fill(mask == 1, float(0.0))


def generate_square_subsequent_mask(sz):
    mask = (torch.triu(torch.ones((sz, sz))) == 1).transpose(0, 1)
    return _mask_to_float(mask).bool()


def _generate_square_subsequent_mask_bug(sz):
    mask = (torch.triu(torch.ones((sz, sz))) == 1).transpose(0, 1)
    return ~mask


token_1_mask = generate_square_subsequent_mask(1).to(device)
correct_mask = generate_square_subsequent_mask(2).to(device)
bug_mask = _generate_square_subsequent_mask_bug(2).to(device)

# The masks are all boolean type and are exactly same
assert correct_mask.dtype == bug_mask.dtype
assert torch.all(correct_mask == bug_mask)

# Forward pass through the decoder
token_1 = transformer_decoder(tgt=tgt[:, :1, :], memory=memory, tgt_mask=token_1_mask)
output_bug = transformer_decoder(tgt=tgt, memory=memory, tgt_mask=bug_mask)
output = transformer_decoder(tgt=tgt, memory=memory, tgt_mask=correct_mask)

print("Token_1 (Ground Truth):", token_1.detach().cpu().numpy())
print("Ground Truth:", output[0, 0].detach().cpu().numpy())
print("Buggy Results:", output_bug[0, 0].detach().cpu().numpy())

```

### Versions

Is debug build: False

ROCM used to build PyTorch: N/A

Apple M3 Max

items.title: [MPS] `F.linear` / `matmul` with a transposed weight is up to 8.7x slower than with a contiguous `[K, N]` weight at large K
items.author: roblennon
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On an M1 Max, `F.linear(x, w)` is much slower than the same product against a pre-transposed contiguous weight, `x @ w.t().contiguous()`, once the inner dimension K is large. At M = 4608, N = 6144 the gap is about 1.9x at K = 16384 and 3.6x at K = 32768 in fp16, and 4.2x and 8.4 to 8.7x in fp32. Outputs are identical (maximum absolute difference zero). Release 2.14.1 and nightly 2.16.0.dev20261009 behave the same.

This is the `nn.Linear` layout: the weight is stored `[N, K]` and multiplied transposed. Large-K projections, such as transformer MLP down-projections in diffusion models or LLM prefill, hit it. Single-token decode (small M) is a different path and is not covered here.

Every variant whose right-hand operand is a transposed `[N, K]` tensor is slow, whichever PyTorch path it takes: `F.linear(x, w)` (on macOS 15, `_mps_linear_nograph`), `F.linear` with a non-contiguous input (the MPSGraph path), `x @ w.t()` and `torch.mm(x, w.t())` (`mm_out_mps_impl`), and `torch.mm(w, x.t()).t()`. They match `F.linear` within noise. Only a contiguous right-hand operand is fast. A transposed left-hand operand (`torch.mm(xt.t(), wt)`) stays within 11% of the contiguous variant.

Because every PyTorch path shows the same behavior, the cause is likely below PyTorch, in how MPS / MPSGraph handles a right-hand operand contiguous along K. That is an inference; no kernel profile was taken.

Repro (standalone, torch only):

```python
import time, torch, torch.nn.functional as F
torch.manual_seed(0)

def best_ms(fn, iters=5):
    t = float("inf")
    for _ in range(iters):
        torch.mps.synchronize(); t0 = time.perf_counter(); fn(); torch.mps.synchronize()
        t = min(t, (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1e3)
    return t

M, N = 4608, 6144
for dtype in (torch.float16, torch.float32):
    for K in (4096, 8192, 16384, 32768):          # K > 32768 takes a separate reroute on M1/M2
        x = torch.randn(M, K, device="mps", dtype=dtype)
        w = torch.randn(N, K, device="mps", dtype=dtype) / K ** 0.5   # nn.Linear layout [N, K]
        wt = w.t().contiguous()                                       # [K, N], made once, not timed
        F.linear(x, w); x @ wt                                        # warm up
        a, b = best_ms(lambda: F.linear(x, w)), best_ms(lambda: x @ wt)
        assert torch.equal(F.linear(x, w), x @ wt)
        print(dtype, K, f"F.linear {a:.1f} ms, x @ wt {b:.1f} ms, ratio {a / b:.2f}")
```

Minimum milliseconds per call, M = 4608, N = 6144, three interleaved rounds of five calls after warm-up. Output allocation is included in every timing; the one-off `w.t().contiguous()` copy is not. At fp32, K = 32768 the script holds about 3.4 GB of tensors.

items.title: DataLoader pin_memory thread: per-batch /dev/shm fd munmap causes significant overhead for large/multi-tensor batches
items.author: zhaozheng09
items.body_excerpt:
# DataLoader pin_memory thread: per-batch shared-memory fd munmap causes significant overhead for large/variable-length multi-tensor batches

## Summary

When using `DataLoader(pin_memory=True, num_workers>0)`, every tensor in each batch is transferred from worker → main process via a fresh `/dev/shm` file descriptor (default `file_descriptor` sharing strategy). The pin_memory thread then consumes the batch, and when the previous batch's tensors are deallocated, each fd is `close()`'d + `munmap()`'d. For workloads with **large, variable-length, multi-tensor batches** (e.g. recommendation systems with KeyedJaggedTensor — dozens of tensors per batch, multi-GB values tensor, rebuilt fresh every step), this per-step fd churn + munmap dominates the pin thread and shows up as a large wall-clock gap in the training step.

We built a solution (SharedMemory slot pool) that reuses persistent `/dev/shm` mappings across batches instead of alloc/munmap per batch, yielding **-279 ms/step (-28.7%)** on a 4×H20 recommendation training workload. We'd like to upstream a generalized version.

## Reproduction

4×H20 GPUs, PyTorch 2.10.0+cu126, recommendation model (TorchRec-style KJT batches). `batch_size=12288`, `num_workers=8`, `pin_memory=True`, `prefetch_factor=2`. Each batch contains a `KeyedJaggedTensor` with a variable-length `_values` tensor (~1.3 GB per rank) plus `_lengths`/`_offsets`/`_weights`.

Steady-state `sec/step` (steps 250-500, filtering inductor recompile spikes <1500 ms):

| config | sec/step |
|---|---|
| baseline (default `file_descriptor`) | **972.8 ms** |
| **SharedMemory slot pool (our solution)** | **693.3 ms** |
| **savings** | **-279.5 ms (-28.7%)** |

### Profiler evidence

Chrome trace (torch.profiler, step 300-305) shows a **~600 ms GPU idle gap** per step that is not GPU-bound (kernels finish, then idle waiting for data). ProfilerStep CPU wall time = **442 ms** vs CUDA active = **7.7 ms** — the GPU spends 98% of the step idle, waiting on the pin thread. The pin thread's critical path is dominated by `del previous_batch`, which triggers `close(fd)` + `munmap()` of the previous batch's `/dev/shm` mappings (native stack captured via py-spy: `MapAllocator::~MapAllocator → close(fd) → munmap`).

### Minimal reproduction (stock PyTorch, no TorchRec dependency)

We extracted the root cause into a self-contained script using only stock PyTorch + Python stdlib `multiprocessing.shared_memory`. A persistent worker process sends real tensors over a `multiprocessing.Queue` (triggering `reduce_storage` → real `/dev/shm` fds). Full repro script: https://gist.github.com/zhaozheng09/81cdeda4b6222fb727bcaa324b4d75f7

**Important: the consumer (pin thread) is the critical path; the producer (worker) is parallelizable.** In production, multiple workers (`num_workers=8`) produce batches concurrently, so producer-side cost is overlapped and not on the critical path. The serial bottleneck is the pin thread's per-step `del previous_batch` → `munmap`. The producer-side numbers below are from a single-worker repro and are not representative of the overlapped production case — they can also be further optimized (see notes).

**Consumer-side critical path** (`del previous_batch` segment only, 4×H20, torch 2.10, 4 large tensors/batch, 20 steps steady-state):

| segment | `del prev_batch` cost |
|---|---|
| BEFORE (`file_descriptor`, munmap `/dev/shm`) | **152.3 ms/step** |
| AFTER (SharedMemory slot pool, `del view` — no munmap) | **45.5 ms/step** |
| **savings on this segment** | **-106.8 ms (-70.2%)** |

Micro-benchmark (400 MB): `munmap` of `/dev/shm` tmpfs mapping = **59 ms** vs anon glibc `free` = **38 ms** (1.6× slower — tmpfs must reclaim page cache + cross-process unref).

**End-to-end comparison (single worker repro, consumer + producer both measured):**

| tensors/batch | BEFORE | AFTER | savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 (4×160 MB, worst case) | 586.9 ms | 461.8 ms | **-125 ms (-21.3%)** |
| 100 (100×6.4 MB, KJT-like) | 518.8 ms | 446.2 ms | **-72.6 ms (-14.0%)** |
| 400 | **`OSError: Too many open files`** — `file_descriptor` strategy exhausts fd limit (default 1024); only AFTER runs | — | — |

The 400-tensor case is particularly illustrative: `file_descriptor` creates one `/dev/shm` fd per tensor per in-flight batch, so 400 tensors × `prefetch_factor=2` × queue depth blows past the default fd limit. The slot pool uses a fixed number of slots regardless of tensor count.

**Notes on the producer side:** The single-worker end-to-end numbers above include producer cost (worker building data + queue transfer). With multiple workers this is overlapped — the consumer `del`/`pin`/`h2d` segments are what matter. The AFTER producer uses `torch.randint(out=shm_view)` to write directly into the slot (zero-copy, no intermediate anon tensor); the remaining producer overhead is from the repro's placeholder data generation, not the slot mechanism itself, and can be further reduced.

#### Bonus: `file_descriptor` resource_sharer fragility

During reproduction we hit a robustness issue: with `file_descriptor` sharing, if a worker exits shortly after `Queue.put()`, the `resource_sharer` daemon thread tears down its Unix domain socket before the main process calls `rebuild_storage_fd`, raising `FileNotFoundError` ([Errno 2] No such file or directory) in `resource_sharer.get_connection`. The workaround is to keep the worker alive (e.g. via an `Event`) until the main process has consumed all batches. This is worth noting as it surfaces under the same large-batch / many-worker conditions.


## Root cause

`torch/multiprocessing/reductions.py::reduce_storage` — for each CPU tensor crossing the process boundary:

1. worker: `storage._share_fd_cpu_()` → creates a **new** `/dev/shm` file + `memcpy`
2. main: `rebuild_storage_fd` → `mmap(fd)`
3. main consumes; on deallocation → `close(fd)` + `munmap()`

`shared_cache` exists but only holds `StorageWeakRef` (weak references for dedup) — it does **not** retain mappings for

items.title: use_deterministic_algorithms(True) costs a fill kernel per empty()
items.author: okolenmi
items.body_excerpt:
It's just an optimization proposed by AI that may be helpful for someone who want to test things precisely without increasing computing cost.
fill kernel per empty() costs +2174 kernels and ~98 ms/step on a real 5B diffusion model on my hardware.

### Summary

`torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` also enables
`torch.utils.deterministic.fill_uninitialized_memory`, which fills every
uninitialised allocation with a known value (NaN for floats). On a large model
there is one `torch.empty`/`empty_like` per temporary, so this becomes one extra
fill kernel per temporary, enqueued on the same stream as the model's real work.
The fill is a debugging aid, but it is not small.

### Minimal repro

```python
import time
import torch

torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)
assert torch.utils.deterministic.fill_uninitialized_memory          # default True

# ... and the fill is observable:
assert torch.isnan(torch.empty(1024)).all()                        # flag on
torch.utils.deterministic.fill_uninitialized_memory = False
assert not torch.isnan(torch.empty(1024)).all()                    # flag off


def alloc_us(n, shape, dev):
    sync = torch.xpu.synchronize if dev == "xpu" else (lambda: None)
    sync()
    t = time.perf_counter()
    keep = [torch.empty(*shape, device=dev) for _ in range(n)]
    sync()
    return (time.perf_counter() - t) / n * 1e6


for fill in (True, False):
    torch.utils.deterministic.fill_uninitialized_memory = fill
    print(fill, "us/alloc:", alloc_us(2000, (3072,), "xpu"))
```

### Measured

torch 2.12.1+xpu, Intel Arc B580 (XPU) and CPU, fp32, `min` of two runs,
2000 / 1000 / 10 allocations per row:

| device | tensor | fill on | fill off | delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| xpu:0 | `(3072,)` | 10.58 us | 1.65 us | **+8.93 us** |
| xpu:0 | `(128, 3072)` | 10.91 us | 1.71 us | **+9.21 us** |
| xpu:0 | `(1, 8192, 3072)` | 181.41 us | 6.16 us | **+175.25 us** |
| cpu | `(3072,)` | 2.69 us | 1.32 us | +1.37 us |
| cpu | `(128, 3072)` | 326.74 us | 4.32 us | +322.42 us |
| cpu | `(1, 8192, 3072)` | 11165.88 us | 6.59 us | +11159.29 us |

Two things stand out:

* On XPU a small fill costs **~9 us regardless of the tensor size** -- it is
  launch-bound, not bandwidth-bound. Large fills run at ~570 GB/s.
* On CPU the cost is pure single-threaded fill bandwidth (~9 GB/s), so it is
  proportionally worse for anything that is not tiny.

### Effect on a real model

42-block DiT (dim 3072, ffn 8192, 24 heads, seq 3973), bf16 activations + int8
weights, 2 forwards per generation step. Measured with `torch.profiler` for
exactly one forward, on XPU:

| per forward | fill on | fill off |
|---|---|---|
| `aten::fill_` calls | 2174 | 510 |
| `aten::fill_` device time | 49.3 ms | 0.4 ms |
| `aten::fill_` host (self) time | 46.6 ms | 12.6 ms |
| total kernel launches | 3073 | 1690 |

That is **~1660 extra fill kernels, ~98 ms of device time and ~68 ms of host
time per step** (7-8% of the step), and the generated image is byte-identical
either way (same PNG md5).

### Ask

1. **Decouple the two.** Deterministic *algorithms* and "fill uninitialised
   memory" are separate concerns; a user should be able to keep reproducible
   kernels without paying for a fill kernel per allocation.
2. Or make the fill cheap: only in debug builds, or lazily on read.
3. At minimum, document that the cost is one kernel per allocation and scales
   with the **number** of allocations, not the tensor size -- for a model with
   many temporaries it dominates the flag.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

### Summary

Memory leak found in quantized Stable Difussion 2.1 (fp8) due to orphaned memory handles in cpp_wrapper_cpu.py when fusing qlinear + add.

### Minimal repro

```python
# RSS grows on every iteration (one leaked buffer per qlinear + add fusion).
import torch
import torch._inductor.config as cfg
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torchao.quantization.pt2e.quantizer.x86_inductor_quantizer
import logging

logging.getLogger("torch.utils._pytree").setLevel(logging.ERROR)

class FP8Linear(torch.nn.Module):
  def __init__(self, c, x_scale=0.05):
    super().__init__()
    lin = torch.nn.Linear(c, c)
    self.w_scale = lin.weight.abs().max().item() / torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max
    self.w = (lin.weight / self.w_scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn).detach()
    self.bias, self.x_scale = lin.bias, x_scale

  def forward(self, x):
    w = torch.ops.torchao.dequantize_affine_float8_non_decomposed.default(
      tensor=self.w, scale=torch.tensor([self.w_scale]), output_dtype=torch.float)
    xq = torch.ops.torchao.quantize_affine_float8_non_decomposed.default(
      tensor=x, scale=torch.tensor([self.x_scale]), float8_dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn)
    xdq = torch.ops.torchao.dequantize_affine_float8_non_decomposed.default(
      tensor=xq, scale=torch.tensor([self.x_scale]), output_dtype=torch.float)
    return F.linear(xdq, w, self.bias)

class M(torch.nn.Module):
  def __init__(self, c=320):
    super().__init__()
    self.a, self.b = FP8Linear(c), FP8Linear(c)

  def forward(self, x):
    h = self.a(x)
    return self.b(h) + h

with torch.autocast("cpu"), torch.no_grad():
  x = torch.randn(2, 9216, 320)
  cfg.freezing = cfg.cpp_wrapper = True
  m = torch.compile(M().eval())
  for i in range(100):
    m(x)
    print("Memory usage:", "iteration", i, open("/proc/self/status").read().split("VmRSS:")[1].split()[0], "kB")

items.title: CI reachability: 45 test files (13,799 lines, 459 tests) match the test glob but are reached by no shard, aggregator, or workflow script at 210bb7ca
items.author: alexisromtz-lab
items.body_excerpt:
Hi PyTorch team,

We run an open metrology project: pre-registered, read-only audits of CI reachability. We audited `pytorch/pytorch` at `210bb7ca5c4e08c40513c389c14b1adbf4a82f8c` and want to report a measurable gap, together with the evidence and the commands to reproduce or falsify it.

**What we measured** (static analysis only; we did not run your CI)

- `A` = files matching the discovery contract's own glob, `test/**/test_*.py`: **1,344**
- `B` = `TESTS`, rebuilt from `tools/testing/discover_tests.py` (10 `startswith` patterns at `:74-85`, 38 exact blocklist entries at `:86-126`, 14 `extra_tests` at `:127-142`): **1,121**
- `A - B` = **223** files not scheduled as a shard
- Of those 223, **153 do run**, but by a path the shard does not declare: transitive import from an aggregator that *is* in `TESTS` (e.g. `test/test_fx.py:51-68`), or a direct `python test_X.py` in `.ci`/`.github`
- **70** remain unreached by any of the three layers. **25 of those were false positives on our side and we hand-rejected them** before publishing: 15 reached by `unittest discover -s .../torch_openreg/tests` via the `--openreg` handler (`test/run_test.py:1196-1221`, invoked from `.ci/pytorch/test.sh:2618-2620`); 2 by direct invocation in `.ci/pytorch/test.sh:2052-2082`; 1 by the `test_cpp_extensions_aot_ninja` handler (`test/run_test.py:1127`); 7 that are launchers or a wrapper, not tests.

**Result: 45 files, 13,799 lines, 459 `def test_` — 3.35% of the corpus — that no CI path we could find executes.** They split into two classes with different responsibility:

| class | files | lines | `def test_` | what it is |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | 33 | 11,093 | 355 | the family's aggregator **exists and is in `TESTS`**, but does not import them (`fx`, `jit`, `quantization`, `autograd`, `ao`; `mobile` has no aggregator at all and its CI job is build-only) |
| II | 12 | 2,706 | 104 | the file carries its **own exact entry** in `blocklisted_tests` — declared, not omitted |

Four rows anyone can check in one grep:

```
grep -n 'from fx\.' test/test_fx.py                            # 12 test imports; fx/test_dynamism, fx/test_graph_pickler, ... are not among them
grep -n 'test_node_lifecycle' test/test_autograd.py            # empty; autograd/test_node_lifecycle.py = 566 lines, 47 tests
grep -rn 'qlinear_packed_params' .ci .github test/run_test.py  # empty
grep -n 'test/inductor/test_aot_inductor_utils' tools/testing/discover_tests.py   # :109
```

**Collateral finding: a blocklist entry that can never match.** `tools/testing/discover_tests.py:109` lists `"test/inductor/test_aot_inductor_utils"`, but keys are compared against names relative to `test/` (`:54`), so that key could only ever match `test/test/inductor/...`. Consequence: `inductor/test_aot_inductor_utils` enters `TESTS` (shard 600 of the 1,121) even though the module contains zero tests: its only two classes are `WrapperModule(torch.nn.Module)` and `AOTIRunnerUtil`, and `grep -cE '^\s*def test_|^\s*class Test'` returns 0 (the `TestCase` string in the file is an import plus three `self: TestCase` type annotations, not a test class). The same contract schedules a ghost shard and omits real orphans, and the pipeline colour does not change in either direction.

**On the class-I files:** we are not claiming anyone decided to skip them. The measurable fact is that the aggregator whose pattern comment says *"executed by test_X.py"* does not import them. Whether the fix is adding the import, adding an explicit blocklist entry (which would at least make the decision visible), or removing the files is a maintainer call — the report deliberately does not prescribe it.

**Pre-registration.** The falsifier was frozen before we looked at the tree: *if every file matching the test glob is reached by a shard or a workflow, the hypothesis falls and we publish a refutation.* It did not fall. We also corrected our own contract upward mid-audit: the pre-registration wrote the universe as `test/test_*.py` (179 files, non-recursive); the real contract is recursive (`discover_tests.py:42`, 1,344 files). The report declares that correction in its §2 instead of quietly using the larger number.

**Published record** (immutable; methodology, declared limits and exact reproduction commands included):
- Report #002, v1: `10.5281/zenodo.23513541`
- Concept DOI (always resolves to the latest version): `10.5281/zenodo.23513540`
- Report #001, same method on a different CI: `10.5281/zenodo.23512292`
- Erratum in preparation: one `grep` printed in §12 of v1 is broader than the claim it supports (it matches `TestCase` in imports/annotations). The measurement stands; the command is being corrected in a new version, and the corrected form is the one quoted above.

The report's §11 states the limits — static analysis; reachability outside `unittest discover` and outside the three layers would not be seen — and its §12 has the commands to rebuild `TESTS` from `discover_tests.py` without trusting our numbers.

If useful, we can post the full 45-row table (file, lines, test count, omission mechanism) as a follow-up comment here; we kept it out of the body to keep this readable.

Thanks for your time, and for `run_test.py` and `discover_tests.py` being readable enough to audit from the outside.

items.title: [RFC]: Support Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) Disaggregation in AIBrix Gateway
items.author: varungup90
items.body_excerpt: ### Summary This RFC proposes adding Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) disaggregation support to AIBrix Gateway. Today, AIBrix supports Prefill/Decode (PD) disaggregation. With growing multimodal workloads, the encoding stage can also become a significant and independently scalable part of inference. EPD disaggregation separates inference into three stages: * Encode (E): Process multimodal inputs such as image, video, or audio and generate intermediate representations. * Prefill (P): Process prompt tokens and encoder outputs and generate KV cache. * Decode (D): Perform autoregressive token generation. The Gateway should become aware of these worker roles and route requests to the appropriate Encode, Prefill, and Decode worker pools. ### Motivation Encode, Prefill, and Decode have different compute and memory characteristics. Running all stages on the same workers can lead to resource contention and makes it difficult to scale each stage independently. EPD disaggregation enables: * Independent scaling of Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. * Better resource utilization for multimodal workloads. * Different hardware or parallelism configurations for each stage. * Isolation of expensive multimodal encoding from Prefill/Decode workloads. * Reuse of the existing AIBrix PD routing architecture for multimodal serving. vLLM has started supporting disaggregated encoder architectures, including EPD-style deployments: * https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/ascend/en/latest/user_guide/feature_guide/epd_disaggregation.html * https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/disagg_encoder/ ### Proposed Change Extend AIBrix Gateway’s existing PD disaggregation support to understand an additional Encode worker role. Conceptually: For multimodal requests, the Gateway should: 1. Identify compatible Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. 2. Select workers using the existing AIBrix load-balancing framework. 3. Pass the required routing/transfer metadata to the inference engine. 4. Allow the inference engine and its connectors to handle encoder-output and KV-cache transfers. For text-only requests, the Encode stage can be bypassed and existing PD routing can continue to be used. The implementation should reuse the existing PD routing infrastructure as much as possible rather than introducing a separate routing architecture. Initial Scope * Add encode as a supported worker role alongside prefill and decode. * Discover and maintain Encode/Prefill/Decode worker pools. * Extend PD routing to select a compatible E/P/D execution path. * Support multimodal requests requiring an Encode stage. * Keep encoder-output and KV-cache transfer outside of the Gateway. * Add basic stage-level routing metrics and failure handling. Future work can explore encoder-cache-aware routing, heterogeneous hardware selection, and independent autoscaling of E/P/D worker pools. Open Questions * Should Encode workers be shared across multiple Prefill/Decode pools? * What metadata should the Gateway provide to coordinate encoder-output transfer? * Should worker selection happen in E → P → D order, or should Decode/Prefill capacity drive the selection first? * How much of the existing PD router can be generalized into an EPD stage-aware router? ### Alternatives Considered _No response_ ### Area Not sure

items.title: [Gluon] async_load accepts a pointer whose element type differs from the shared memory buffer
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Gluon's `async_copy.async_load` (and `async_copy_global_to_local` in general) does not check that the pointer element type matches the shared memory element type. Copying from an fp32 pointer into an fp16 buffer compiles and copies raw bytes, and the reverse faults with a misaligned address. `smem.store` rejects the same mismatch at compile time.

```python
import torch
from triton.experimental import gluon
from triton.experimental.gluon import language as gl
from triton.experimental.gluon.language.nvidia.ampere import async_copy


@gluon.jit
def kernel(inp, out, SMEM_DTYPE: gl.constexpr, N: gl.constexpr):
    L: gl.constexpr = gl.BlockedLayout([4], [32], [4], [0])
    offs = gl.arange(0, N, L)
    smem = gl.allocate_shared_memory(SMEM_DTYPE, [N], gl.SwizzledSharedLayout(1, 1, 1, [0]))
    async_copy.async_load(smem, inp + offs)
    async_copy.commit_group()
    async_copy.wait_group(0)
    gl.store(out + offs, smem.load(L))


N = 512
inp = torch.arange(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32) + 0.5
out = torch.zeros(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
kernel[(1, )](inp, out, gl.float16, N)  # fp32 pointer -> fp16 smem: compiles, wrong values
print(out[:8].tolist())

inp = torch.arange(N, device="cuda").to(torch.float16)
out = torch.zeros(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
kernel[(1, )](inp, out, gl.float32, N)  # fp16 pointer -> fp32 smem
torch.cuda.synchronize()                # RuntimeError: CUDA error: misaligned address
```

```
[0.0, 1.75, 0.0, 1.9375, 0.0, 2.28125, 0.0, 2.34375]
RuntimeError: CUDA error: misaligned address
```

The first kernel should print `[0.5, 1.5, 2.5, ...]`; instead each 8-byte copy moves the raw bytes of two fp32 values into four fp16 slots.

Expected: a compile-time error for both, like `smem.store` gives for a value whose dtype does not match the buffer.

The frontend (`python/triton/experimental/gluon/language/nvidia/ampere/async_copy.py`, and the AMD `cdna4`/`cdna5` versions) only checks the shapes, and `AsyncCopyGlobalToLocalOp::verify` only checks that the destination is mutable. The lowering sizes each copy by the shared memory element type, so a mismatch reads with the wrong stride.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Opened #12341, picking up where the closed #12250 left off (same verifier + frontend-check shape, extended to both AMD copy directions).

The builtins now reject the mismatch at the frontend on every NVIDIA and AMD async-copy path, and AsyncCopyGlobalToLocalOp verifies it for non-Gluon producers. The regression test is red without the frontend check and green with it on this machine (no GPU here, so the byte-level runtime repro stays as documented in the issue).

items.title: Non-persistent `triton_kernels.matmul` with a fused SwiGLU masks the MX output scales with the pre-activation `N` instead of `N // 2`, silently writing past each row's scales
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


**TL;DR.** #8865 fixed the MX scale store mask of the persistent `triton_kernels.matmul` kernel to count scale blocks from the output width `yN = N // 2` of a fused SwiGLU instead of the pre-activation `N` ("there is a bug in mask_n_scale which should use yN (N // ACTIVATION_REDUCTION_N) instead N"), but did not change the same mask in the non-persistent kernel (`_matmul.py`), which still uses `N_MX_BLOCK = cdiv(N, 32)`. There, with an MXFP8 or MXFP4 output, the last output tile of a row also stores the scale blocks past the row's `cdiv(yN, 32)` (up to 3 bytes per row at the default `BLOCK_N = 256`, for example N = 576): onto the first scales of the next row, and past the end of the scale tensor for the last row. Possible fix: count from `yN` in the non-persistent kernel too, as #8865 does in the persistent one.

`test_matmul.py` checks this combination under "swiglu together with mxfp8 downcast", but only for the persistent kernel on Blackwell. The script below runs the non-persistent kernel with N = 576 (yN = 288, so 9 scale bytes per row; the output tile is 128 columns, 4 scale bytes) and leaves 3 spare bytes behind every row of the scale tensor, which nothing should write to. N = 512 is the control (yN is a multiple of the output tile):

```python
import sys

import torch
from triton_kernels.matmul import matmul, PrecisionConfig, FusedActivation, FnSpecs, FnName, Epilogue
from triton_kernels.matmul_details import opt_flags
from triton_kernels.numerics_details.mxfp import quantize_mxfp8_fn
from triton_kernels.swiglu import swiglu_fn

swiglu = FusedActivation(FnSpecs("swiglu", swiglu_fn, ("alpha", "limit"), reduction_n=2), (1.0, 1.0))
quantize = Epilogue(FnSpecs(FnName.QUANTIZE_MXFP8.name, quantize_mxfp8_fn, (), ()), (), ())
M, K = 64, 512
bug = False
for N in (512, 576):  # SwiGLU halves N; one scale byte per 32 outputs: 256 outputs = 8 scales per row, 288 outputs = 9
    n_scale = N // 2 // 32
    a = torch.randn(M, K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    b = torch.randn(K, N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    scales = torch.full((M, n_scale + 3), 0xA5, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")  # 3 spare bytes after each row
    config = PrecisionConfig(out_dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, c_mx_scale=scales[:, :n_scale])
    with opt_flags.scoped_opt_flags_constraints({"is_persistent": False}):
        matmul(a, b, None, precision_config=config, epilogue=quantize, fused_activation=swiglu)
    written = int((scales[:, n_scale:] != 0xA5).sum())
    print(f"N={N}: {written} of {M * 3} spare bytes written (expected 0)")
    bug |= written > 0
sys.exit(1 if bug else 0)
```

Observed on main @6fe3348e6 (exit code 1):
```
N=512: 0 of 192 spare bytes written (expected 0)
N=576: 192 of 192 spare bytes written (expected 0)
```
Expected: 0 for both. Every row of N = 576 gets 3 stores at scale columns 9 to 11, which the row does not have. The stored bytes hold 119, the scale byte the epilogue computes for a block that is entirely padding: masked lanes enter the max as -1 ([_downcast_to_mxfp.py#L45](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton_kernels/triton_kernels/numerics_details/mxfp_details/_downcast_to_mxfp.py#L45)), and `-1 / 448` gives byte 119 in the rounding formula at [L55-L56](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton_kernels/triton_kernels/numerics_details/mxfp_details/_downcast_to_mxfp.py#L55-L56) (`-1 / 6` gives 125, the byte seen with an MXFP4 output). A caller passes a contiguous `[M, 9]` scale tensor, where column 9 + j of row r is column j of row r + 1: the stores overwrite the first three scales of the next row (wrong outputs, see below) and, behind the last row, fall outside the tensor. With the change below the script prints 0 for both sizes (exit code 0). On the 3.8.0 wheel with `triton_kernels` from the v3.8.0 tag the output is identical to main.

<details>
<summary>The same with a contiguous scale tensor and a torch reference (3298 of 18432 outputs wrong)</summary>

```python
import sys

import torch
import triton
from triton_kernels.matmul import matmul, PrecisionConfig, FusedActivation, FnSpecs, FnName, Epilogue
from triton_kernels.matmul_details import opt_flags
from triton_kernels.numerics_details.mxfp import quantize_mxfp8_fn, upcast_from_mxfp
from triton_kernels.swiglu import swiglu_fn

M, K, ALPHA, LIMIT = 64, 512, 1.702, 7.0
SENTINEL = 0xA5


def run(N):
    y_n, n_scale = N // 2, triton.cdiv(N // 2, 32)
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    a = torch.randn(M, K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    b = torch.randn(K, N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    swiglu = FusedActivation(FnSpecs("swiglu", swiglu_fn, ("alpha", "limit"), reduction_n=2), (ALPHA, LIMIT))
    quantize = Epilogue(FnSpecs(FnName.QUANTIZE_MXFP8.name, quantize_mxfp8_fn, (), ()), (), (), effective_itemsize=6.0)
    # the [M, n_scale] scales, followed by 64 bytes that nothing should write to
    scale_buf = torch.full((M * n_scale + 64, ), SENTINEL, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
    scale = scale_buf[:M * n_scale].view(M, n_scale)
    config = PrecisionConfig(out_dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, c_mx_scale=scale, c_microblock_size=32)
    with opt_flags.scoped_opt_flags_constraints({"is_persistent": False}):
        y = matmul(a, b, None, precision_config=config, epilogue=quantize, fused_activation=swiglu)
    got = upcast_from_mxfp(y, scale, torch.bfloat16, axis=-1).float()
    acc = a.float() @ b.float()
    g, lin = acc[:, ::2].clamp(max=LIMIT), acc[:, 1::2].clamp(-LIMIT, LIMIT)
    want = g * torch.sigmoid(ALPHA * g) * (lin + 1)
    wrong = (got - want).abs() > 0.15 * want.abs() + 0.1  # fp8 e4m3 rounding stays below 15%
    past_end = int((scale_buf[M * n_scale:] != SENTINEL).sum())
    print(f"N={N} (yN={y_n}, {n_scale} scale blocks per row): {int(wrong.sum())}/{wrong.numel()} output elements wrong, "
          f"{past_end} bytes written past the end of the scale ten

items.title: [Bug]: Kimi K3 / MLA unit tests on SM107: two KDA files skip SM107, a cute_dsl_mla routing case contradicts the perf table, and an indexed-pool decode test compares two code paths bit-exactly
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM main @ e88d19ca3b, PyTorch backend
- GPU with compute capability 10.7 (SM107). Item 2 is a host-side routing test (it monkeypatches the SM version) and fails independently of the GPU.

### Who can help?

Related: #19960 (adds the `test_cute_dsl_mla` case below and extends Kimi K3 to SM107), #18599 (the `(96, 1)` entry in the FP8 perf table), #18938 (the KDA decode kernel and dispatch).

### Reproduction

Three test-only problems seen when running the Kimi K3 / MLA unit tests on SM107. They are grouped here to keep the noise down. None of them is a product bug as far as I can tell. Each item lists the fix I verified.

**1. Two KDA test files skip everything on SM107**

`tests/unittest/_torch/modules/kimi_kda/test_kda_cache_soundness.py:57` and `test_kda_prefill_state_parity.py:40` gate on

```python
torch.cuda.get_device_capability(0) in {(10, 0), (10, 3)}
```

with reason "Kimi K3 is supported only on Blackwell (SM100/SM103)". The runtime predicate `is_kda_optimized_supported()` (`_torch/modules/kimi_kda/_kda_kernels.py:66`) accepts `(100, 103, 107)`, and the neighbouring files (`test_kda_decode_op.py`, `test_kda_prefill_op.py`) already gate on it. So on SM107 these two files report 6 and 15 skips and cover nothing.

Fix: gate on `is_kda_optimized_supported()` like the other files. With `(10, 7)` added, `test_kda_cache_soundness.py` gives 5 passed and 1 skipped on SM107; the remaining skip is its own runtime condition, "could not obtain a recycled cu_seqlens tensor ID". `test_kda_prefill_state_parity.py` gives 15 passed.

Related stale comment: the `_has_supported_gpu()` comments in `test_kda_decode_op.py:33` and `test_kda_prefill_op.py:38` still say the predicate "accepts SM100/SM103 only; SM107 takes the FLA fallback".

**2. `test_cute_dsl_mla.py::test_mla_generation_routes_wide_head_fp8_verify_away_from_trtllm_gen[103-96-1-True-False-cute_dsl_mla]` fails independently of the GPU**

```
pytest tests/unittest/_torch/attention/test_cute_dsl_mla.py -k routes_wide_head
E       AssertionError: assert 'trtllm_gen' == 'cute_dsl_mla'
```

The case `(103, 96, 1, True, False, "cute_dsl_mla")` ("Single-token H=96 is unchanged (measured perf-table entry)") goes through the FP8 perf gate. `_PERF_MIN_BATCH_FP8[(96, 1)] = 8` (`attention/backends/fmha/cute_dsl_mla.py:419`), but `_select_mla_generation_fmha` always builds a decode batch of `batch_size = 4` (`test_cute_dsl_mla.py:148`). So the gate rejects CuTe DSL MLA and the selection falls through to the TRTLLM-Gen stub. The code behaves as the table says; the expectation is wrong for batch 4.

Fix: either expect `"trtllm_gen"` for that case (verified: the parametrization then gives 10/10 passed), or add a `batch_size` parameter to the helper and assert `"cute_dsl_mla"` at batch 8, which would test the table entry the comment refers to.

**3. `test_kda_decode_op.py::test_optimized_decode_updates_indexed_recurrent_state_pool_in_place` (all 3 ids) fails on SM107**

```
torch.testing.assert_close(indexed_output, local_output, rtol=0, atol=0)
E       Mismatched elements: 2154 / 21504 (10.0%)
E       Greatest absolute difference: 0.00048828125
```

The test compares two different code paths bit-exactly:

- The "local" reference calls `_run_production_decode(...)` without `ssm_state_indices`. `KimiKDALinearAttention.forward_decode` then routes to `forward_decode_fallback` (`ssm_state_indices is None`), which runs separate q/k/v/g projections.
- The indexed call passes `ssm_state_indices` and takes the optimized path with the fused `qkvg` projection.

On SM107 the two GEMM shapes round differently, by one bf16 ulp on 10% of the elements. That difference then also shows up in the fp32 recurrent state. Each path is deterministic: two local runs are bit-identical. Running the same core output through `_project_output` twice is bit-identical too.

Fix: compute the local reference on the same path with dense indices, so that the test checks only the pool addressing:

```python
dense_indices = torch.arange(batch_size, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
local_output, local_cache = _run_production_decode(
    optimized,
    hidden_states,
    copy.deepcopy(initial_cache),
    slot_indices=dense_indices.long(),
    ssm_state_indices=dense_indices,
)
```

With this, the indexed output and the indexed recurrent state are bit-identical to the reference for `many-dense-pool`, `many-strided-pool` and `compact-dense-pool`. The test then gives 3 passed on SM107. I have not checked whether the two paths happen to agree bit-exactly on SM100/SM103.

### Expected behavior

These tests run and pass on SM107 (items 1 and 3), and item 2 passes on any GPU.

### Actual behavior

On SM107, item 1 skips everything and item 3 fails as shown above. Item 2 fails independently of the GPU.

### Additional notes

All three fixes are test-only. I can put them in one PR.

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

`trtllm-serve` on the model above, with the multimodal encoder enabled, dies on every rank while estimating KV-cache capacity, in the dummy image encode:

```
_util.py configure_kv_cache_capacity -> _encode_dummy_inputs
modeling_deepseekv41_multimodal.py encode_multimodal_inputs
deepseek_v41_vision.py -> F.scaled_dot_product_attention
RuntimeError: cuDNN Frontend error: [cudnn_frontend] Error: No valid execution plans built.
```

Standalone (1 GPU, compute capability 10.7, torch 2.14 + cuDNN 9.24), the same shape the vision attention uses for the 8192-patch profiling dummy:

```python
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
x = torch.randn(8192, 3 * 1024, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
q, k, v = (t.reshape(8192, 16, 64).transpose(0, 1).unsqueeze(0) for t in x.chunk(3, -1))
F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)  # RuntimeError: ... No valid execution plans built.
```

### Expected behavior

The server starts and image requests are served, as on SM100/SM103.

### actual behavior

Startup fails as above. Only `disable_mm_encoder: true` gets the server up (text only).

### additional notes

Root cause:
- PyTorch 2.14 (CUDA >= 13 builds) prefers the cuDNN SDPA backend on every SM 10.x device, including 10.7, and does not fall back to another backend when cuDNN plan building fails.
- cuDNN 9.24 offers only runtime-compiled engines (eng8/eng10) for SM 10.7 SDPA forward, and all of them fail NVRTC compilation (`CUDNN_STATUS_INTERNAL_ERROR_COMPILATION_FAILED`). This holds for every shape that dispatches to cuDNN (head_dim 32/64/128, BF16/FP16, contiguous or strided), with NVRTC 13.2 or 13.4. cuDNN 9.25.1.1, 9.26.1.1 and 9.27.0.42 provide an engine (eng18) that builds on SM 10.7.
- A try/except fallback in the model is not safe: after a failed build PyTorch caches a null graph for that shape and the next call on the same shape segfaults. Reported upstream as pytorch/pytorch#201420.
- The vision tower's unit tests are CPU-only, and the V4.1 GPU tests (added with #19727) are text-only and do not run on SM 10.7, so CI does not cover this path.

Vision tower forward on one Vera Rubin GPU (full 32-layer tower + aligner, real weights, BF16; 1022x1022 image = 5329 patches / 8192-patch profiling dummy):

| SDPA backend | 5329 patches | 8192 patches |
|---|---|---|
| cuDNN 9.24 (as shipped) | fails | fails |
| FLASH | 30.8 ms | 53.0 ms |
| EFFICIENT | 44.6 ms | 86.3 ms |
| MATH | 260 ms | 567 ms |
| cuDNN 9.27 | 22.8 ms | 35.5 ms |

Against an FP32 reference (the checkpoint's `inference/vision.py`), every BF16 backend has a relative L2 error of 3.5–3.8% at the aligner output (MATH in BF16: 3.7%), so the choice of backend is within BF16 noise.

Proposed fix: on SM 10.7 with cuDNN < 9.25, exclude only the cuDNN backend around the vision SDPA call; leave every other configuration unchanged, since cuDNN is the fastest backend where it works. PR to follow.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL >= 4.6: FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward with block-sparse masks spills registers, up to 1.8x slower than 4.5.3 (same kernel source)
items.author: janhuenermann
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

With the same kernel source, CuTe DSL 4.6.0.dev0 and later generate PTX for the FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward kernel (`flash_attn.cute.flash_bwd_sm100.FlashAttentionBackwardSm100`) that spills registers. The spills appear when the kernel is specialized for block-sparse attention with a `mask_mod`. That is the path `torch.nn.attention.flex_attention(..., kernel_options={"BACKEND": "FLASH"})` takes. With CuTe DSL 4.5.3, the same source compiles to PTX with no spills, or almost none. The kernel is at the 128-register cap (512 threads per CTA), so the extra pressure becomes local-memory traffic. On B200 the backward kernel is 22% slower with a sliding-window mask and 82% slower with a document mask. The dense, causal, GQA and native `window_size` specializations of the same kernel are not affected.

This looks like the backward counterpart of #3701 (forward kernel, 4.7/4.8 vs 4.5.1), and it narrows down where the regression landed. 4.5.3 is fine. 4.6.0.dev0 already regresses, and it is the first release whose PTX header says `Based on NVVM 23.0.0` (4.5.3: `NVVM 20.0.0`).

**Backward kernel GPU time**, ms (B200, bf16, head dim 128, 16 heads; median of 50; main backward kernel only, from the torch profiler; a repeat run agrees within 1% for the block-sparse rows and within 5% for the others)

| attention | 4.5.3 | 4.6.0.dev0 | 4.8.0 ¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| full, batch 2 × 8192 | 2.039 | 2.010 (−1%) | 2.084 |
| causal, 2 × 8192 | 1.121 | 1.140 (+2%) | 1.177 |
| GQA causal (32 q / 4 kv heads), 2 × 8192 | 2.287 | 2.266 (−1%) | 2.366 |
| native sliding window 1024 (`window_size`), 2 × 16384 | 0.714 | 0.713 (0%) | 0.756 |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: sliding window 1024**, 2 × 16384 | 0.858 | **1.045 (+22%)** | **1.027 (+20%)** |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: document mask** (causal within random-length documents), 1 × 32768 | 1.279 | **2.329 (+82%)** | **2.209 (+73%)** |

The 4.5.3 and 4.6.0.dev0 columns run the same FA4 source (b20, see "Same source" below).
¹ The 4.8.0 column runs FA4 4.0.0b32, the latest release at the time of testing (b33 has a byte-identical backward kernel). FA4 changed between b20 and b32, so this column shows that the regression persists; it is not a clean A/B.

**The same PTX files assembled by one ptxas** (CUDA 13.0, V13.0.88, `ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v`)

| backward specialization | PTX from | spill stores / loads | SASS instr. | IMAD | STL / LDL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| causal | 4.5.3 (CUDA 12.9 / NVVM 20.0.0) | 0 / 0 B | 3496 | 242 | 0 / 0 |
| causal | 4.6.0.dev0 (CUDA 13.3 / NVVM 23.0.0) | 0 / 0 B | 3360 | 216 | 0 / 0 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.5.3 | 0 / 0 B | 3800 | 294 | 0 / 0 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.6.0.dev0 | 124 / 228 B | 4528 | 703 | 31 / 57 |
| sliding window `mask_mod` | 4.8.0 (CUDA 13.4 / NVVM 23.0.0) ¹ | 260 / 264 B | 4192 | 318 | 65 / 55 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.5.3 | 28 / 16 B | 4512 | 653 | 7 / 4 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.6.0.dev0 | 204 / 204 B | 5952 | 1049 | 51 / 42 |
| document `mask_mod` | 4.8.0 ¹ | 184 / 184 B | 5456 | 968 | 46 / 37 |

All of these are at 128 registers (`.reqntid 512`), with warp-specialized budgets (`setmaxnreg.inc` 136/152, `setmaxnreg.dec` 88/24). The PTX files have no `.local` declarations, so ptxas introduces the spills from register pressure in the NVVM 23 PTX. The SASS that 4.8.0 ships through its own ptxas has 50 STL / 42 LDL for the document mask and 35 / 26 for the sliding window (causal: 2 / 2).

**Likely pressure region.** `CUTE_DSL_COMPILER_OPT="remarks{ptx}" CUTE_DSL_LINEINFO=1` on 4.8.0 marks `flash_attn/cute/block_sparse_utils.py:1564` in `get_block_sparse_iteration_info_bwd`. That line loads the block-sparse count and index tensors: `curr_q_cnt = q_cnt[batch_idx, head_idx, n_block]` and `q_idx[batch_idx, head_idx, n_block, None]`. #3701 found the same kind of small metadata-tensor load for the forward kernel (`cu_seqlens` in the varlen scheduler). Here the IMAD count rises together with the spills (document mask: 653 → 1049). We suspect the address arithmetic of these indexed loads, but have not verified it.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

The attached `nvvm23-sm100-bwd-repro.zip` has the scripts, the nine PTX files and our raw results. Its README has more detail.

*1. No GPU needed.* Assemble the attached PTX pair:

```
ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v ptx/bwd.document_mask.fa4-b20.cutlass-dsl-4.5.3.nvvm20.ptx -o /dev/null
    16 bytes stack frame, 28 bytes spill stores, 16 bytes spill loads
ptxas -arch=sm_100a -O3 -v ptx/bwd.document_mask.fa4-b20.cutlass-dsl-4.6.0.dev0.nvvm23.ptx -o /dev/null
    152 bytes stack frame, 204 bytes spill stores, 204 bytes spill loads
```

*2. On a B200: time the backward* with the script below (FA4 through `flex_attention`, about 50 lines), once per environment:

```
python3.12 -m venv nvvm20 && . nvvm20/bin/activate
pip install torch==2.14.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
pip install torch==2.14.0 numpy flash-attn-4==4.0.0b19 nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.5.3 quack-kernels==0.5.0 apache-tvm-ffi==0.1.11
python minimal_repro.py

python3.12 -m venv nvvm23 && . nvvm23/bin/activate
pip install torch==2.14.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
pip install torch==2.14.0 numpy flash-attn-4==4.0.0b20 nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.6.0.dev0 quack-kernels==0.5.3 apache-tvm-ffi==0.1.12
python minimal_repro.py

comments.author: dongxiao92
comments.body: Hey @janhuenermann , I did some investigation and could reproduce your issues. Basically it's a specific pattern in PTX triggering pathological transformation in ptxas. We have started to work with compiler team to see how to fix it. Meawhile, there're a few options for you to WAR it: - option1: using O2 in cute.compile for impacted kernels. This is the most straightword path in my understanding. - option2: removing the cutlass prefix in kernel name through `FlashAttentionBackwardSm100.kernel.set_name_prefix("", remove_cutlass_symbol=True`. But this API is only available from 4.6.2 so an update will be necessary. - option3: patching the FA4 code. I list the perf results with different WARs below. Could you help to comment which one may be helping your case before we have a clean fix in future release?

items.title: Experimental tracking: Qwen 3.5 gated attention block on Rubin (cuDNN Frontend FROST kernels), the proof of concept before Qwen 3.8 Flash-Next
items.author: RomanAnders90
items.body_excerpt:
Owner: @RomanAnders90

This tracks the experimental `flashinfer.qwen_3_5_block` API (PR #6573), with its backend in `flashinfer/experimental/qwen_3_5_block/`: the Qwen 3.5 full-attention sub-layer as one call, from the post-layernorm hidden states to the attention output, over the serving stack's own paged KV cache. One plan runs the QKV + gate projection, QK-RMSNorm with partial RoPE, the paged-KV write-through, GQA attention at head dim 256 with split-KV, the sigmoid output gate and the out projection. Three serving forms, each its own compiled plan: dense prefill, extend (chunked prefill, prefix-cache hit, speculative verify) and decode (`q_len = 1 + drafts`). The kernels are CuTe DSL kernels vendored from cuDNN Frontend (the FROST kernels), with the import roots rewritten and a small set of declared patches; the deployed process imports neither the `cudnn` package nor the cuDNN library. The intended consumer is vLLM's Qwen 3.5 attention layer through FlashInfer.

It fits the experimental path as a model-specific fused block on one part: bf16 and SM107 (Rubin, cc 10.7) only, deliberately overfit to one model family; the kernels are still moving on the cuDNN Frontend side (the vendored pin follows cuDNN Frontend `develop` and is re-vendored as that side lands improvements); the SDPA launch binder is served in Python rather than by the native extension; and the API should settle once the vLLM integration is in use. It is explicit-only, with no `backend="auto"` routing and no AOT packaging.

Execution contract: compute capability 10.7, bf16 activations and weights, head_dim 256, `rope_dim` a positive multiple of 64 below head_dim (64 default), GQA with the model's head counts, a paged KV cache addressed by `slot_mapping` for the write-through and by block tables for the reads, `page_size` a positive multiple of 16 (16 / 32 / 64 / 128 validated), int32 index tensors whose form is checked host-side before any launch so a first `run` can be captured into a CUDA graph. Every other device, DSL version, dtype or geometry is a typed `NotImplementedError`; `qwen_3_5_block_support()` is the init-time dispatch predicate.

Roadmap: Qwen 3.5 is the proof of concept. The next step is Qwen 3.8 Flash-Next, whose attention layers add Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA) with an indexer on top of this block: decode first, then prefill. Those kernels land in cuDNN Frontend first and are then vendored here, either as an extension of this API or as a sibling experimental API under this issue, decided with the maintainers when the 3.8 PR opens.

Graduation target: the first release on or after **2026-11-04**, subject to maintainer review. Before graduation:

- Run the GPU tests through the experimental CI lane on an SM107 runner once one is available (today the CPU tests run everywhere and the GPU tests skip in CI; they are validated on the intended hardware before each push).
- Land the vLLM integration of the Qwen 3.5 attention layer and confirm the API needs no change for it.
- Pin the vendored cuDNN Frontend sources to a released version instead of a `develop` commit, and keep the one-command re-vendor path.
- Decide whether the Python SDPA launch binder stays or the native binder is adopted.
- Settle the stable name and module, and the relation to the Qwen 3.8 Flash-Next work.
- Remove the backend instead if vLLM does not adopt it.

This issue tracks qualification and API integration of the Qwen 3.5 block; the Qwen 3.8 Flash-Next kernels get their own PR(s).

items.title: [Perf] v0.7.2rc5: #6167 warp split-K MXFP8 GEMM becomes the untuned mm_mxfp8 cute-dsl default on SM100/SM103 (m16 n6144 k1536 ~0.83x)
items.author: jimmyzho
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

#6167 (warp-level split-K MXFP8 GEMM, commit 896909a6a, on `release-v0.7.2` since v0.7.2rc5) registers its new kernel as the **first** runner for `mm_mxfp8(backend="cute-dsl")` when M <= 8 or K <= 2048 on SM100 and SM103. The first runner is the untuned default, and on at least one Core-Models shape (the MiniMax-M3 dense FFN GEMM, m 16, n 6144, k 1536) that default is slower than the previous kernel. SM107 keeps the old path and is unaffected.

Measured same-node, interleaved A/B, 5 rounds, fresh process per run, CUDA-event timing, tree before #6167 vs tree at #6167 (ratio = t_before / t_after, so < 1 means slower after); the m 16 result reproduced on two different GB300 nodes:

| `mm_mxfp8`, bf16 in / bf16 out, 128x4 scale layout, untuned | SM103 (GB300) | SM100 (B200) | SM107 |
|---|---|---|---|
| cute-dsl, m 16, n 6144, k 1536 | 0.84x / 0.855x (two nodes) | 0.83x | 1.00x (gated) |
| cute-dsl, m 8, n 6144, k 1536 | 0.92-0.95x (marginal) | not run | 1.00x |
| cute-dsl, m 1 / m 4 / m 32, n 6144, k 1536 | 0.98 / 0.98 / 1.01x | 0.99 / 1.03x | 1.00x |
| cute-dsl, m 16, n 1536, k 6144 (K > 2048 control) | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x |
| cutlass / trtllm backends, every shape above | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x |
| cute-dsl, m 16, n 6144, k 1536, `--autotune` | ~1.0x, but 15-27 % run-to-run spread at this size | 1.05x (m 4) | 1.00x |

Bisecting the following commits on the branch (#6089, #5276, #5663, then #6309 / #6503 / #6726 / #6555 / #6546 / #6521) shows no further movement on these cells, so the change is #6167 alone.

## Root cause

In `flashinfer/gemm/gemm_base.py` the new warp-level split-K runner is inserted ahead of the existing tcgen05 runner whenever M <= 8 or K <= 2048, so it becomes the untuned default for every small-K call on SM100 / SM103 even where the existing kernel is faster (M 16 at K 1536 here). Autotuning picks the better of the two, but the untuned path is what `backend="cute-dsl"` callers get.

Suggested fix: keep the existing runner first for M > 8 (or narrow the shape rule to where the new kernel measured faster), or register the new kernel only as an autotune candidate.

## Reproduce

Run from `benchmarks/` on two checkouts, back to back on the same GPU, with a separate JIT cache (`FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_BASE`) per checkout. Good tree: `198c6d2ef` (the commit before #6167 on `release-v0.7.2`). Bad tree: `896909a6a` (#6167) or `v0.7.2rc5`. Compare the `-vv` median of the `cute-dsl` backend.

```bash
# regressed cell (MiniMax-M3 dense FFN shape)
python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py --routine mm_mxfp8 --m 16 --n 6144 --k 1536 --input_dtype bfloat16 --out_dtype bfloat16 --backends cute-dsl --use_128x4_sf_layout --refcheck --random_seed 42 -vv --use_cuda_events --generate_repro_command
# same shape, all three backends side by side (cutlass and trtllm should not move)
python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py --routine mm_mxfp8 --m 16 --n 6144 --k 1536 --input_dtype bfloat16 --out_dtype bfloat16 --backends cutlass cute-dsl trtllm --use_128x4_sf_layout --refcheck --random_seed 42 -vv --use_cuda_events --generate_repro_command
# M ladder at the same N / K
python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py --routine mm_mxfp8 --m 8 --n 6144 --k 1536 --input_dtype bfloat16 --out_dtype bfloat16 --backends cute-dsl --use_128x4_sf_layout --refcheck --random_seed 42 -vv --use_cuda_events --generate_repro_command
python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py --routine mm_mxfp8 --m 4 --n 6144 --k 1536 --input_dtype bfloat16 --out_dtype bfloat16 --backends cute-dsl --use_128x4_sf_layout --refcheck --random_seed 42 -vv --use_cuda_events --generate_repro_command
python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py --routine mm_mxfp8 --m 32 --n 6144 --k 1536 --input_dtype bfloat16 --out_dtype bfloat16 --backends cute-dsl --use_128x4_sf_layout --refcheck --random_seed 42 -vv --use_cuda_events --generate_repro_command
# control: K > 2048, the new runner is not first here, should be flat
python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py --routine mm_mxfp8 --m 16 --n 1536 --k 6144 --input_dtype bfloat16 --out_dtype bfloat16 --backends cute-dsl --use_128x4_sf_layout --refcheck --random_seed 42 -vv --use_cuda_events --generate_repro_command
# control: autotuned (recovers; expect wide spread at this size, repeat a few times)
python3 flashinfer_benchmark.py --routine mm_mxfp8 --m 16 --n 6144 --k 1536 --input_dtype bfloat16 --out_dtype bfloat16 --backends cute-dsl --use_128x4_sf_layout --refcheck --random_seed 42 -vv --use_cuda_events --autotune --generate_repro_command
```

Environment used: CUDA 13.4 toolkit image, cuDNN frontend 1.31.0, CUTE_DSL_LIBS for cu13 (cutlass-dsl 4.8). The kernel is only a few microseconds, so alternate the two trees for 3 to 5 repeats rather than relying on a single pair.

## Related

- #6167 (the PR). #6521 and #6709 (SM107 GEMM selection and small-M MXFP8 kernels) were bisected and are not involved on SM100 / SM103.

items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting
- [x] I searched existing issues. This is separate from the out-of-pool page-ID validation tracked in #6741.

### Bug description
`BatchMLAPagedAttentionWrapper(backend="cutlass")` can return NaN in valid output rows when only KV storage outside a request is NaN. All page IDs in this reproduction are in bounds, and all logically valid Q/K/V elements are finite.

Two independently reproduced sources are:
1. The unused tail of the request's last page, after `kv_len % page_size`.
2. A valid physical page referenced only by unused slots after the request's last page in dense `block_tables`.

Both are confirmed on B300 (SM103). The in-bounds, unpoisoned controls pass the independent FP32 MLA reference; FA2 stays finite and matches the reference with the same poison. The observations are consistent with loading past `kv_len`, masking scores, and then allowing `0 * NaN` to enter P@V; that is a suspected mechanism, not a proven kernel-level root cause.

### B200 and B300 evidence
Yang Xu independently reported the same two sources on B200 (SM100), using seeds 1, 9 and 92, in [this review](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6743#pullrequestreview-5584279162). The B300 reproduction used the same seeds and separately tested both CSR and dense metadata. For example, seed 9 has page size 64 and KV lengths `[127,64,64,1,128,4096]`:

| B300 seed 9 | Requests with non-finite output (zero-based) |
| --- | --- |
| Unpoisoned, CSR or dense | none |
| Last-page tail only, CSR or dense | 0, 3 |
| Padding page only, CSR | none (wrapper-generated padding refers to finite page 0) |
| Padding page only, dense | 1, 2, 3 |

Each affected Q=1 request has 65,536 non-finite output elements (128 heads × 512 values). Seeds 1 and 92 confirm the same distinction. This is not a cross-GPU performance comparison.

### Minimal standalone reproduction
This smaller confirmed B300 example uses two requests with lengths 63/64 and page size 64. Page IDs 1/2 contain the requests, page 0 stays finite, and page 3 is used only for dense-table padding.

```python
import json

import torch

from flashinfer.mla import BatchMLAPagedAttentionWrapper, MLAPlanMetadata

torch.manual_seed(0)
query = torch.randn(2, 128, 576, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16) * 0.25
original = torch.randn(4, 64, 576, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16) * 0.25
workspace = torch.empty(128 << 20, device="cuda", dtype=torch.uint8)
records = []
for backend in ("cutlass", "fa2"):
    for form in ("csr", "dense"):
        for region in ("control", "last_page_tail", "table_padding"):
            cache = original.clone()
            if region == "last_page_tail":
                cache[1, 63:].fill_(float("nan"))
            if region == "table_padding":
                cache[3].fill_(float("nan"))
            qptr = torch.tensor([0, 1, 2], dtype=torch.int32)
            lengths = torch.tensor([63, 64], dtype=torch.int32)
            if form == "csr":
                metadata = MLAPlanMetadata.csr(
                    qptr,
                    torch.tensor([0, 1, 2], dtype=torch.int32),
                    torch.tensor([1, 2], dtype=torch.int32),
                    lengths,
                )
            else:
                metadata = MLAPlanMetadata.dense(
                    qptr, torch.tensor([[1, 3], [2, 3]], dtype=torch.int32), lengths, 1
                )
            wrapper = BatchMLAPagedAttentionWrapper(workspace, backend=backend)
            wrapper.plan(
                metadata=metadata,
                num_heads=128,
                head_dim_ckv=512,
                head_dim_kpe=64,
                page_size=64,
                causal=False,
                sm_scale=192**-0.5,
                q_data_type=torch.bfloat16,
                kv_data_type=torch.bfloat16,
                query_layout="packed",
                kv_cache_layout="packed",
                lse_mode="none",
            )
            out = wrapper.run(query=query, kv_cache=cache)
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
            records.append(
                dict(
                    backend=backend,
                    metadata=form,
                    region=region,
                    nonfinite_per_request=(~torch.isfinite(out)).flatten(1).sum(1).tolist(),
                )
            )
print(json.dumps(records))

```

Expected: both outputs remain finite in every case.
Observed non-finite counts per request:
- CUTLASS unpoisoned: `[0,0]`.
- CUTLASS last-page-tail poison: `[65536,0]` for CSR and dense.
- CUTLASS padding-page poison: CSR `[0,0]`, dense `[65536,65536]`.
- FA2: `[0,0]` for every region/metadata combination.

The original PR corpus can reproduce the affected seeds with:
```bash
FLASHINFER_MLA_FUZZ_ONLY_SEED=1,9,92 pytest -s tests/attention/test_mla_paged_attention_fuzz.py -k 'cutlass and valid'
```
This command reproduces the hard failure at PR #6743 commit `cedd295f`. The follow-up quarantine will retain the unpoisoned control as a gate before isolating only the poisoned-padding phase; the standalone reproduction above bypasses that test-only quarantine.

items.title: [Bug] CuTe DSL monolithic MLA propagates padding NaNs into valid output on SM103
items.author: leonardHONG
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting
- [x] I searched existing issues. This tracks the CuTe DSL monolithic MLA backend separately from CUTLASS padding contamination (#6860) and invalid page IDs (#6741).

### Bug description
On B300/SM103, `BatchMLAPagedAttentionWrapper(backend="auto")` selects `cute-dsl-monolithic` for fuzzer seeds 90 and 112. Both pass the unpoisoned control against the independent FP32 reference, but NaN in storage outside a request propagates into valid output rows. Explicitly selecting `cute-dsl-monolithic` reproduces it, while explicitly selecting FA2 on the identical inputs stays finite and matches the reference.

All page IDs are in bounds and all logically valid Q/K/V elements are finite. Regions were poisoned independently, not just together:

| Seed | KV lengths / page size | Last-page-tail poison: affected requests | Dense padding-page poison: affected requests |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 90 | `[4096,127]` / 16 | request 1: 524,288 non-finite elements | none |
| 112 | `[4096,129,64,128,65]` / 64 | request 1: 131,072; request 4: 540,672 | request 1: 131,072; request 2: 16,384 |

Request indices are zero-based. Seed 90 uses 128 heads and query lengths `[33,8]`; seed 112 uses 32 heads and query lengths `[33,8,1,8,33]`. Both use BF16 and dense metadata. The observed auto backend name was read after executing the control, not inferred from the requested string `auto`.

This is consistent with masked padding values still entering P@V. The exact CuTe kernel mechanism remains to be confirmed. These B300 results should not be interpreted as an identification of the separate extra `auto` failure reported on B200 in the PR review.

### Reproduction
On PR #6743, run:
```bash
FLASHINFER_MLA_FUZZ_ONLY_SEED=90,112 pytest -s tests/attention/test_mla_paged_attention_fuzz.py -k 'auto and valid'
```
This reproduces the hard failures at commit `cedd295f`. The follow-up ledger will quarantine only the poisoned-padding phase for the actual selected backend, after its unpoisoned control passes. The direct diagnostic below bypasses that ledger, selects each backend explicitly, and separates the two poison regions. It uses the PR's input/reference helpers:

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path

import torch

from tests.attention.test_mla_paged_attention_fuzz import (
    _check_numeric,
    _run_kwargs,
    _structure,
    _wrapper,
    make_problem,
    reference_mla,
    sample_config,
)


@torch.inference_mode()
def main():
    torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False
    workspace = torch.empty(128 << 20, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
    records = []
    for seed in (90, 112):
        cfg = sample_config(seed, "auto")
        for backend in ("cute-dsl-monolithic", "fa2"):
            for region in ("control", "last_page_tail", "table_padding", "both"):
                p = make_problem(cfg, poison_padding=False)
                if region in ("last_page_tail", "both"):
                    for ids, length in zip(p.pages, cfg.kv_lengths, strict=True):
                        tail = length % cfg.page_size
                        if tail:
                            p.cache[ids[-1], tail:].fill_(float("nan"))
                if region in ("table_padding", "both"):
                    p.cache[p.nan_page].fill_(float("nan"))
                p.kv_cache = _structure(p.cache, cfg.kv_layout)
                wrapper = _wrapper(p, backend, workspace)
                out = torch.empty_like(p.q[..., :512])
                lse = torch.empty(p.q.shape[:2], dtype=torch.float32, device=p.q.device)
                wrapper.run(**_run_kwargs(p, out, lse))
                torch.cuda.synchronize()
                counts = [
                    int((~torch.isfinite(rows)).sum())
                    for rows in out.split(cfg.q_lengths)
                ]
                numeric = None
                if bool(torch.isfinite(out).all()):
                    _check_numeric(out, lse, p, reference_mla(p))
                    numeric = True
                if region == "control" or backend == "fa2":
                    assert numeric is True
                records.append(
                    dict(
                        seed=seed,
                        backend=backend,
                        selected=wrapper._planned_backend_name,
                        region=region,
                        metadata=cfg.metadata_form,
                        page_size=cfg.page_size,
                        lengths=cfg.kv_lengths,
                        q_lengths=cfg.q_lengths,
                        heads=cfg.heads,
                        dtype=str(cfg.dtype),
                        nonfinite_per_request=counts,
                        finite_reference_check=numeric,
                    )
                )
    Path(__file__).with_suffix(".json").write_text(json.dumps(records, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(records))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```

items.title: [Feature]: Track experimental ResInfer MEXT, ResAttn, and KEXT kernels
items.author: ShawRong
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and this request has not been filed yet.

### Problem

ResInfer uses base-plus-residue NVFP4 representations for linear layers and
decode attention. Integrating these kernels through FlashInfer's public APIs
would let users compose them with FlashInfer GEMM and paged KV caches without
maintaining a separate Torch extension.

### Requested outcome

Track three experimental features, owned by @ShawRong:

- **MEXT:** row-pair residue quantization and GEMM with FP32 Fold.
- **ResAttn:** grouped-Q residue attention over a paged NVFP4 KV cache.
- **KEXT:** selected-channel residue quantization feeding upstream FP4 GEMM.

These implementations come from **ResInfer**, public commit
[51b9068](https://github.com/ShawRong/resinfer/commit/51b906836a69fa43915040314df57bc9f23030ad).
The integration retains the original copyright and license notices.
Implementation and validation are available in [the fork PR](https://github.com/ShawRong/flashinfer/pull/1).

### Target hardware

SM100 (B200, GB200); validated on B200.

### Inference engine

PyTorch native.

### Why experimental

The residue representation introduces distinct activation, weight and KV-scale
contracts. The proposed APIs are explicit opt-ins while those contracts and
the SM100 implementation receive review. They use deferred imports and are
excluded from automatic backend selection and AOT registration.

### Acceptance criteria and graduation plan

- [x] Pass reference correctness and CUDA Graph replay tests on SM100:
  MEXT 30, ResAttn 15, KEXT 43.
- [x] Pass the repository's pre-commit hooks.
- [x] Include and validate runnable examples for all three features.
- [ ] Finalize the API and layout contracts with maintainers.
- [ ] Pass the upstream experimental CI lane for the declared tests.
- [ ] Publish matched kernel performance measurements with shapes, runtime and
  timing boundaries; include activation quantization in pipeline measurements
  and exclude offline weight/cache preparation.
- [ ] Review each feature for graduation, continued incubation or removal.

### Timing or release need

Proposed graduation target: **v0.8.0**, subject to maintainer agreement.
Review progress within four weeks of experimental admission. If a feature is
not ready, document its remaining blockers and request a maintainer-approved
extension with an updated target.
