items.title: GDN chunk_gated_delta_rule: much higher incomplete-generation rate on Hopper (SM90) vs Blackwell (SM120), same model/LoRA/config
items.author: anhngml
items.body_excerpt:
## GDN chunk_gated_delta_rule on Hopper (SM90): significantly higher rate of premature/incomplete generation vs Blackwell (SM100/SM120), same model/weights/config — suspect numerical difference, not a config issue

**flashinfer version**: `0.6.16.post3`
**Model**: `numind/NuExtract3` (Qwen3.5-family, hybrid Mamba/GDN attention) + a LoRA adapter, served via `vllm/vllm-openai:latest` (vLLM 0.28.0)
**GPUs compared**: NVIDIA H100 NVL (Hopper, SM90) vs NVIDIA RTX 5090 (Blackwell, SM120)

### Summary

Running the exact same model + exact same LoRA adapter (verified byte-identical, SHA256 match) + exact same serving config against the exact same input documents, we see a **~20-45% rate of incomplete generation** (model emits a natural stop token, `finish_reason='stop'`, before finishing valid JSON — output is missing a closing bracket at the very end) on an H100 (SM90), but **0/10 on an RTX 5090 (SM120)** in a matched test. We've ruled out every config-level variable we could think of and are left suspecting something in the GDN chunk_gated_delta_rule computation itself behaves differently (numerically) between SM90 and SM100/SM120.

### What we're doing

Structured extraction: model is prompted (via `chat_template_kwargs.template`, the NuExtract-style type-marker DSL) to fill in a JSON template for a large, deeply-nested schema (~19 repeating array/table fields, up to 5 levels of nesting, template itself ~8.6KB as JSON). Generation is **free-text** (no `response_format`/grammar constraint) — nothing enforces the model to close every bracket before stopping. `temperature=0.0`.

### The failure signature (confirmed by directly capturing raw model output + `finish_reason`)

For the majority of failures on H100:
- `finish_reason == "stop"` (NOT `"length"` — not a token-budget truncation; `completion_tokens` typically 1500-3700, nowhere near any configured ceiling)
- The resulting text fails `json.loads()` with `Expecting ',' delimiter` at a position exactly equal to `len(content)` — i.e. the model produced a fully well-formed JSON body but is missing exactly the outermost closing `}` (verified by manual bracket-depth counting: final depth = 1 on one captured example)
- The **same physical input document** reproducibly fails on some runs and succeeds on others (not a per-document deterministic thing) — confirmed directly: one specific document failed in one sequential run and succeeded in a later sequential run, same everything.

### What we ruled out (each tested directly, not assumed)

- **Not batching/preemption/concurrency**: fully sequential (1 request in flight at a time, `vllm:num_preemptions_total` stayed at 0 throughout) still reproduces the failure at the same rate (20-44% across several N=8-18 runs) as under concurrent load.
- **Not KV-cache size**: A/B test going from a 20G fixed KV cache pool (with heavy preemption under load) to a ~43GB auto-sized pool (zero preemption) left the failure rate unchanged (27.5% → 25%).
- **Not `--max-model-len`/token budget**: raised 65536 → 131072; a separate, distinct failure mode (genuine context overflow, `finish_reason='length'`) went away, but this premature-stop mode is unaffected (still ~20% after the change).
- **Not the vLLM version**: tried `0.26.1rc1.dev1046+gba07e4a48` (pinned via `pip install --no-deps` over the same base image, same torch 2.13.0/CUDA 13.0 — confirmed compatible, no start-up errors) on the H100 — failure rate was *higher* (45%), not lower.
- **Not `--gdn-prefill-backend`**: tried `triton` explicitly — same failure rate (20% over N=15) and same failure signature.
- **Not the LoRA adapter**: `sha256sum` of `adapter_model.safetensors` is byte-identical between the H100 and RTX 5090 hosts.
- **Not the prompt/template construction**: the reverse-derived `chat_template_kwargs.template` DSL we send matches, byte-for-byte (diffed programmatically), the template used to fine-tune the LoRA adapter in the first place.
- **Not the pipeline config**: identical JSON config (temperature, `pages_per_call`, all flags) on both hosts.

### The one variable we couldn't equalize: GPU architecture

| | H100 NVL (SM90) | RTX 5090 (SM120) |
|---|---|---|
| Failure rate, same 10-15 sequential requests, same documents | 20-45% (multiple runs) | **0/10** |
| `--gdn-prefill-backend` | default (`flashinfer`) and `triton` both tested, same result | default |

We traced flashinfer's own dispatch (`gdn_prefill.py`) and confirmed that on SM90 the default (non-CP) path already calls `chunk_gated_delta_rule_sm90` — i.e. we are *not* stuck on some older code path; this is the current SM90 kernel. We also found and briefly tried forcing vLLM's `--gdn-prefill-backend cutedsl`, but stopped immediately once we realized that vLLM's in-tree `cutedsl` GDN kernel (`vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/ops/gdn_chunk_cutedsl/`) is a separate, SM100-specific implementation (`Sm100ChunkUWKernel`) — forcing it onto SM90 risks silently wrong results rather than a real fix, so we didn't pursue that path further or measure accuracy under it.

### Question

Is there a known numerical-precision or algorithmic difference between the SM90 and SM100/SM120 `chunk_gated_delta_rule` kernels that could plausibly manifest as occasional incorrect/divergent output for the *same* input at `temperature=0`? Or any pointers on how to get a tighter repro (we can build a minimal standalone script calling `flashinfer.gdn_prefill.chunk_gated_delta_rule` directly with saved intermediate tensors, if that would help — we currently only have this at the full vLLM-serving level; the exact input documents are real government records and can't be shared, but the schema shape and reproduction steps can be shared/generalized).

Happy to run any diagnostic you'd suggest — we have both a Hopper and a Blackwell machine available for A/B testing.

items.title: [Feature] Remote call timeout required.
items.author: MissiontoMars
items.body_excerpt:
### Search before asking

- [X] I had searched in the [issues](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues) and found no similar feature requirement.


### Description

### Why the feature needed?
 Feature required from our users. The current remote call design lacks a timeout mechanism, `actor.foo.remote()` will be executed in the end. The user may expect the remote call to be completed in a certain period of time, if not, then give up. If the producer actor send lots of calls in a short time, some calls which destined to be timeout will also be executed, that's unnecessary.

### API
Set `timeout_ms` option when do remote call. e.g.:

```
@ray.remote
    class Foo:
        def method(self):
            return 1
    f = Foo.remote()
    f.method.options(timeout_ms=500).remote()
```

When the caller actor send out the task, put the current timestamp in taskspec, and on the callee actor side, check the timestamp with current system time when prepare to execute the task, if timeout, give up.

### Other considerations
1. The user can do the similar things by themself. Add an extra timestamp parameter in mthod, and do not execute the bussiness code when timeout.  But I think it would be more convenient to support this option in Ray.
2. The time synchronization problem in distributed systems, makes the timeout not 100% accurate.  But in most cases it's not a problem.

items.title: Batch requests ignore the job's client.request_timeout_seconds and always use a 30 s read timeout
items.author: wguo7
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

A batch job can set `client.request_timeout_seconds` (`ClientConfig` in `python/aibrix/aibrix/batch/job_entity/aibrix_metadata.py`, added in #2492, default `None`). The batch code reads it in two places: the request lock lifetime (`BatchStorageAdapter._request_lock_timeout_seconds`) and the pending-request retry poll interval (`BaseJobDriver._pending_request_retry_poll_seconds`). It never reaches the HTTP request itself.

Every runtime builds its endpoint source without a timeout (`worker.py`, `ssh_launch.py`, `k8s_deployment.py`), so `HttpChannel` uses its default `timeout=30.0` as the read timeout. As a result:

- Long-generation jobs that set a longer timeout still fail, and retry, every request that takes over 30 s.
- A job that sets a shorter timeout still waits up to 30 s for each request.

### Steps to Reproduce

The script below runs one request through `BaseJobDriver` the way the batch worker pod does (`ExternalRuntime(GatewayEndpointSource(url))`, `worker_mode=True`), against a local server that answers after 3 s, with `client.request_timeout_seconds=1` and retries off. Output on main (8e96742):

```
job request_timeout_seconds=1.0, HttpChannel read timeout=30.0
actual: completed=1 failed=0 elapsed=3.2s expected: failed=1 (read timeout after ~1s)
```

<details><summary>repro.py</summary>

```python
"""Batch requests ignore client.request_timeout_seconds: the HTTP read timeout stays 30 s."""
import asyncio
import json
import os
import tempfile
import threading
import time
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer

tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
os.environ["STORAGE_LOCAL_PATH"] = tmp
DELAY = 3.0


class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        self.rfile.read(int(self.headers.get("content-length", 0)))
        time.sleep(DELAY)
        body = json.dumps({"id": "x", "object": "chat.completion", "choices": [],
                           "usage": {"prompt_tokens": 1, "completion_tokens": 1}}).encode()
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("content-type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("content-length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

    def log_message(self, *a):
        pass


srv = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), H)
threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
BASE = f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv.server_address[1]}"

from aibrix.batch.client import GatewayEndpointSource  # noqa: E402
from aibrix.batch.job_driver.base import BaseJobDriver  # noqa: E402
from aibrix.batch.job_driver.runtime import ExternalRuntime  # noqa: E402
from aibrix.batch.job_entity import BatchJob, BatchJobSpec, BatchJobState  # noqa: E402
from aibrix.batch.storage import batch_metastore, batch_storage  # noqa: E402
from aibrix.batch.worker import SingleJobRunner  # noqa: E402
from aibrix.context.infra import InfrastructureContext  # noqa: E402
from aibrix.storage import StorageType  # noqa: E402


async def main():
    batch_metastore.initialize_batch_metastore(StorageType.LOCAL)
    batch_storage.initialize_batch_storage(StorageType.LOCAL, {"base_path": tmp})
    line = json.dumps({"custom_id": "r0", "method": "POST", "url": "/v1/chat/completions",
                       "body": {"model": "m", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]}})
    await batch_storage.p_storage.storage.put_object("in-1", line + "\n", "application/jsonl")

    spec = BatchJobSpec.from_strings(
        input_file_id="in-1", endpoint="/v1/chat/completions",
        aibrix={"client": {"request_timeout_seconds": 1.0,
                           "retry_policy": {"max_retries": 0}}},
    )
    job = BatchJob.new_local(spec, request_count=1)
    job.status.state = BatchJobState.IN_PROGRESS
    job = await batch_storage.prepare_job_ouput_files(job)

    runner = SingleJobRunner(job)
    source = GatewayEndpointSource(BASE)  # as the batch worker does
    driver = BaseJobDriver(InfrastructureContext(), runner, ExternalRuntime(source), worker_mode=True)
    t0 = time.monotonic()
    try:
        await driver.execute(job.job_id)
    except Exception as e:  # worker_mode re-raises on failure
        print("execute raised:", type(e).__name__, e)
    elapsed = time.monotonic() - t0
    rc = runner._meta.status.request_counts
    read_timeout = source._channel._timeout_config.read
    print(f"job request_timeout_seconds=1.0, HttpChannel read timeout={read_timeout}")
    print(f"actual: completed={rc.completed} failed={rc.failed} elapsed={elapsed:.1f}s "
          f"expected: failed=1 (read timeout after ~1s)")


asyncio.run(main())
srv.shutdown()
```

</details>

### Expected behavior

When a job sets `client.request_timeout_seconds`, each inference request uses it as the HTTP read timeout. Jobs that do not set it keep today's 30 s.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: main at 8e96742
- Deployment environment: none. The repro runs the batch driver in-process with local storage (macOS arm64, Python 3.12.15)
- LLM(s) being used: none (local HTTP server)

### Area

Batch

I have a fix with tests ready and will open a PR.

items.title: [Perf] DeepSeek-V4.1 CSA2: BF16 wq_a / wkv projections at decode reach 0.9-2 TB/s on Vera Rubin; tinygemm2 is 1.6-3x faster
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- GPU: Vera Rubin, compute capability 10.7, single node, TP4/EP4
- TensorRT-LLM main, PyTorch backend, CUDA graphs; CSA2 projections in BF16 (the SM107 path of #20512)
- Model: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash`, batch 1 decode, 32K context

### Who can help?

@NVIDIA/trt-llm-torch-models-devs

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

Serve DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with BF16 CSA2 projections, run a single-request decode and profile it with nsys (`--cuda-graph-trace=node`). Look at the two hidden-state projections of `DeepseekV41Attention.forward` (`csa2/module.py`): `wq_a` (5120 -> 1280) and `wkv` (5120 -> 512).

### Expected behavior

At M = 1 these are weight-streaming GEMVs (13 MB and 5 MB of BF16 weight per layer), so they should run close to memory bandwidth.

### Actual behavior

cuBLAS picks 16x64 / 32x64 nvjet tiles for these N-small, K=5120 shapes and reaches only 0.9-2 TB/s. Single-GPU timing on Vera Rubin, CUDA graph replay, weights rotated past L2, M = 1 (M = 4 and 6 behave the same):

| projection (N x K) | cuBLAS (nvjet) µs | `trtllm::tinygemm2` µs |
|---|---|---|
| wq_a 1280 x 5120 | 6.64 | 3.85 |
| wkv 512 x 5120 | 5.86 | 3.67 |
| [wq_a; wkv] concatenated, 1792 x 5120 | 6.87 | 4.67 |

Both projections read the same input, so for one token they can run as a single tinygemm2 over the row-concatenated weight: 4.13 µs for both, against 12.5 µs for the two cuBLAS calls (-8.4 µs per layer, 40 layers). The N-large projections (`wq_b`, `o_b`) are faster on cuBLAS and are not affected.

End-to-end (TP4/EP4, same server configuration, only this change): decode step period 5.97 ms -> 5.70 ms (-0.27 ms); GSM8K (100 questions) 99 -> 99, passkey 8K/32K/128K 5/5 in both.

### Additional notes

- `trtllm::tinygemm2` already accepts SM90 and the SM100 family including SM107 (`thop/tinygemm2.cpp`); today only the gpt-oss router uses it.
- Known risk: `tinygemm2_kernel.cuh` calls `cudaTriggerProgrammaticLaunchCompletion()` before its output stores and the kernel is always launched with programmatic stream serialization; #15729 reported wrong gpt-oss results from this and was closed together with #15790 without a change. A PDL consumer that calls `griddepcontrol.wait` before reading should still see complete output (the wait covers completion and memory visibility of the primary grid). We stress-tested the decode pattern here (PDL RMSNorm -> tinygemm2 -> PDL RMSNorm on each half, in a CUDA graph, new input before every replay, bitwise against the same ops run without PDL and with a sync between them): 0 mismatches in 20,000 replays for the fused M = 1 call and for separate calls at M = 1/4/8. We do not have a positive control showing that this test would catch the race, so moving the trigger after the stores would still be the safer kernel-side fix.
- We have a patch (one-token fused call plus per-projection calls for M <= 8, falling back to `Linear` otherwise) and are happy to send it as a PR if the approach looks right.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the documentation and examples for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: How to make Tensor static and only call kernel by pointer?
items.author: peterbjorgensen
items.body_excerpt:
I am trying to turn Python cute dsl kernels into TensorRT QDP Plugins. It restricts the kind of parameters the PTX can have to (input_pointers..., scalar_arguments..., output_pointers...). I have it working for a simple "add_one_kernel" (see the program listing below if interested).

Instead of writing the kernel with pointer arguments, I would like to write it with some StaticTensorPointer class that automatically turns the layout etc. into compile-time variables and only the pointer ends up as a PTX parameter. I guess it's possible with a custom `DynamicExpression`, but I find the documentation a bit vague on this. Any ideas how to achieve this?

Another question: Is it possible to get the shared memory needed for a compiled kernel? I need it for the kernel launch parameters of the kernel in the plugin.

```
import tensorrt as trt
import numpy as np
from quack.cute_dsl_utils import torch2cute_dtype_map
import tensorrt.plugin as trtp
import torch
import torch_tensorrt
import cutlass.cute as cute

from quack.cute_dsl_utils import torch2cute_dtype_map

trt_logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.VERBOSE)

STATIC_SHAPE = (16, 16)
STATIC_STRIDE = (1, 16)

@cute.kernel
def add_one_kernel(x: cute.Pointer, y: cute.Pointer):
    STATIC_LAYOUT = cute.make_layout(shape=STATIC_SHAPE, stride=STATIC_STRIDE)
    tensor_x = cute.make_tensor(x, STATIC_LAYOUT)
    tensor_y = cute.make_tensor(y, STATIC_LAYOUT)
    tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
    bidx, _, _ = cute.arch.block_idx()
    idx = bidx * cute.arch.block_dim()[0] + tidx
    if idx < cute.size(tensor_x):
        tensor_y[idx] = tensor_x[idx] + 1

@cute.jit
def apply_add_one_kernel(x: cute.Pointer, y: cute.Pointer):
    BLOCK_SIZE = 256
    num_blocks = (np.prod(STATIC_SHAPE).item() + BLOCK_SIZE - 1) // BLOCK_SIZE

    add_one_kernel(x, y).launch(
        grid = [num_blocks, 1, 1],
        block = [BLOCK_SIZE, 1, 1],
    )


@torch.library.custom_op("my::add_one", mutates_args=())  # type: ignore[misc]
def add_one(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    assert x.is_cuda
    y = torch.empty_like(x)
    input_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[x.dtype]
    y_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, y.data_ptr(), cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)
    x_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, x.data_ptr(), cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)

    compiled = cute.compile(apply_add_one_kernel, x_ptr, y_ptr, options="--keep-ptx")
    compiled(x_ptr, y_ptr)

    return y


@torch.library.register_fake("my::add_one")
def _(X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    return X

@trtp.register("my::add_one")
def add_plugin_desc(X: trtp.TensorDesc) -> tuple[trtp.TensorDesc]:
    # Output has the same shape and dtype as the input.
    return X.like()


@trtp.aot_impl("my::add_one")
def add_plugin_aot_impl(
    X: trtp.TensorDesc, outputs: tuple[trtp.TensorDesc], tactic: int
) -> tuple[
    str | bytes, str | bytes, trtp.KernelLaunchParams, trtp.SymExprs
]:
    # Choose the pointer type based on the input dtype.
    if X.dtype == trt.float32:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.float32]
    elif X.dtype == trt.float16:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.float16]
    elif X.dtype == trt.bfloat16:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.bfloat16]
    else:
        raise ValueError("Unexpected dtype")
    input_dtype = x_dtype
    y_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, 32, cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)
    x_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, 64, cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)

    compiled_kernel = cute.compile(apply_add_one_kernel, x_ptr, y_ptr, options="--keep-ptx")


    # Build symbolic launch parameters.
    BLOCK_SIZE = 256
    num_blocks = (np.prod(STATIC_SHAPE).item() + BLOCK_SIZE - 1) // BLOCK_SIZE
    launch_params = trtp.KernelLaunchParams()
    launch_params.grid_x = num_blocks  # number of thread blocks
    launch_params.block_x = BLOCK_SIZE  # threads per block
    launch_params.shared_mem = 0  # bytes of shared mem (I have no idea how to get this)

    # ``extra_args`` are scalar arguments appended to the kernel's argument list at
    # launch. Here ``n_elements`` is passed as a 32-bit symbolic integer so TRT
    # evaluates it from the actual tensor size at runtime.
    extra_args = trtp.SymIntExprs(0)

    kernel_name_ptx = list(compiled_kernel.kernel_info.keys())[0]
    return (
        kernel_name_ptx,  # kernel function name in PTX
        compiled_kernel.artifacts.PTX,  # PTX source — embedded in TRT engine
        launch_params,
        extra_args,
    )


torch_tensorrt.dynamo.conversion.plugins.generate_plugin_converter(
    "my::add_one",
    supports_dynamic_shapes=False,
    requires_output_allocator=False,
    use_aot_if_available=True,
)


class MyModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def forward(self, X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        res = torch.ops.my.add_one.default(X)
        return res


if __name__ == "__main__":


    my_model = MyModel().to("cuda").eval()
    m = torch.full(STATIC_SHAPE, 2, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)

    assert my_model(m)[0][0] == 3.0
    assert my_model(m)[1][1] == 3.0

    with torch_tensorrt.logging.debug():
        trt_inputs = [m]
        model_trt = torch_tensorrt.compile(
            my_model,
            inputs=trt_inputs,
            min_block_size=1,
        )
        print("Model compiled successfully!")
        print("Running inference with compiled model...")
        with torch.no_grad():
            for i in range(10):
                res = model_trt(m)
                assert torch.allclose(res, my_model(m)), "Results do not match!"

        program = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.trace(
            my_model,
            arg_inputs=trt_inputs,
        )
        engine_bytes: bytes = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.convert_exported_program_to_seri

items.title: attn_scores: compute_paged_mqa_logits_schedule compiles a new kernel per 32-row bucket (seconds each), stalling eager large-batch callers
items.author: akhilg-nv
items.body_excerpt:
[by Claude Code]

## Summary
`compute_paged_mqa_logits_schedule` (GPU path, `_gpu_schedule`) specializes
`PagedMQALogitsScheduleKernel` on `_schedule_bucket(B) = ceil(B/32)*32`, and the kernel fully unrolls
(`range_constexpr`) over `B/32` chunks of a shared-memory prefix sum. Every new bucket is a fresh
`cute.compile`, and its cost grows with B. Callers whose row count varies call to call and is not
graph-captured, such as a paged indexer during prefill (one row per prompt token), hit a multi-second
compile on nearly every new prompt length while serving.

## Measurement (B200, flashinfer 0.7.1, empty FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_BASE, fp8, next_n=1)
The schedule kernel and `_schedule_bucket` are unchanged on main as of 3bf6d3202.

| rows | bucket | first call | repeat |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 16 | 32 | 365 ms | 0.075 ms |
| 64 | 64 | 250 ms | 0.061 ms |
| 1024 | 1024 | 478 ms | 0.062 ms |
| 4096 | 4096 | 1564 ms | 0.088 ms |
| 8159 | 8160 | 2325 ms | 0.116 ms |
| 8160 | 8160 | 0.1 ms (cached) | 0.054 ms |
| 8192 | 8192 | 2335 ms | 0.125 ms |
| 8193 | 8224 | 2346 ms | 0.126 ms |
| 16384 | 16384 | 8451 ms | 0.194 ms |

Probe: time the first and a repeat call of `compute_paged_mqa_logits_schedule(seq_lens)` on a CUDA int32 `seq_lens` of each length, with an empty JIT workspace.

## Impact seen
An experimental (unmerged) SGLang integration routed the DeepSeek-V4-Flash C4 indexer through
`fp8_paged_mqa_logits` in eager prefill as well (TP4, B200). Median TTFT at concurrency 1 with 8K
prompts went from 181 ms to 2565 ms, and the slow prefills were exactly the first prompt length in
each new 32-row bucket. The on-disk cache only helps later process starts, not the first time a
bucket appears. Decode and verify were unaffected: they are graph-captured, so their few buckets
compile at capture time.

## Suggestions (any one)
1. Loop over chunks at runtime (`cutlass.range`, dynamic smem or a two-pass/grid prefix sum) so one
   compiled kernel serves every B, like DeepGEMM's `get_paged_mqa_logits_metadata`.
2. Keep the unrolled kernel for small B (decode), and above a threshold (e.g. B > 512) round up to
   powers of two or use a generic kernel.
3. At minimum, document the per-bucket compile in the `compute_paged_mqa_logits_schedule` docstring
   and point eager callers to `precompile_paged_mqa_logits(batch_sizes=...)`.

items.title: [Bug] b12x fused_moe w4a8_mx: tiny-decode path (T<=4) ignores swiglu_limit (DeepSeek-V4.1 decode)
items.author: thenaxon
items.body_excerpt:
### Before submitting

- [x] I have searched existing issues and did not find a solution or an existing report.

### Environment

`flashinfer.collect_env` output is not attached yet. We hit this with the **standalone b12x 1.5.1 wheel (PyPI)**, before its move into FlashInfer. I checked that the relevant code is unchanged in `flashinfer/experimental/b12x` on `main` @ `8dc1163` (line refs below). I will follow up with a standalone repro and `collect_env` from a FlashInfer build.

- GPU: RTX 5090 (SM120), driver 595.99.02 (CUDA 13.2)
- torch 2.13.0+cu132, b12x 1.5.1, nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04 (container `nvidia/cuda:13.2.1-devel-ubuntu24.04`)

### Bug description

For b12x `fused_moe` with `quant_mode="w4a8_mx"` / `source_format="fp4_e8m0_k32"`, the **tiny-decode path (1 ≤ T ≤ 4 tokens, enabled by default) silently ignores `Caps.swiglu_limit`**. It computes plain SiLU(gate)·up with no clamp. The dynamic paths apply the clamp correctly.

This affects models that rely on the clamp, e.g. **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash** (`swiglu_limit: 10.0`). Single-stream decode (T ≤ 4, including small spec-decode verify batches) is exactly the case that selects tiny-decode.

**Expected:** every path honours `swiglu_limit`, or tiny-decode is not selected when a limit is set.

**Where it happens (FlashInfer `main` @ `8dc1163`):**
- `flashinfer/experimental/b12x/moe/fused_moe/_impl.py:2593`: path selection `_tiny_decode_enabled() and _tiny_decode_supports(...)`.
- `_impl.py:12785` `_tiny_decode_supports`: checks only `num_tokens`, `k`, `n` and `activation`, not `swiglu_limit`/alpha/beta.
- `_impl.py:12859` `_launch_tiny_decode_flat` and `b12x::tp_moe_tiny_decode_launch` (`:12904`): take no swiglu limit/alpha/beta.
- `flashinfer/experimental/b12x/moe/_shared/kernels/tiny_decode.py`: no clamp anywhere (`activation == "silu"` only).

**Workaround:** `B12X_W4A8_TINY_DECODE=0`

**Suggested fix:** implement the clamp in the tiny-decode kernel, or return `False` from `_tiny_decode_supports` when `swiglu_limit` (or alpha/beta) is set, so these models fall back to the dynamic path.

### Minimal reproduction

So far the repro uses real DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 layer-2 routed experts (384 × MXFP4 with UE8M0/32 scales, hidden 5120, intermediate 2304, top-6, `w13_layout="w31"`). A self-contained random-weight script will follow. Call sequence (b12x 1.5.1 tensor API):

```python
import torch, b12x
fm = b12x.moe.fused_moe
wplan = fm.plan_weights(quant_modes="w4a8_mx", source_format="fp4_e8m0_k32", activation="silu",
                        params_dtype=torch.bfloat16, num_experts=E, hidden_size=5120,
                        intermediate_size=2304, w13_layout="w31")
experts = fm.prepare_weights(plan=wplan, params_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
                             w1_fp4=w13_u8, w2_fp4=w2_u8,                      # raw checkpoint FP4 bytes
                             w1_blockscale=s13_u8, w2_blockscale=s2_u8,        # UE8M0 per-32
                             w1_global_scale=ones, w2_global_scale=ones, a1_gscale=ones, a2_gscale=ones)
caps = fm.Caps(max_tokens=T, num_topk=6, device="cuda", weight_plan=wplan,
               quant_mode="w4a8_mx", swiglu_limit=10.0)
plan = fm.plan(caps)
scratch = tuple(torch.zeros(s.shape, dtype=s.dtype, device=s.device) for s in plan.scratch_specs())
b = fm.bind(plan, scratch=scratch, a=x_bf16, experts=experts, topk_weights=w_f32, topk_ids=ids_i32,
            output=out_bf16, input_scales_static=True)
fm.run(binding=b)
# compare `out` to an fp32 torch reference with and without the clamp
# (gate clamped to <= L, up clamped to [-L, L], same convention as moe/_shared/kernels/reference.py)
```

To make the clamp active, use hidden states with std 8. About 33 % of gate/up values then exceed the limit.

### Error messages / logs

No error is raised; the result is silently wrong:

| Path | T | cos vs **clamped** fp32 ref | cos vs unclamped ref |
|---|---|---|---|
| default → tiny-decode | 1 | **0.788** | ≈ 1 (matches unclamped) |
| `B12X_W4A8_TINY_DECODE=0` → dynamic | 1 | 0.9985 | ~0.7 |
| `B12X_W4A8_TINY_DECODE=0` + grouped route | 1 | 0.9985 | ~0.7 |
| default → dynamic (not tiny) | 7 | 0.9986 | 0.80 |

With normal-scale inputs (std 1, clamp rarely active), all paths match the clamped reference at cos ≥ 0.999.

Side note: expert id `-1` masking (local-expert subsets for EP) works correctly on every path, tiny-decode included.

items.title: [Inductor][PDL] triton.enable_pdl: mix-order reduction issues pipelined loads before gdc_wait(), giving wrong results
items.author: shino16
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

With `triton.enable_pdl=True`, a mix-order reduction kernel (one kernel computing both `y.sum(1)` and `y.sum(0)`) can read its input before the producing kernel has finished writing it. Inductor emits `tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait()` inside the mix-order loop `for _ in tl.range(0, split_size, XBLOCK, num_stages=NUM_STAGES)`, and Triton's software pipeliner issues the first iterations' loads (`cp.async`) in the loop prologue, before `griddepcontrol.wait`. The results are wrong on most calls; they are correct with `triton.enable_pdl=False`, with `triton.mix_order_reduction=False`, or with `TORCHINDUCTOR_MIX_ORDER_REDUCTION_ALLOW_MULTI_STAGES=0`.

```python
import torch
import torch._inductor.config as ic

M, N, CH = 6144, 4000, 256

def f(x):
    y = x
    for _ in range(CH):  # long producer kernel writing y
        y = torch.sin(y) * 0.999 + 0.001
    return y.sum(dim=1), y.sum(dim=0), y  # mix-order reduction kernel reads y

xs = [torch.randn(M, N, device="cuda") for _ in range(4)]
refs = [f(x) for x in xs]
with ic.patch({"triton.enable_pdl": True}):
    fc = torch.compile(f)
    fc(xs[0])
torch.cuda.synchronize()
bad = 0
for i in range(100):
    o = fc(xs[i % 4])
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    r = refs[i % 4]
    bad += max((o[0] - r[0]).abs().max().item(), (o[1] - r[1]).abs().max().item()) > 1e-2
print(f"{bad}/100 calls wrong")
```

Output on main (`210bb7ca5c4`), RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm_120):

| Config | Wrong calls |
|---|---|
| `triton.enable_pdl=True` | 97/100 and 98/100 in two runs (54/100 with `CH=64`) |
| `triton.enable_pdl=False` | 0/100 |
| `enable_pdl=True`, `triton.mix_order_reduction=False` | 0/100 |
| `enable_pdl=True`, `TORCHINDUCTOR_MIX_ORDER_REDUCTION_ALLOW_MULTI_STAGES=0` | 0/100 |

Generated mix-order kernel (`TORCH_LOGS=output_code`, `CH=2`, abridged):

```python
accum0 = tl.full([R0_BLOCK], 0, tl.float32)[None, :]
split_size = min(RSPLIT_SIZE, xnumel - xoffset)
for _ in tl.range(0, split_size, XBLOCK, num_stages=NUM_STAGES):
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    x0 = xindex
    xindex += XBLOCK
    tl.extra.cuda.gdc_wait()
    tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (r0_1 + 4000*x0), r0_mask & xmask, eviction_policy='evict_first', other=0.0)
    tl.extra.cuda.gdc_launch_dependents()
    ...
```

The PTX of that kernel issues two prologue batches of `cp.async.cg.shared.global` (each ending in `cp.async.commit_group`) before the first `griddepcontrol.wait`:

```
68:   cp.async.cg.shared.global [ %r11 + 0 ], [ %rd7 + 0 ], 0x10, %r13;
...
91:   cp.async.commit_group;
112:  cp.async.cg.shared.global [ %r17 + 0 ], [ %rd11 + 0 ], 0x10, %r19;
...
135:  cp.async.commit_group;
199:  griddepcontrol.wait; // dummy %r38
203:  cp.async.wait_group 1;
```

Cause: `TritonKernel._handle_pdl_before_access` in `torch/_inductor/codegen/triton.py` hoists the wait out of the loop only for looped reductions (`self.inside_reduction and self.range_trees[-1].is_loop`). Mix-order kernels are persistent reductions that wrap the loads in their own pipelined `tl.range` loop, so the wait stays inside the loop body, where it does not order the prologue loads.

A possible fix is to also hoist for mix-order kernels, which places the wait before the loop (this makes the repro above 0/100):

```diff
-        if self.inside_reduction and self.range_trees[-1].is_loop:
+        if self.inside_reduction and (
+            self.range_trees[-1].is_loop or self.mix_order_reduction
+        ):
             wait_buffer = self.body
```

Related: #199165. On current main, an in-place producer (for example `x.index_put_(...)` followed by `x.sum(1), x.sum(0)`) also fails with mix-order disabled because of #199165, so the repro above uses an out-of-place producer.

### Versions

PyTorch main `210bb7ca5c4` (source build, `2.16.0a0+git210bb7c`), CUDA 13.4, Triton 3.8.0, driver 580.178.04, NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition (sm_120).


cc @chauhang @penguinwu @voznesenskym @EikanWang @jgong5 @Guobing-Chen @XiaobingSuper @zhuhaozhe @blzheng @wenzhe-nrv @jiayisunx @ipiszy @kadeng @muchulee8 @amjames @aakhundov @coconutruben @jataylo

items.title: [Core] After a failed ray:// connect, ray.init() raises a bare AssertionError and an allow_multiple=True retry times out
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

After `ray.init("ray://...")` fails, the process stays in Ray Client mode, and every later `ray.init()` in that process fails:

- A local `ray.init()` raises a bare `AssertionError` that doesn't say what went wrong.
- `ray.init("ray://<live address>", allow_multiple=True)` fails with `ConnectionError: ray client connection timeout`, although a fresh process connects to the same address.

```
ray:// connect failed: ConnectionError ray client connection timeout
client mode enabled after failure: True
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File "python/ray/_private/node.py", line 2272, in _record_stats
    assert ray.experimental.internal_kv._internal_kv_initialized()
AssertionError
```

The `AssertionError` happens because `RayAPIStub.connect` in `python/ray/util/client/__init__.py` calls `_explicitly_enable_client_mode()` before connecting, and on failure its `except` calls only the per-context `disconnect()`, which never resets the flag. Only the module-level `ray.util.disconnect()` calls `_explicitly_disable_client_mode()`. I haven't found the cause of the `allow_multiple=True` timeout.

Expected, after the first `ray://` connect fails:

1. A local `ray.init()` still fails, but with an error that says `Ray Client is already initialized.` instead of a bare `AssertionError`.
2. `ray.init("ray://<live address>", allow_multiple=True)` connects.

As a workaround for the local `ray.init()`, call `ray.util.disconnect()` after the failed connect.

### Versions / Dependencies

The `AssertionError` reproduces on master 3e2f0b5c2a with ray-project/ray#67126 applied. At that point the PR hadn't changed `python/ray/util/client/__init__.py` or `python/ray/_private/client_mode_hook.py`. I saw the `allow_multiple=True` timeout on ray-project/ray#67126 at cd9a46ee9a, which does change the Ray Client files, so I haven't confirmed it on master alone. Python 3.12.15, Linux.

### Reproduction script

Start a head node with auth off first: `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled ray start --head`.

```python
import ray
from ray._common.network_utils import find_free_port

try:
    # Nothing listens on this port.
    ray.init(f"ray://127.0.0.1:{find_free_port()}")
except ConnectionError as e:
    print("ray:// connect failed:", type(e).__name__, e)

try:
    ray.init()  # Today: bare AssertionError in node.py _record_stats
except Exception as e:
    print("local ray.init() failed:", type(e).__name__, e)

ray.init("ray://127.0.0.1:10001", allow_multiple=True)  # Today: ConnectionError, ray client connection timeout
```

### Issue Severity

Low: It annoys or frustrates me.

items.title: On sm_89, fp8 `acc += tl.dot(a, b)` is silently rewritten into the lower-precision `tl.dot(a, b, acc)` instead of keeping the fp32 add
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


**TL;DR.** On sm_89, `acc += tl.dot(a, b)` with fp8 inputs and an fp32 `acc` is silently rewritten into `tl.dot(a, b, acc)`, which accumulates the running sum inside the fp8 `mma.sync` at lower precision: ones with K = 20000 give 16384, and random data in [0.5, 1.5) at K = 8192 is off by up to 15%. The `+=` form is how a kernel asks for precise accumulation (Inductor writes it for `torch._scaled_mm(..., use_fast_accum=False)`), and the same rewrite on sm_90 was treated as a bug in #8056.

Reproducer (fp8 ones, 625 tiles of 32 products each; `max_num_imprecise_acc=32` is the control, it only keeps the add from being folded into the dot):

```python
import sys

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, MNIA: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, 16)
    ok = tl.arange(0, 32)
    acc = tl.zeros((16, 16), tl.float32)
    for _ in range(625):  # 625 tiles of 32 products of 1.0 = 20000
        a = tl.load(a_ptr + om[:, None] * 32 + ok[None, :])  # [16, 32]
        b = tl.load(b_ptr + ok[:, None] * 16 + om[None, :])  # [32, 16]
        acc += tl.dot(a, b, max_num_imprecise_acc=MNIA)
    tl.store(c_ptr + om[:, None] * 16 + om[None, :], acc)


a = torch.ones(16, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn)
b = torch.ones(32, 16, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn)
bad = False
for mnia in (None, 32):  # 32 is the control: the add is not folded into the dot
    c = torch.zeros(16, 16, device="cuda")
    h = kernel[(1, )](a, b, c, MNIA=mnia)
    print(f"max_num_imprecise_acc={mnia}: {c.unique().tolist()} (expected [20000.0]), "
          f"fp32 add kept in TTIR: {'arith.addf' in h.asm['ttir']}")
    bad |= bool((c != 20000).any())
sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)
```

Output on an L40S, main 6fe3348e6 (exit code 1); the 3.0.0, 3.1.0, 3.2.0, 3.3.1, 3.4.0, 3.5.0, 3.6.0 and 3.8.0 wheels print the same:

```
max_num_imprecise_acc=None: [16384.0] (expected [20000.0]), fp32 add kept in TTIR: False
max_num_imprecise_acc=32: [20000.0] (expected [20000.0]), fp32 add kept in TTIR: True
```

Expected: 20000 in both cases. The 3.0.0 to 3.8.0 wheels print the same.

**Root cause.** `TritonCombineOps` folds `acc + tl.dot(a, b)` into `tl.dot(a, b, acc)` when the dot's `max_num_imprecise_acc` is 0 ([Combine.cpp#L270-L277](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/lib/Dialect/Triton/Transforms/Combine.cpp#L270-L277)), assuming such a dot accumulates precisely, and 0 is the default on sm_89 ([compiler.py#L256](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/third_party/nvidia/backend/compiler.py#L256)). But the sm_89 fp8 dot is an fp8 `mma.sync`, whose accumulation is lossy, so the fold moves the user's precise fp32 add into it.

<details>
<summary>Measurements on the L40S</summary>

| form | ones, K=20000 | random [0.5, 1.5), K=8192: max rel. error |
|---|---|---|
| `acc += tl.dot(a, b)` (default) | 16384 | 0.152 |
| `acc += tl.dot(a, b, max_num_imprecise_acc=32)` | 20000 | 0 (BK=32), 2.3e-5 (BK=64), 1.7e-4 (BK=128) |
| `acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc)` (any `max_num_imprecise_acc`) | 16384 | 0.152 |
| same tiles upcast to fp16 (control) | 20000 | 0 |

- Ones: exact up to K=16384, and 16384 for every larger K tried (16416, 20000, 32768, 65536), for BK 32, 64 and 128, e4m3 and e5m2, 4 and 8 warps.
- Zero-mean data (`randn`, K=8192, BK=32, e4m3): the largest error is 3.4e-3 to 4.9e-3 of the largest output with the default and 5.2e-5 to 5.6e-5 after the change; the 15% is for data in [0.5, 1.5).
- One `mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k32.row.col.f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32` adding 32 products of 1.0 to an accumulator of 2^e drops all of them for e >= 14 and is exact for e <= 13 (e5m2 the same; with f16 operands all are kept up to e = 24). So a single `tl.dot(a, b) + c` is affected too, since it is folded the same way: on main `(tl.dot(a, b) + c) - c` is 0 instead of 32 for `c` = 2^14, 2^16, 2^20.
- Compile-only: the add is folded on sm_89, sm_100 and sm_120 and kept on sm_90 (default 2**30); sm_80/86 upcast fp8 to fp16. sm_120 and sm_121 emit the same `mma.sync ... e4m3.e4m3.f32` as sm_89 and get the same fold; they are not changed here, because I could not measure the accumulation precision of sm_12x or of tcgen05 (sm_100).
- The repro gives 16384 (control 20000) on the 3.0.0, 3.1.0, 3.2.0, 3.3.1, 3.4.0, 3.5.0, 3.6.0 and 3.8.0 wheels and on main (3.0.0 to 3.2.0 ran with torch 2.5.1+cu124 on Python 3.12). On the 2.2.0 wheel, which predates #3479, the fp8e5 version of the repro gives 20000 and fp8e4nv dots are rejected on sm_89 (`Dot op does not support fp8e4nv on CUDA arch < 90`).
- sm_90 is not affected. On an H100 the repro gives 20000 for both lines, before and after the change. With an M=32 tile, which cannot use WGMMA either (M must be a multiple of 64), the fp8 operands are upcast to fp16 there and even the chained form gives 20000. With M=64, N=64 (WGMMA), `acc += tl.dot(a, b)` gives 20000 with the default, because the default there is already 2**30 and the add is kept, and is the same before and after the change. The chained `acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc)` gives 16384 at M=64 with the default (WGMMA without promotion), and 20000 with an explicit `max_num_imprecise_acc` of 32 (WGMMA promotes) or 0 (Triton falls back to an fp16-upcast `mma.sync`).
- Through PyTorch (torch 2.11.0, Triton 3.6.0): `torch.compile(mode="max-autotune-no-cudagraphs")` of `torch._scaled_mm(a, b, scale_a, scale_b, out_dtype=torch.float32, use_fast_accum=False)` with only Triton GEMM templates (M=N=64, K=8192, random data) has a max relative error of 0.153, against 1.7e-4 for eager cuBLAS. Inductor's template writes `acc += tl.dot(a, b)` for `use_fast_accum=False` and `acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc)` for `True`. With the default GEMM backends (ATEN,TRITON) the autotuner picked a Triton template over cuBLAS for all five shapes tried (M, N, K = 64, 64, 8192; 16, 4096, 4096; 128, 4096, 8192; 1024, 1024, 8192; 4096, 4096, 4096

items.title: [Hopper] `warp_specialize=True` places loop ops by who uses their result, silently dropping or repeating atomics and `gdc_*`
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


**TL;DR.** On Hopper, side effects in a `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)` loop body are silently dropped or repeated: a `tl.atomic_*` whose result is unused never runs, `gdc_wait()` / `gdc_launch_dependents()` disappear from the PTX, and an atomic whose result feeds a store runs once per consumer warp group. Root cause: the pass places an op that is not a dot, load or store in the partitions of the ops that use its result, so an op with side effects and no used result is placed in no partition and is not emitted.

Reproducer (one program, a 128 x 128 tile, the default `num_warps=4`; control: `warp_specialize=False`):

```python
import sys

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl
from triton.language.extra.cuda import gdc_launch_dependents, gdc_wait

triton.set_allocator(lambda size, align, stream: torch.empty(size, dtype=torch.int8, device="cuda"))


@triton.jit
def kernel(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, cnt_ptr, WS: tl.constexpr):
    a_desc = tl.make_tensor_descriptor(a_ptr, shape=[128, 128], strides=[128, 1], block_shape=[128, 64])
    b_desc = tl.make_tensor_descriptor(b_ptr, shape=[128, 128], strides=[128, 1], block_shape=[64, 128])
    c_desc = tl.make_tensor_descriptor(c_ptr, shape=[128, 128], strides=[128, 1], block_shape=[128, 128])
    acc = tl.zeros((128, 128), tl.float32)
    for k in tl.range(0, 128, 64, warp_specialize=WS):  # 2 iterations
        acc = tl.dot(a_desc.load([0, k]), b_desc.load([k, 0]), acc)
        tl.atomic_add(cnt_ptr, 1)  # the result is unused
        gdc_wait()
        gdc_launch_dependents()
    c_desc.store([0, 0], acc)


x = torch.zeros(128, 128, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)  # A and B: the values do not matter
c = torch.zeros(128, 128, device="cuda")
for ws in (False, True):
    cnt = torch.zeros(1, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
    ptx = kernel[(1, )](x, x, c, cnt, ws).asm["ptx"]
    gdc = [line.strip() for line in ptx.splitlines() if "griddepcontrol" in line]
    print(f"warp_specialize={ws}: atomic_add ran {cnt.item()} times (expected 2), griddepcontrol in the PTX: {gdc}")
sys.exit(1 if cnt.item() != 2 or len(gdc) != 2 else 0)
```
Observed on an H100 with main @6fe3348e6 (exit code 1):
```
warp_specialize=False: atomic_add ran 2 times (expected 2), griddepcontrol in the PTX: ['griddepcontrol.wait ;', 'griddepcontrol.launch_dependents ;']
warp_specialize=True: atomic_add ran 0 times (expected 2), griddepcontrol in the PTX: []
```
Expected: the same as with `warp_specialize=False`. Each call is dropped on its own, `tl.atomic_cas` included. The 3.5.0, 3.6.0, 3.7.1 and 3.8.0 wheels give the same result.

Under programmatic dependent launch the missing `griddepcontrol.wait` changes `C`: with a producer kernel that calls `gdc_launch_dependents()`, sleeps 1 ms and then writes `A`, and a consumer of this form (M = N = 128, K = 512, `gdc_wait()` before the `A` load in the loop body) launched with `launch_pdl=True` in a CUDA graph, 20 of 20 replays gave a wrong `C` (max error 512, the full sum), also with #11989; with `warp_specialize=False`, with `gdc_wait()` before the loop, or without PDL, 0 of 20.

<details>
<summary>The same with five atomic kinds, a used atomic result and the result tile compared with torch, on main and with #11989</summary>

```python

import triton
import triton.language as tl
from triton.language.extra.cuda import gdc_launch_dependents, gdc_wait

triton.set_allocator(lambda size, align, stream: torch.empty(size, dtype=torch.int8, device="cuda"))


@triton.jit

           WS: tl.constexpr, KIND: tl.constexpr):

    b_desc = tl.make_tensor_descriptor(b_ptr, shape=[K, N], strides=[N, 1], block_shape=[BK, BN])

items.title: [Feature]: Whisper serving parity in trtllm-serve — /v1/audio/transcriptions, long-form audio, verbose_json segments, decoder biasing
items.author: ravo42-maker
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

`openai/whisper-large-v3` runs on the PyTorch backend once the pending KV-cache fixes land (#19302 for #18609 / #19515, #19516 for #19514), and the engine itself is fast: on an RTX 5070 Ti, fp16, 0.34 s per 30 s clip warm (~87x realtime; ~14x for faster-whisper large-v3 float32 on the same clip). But it is still not usable as a drop-in STT service, because the serving layer is missing. Our use case is clinical dictation (10–20 minute recordings), currently served by faster-whisper and vLLM; every gap below is something those two already provide. Ordered by how blocking it is:

1. **`/v1/audio/transcriptions` (and `/v1/audio/translations`) in `trtllm-serve`.** Today audio reaches the model only through `/v1/chat/completions` with `input_audio` or the Python `LLM` API. Every OpenAI-compatible STT client uses the audio route: multipart `file`, `model`, `language`, `prompt`, `temperature`, `response_format`, `timestamp_granularities`. Nothing under `tensorrt_llm/serve/` implements it on current `main`.

2. **Long-form audio.** `WhisperInputProcessor` accepts exactly one clip of at most `max_source_positions` (1500 frames = 30 s) and rejects longer input with "chunk the audio" (`modeling_whisper.py`, the `max_audio_seconds` check). A 16-minute file needs windowing on the server, ideally seek-based — the next window starts at the last complete segment's end timestamp, as openai/whisper and faster-whisper do. Fixed pre-cut 30 s chunks lose words at mid-sentence cuts (vllm-project/vllm#58029 documents that failure mode), so this depends on item 3.

3. **`verbose_json` output: per-segment `start`/`end`, `text`, `avg_logprob`, `compression_ratio`** (and `no_speech_prob` where available). The input processor currently forces `<|notimestamps|>` in the decoder prompt, so timestamps are never produced. Per-segment `compression_ratio` is what production pipelines use to detect Whisper's repetition loops; without it the service cannot be monitored.

4. **Decoder biasing:** `prompt` (previous-text conditioning across windows) and a `hotwords`-style bias for proper nouns. faster-whisper exposes both; vLLM accepts `hotwords`.

5. **Whisper-specific input validation.** A user-supplied `max_seq_len` below `max_source_positions` should be rejected: with `max_batch_size=2` it fails at the micro-batch scheduler, but with `max_batch_size=8` it passes and silently drops phrases from the transcript (details in #19514).

Items 1 and 3 are the ones that would let a maintainer or contributor close the gap to vLLM's `/v1/audio/transcriptions`; 2 builds on 3; 4 and 5 are independent.

### Alternatives

A thin service in front of the `LLM` API that does windowing, emits segment timestamps and emulates the OpenAI response shape. That duplicates what vLLM already ships and every TensorRT-LLM Whisper user would have to write it.

### Additional context

Hardware verification runs, the rc25 + patch wheel and the repro kit are described in #18609, #19450, #19514, #19515, #19516 and in the #19302 thread. Happy to test any of the above on sm_120 and on real multi-minute dictations.

items.title: CuTeDSL: width-only f-string format spec emits a malformed device printf format (%8) and silently drops the value
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`FormattedValue.to_str` in `cutlass/base_dsl/ast_helpers.py` (~lines 731-737) converts a non-empty single-token `format_spec` into a printf conversion by emitting `"%{format_spec[0]}"`. That is only valid when the spec actually ends in a conversion character. A width-only spec such as `{x:8}` is legal Python but produces the literal format `%8`, which consumes no argument and prints garbage.

Unit-level repro (against `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.7.0`):

```python
from cutlass.base_dsl.ast_helpers import FormattedValue
import cutlass

fv = FormattedValue(value=cutlass.Int32(7), conversion=-1, format_spec=["8"])
print(fv.to_str()[0])    # prints: %8
fv = FormattedValue(value=cutlass.Int32(7), conversion=-1, format_spec=[".2f"])
print(fv.to_str()[0])    # prints: %.2f  (fine)
```

End-to-end, `cute.printf(f"[{x:8}]")` with a dynamic `x` makes the device print `[     8]`-style text where the value never appears: the kernel receives format string `[%8]` plus an unconsumed vararg. No diagnostic is raised.

### Suggested fix

Validate that the spec terminates in a known conversion character. Either raise `DiagId.UNSUP_FSTRING_FORMAT` for specs without one, or map a bare numeric spec to a sensible default conversion per the value's dtype (e.g. append `d` for integer types, `f`/`g` for float types) so `{x:8}` keeps its Python meaning.

items.title: CuTeDSL: print_warning_once re-warns when more than one distinct message is used (lru_cache maxsize=1)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`BaseDSL.print_warning_once` (`cutlass/base_dsl/dsl.py` ~line 813) caches on `(self, message)` with `@lru_cache(maxsize=1)`:

```python
@lru_cache(maxsize=1)
def print_warning_once(self, message: str) -> None:
```

With more than one distinct message, every new message evicts the previous cache entry, so alternating messages re-warn forever instead of once each.

Repro against `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.7.0`:

```python
import warnings
from cutlass.base_dsl.dsl import BaseDSL

dsl = object.__new__(BaseDSL)
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as rec:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    for msg in ["A", "B", "A", "B", "A"]:
        dsl.print_warning_once(msg)
print(len(rec))   # 5 warnings emitted; correct behavior is 2 (one per unique message)
```

Actual output: `5`.

### Suggested fix

Keep an instance-level `set` of already-emitted messages, or move the cache to a module-level function keyed on the message alone with unbounded size.

items.title: Fused fprop scale/bias iterator advances without the split-k factor and drifts from activation channels
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

In the fused (scale/bias) fprop mainloop, the scale/bias vector iterator and the activation/filter iterators disagree on the per-R*S-cycle channel stride when `split_k_slices > 1`, so scale/bias drift to the wrong channel blocks.

- Activation iterator on gemm-k wrap (include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv2d_fprop_activation_tile_access_iterator_analytic.h ~line 216, `_optimized` analogue ~314): `filter_c_ += Shape::kColumn * problem_size_.split_k_slices;`
- Scale/bias iterator on the same wrap (include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/predicated_scale_bias_vector_access_iterator.h:247-262): calls `add_tile_offset(TensorCoord(1, 0))`, which advances by a single `ThreadblockShape::kContiguous`, with no split-k factor.

Both start consistently at channel `threadblock_tile_idx.k() * kK` (implicit_gemm_convolution_fusion.h ~296-337), so the divergence accumulates once the loop wraps past R*S. With interleaved slice partitioning, each additional R*S cycle applies bias/scale from one kK-block earlier than the channels the activations actually carry. This needs `split_k_slices > 1` and more than one C-channel block per slice (`ceil(ceil(C/S)/kK) >= 2`) to appear, e.g. split_k_slices=4, C=256, ThreadblockShape::kK=32, R*S>=2: from the second cycle on, bias[64+j*32] is applied where the activations come from channels 192+. The result is silent wrong numerics, not an OOB.

The same pattern exists in the conv3d fusion headers (conv3d_fprop_activation_tile_access_iterator_analytic/_optimized vs the shared scale/bias iterator). Wgrad fusion is unaffected: it loads scale/bias once, with no per-tile advance.

The device layer explicitly supports split-k for fused fprop (workspace handling in include/cutlass/conv/device/implicit_gemm_convolution_fusion.h ~148-175), so the combination is reachable through the public API.

This finding is from static verification of the two advance paths; I have not built an end-to-end failing kernel, but the stride mismatch is exactly the missing `split_k_slices` factor and the start offsets agree.

### Suggested fix

Multiply the scale/bias iterator's wrap stride by `problem_size.split_k_slices` in `advance()`, mirroring the activation iterators.

items.title: [BUG] Example 77 MLA fused split-KV reduction (--fuse_reduction) can hang or return wrong output
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CUTLASS C++

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

**Summary.** In the Blackwell MLA example's fused split-KV reduction (`--fuse_reduction`, `split_kv > 1`), the counter wait that synchronizes the split CTAs in `epilogue_lse_reduction` can hang the whole split group, and can let peer CTAs read the LSE exchange buffers before every contribution has landed, which gives wrong output. File: `examples/77_blackwell_fmha/kernel/sm100_fmha_mla_tma_warpspecialized.hpp`, lambda at lines 1952–1960, called at 1971 and 1981. #3763 fixes both by building the wait from `cutlass::GenericBarrier`'s `arrive_inc` and `wait_lt`.

#### Cause

Below, S is `local_split_kv`, the group's number of non-empty splits (at most `--split_kv`).

- **Overtaken equality wait (hang).** Phase 1 spins until `atomicCAS(lock, count, count)` returns exactly S (line 1956). A CTA that has already passed can add its phase-2 increment before a slower peer polls again; the slower peer then never sees S and never adds its own phase-2 increment, so the counter stops below 2S and every CTA of the group spins forever.
- **Arrival before contribution (wrong output).** Thread 0 increments the counter without waiting for the CTA's other contributing threads (in practice warp 1 of the 2-SM kernel): the lambda's only barrier comes after the spin, and a `__threadfence()` publishes only writes already in the fencing thread's causality past. A peer that sees the count can then read the LSE max (1973) before warp 1's `atomicMax` lands, or the LSE sum (1983) before its `atomicAdd` lands.

#### Suggested fix

See #3763. `arrive_inc` syncs the compute warps before thread 0's release increment, and `wait_lt` has thread 0 wait with an acquire load until the counter is at least the target.

#### Scope

- Affected: only `--fuse_reduction` with `split_kv > 1`; `is_fused_reduction` defaults to false (`77_blackwell_mla.cu`, line 87). The default split-KV path uses the separate `Sm100FmhaMlaReductionKernel` and is not affected. The lambda is unchanged from v4.2.0 to main `91843b7`.
- Evidence, from `77_blackwell_mla_2sm_fp16` on a B300 that was time-shared with another user's job (details and method in #3763):
  - Hang without any injected delay: 13 of 18 stress processes (1001 back-to-back launches each, six configurations with `--split_kv` 8 to 64) hung until killed at 300 s. With only a watchdog added to the same wait, every hang burst (1108 over 13 of 18 processes) contains a CTA waiting for exactly S that read a counter value above S. The `TEST_MLA_FUSE_REDUCTION` configuration (b=1, `--split_kv` 8) did not hang in 3 of 3 processes.
  - Hang under a forced legal schedule (thread 0 of one split waits 100 µs before each phase-1 poll): 60 of 60 runs, with peers waiting for 2S and the counter at 2S − 1.
  - Wrong output only under a forced legal schedule (warp 1 of one split waits 100 µs before its phase-2 `atomicAdd`): 60 of 60 runs fail `--verify`. Apart from near-threshold misses at `--split_kv` 64, which are a separate numerical issue (see #3763), we have not seen wrong output without a delay; a stress process verifies only its last launch.
- With #3763: none of 18 stress processes hung (18,018 launches). With its barrier inlined into our test patch, neither forced schedule hung or produced a race failure in 60 runs; 3 of them missed the 1e-2 threshold with max diff 0.0117, the size of the numerical misses, against 0.2 or more for every race failure.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

Unmodified example, built with CMake `-DCUTLASS_NVCC_ARCHS=103a`, on a B300:

```
./77_blackwell_mla_2sm_fp16 --b=8 --k=8192 --split_kv=20 --page=128 --fuse_reduction --verify --iterations=1000
```

Expected: the process finishes and `--verify` passes. Actual: it hung in 3 of 3 attempts until killed at 300 s.

The wrong output needs one late warp: a 100 µs `%globaltimer` busy-wait in warp 1 of one split per group, placed just before the `atomicAdd` at line 1979, makes `--verify` report "failed O" in every run.

**Expected behavior**

The fused reduction completes and matches the reference however the split CTAs are scheduled.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
 - Environment location: Bare-metal. NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC, driver 610.57.04, CUDA 12.9, CUTLASS `0b55a2f` (the file is byte-identical on main `91843b7`). The GPU was time-shared with another user's job during the runs.

items.title: [Feature Request] [Inductor][dynamic_shape]Size-specialized autotune config for non-template (pointwise & reduction) kernels under dynamic shapes
items.author: markc-614
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Under dynamic shapes, Inductor autotunes a single launch config for a given kernel and reuses it for every subsequent runtime shape. The chosen config (e.g. block size for pointwise, or split factor / RSPLIT for reduction) is decided by the first shape the kernel is autotuned with. A config that is optimal for a small shape can be catastrophic for a large shape — even though the shape is dynamic and the kernel could have been re-tuned.

This affects non-template triton kernels in general:

- pointwise kernels (block size XBLOCK / YBLOCK / ZBLOCK, num_warps)
- reduction kernels (split factor / RSPLIT, XBLOCK, num_warps)

and is backend-independent (CUDA, MLU, or any SIMD backend).

## Root cause

- CachingAutotuner.run benchmarks once and sets self.launchers = [best]; all later shapes reuse that one config.
- Pointwise/reduction configs are generated from compile-time size_hints, which is a single hint for dynamic shapes.
- Block size / split factor / num_warps are compile-time constants in Triton, so adapting to size requires different configs/binaries rather than a single adaptive binary.

Concrete CUDA (B300, PyTorch version: 2.13.0+cu130) reproductions with torch.sum (reduction) and torch.add (pointwise), using dynamic=True + mode="max-autotune".

## Repro 
### reduction
```
import os
import torch
torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high")

def red(x):
    return torch.sum(x)

c = torch.compile(red, dynamic=True, mode="max-autotune")

start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)

def time_it(fn, x, warmup=5, reps=7):
    for _ in range(warmup):
        fn(x)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    ts = []
    for _ in range(reps):
        start.record(); fn(x); end.record(); torch.cuda.synchronize()
        ts.append(start.elapsed_time(end))
    return sorted(ts)[len(ts) // 2]

x_small = torch.randn(128, 128, device="cuda")
print("small, small-tuned:", time_it(c, x_small))

x_large = torch.randn(8192, 8192, device="cuda")
print("large, reusing small-tuned:", time_it(c, x_large))

os.environ["TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR"] = f"/tmp/tc_d_{os.getpid()}"
torch._dynamo.reset()

d = torch.compile(red, dynamic=True, mode="max-autotune")
print("large, fresh autotune:", time_it(d, x_large))
```

output
```

small, small-tuned:            0.016 ms
large, reusing small-tuned:   12.576 ms
large, fresh autotune:         0.223 ms
```
-> slow / fast ratio: 56.3x

### pointwise
```
import os
import torch

def binary(x, y):
    return torch.add(x, y)

c = torch.compile(binary, dynamic=True, mode="max-autotune")

start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)

def time_it(fn, args, warmup=5, reps=7):
    for _ in range(warmup):
        fn(*args)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    ts = []
    for _ in range(reps):
        start.record()
        fn(*args)
        end.record()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        ts.append(start.elapsed_time(end))
    return sorted(ts)[len(ts) // 2]

x_small = torch.randn(128, 128, device="cuda")
y_small = torch.randn(128, 128, device="cuda")
print("small, small-tuned:", time_it(c, (x_small, y_small)))

x_large = torch.randn(16384, 16384, device="cuda")
y_large = torch.randn(16384, 16384, device="cuda")
print("large, reusing small-tuned:", time_it(c, (x_large, y_large)))

os.environ["TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR"] = f"/tmp/tc_d_{os.getpid()}"
torch._dynamo.reset()

d = torch.compile(binary, dynamic=True, mode="max-autotune")
print("large, fresh autotune:", time_it(d, (x_large, y_large)))
```
output
```
small, small-tuned:            0.019 ms
large, reusing small-tuned:    1.489 ms
large, fresh autotune:         1.142 ms
```
-> slow / fast ratio: ~1.30x

The regression is operator-dependent (dramatic for reduction, milder but consistent for pointwise), but the root cause is the same: a single small-shape-tuned config is frozen and reused for large shapes.

## Desired behavior

Make config selection size-specialized for non-template triton kernels: partition the input-size space into buckets (or generate a small set of size-hinted kernels) and dispatch to the config/kernel appropriate for the observed runtime size — for both pointwise and reduction.


### Alternatives

### size-bucketed autotune

A working prototype patches CachingAutotuner._precompile_worker and CachingAutotuner.run to make config selection size-dependent. In brief:

1. At codegen, record each dynamic dim's value range into inductor_meta.
2. At runtime, geometrically sample the size space (growth factor ~4) into buckets, capped at an empirical max (2^20) above which the best block size stops changing.
3. Eagerly precompile one best config per bucket, then dispatch to the bucket whose size is closest to the actual runtime size.

This works and fixes the large-shape slowdown, but has downsides:

- Increased device memory: every per-bucket kernel is compiled and kept resident, so binary/workspace footprint grows with the number of buckets.
- OOM risk during autotune: benchmarking each bucket requires constructing example inputs at that bucket's scale (up to the empirical cap), which can exhaust device memory — especially for large buckets or many buckets.

### Shape-range guards at the dynamo level

Partition the size space into ranges and rely on dynamo guards so that crossing a range boundary triggers a recompile, each specialization autotuning for its own range. Trade-offs:

- P99 latency fluctuation: crossing a range boundary triggers a recompile + re-autotune on the critical path, producing a latency spike.

### Extend multi_kernel_hints / SizeHintMultiKernel to non-template kernels

Reuse the existing size-hint multi-kernel dispatch (compile-time N kernels + runtime log2-L1 distance selection) for pointwise and reduction. This avoids the eager per-bucket precompilation and the resulting memory blow-up, but requires a non-template analog of MultiTemplateBuffer.

items.title: Deterministic index_put_(accumulate=True) / index_add_ on CUDA collapses to a single block when nElemBefore is in [2^31, 2^32) due to int narrowing in grid size
items.author: wipemble-jumptrading
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

With `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)`, CUDA `index_put_(accumulate=True)` launches its backward kernel with a grid that collapses to a single block when the number of elements before the indexed dimension (`nElemBefore`) is in [2^31, 2^32). One block then walks all of those elements serially, so the operation becomes _siginificantly_ slower. The same path is used by deterministic `index_add_` and by the backward of `index_select`.

In `index_put_with_sort_kernel` (`aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Indexing.cu`, line 719):

```cpp
std::clamp<int>(nElemBefore, 1, at::cuda::getCurrentDeviceProperties()->maxGridSize[2])
```

`nElemBefore` is `int64_t`, but `std::clamp<int>` narrows it to `int` before clamping. In [2^31, 2^32) the narrowed value is negative, so `grid.z = 1`. 

```python
import time

import torch

torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)


def backward_seconds(n: int) -> float:
    x = torch.zeros(n, 1, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16, requires_grad=True)
    index = torch.tensor([0], device="cuda")
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    start = time.monotonic()
    x.index_select(1, index).sum().backward()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    return time.monotonic() - start

print(backward_seconds(1_879_048_192))   # below 2**31: grid.z = maxGridSize[2]
print(backward_seconds(2_415_919_104))   # in [2**31, 2**32): grid.z = 1
print(backward_seconds(4_563_402_752)) # above 2**32: grid.z = maxGridSize[2]
```

gives 

```
1.14 s
979.66 s
2.37 s
```

items.title: [RayTrain] Manual checkpoint persistence to storage
items.author: mgharbi
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

It would be neat to be able to bypass RayTrain's automatic persistence of checkpoints to the storage backend (e.g. S3 or GCS). There is currently no way around that.

In my use case, I am writing custom code to persist checkpoint to GCS using PyTorch's distributed checkpointing library (which does not require staging to disk before asynchronous upload). Ray's current `report` API forces a copy of my uploaded checkpoint, even though it is already stored in the cloud.

Ideally, I would like to simply "inform" the Ray TorchTrainer of that custom checkpoint, so it can be used in the Ray Result, e.g. for auto-resume functionalities.

```python
# Current API
ray.train.report(metrics, checkpoint=persisted_ckpt)
# This will create a new checkpoint on the backend storage.

# Code to achieve the desired effect: bypass RayTrain's automatic checkpoint upload
from ray.train._internal.session import _TrainingResult
from ray.train.v2._internal.execution.context import (
    get_train_context as get_internal_train_context,
)
result = _TrainingResult(checkpoint=persisted_ckpt, metrics=metrics)
get_internal_train_context().get_result_queue().put(result)
```

items.title: [Data] JoinOperator receives GPU budget it never uses, preventing GPU actor pools from upscaling
items.author: albertcthomas
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

`HashShufflingOperatorBase` and therefore `JoinOperator` don't override `min_max_resource_requirements()`. They inherit the default `(zero, inf)`, so `ReservationOpResourceAllocator` reserves GPU budget for them and also hands them the leftover shared GPU budget, even though they never use a GPU (they report `gpu=0` in `base_resource_usage`, `incremental_resource_usage` and `per_task_resource_allocation`). PR #59789 added the zero-GPU cap for map operators only. Wondering if this is expected for `JoinOperator`.

The issue is that this budget blocks GPU actor pool upscaling on fixed-size clusters, for example a `map_batches(num_gpus=1)` pool upstream of a `Dataset.join`. A new actor needs a full GPU of budget, but part of the cluster's GPUs sits in the Join's budget, unused:

| Setup | GPU pool | Pool alloc / budget | Join alloc | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Repro below (2 logical GPUs) | 1 actor, 10 queued blocks | `gpu=1.2` / `gpu=0.2` | `gpu=0.8` | 1 of 2 GPUs used (2 without the join) |

With 4 GPUs, running the allocator code on the same operators gives a pool that can only recover to 3 actors (pool budget `0.19–0.33 GPU`, Join `0.67–0.81 GPU`), so one GPU stays idle.

Related: #59789, #59144.

### Versions / Dependencies

Tested on Ray 2.56.0, Python 3.11, Linux.

### Reproduction script

GPUs are logical (`ray.init(num_gpus=2)`), so no real GPU is needed.

```python
import os
import sys
import time

import numpy as np
import ray
from ray.data import ActorPoolStrategy

WITH_JOIN = sys.argv[1] == "join"

ray.init(num_cpus=8, num_gpus=2, include_dashboard=False)
ray.data.DataContext.get_current().enable_progress_bars = False

ds = ray.data.range(2_000, override_num_blocks=40).materialize()

class FakeGpuModel:
    def __call__(self, batch):
        time.sleep(0.5)  # simulate a slow GPU forward pass
        return {"id": batch["id"], "emb": np.zeros(len(batch["id"])), "pid": np.full(len(batch["id"]), os.getpid())}

emb = ds.map_batches(
    FakeGpuModel,
    num_gpus=1,
    batch_size=50,
    compute=ActorPoolStrategy(min_size=1, max_size=2),  # should scale 1 -> 2 (2 GPUs, many queued blocks)
    batch_format="numpy",
)
out = ds.join(emb, join_type="inner", num_partitions=4, on=("id",)) if WITH_JOIN else emb

n_actors = len(set(out.to_pandas()["pid"]))
print(f"with_join={WITH_JOIN}: GPU actors used = {n_actors} (cluster has 2 GPUs)")
```

```
$ python repro.py nojoin
with_join=False: GPU actors used = 2 (cluster has 2 GPUs)
$ python repro.py join
with_join=True: GPU actors used = 1 (cluster has 2 GPUs)
```


### Issue Severity

None

items.title: [Serve][Core/Auth] HAProxy ingress serves `/metrics` without the auth token when token auth is on
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
With token auth on, Ray's own metrics endpoints (each node's metrics port, the dashboard head and the autoscaler) will require the auth token once #67128 lands for #67119. Serve's HAProxy ingress still serves HAProxy's own Prometheus exporter with no token check.

The `prometheus` frontend in the HAProxy config template binds `RAY_SERVE_HAPROXY_METRICS_PORT` (default 9101) on all interfaces and answers `/metrics` with HAProxy's built-in exporter, with no `Authorization` check:

```
frontend prometheus
    bind :{{ config.metrics_port }}
    ...
    http-request use-service prometheus-exporter if { path {{ config.metrics_uri }} }
```

- Template: https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be/python/ray/serve/_private/haproxy_templates.py#L136-L139
- `metrics_port` and `metrics_uri = "/metrics"` defaults: https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be/python/ray/serve/_private/haproxy.py#L652-L653

This exposes HAProxy's stats (backends, request and error counts per route), not Ray's metrics registry. I found it by reading the template and haven't confirmed it with a running request.

Writing the token into the HAProxy config isn't an option: #67047 rules out new copies of the token on disk, with one exception for `ray metrics launch-prometheus`'s 0600 config. The approach is open. Options include having HAProxy check the header against the token some other way, or serving the exporter through a Python handler that runs the same check as Ray's other metrics endpoints.

Related: #67047, #67119.

items.title: [Core/Auth][Autoscaler] CloudWatch Prometheus scrape config gets 401 from Ray metrics endpoints when token auth is on
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
The Prometheus scrape config that the AWS CloudWatch integration for `ray up` ships has no `authorization` block, so once Ray's metrics endpoints require the auth token, every Ray target the CloudWatch agent scrapes returns 401 and CloudWatch metrics stop arriving.

Config: [`python/ray/autoscaler/aws/cloudwatch/prometheus.yml`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be/python/ray/autoscaler/aws/cloudwatch/prometheus.yml). The commented `head_setup_commands` in [`example-cloudwatch.yaml`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/f178b1887d2f9bb43a323678dc54c14aae7378be/python/ray/autoscaler/aws/example-cloudwatch.yaml#L99-L112) copy it to `/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/prometheus.yml`. Its `ray` job is:

```yaml
- job_name: 'ray'
  file_sd_configs:
  - files:
    - '/tmp/ray/prom_metrics_service_discovery.json'
    refresh_interval: 1m
```

When this starts to matter:

- #67119 (PR #67128) makes each node's metrics port, the dashboard head and the autoscaler return 401 without the token when token auth is on.
- Local clusters have run with token auth on by default since 2.59, and #67055 turns it on for every cluster in 2.61.
- #67047's goal is that every tool in this repo works with auth on.

Open questions:

- Does the CloudWatch agent's Prometheus scraping accept `authorization: {type: Bearer, credentials_file: ...}` in this file? I haven't checked.
- Which token path to point at on the node. The agent runs under `sudo`, so `~/.ray/auth_token` may resolve to root's home rather than the user who started Ray.

I haven't run this on AWS; this comes from reading the config and the endpoint changes in #67128.
