items.title: [Serve] [RFC] Computed Retry-After for backpressure rejections
items.author: vinay7373
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

PR #65193 added `BackpressureConfig`. Deployments can now reject backpressured requests with a 429 and a static `Retry-After` header. Each caller (proxy or `DeploymentHandle`) has its own request queue, and at the time of a backpressure rejection a static `Retry-After` value can be incorrect in both directions. If the queue is deep and the static value is too short, clients retry into another rejection, adding load exactly when the system is trying to shed it. If the queue drains fast and the value is too long, capacity sits idle while clients wait.

This proposal computes the `Retry-After` value from observed load. This makes the header a reliable estimate of when capacity will be available, instead of a number the operator guessed. This was the original shape of the production request behind #65193 and it fits the discussion there about making 429 the default at some point.

No OSS inference server does this today (TGI, Triton, NVIDIA Dynamo and TorchServe all reject without a retry hint). The closest prior art is cloud-side (Azure OpenAI's `retry-after-ms`, AWS's `x-amz-retry-after`) and per-client rate limiters, where the value can be exact because a rate window is a clock. Capacity recovery is not a clock, so here the value is an estimate at any layer.

## Goals

- An opt-in `BackpressureConfig` policy that computes `Retry-After` from load signals the rejecting component already has.
- Keep the rejection path as cheap as it is today. No RPCs, locks or extra work on reject-and-respond.
- Degrade gracefully: computed, else static, else no header. Never fail or delay a rejection.

## Non-goals

- Changing when requests are rejected. Admission control is a separate discussion.
- Guaranteeing admission at the suggested time. The header is a hint, not a reservation: it estimates when the current backlog will have drained, and admission at that time also depends on other arrivals.
- Changing the default rejection status code. Tracked separately.
- Implementing any further policy, such as the cluster-informed one (see "Future policies").

## Proposed API

```python
from ray.serve.config import BackpressureConfig

@serve.deployment(
    max_queued_requests=64,
    backpressure_config=BackpressureConfig(
        status_code=429,
        retry_after_policy="queue_drain_rate",   # NEW: "static" (default) | "queue_drain_rate"
        retry_after_s=5,                         # static value; also the fallback for computed policies
    ),
)
```

`retry_after_policy` is a named policy instead of a bare `"auto"` so future strategies can be added without changing what existing configs mean.

## Proposed design

This design adds a new field to `BackpressureConfig` called `retry_after_policy`, and one new policy named `queue_drain_rate` that computes `Retry-After` from the rejecting component's observed queue depth and drain rate.

The overall mechanism has 3 basic aspects: (i) how to compute the `Retry-After` value (what the `queue_drain_rate` policy implements), (ii) where to compute it, and (iii) who stamps the header and emits it to the client.

These boil down to emission and estimation. Emission answers (iii) and is fixed: the rejecting component stamps the header. Estimation covers (i) and (ii): one shared implementation, invoked at the two places Serve rejects today, each feeding its own local signals.

### The `queue_drain_rate` policy (this proposal)

```
retry_after = ceil(observed_queue_depth / drain_rate)
```

- **The numerator is the depth observed at rejection.** It is at least `max_queued_requests`, since a rejection only fires once the queue has reached the cap, and occasionally a little above it: the router's check is not atomic, and replica-rejected requests re-enter the queue behind new arrivals. The raise site already holds this number (it is in the `BackPressureError` message today), so using the observed value costs nothing and is exact.
- **`drain_rate` is the live signal**: how fast the queue empties, updated at the end of every interval as `drain_rate = 0.3 * rate_over_last_interval + 0.7 * previous_drain_rate`. `rate_over_last_interval` is the fresh measurement: requests drained during the interval that just ended. `previous_drain_rate` is this same formula's output from the previous update, so it carries the whole history with older intervals fading out. The 70% weight on the trend keeps lumpy traffic from whipping the value around (completions land in bursts, so a single interval can read 0 or 3x the true rate), and the 30% on the fresh measurement keeps the estimate chasing real load changes within a few intervals. The split, the interval length and the warmup threshold are implementation constants with environment-variable overrides, like Serve's other internal tunables, not new `BackpressureConfig` fields. The update runs on a lightweight background timer in the component's existing metrics machinery (default 1s). An interval with zero completions counts as a real observation when work is in flight, since that is what slow drain looks like, but idle intervals (nothing running or queued) skip the update instead of decaying the rate. The rate counts as warm after a configurable minimum number of counted intervals; until then the fallback applies.
- **Two call sites, one implementation.** On the proxy path the router rejects; its drain rate is its own assignment throughput, from a monotonic counter added at the existing send event (the current per-replica counter is an in-flight gauge, so it can't provide a rate). The rate is fleet-blended: faster replicas take more assignments, so mixed hardware is priced in. On direct ingress the replica rejects; its drain rate is its own completion rate, and its queue is drained only by itself. Same formula, different local inputs, different values, each describing its own queue. A replica's value is a conservative upper bound, since a retry may be re-balanced to a replica that frees up sooner.
- **Clamp to [1, 60] seconds.

comments.author: abrarsheikh
comments.body: @suppagoddo can you review this please

comments.author: suppagoddo
comments.body: @abrarsheikh - Sure, Will review

comments.author: johntaylor-cell
comments.body:
My main concern is how this RFC and direct-ingress work together.  Serve is moving toward direct-ingress with HAProxy as the default, and on that path the router is no longer the module that rejects the request.  HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve, and it already has retry-after functionality (as does Envoy).  Both implement it very differently from what the RFC proposes.  Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction.  It is also per-client, and HAProxy exposes queue-based metrics so the limit can fire only under real back pressure.  I suggest we provide a way to enable that functionality in HAProxy, which Serve already generates config for but does not use today.

If we also want retry-after on the router path (when direct-ingress is disabled), I would try to duplicate HAProxy's time-based functionality, rather than use a forecast. That is a larger change than this RFC scopes, since admission control is listed as a non-goal, but I think it is worth deciding explicitly rather than estimating.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Thanks for the review. Breaking it down into where we agree and where we don't.

**Where we agree:**

1. The RFC did not cover the direct-ingress path. That was a real gap and I updated the RFC. Short version: on direct ingress the same policy runs at the replica, using its own queue depth divided by an EWMA of its own completion rate. Same formula, one shared estimator implementation, two call sites. A replica's queue is drained only by itself, so that vantage is even simpler than the router's.

2. Per-client rate limiting at the HAProxy layer is valuable. It answers "this client exceeded its quota", and its Retry-After can be exact because a rate window is a clock. That is complementary to this RFC, which answers "the deployment is out of capacity, here is when to come back". I would support that as a separate proposal and am happy to file it.

**Where we don't agree, and why:**

1. "HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve" as the rejector. Not for backpressure today. On the direct-ingress path the replica rejects the request (see the "Request dropped due to backpressure" emission sites in [replica.py on the ray-2.58.0 tag](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/python/ray/serve/_private/replica.py)). HAProxy passes the replica's response through, and its errorfiles only rewrite HAProxy-generated errors. #65193 shipped 429 + Retry-After on this path, tested with `RAY_SERVE_ENABLE_DIRECT_INGRESS=1`.

2. "Functionality Serve already generates config for but does not use". I checked `haproxy_templates.py`: no stick-tables, no track-sc, no deny rules, no Retry-After anywhere in the generated config. Enabling this would be new work, not switching on something dormant.

3. "Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction". I checked the [HAProxy docs](https://www.haproxy.com/documentation/haproxy-configuration-tutorials/security/traffic-policing/) on this. HAProxy's computed Retry-After is `http-after-response set-header Retry-After %[src,table_expire(...)]`: the time until the client's stick-table rate-limit record expires. That is per-client policing, and it is exact because a rate window is deterministic. For capacity overload (server maxconn queue full, `timeout queue` expiring) the docs show no Retry-After computation: that 503 ships without a hint. The queue timer measures elapsed wait, not time until capacity returns. When capacity frees depends on service completions and arrivals, and no layer can know that exactly, including HAProxy, which cannot see how long the inference ahead of a request will take. Any capacity Retry-After is an estimate at every layer. That is why the RFC ships an acceptance criterion and telemetry to measure the estimate, instead of claiming exactness.

Rate limiting and capacity backpressure are different problems. An exact time-based Retry-After exists for the first and cannot exist for the second. This RFC is scoped to the second, now explicitly works on both ingress paths, and leaves room for a HAProxy rate-limiting proposal alongside it.

comments.author: suppagoddo
comments.body:
@vinay7373 - Couple of questions or feedback on this:

1. In case of direct-ingress path, the `router_queue_drain_rate` would become a bit misleading as the requests are rejected by the replicas here. 
2. For the direct-ingress path, I am thinking can we also add another saturation_factor. Fleet level info does not exists here, so it can be local value here.
3. For the EWMA warmup, I am thinking can this be a configurable variable.

Also I agree on the Rate limit and capacity back-pressure differentiation made above. 

Overall, I like the idea of calculating the `retry_after_s` on router/replica level before the `cluster_informed` policy.

comments.author: suppagoddo
comments.body:
@vinay7373 - For 
> retry at the suggested delay is admitted X% of the time” 

metric, in case of arbitrary production traffic, how can the serve proxy/router reliably correlate a 429 with a subsequent retry, because the client may generate a new request ID, retry through a different proxy/router, or not retry at all.

In order to measure efficiency without client correlation, shall we also compare the suggested/computed delay against an observable local recovery/drain-time metric [The calculation for this might get tricky under continuous load]?

comments.body:
@vinay7373 @johntaylor-cell - In the current scenario `own_queue_depth` is effectively equivalent to `max_queued_requests` whenever backpressure rejection happens. comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@johntaylor-cell 

My thoughts on your a HA Proxy based admission control and what I see as limitations:

- As you mentioned the HAProxy queue resets on every reload and Serve reloads HAProxy on every replica-set change. So the primary queue evaporates exactly during autoscaling churn (your own finding).
- Composition traffic never passes HAProxy, so the Serve backstop must stay. That means 3 admission systems with 3 threshold vocabularies to keep coherent.
    - Users configuring three queueing layers instead of one: per-server `maxconn` plus timeout queue in HAProxy, `max_queued_requests` at handles, `max_ongoing_requests` at replicas. Three knobs at three levels in different units (connections vs requests, per instance vs per caller vs per replica) that all have to be sized against each other and re-sized as the cluster scales. Mis-size any pair and you get double queueing or shedding while replicas sit idle. That is more error prone, not simpler.
- The default proxy path gets nothing from it.
- Per-deployment BackpressureConfig granularity would have to be re-expressed in generated HAProxy config.
- Moving where queueing happens is an admission-control redesign, which this RFC explicitly scopes out as a non-goal.
- On jittered-static vs computed: 
    - jitter only spreads retries around a center, it cannot make the center reliable. With `retry_after_s` we already ship the option to set a fixed, guessed value at config time, so a jittered constant is not a new proposal, it is [#65193](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65193) plus jitter. Drain rate moves 10-100x across load regimes, so the constant is wrong exactly when it matters. A 5s center against a 60s real drain means every jittered retry comes back early and gets refused again. Guessing that constant is the problem this RFC exists to remove. So a computed value using drain rate is more reliable. And @suppagoddo 's suggestion for A/B against a jittered-static baseline will show it under real workloads and make this measurable.

@johntaylor-cell took your 6 and 7 into the RFC:

On 6: you are right that queue depth is the configured cap at rejection, and right about occupancy. I checked: `serve.llm` sets `DEFAULT_MAX_ONGOING_REQUESTS = int(1e9)` (python/ray/llm/_internal/serve/constants.py), so occupancy against configured capacity reads zero. The saturation factor is dropped entirely and the formula is now `ceil(max_queued_requests / drain_rate)`.

On 7: agreed and adopted. Jitter moves into the shared header helper, so the static retry_after_s path gets it too, which both fixes today's verbatim emission and keeps the A/B fair. Good catch, credited in the RFC.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@suppagoddo thanks for your review, all of your points are in the updated RFC:

1. Renamed to queue_drain_rate, since the same policy runs at the router or the replica, whichever rejects.
2. On a local saturation factor for direct ingress: we ended up dropping the saturation factor everywhere instead. From @johntaylor-cell 's finding `serve.llm` defaults `max_ongoing_requests` to `1e9`, so occupancy measured against configured capacity reads zero for the main workload class, and the backoff term had no existing signal behind it. It isn't gone forever though: if the A/B data shows the simple formula consistently errs in a way a saturation signal would fix, that data is the justification to bring one back. Evidence first, term later.
3. EWMA warmup is configurable as an implementation constant with an environment-variable override, alongside the smoothing split and the interval length, same as Serve's other internal tunables. Deliberately not a new BackpressureConfig field, to keep the public API at two fields plus the policy name.
4. Adopted your measurement point: since retries can't be reliably correlated (new request IDs, different proxy, or no retry at all), the primary measure is suggested delay vs the locally observed queue drain time, with admitted-retry rate secondary where correlation does exist.
5. Your A/B against a jittered-static baseline is now the acceptance test itself.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@abrarsheikh to summarize the whole review thread and the current state of RFC:

Updated the RFC based on the review so far and it came out simpler. 
One policy, `queue_drain_rate` which computes `retry_after` on rejection using below formula:
```
retry_after = ceil(max_queued_requests / drain_rate)
```
Where:
- `max_queued_requests`: the numerator is the configured cap (depth at rejection is always the cap) and 
- `drain_rate` is a smoothed measure of how fast the rejecting component's queue empties which is assignment throughput at the router, completion rate at the replica. 

The value is clamped to [1, 60]s and jittered in the shared header helper so the static path gets jitter too, falls back to the static retry_after_s when the rate isn't warm, and the acceptance test is an A/B against a jittered-static baseline measured on suggested delay vs observed local drain time.

comments.author: JerryChaox
comments.body:
hello guys, some information and test for this RFC.

I tested the proposal on Ray 2.58.0 and found two implementation details worth checking before coding it.

First, num_requests_sent_to_replicas is an in-flight gauge: it increments on send and decrements on completion. It cannot directly provide assignment throughput, so the router likely needs a monotonic counter at the accepted-assignment event.

Second, router queue depth is not always equal to max_queued_requests at rejection. Internal replica rejection can cause requests to re-enter after new requests occupy temporarily freed slots. With a cap of 8, 1,418 of 17,270 router rejection events had an observed depth of 9–11. I did not observe this on the direct-replica path.

I also compared the computed policy with a tuned jittered-static baseline over 90 held-out distributed runs. Conditional local-drain header MAE was 1.865s for the computed policy and 1.141s for static 2s. The computed policy generated fewer attempts, so this looks like a precision versus retry-cost tradeoff rather than a clear winner.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@JerryChaox Thanks for testing the approach and for those valuable findings. Here are my thoughts on each of them:

1. Agree (and my earlier comment was wrong on this) that `num_requests_sent_to_replicas` is an in-flight gauge, increments on send (`router.py:404`) and decrements on completion (`router.py:412`). I will fix this by adding a new monotonic assignment counter at the same send event. So the raise site and the counters live on the same object and the drain rate is still a derivation over local state.

2. This is a great find. Agreed. This finding makes the formula better: use the observed depth at rejection as the numerator instead of the configured cap. The raise site already holds that number, it is in the BackPressureError message today.

3. On your third observation, the A/B test: I see how a static value wins on a homogeneous workload, where a good constant like your 2s can be guessed or tuned in advance. But the whole purpose of this RFC is the case where the constant cannot be guessed in advance, because load regimes vary and move the drain rate. I'd like to know: a) Did drain time vary across your 90 runs? b) Was the 2s tuned per workload or once overall?

Your fewer attempts observation is the most interesting part. MAE weighs a 1s early and a 1s late suggestion equally, but the costs are not equal: early means a wasted attempt plus more load on a system that is already shedding, late means idle wait. So I think we should use a asymmetric or composite metric that penalizes wasted attempts (penalize early more than late).

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Acceptance criteria spec:

1. Ground truth: Each rejection records the observed depth D and the drain counter value at that moment. Ground truth T is the wall time until the counter advances by D: assignments at the router, completions at the replica on direct ingress. This measures what the header claims, that the observed backlog clears. It does not measure whether a specific retry gets admitted, since that depends on other clients' arrivals. T stays measurable under continuous overload because the counter keeps advancing even when the queue never dips below the cap.
2. Metric: An asymmetric loss between the suggested delay `s` and `T`: `0.75 * max(T - s, 0) + 0.25 * max(s - T, 0)`. One second too early costs 3x one second too late, because an early retry wastes an attempt and adds load while the system is shedding and a late one only waits, bounded by the clamp. The minimizer of this loss is the 75th percentile of the drain time distribution, so the estimator gets a concrete target. MAE is reported as secondary for comparability. Scoring is offline over logged pairs, on the pre-jitter post-clamp value.
3. Baseline: The comparison arm is jittered static, with the constant tuned only on calibration runs disjoint from the evaluation set (rule: 75th percentile of calibration drain times, one global constant). A per-scenario tuned static is also reported. Runs are open loop (clients ignore the header) with autoscaling off and a pinned replica set.

@suppagoddo For me to run the above acceptance test I'll need one structured record per rejection with `policy id, fallback rung used, observed depth, drain rate estimate and warm flag, pre-jitter and post-jitter values, and the counter value at rejection`. Plus the counter itself readable by a test harness at sub-second granularity. Everything already exists at the raise site or in estimator state; the cost is one log line on a path that already logs a warning today. Please make sure this record emission is part of your implementation.

Pass bar (proposal): 
- Computed beats the static baseline on the primary loss by at least 20% in aggregate across the scenarios
- is never more than 10% worse in any single scenario
- the undershoot rate lands at 25 +/- 10 points
- and cold start falls back to the static value cleanly.

cc. @JerryChaox @abrarsheikh @johntaylor-cell

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
**AI serving regimes for the acceptance runs**

Now that the implementation is up for review (#66798), here are the regimes the acceptance runs will cover. The runs collect the metrics defined in my acceptance comment above. The scenarios its pass bar refers to are drawn from these regimes. I'm deriving the regimes from real-world AI serving, using two characteristics: load and completion.

What a regime is: An AI serving regime is a recurring pattern of load and completion at the component that rejects requests. Load is how requests arrive. Completion is how they finish: how long each one runs, how many run at once, and whether they finish one at a time or in batches.

**Why these two (load and completion)?**
Ground truth in the acceptance spec is the time for the drain counter to advance by the observed depth: assignments at the router, completions at the replica on direct ingress. Both count the completion process, seen from each vantage, since the router hands a queued request to a replica when one finishes. So completion sets the drain time directly. Load decides when the queue overflows and what the estimator sees between rejections, such as idle gaps. Latency is an outcome of both, not an input.

Completion is the important half in AI serving, because processing time is not known when a request arrives. A generative model decides its output length while it generates, and in production "the remaining output length of an LLM request is not conditioned on the generated length so far" [1]. Drain speed cannot be computed from what is in the queue. It has to be measured from completions.


**Completion regimes:** 
The estimator samples once per second, so what matters is how far apart completions arrive at that scale.

| Regime | Examples | Completions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| W1 Real-time predictive | vision, ranking, LLM code completion | Dense: many per second | Latency bounds of 15 to 250 ms [2]. Code completion has a median output of 13 tokens [3] |
| W2 Batched execution | `@serve.batch`, dynamic batching | Grouped: a batch finishes together | Each response returns once its whole batch is evaluated [4] |
| W3 Interactive LLM | chat on continuous batching | Dense to moderate: seconds each, many at once | A median of 129 output tokens [3] at 20 to 50 tokens/s [5] |
| W4 Long-running LLM | reasoning, long context, agent steps | Sparse: minutes each, few at once | A mean of 3,880 output tokens [6]. Long contexts limit how many run at once [7] |

**Load regimes:**

| Regime | Arrivals | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| L1 Steady | A constant rate. The runs use fixed-interval schedules so repeated runs are comparable | MLPerf's Server scenario models online load with Poisson arrivals [2] |
| L2 Bursts and idle gaps | High-rate bursts separated by silence | API traffic is "aperiodic... characterized by burstiness" [8]. Short-term arrivals are "often bursty (CV > 1)" [1] |
| L3 Mix shift | A steady rate, but the request mix changes, so completions speed up or slow down | Services have "widely different prompt and token distributions" [3]. In one 48-hour window, 29 of 2,412 clients sent 90% of requests [1] |

**Scenarios:** 
|# | Cell | Completions | Expected drain time | Load |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | W1, L1 | every 0.25 s | 2 s | 2x drain |
| S2 | W3, L1 | every 2.5 s | 20 s | 2.5x drain |
| S3 | W1 to W3, L3 | every 0.25 s, then every 1 s | 4 s, then 16 s | 2x drain |
| S4 | W1, L2 | every 0.25 s during bursts | 4 s | 3x drain for 20 s, then idle for 25 s |
| S5 | W3, L1, mixed fleet | every 0.4 s, from one fast and one 4x slower replica | 10 s | 2.4x drain |
| S6 | W4, L1, beyond cap | every 8 s | 240 s | 4x drain |
| S7 | W1, L1, cold start | every 0.25 s | 4 s | 3x drain from the first second |
| S8 | W3, L1, pipeline | every 1 s at the inner deployment | 8 s | 3x drain |
| S9 | W2, L1 | 8 at once every 4 s | about 8 s | 2x drain |
| S10 | W4, L1 | every 8 s | about 48 s | 2x drain |

[1] ServeGen, NSDI'26: https://

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
From the above clearly EWMA's loss is 74% lower overall than static jitter. Though the results above show a clear gain, it falls short when completions are seconds apart:
1. Long requests, one completion every 8 s: never early, but clients waited 15 to 17 s longer than needed on average.
2. Batched, 8 requests finishing together every 4 s: early only 2 to 3% of the time, and clients waited about 6 s longer than needed.
3. Steady slow, one completion every 2.5 s: the estimate swings both ways. On the proxy path it was early 45% of the time. On both paths, when it was late, clients waited 9 to 12 s longer than needed.
4. Beyond cap, one completion every 8 s with 30 requests waiting: the true wait is 240 s. Without the 60 s cap, the EWMA would have sent a median of 382 s, and up to about 2,400 s (40 minutes). These are rejections from the first 180 s of each run, while the drain held at one every 8 s.

**Main cause for the above limitation:** The EWMA counts drains in each one-second sample and divides the depth by that rate. When completions are seconds apart, most samples count zero. The rate falls at every empty second and dividing by a small rate gives a long wait. When the next completion comes, the rate jumps back up. So the estimate follows the time since the last completion, not the real drain speed. For example, with one completion every 4 s and 8 requests ahead, the true wait is 29 to 32 s, but the EWMA's estimate moves between 20 and 59 s.

Lets take LLM serving as an example. After bit research on how requests complete in LLM serving, I found that what matters is not just how long each request runs, but how far apart completions are at the component that rejects. That gap is about how long one request runs, divided by how many requests run at the same time. For example, if a replica runs 40 requests at once and each takes 20 s, one finishes every 0.5 s or if it can run only 2 at once, one finishes every 10 s. LLM requests run for seconds to minutes. Memory for long contexts limits how many run at once on a replica and batched work finishes in groups. So in Batched execution (W2), Long-running LLM (W4) and Interactive LLM (W3) when a replica runs only a few requests at once, completions at the rejecting component are seconds apart or come in groups. These patterns are common in LLM serving and they are where a per-second rate breaks down. So we want to measure the drain in a way that does not depend on completions landing inside each one-second sample.

To address the above, I would like to propose **The busy clock**:
The PR already keeps one running total for each component, the drain counter. The busy clock adds a second running total: busy seconds.
- A drain is one step of the drain counter: an assignment at the router, or a completion at a replica.
- A busy second is a second in which the component had work pending or saw a drain. These are the seconds the PR's sampler already counts. Idle seconds, which the PR skips, are not added, so the busy clock stops when the component is idle.
- Seconds per drain is busy seconds divided by drains over a recent window. It is the average time the component needs for one drain while it is working.
- The window is the most recent stretch of busy time that holds at least 8 drains and at least 10 busy seconds. Each limit protects one kind of workload:
  - When completions are seconds apart, the 8 drains matter. They keep the estimate from resting on one or two gaps. With one completion every 8 s, the window stretches to about 64 s.
  - When there are many completions per second, 8 drains can pass in a fraction of a second. The 10 busy seconds keep the estimate from jumping with every small burst.
  - The window only sets how far back the estimate looks. The estimate is still updated every second and every rejection is answered at once. Until 10 busy seconds have passed, the window is all the busy time so far, so warmup still takes 3 counted seconds. If the last 10 minutes of busy

@suppagoddo, 
Following up on your uneven jitter range idea (for example -5% to +15%, so fewer clients come back early).

The tables above score the value before jitter. Clients see the header after jitter and rounding up to whole seconds. So I replayed the final acceptance round the way the PR builds the header: jitter, round up, then clamp to [1, 60] (cap enforced only to keep the experiment consistent with previous ones here, I still prefer no cap with busy clock implementation) for computed values. Same rejections and measured drain times as before. The numbers are the average loss, with the share of clients told to come back early:

| Jitter range | Busy clock | EWMA |
|---|---|---|
| None (rounding up only) | 0.687 (15% early) | 1.321 (12% early) |
| ±5% | 0.722 (12%) | 1.309 (12%) |
| **±10%** | **0.759 (14%)** | 1.298 (13%) |
| ±20% (current default) | 0.882 (20%) | 1.302 (17%) |
| -5% to +15% | 0.834 (8%) | 1.384 (9%) |
| 0% to +20% | 0.948 (4%) | 1.464 (6%) |

**Why the uneven range does not help.** Compare it with ±10%, which has the same spread. -5% to +15% does cut early clients, from 14% to 8%. But its loss is 10% higher (0.834 against 0.759), and it is worse in all 15 scenario and path pairs. The EWMA shows the same pattern (1.384 against 1.298).
- An early second costs three times a late one, so the loss is lowest when about a quarter of clients are early. Below that, everyone else waits longer than needed, and that costs more than the early retries it saves.
- The busy clock already sits close to that point before jitter: 24% of its values are early.
- Rounding up to whole seconds already makes every header later by up to 1 s. Shifting the jitter range up adds more of the same.

**I prefer ±10% instead of ±20%:**
- It lowers the busy clock's loss on the wire from 0.882 to 0.759. The EWMA barely changes, because its own errors are larger than the jitter.
- It keeps most of the spreading. Headers are whole seconds, so for waits up to about 5 s, ±10% and ±20% give nearly the same headers: a 4 s estimate becomes 4 or 5 s either way. For longer waits, ±10% still spreads a 30 s wait over 27 to 33 s.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@suppagoddo, regarding the busy clock's history that we discussed offline, so it is on record here.

**Change:** keep the busy clock's history by drains, not by time. My first version kept the last 10 minutes of history of busy time. This change keeps at least the last 8 drains, however long ago they were. The window rule itself stays the same: at least 8 drains and at least 10 busy seconds.

**Why:** with a 10 minute history, a component that finishes a request less often than once every 75 s (600 / 8) cannot hold 8 drains in its window. Past one completion every 10 minutes, it cannot even see one full gap, so the estimate comes out too low. This happens with very long requests, such as LLM research or agent tasks that run for about 15 minutes, when a replica runs only a few at a time.

**Other benefits:**
- It removes a jump during long stalls. With a 10 minute history, once the last 8 drains are out of history, the estimate jumps to D x 600 s (5 hours for D = 30). With this change it keeps growing steadily, by D / 8 for each stalled second.
- For very slow workloads the window gets long, about 2 hours for 15 minute requests, so it follows changes slowly. There is no way around this: a request's length can only be learned by watching such requests finish.
- Memory stays small.

comments.author: suppagoddo
comments.body:
@vinay7373 - In both the EWMA and Busy second we are considering the current load on the system, shall we also include the number of incoming requests too in the calculation? Imagine this scenario:
```
T0:
 -> Queue Depth is full and We cannot take a new Request.
 -> Request R1 comes: We calculate the retry after and return xx sec
 -> Request R2 comes: We calculate the retry after and return xy sec
 -> The only difference between xx and xy is jitter-delta

T0 + xx:
 -> R1 retry occurs and we let it in. Queue depth have 1 empty slot.

T0 + xy:
 -> R2 retry occurs and we reject it as Queue depth is full because R1 got it.
```

Basically the current estimator is predicting backlog-clear time, which might not be 100% equal to future admission time, which I think seems reasonable as it is a hint. But I think we should make this distinction clear.

comments.author: vinay7373
suppagoddo
comments.body:
>  If we ever want admission guarantees, the right tool is a reservation: return a token with the 429 and give returning clients priority at their time. That is a separate feature, so I would list it as future work.

This as a future works sound good and reasonable. And thanks for adding it to the RFC.

items.title: [Serve] gRPC servers keep SO_REUSEPORT on with enable_so_reuseport=False, so direct ingress ports can be shared
items.author: xyuzh
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

`start_grpc_server` takes `enable_so_reuseport`, and direct ingress replicas (`RAY_SERVE_ENABLE_HA_PROXY=1`) pass `False`, so that binding a port another process listens on fails and Serve allocates another port. The flag has no effect. The option reaches gRPC as a string, `("grpc.so_reuseport", str(int(enable_so_reuseport)))` in `python/ray/serve/_private/grpc_util.py`. gRPC reads `grpc.so_reuseport` as an integer and ignores a string, so SO_REUSEPORT stays on (gRPC's default). A second server then binds a port that is in use without an error, and the kernel splits new connections between the listeners.

Expected: with `enable_so_reuseport=False`, binding a port that is in use fails.

We hit this on a 12-replica gRPC deployment behind HAProxy after an in-place rolling update. The process of one replica, which the controller had allocated gRPC port 40010, also listened on 40011, the port of another replica:

```
LISTEN *:40010  users:(("ray::ServeRepli",pid=157869,fd=65))  ino:95078843
LISTEN *:40011  users:(("ray::ServeRepli",pid=157869,fd=67))  ino:95078844
LISTEN *:40011  users:(("ray::ServeRepli",pid=157968,fd=65))  ino:95012385
```

The second listener of pid 157869 had none of the deployment's servicers. Connections that the kernel gave it got `UNIMPLEMENTED: Method not found!` for every RPC, and about 8% of requests failed until we killed pid 157869 and Serve replaced the replica. The controller's log shows it allocated only 40010 to that replica, so it isn't clear from the logs how the second socket came about (replica INFO logs were off). Either way, the replica could bind 40011 next to the other replica only because both sockets had SO_REUSEPORT on. With the option passed as an integer, that bind fails instead.

### Versions / Dependencies

Ray 3.0.0.dev0 (6703877370); the same code is on master (49bb8191b1). grpcio 1.75.0, Python 3.12, Linux (EKS). Serve with `RAY_SERVE_ENABLE_HA_PROXY=1`.

### Reproduction script

```python
import asyncio
import socket

import grpc


def free_port():
    with socket.socket() as s:
        s.bind(("", 0))
        return s.getsockname()[1]


async def second_bind(value):
    port = free_port()
    first = grpc.aio.server(options=[("grpc.so_reuseport", value)])
    first.add_insecure_port(f"[::]:{port}")
    await first.start()
    second = grpc.aio.server(options=[("grpc.so_reuseport", value)])
    try:
        second.add_insecure_port(f"[::]:{port}")
        return "bound (port shared)"
    except RuntimeError:
        return "failed (port in use)"
    finally:
        await second.stop(0)
        await first.stop(0)


async def main():
    for value in ("0", 0):
        print(f"grpc.so_reuseport={value!r}: second bind {await second_bind(value)}")


asyncio.run(main())
```

Output on Linux with grpcio 1.75.0:

```
grpc.so_reuseport='0': second bind bound (port shared)
grpc.so_reuseport=0: second bind failed (port in use)
```

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

items.title: [Core/Auth] Enable token authentication by default for all clusters in Ray 2.61
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
Since Ray 2.59, token authentication is on by default only for local clusters. Every other cluster (started by hand, by `ray up` and the autoscaler, by KubeRay, or by the Anyscale platform) still runs with auth disabled, so anyone who can reach its ports can run arbitrary code. Ray 2.61 makes token auth the default for every cluster. `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` stays the opt-out.

Goals:

- Every newly started cluster, local or remote, has token auth on unless the user sets `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled`.
- A bare `ray.init()`, C++ and Java drivers that start their own local cluster, and `ray.cluster_utils.Cluster()` stay zero-config; `ray start --head` needs a token created first. Every tool in this repo works with auth on.
- The local-cluster special cases are deleted, with no dead branches left.

Design:

- `AUTH_MODE` defaults to `"token"` in `src/ray/common/ray_config_def.h`. The local-cluster special cases added in #64755, #66467 and #66778 are deleted, since every path is already in token mode.
- `ray start --head` never creates a token; with none, it fails with an error that says to run `ray get-auth-token --generate` and put the token on every node. A bare `ray.init()`, `ray.cluster_utils.Cluster()` and C++/Java drivers that start their own cluster create a missing one. Connecting nodes and clients never create one; without a token they fail fast with an error that names `ray get-auth-token` and the `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` opt-out.
- The token never goes on a command line. `ray up` ships it to the head node as a file mount, and the head ships it to the worker nodes it launches. `image_uri`/`container` workers get it as a read-only file mount when the node's token is a file, and by name from podman's environment when the node has it only in `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN`.
- A client in token mode talking to a cluster that opted out gets an error instead of silent success. gRPC servers in disabled mode reject requests that carry a token. HTTP clients check `GET /api/authentication_mode` instead, because reverse proxies in front of a disabled dashboard can send their own `Authorization` header (the former `kuberay-auth.md` guide set one up with kube-rbac-proxy; also ray-project/kuberay#1824, #42606).
- Ray's Prometheus metrics endpoints (nodes, autoscaler, dashboard head) require the token when auth is on. `ray metrics launch-prometheus` puts the token inline in its own config when `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` is set, and otherwise points it at `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` or `~/.ray/auth_token`. The dashboard's template config for users' own Prometheus never gets the token.


How users use it in 2.61. Every sub-issue PR must keep these flows working as shown:

1. Local development. A bare `ray.init()` needs no setup: it connects to the running local cluster if there is one, and otherwise starts a new one and creates `~/.ray/auth_token` if it is missing. Before `ray start --head`, create the token once; everything in the same HOME then reads it.

```bash
ray get-auth-token --generate        # once; creates ~/.ray/auth_token if missing
ray start --head
ray start --address=127.0.0.1:6379   # a second node on the same machine
python -c "import ray; ray.init()"   # a driver
```

Without a token, `ray start --head` fails at once, before starting anything, with an error that says to run `ray get-auth-token --generate` and put the token on every node. C++ and Java drivers that start their own cluster, and `ray.cluster_utils.Cluster()`, create the token themselves.

2. A cluster built by hand across machines. The token file must be copied from the head to each machine; the token never goes on a command line.

```bash
# head machine
ray get-auth-token --generate
ray start --head
# worker machine, after the head's ~/.ray/auth_token is copied here
ray start --address=<head-ip>:6379
```

Without the copy, `ray start --address` fails at once with an error that says to run `ray get-auth-token` on the head and copy the token.

3. `ray up`. No token steps: `ray up` creates the token on the operator's machine if needed and ships it to the head node. The head ships it to every worker node it launches, including ones the autoscaler adds later.

```bash
ray up cluster.yaml
ray dashboard cluster.yaml &
ray job submit --address http://127.0.0.1:8265 -- python script.py
```

4. A client on another machine. Clients on the head machine, or on the machine that ran `ray up`, already have the token. Any other machine needs the token file copied to it.

```bash
# after the head's ~/.ray/auth_token is copied to this machine
ray job submit --address http://<head-ip>:8265 -- python script.py
```

`RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` is only needed when the token file lives somewhere other than `~/.ray/auth_token`.

5. Opting out. Every node and every client sets `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled`. The head logs a warning that auth is disabled.

```bash
RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled ray start --head
RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled ray start --address=<head-ip>:6379
RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled ray job submit --address http://<head-ip>:8265 -- python script.py
```

A node or client that leaves out `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` fails with an error telling it to set it: AuthModeMismatch if it has a token, the missing-token error if it doesn't. For `ray up`, put `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` in the cluster YAML's start commands.

6. Mismatches never fall back to auth off. A worker or client with no token, a different token, or a different auth mode than the head fails right away with an error that names the fix. It does not hang or connect without auth.

7. Prometheus scraping. `ray metrics launch-prometheus` works with no change. With `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` set, it writes the token into its own config (`./prometheus-<version>.linux-amd64/ray_prometheus.yml`, mode 0600); otherwise the config reads `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` or `~/.ray/auth_token`. With auth on, no `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN`, and a missing, unreadable or empty token file, it fails with an error. An external Prometheus, including one that uses the dashboard's template c

items.title: [Core/Auth] Keep the auth token off the podman command line in image_uri and container runtime envs
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
`image_uri.py` copies every host `RAY_*` variable onto the podman command line as `--env NAME='value'`, so `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` shows up in `ps` on the node. Only the log line is redacted.

PR: #66975. It passes every host `RAY_*` variable to podman by name (`--env NAME`), including `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` and `RAY_RUNTIME_ENV_BEARER_TOKEN`. Podman reads the values from its own environment, so none appears on podman's command line or in `ps`. When the node's token comes from a file (`RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` or `~/.ray/auth_token`), that file is still mounted read-only into the container with `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH`, resolved from the node's environment only. When the node has the token only in `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN`, the container gets it as an environment variable, and no token file is written.

items.title: [Core/Auth] Create the auth token for ray.init() and Cluster() heads, and require one for ray start --head
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
Under a token default, every head start needs a token. `ray start --head` must not create one. It only starts a head node, and the worker nodes of a cluster started that way need the same token, so it fails with an error telling the user to create a token and distribute it. A bare `ray.init()`, `ray.cluster_utils.Cluster()` and C++/Java drivers that start their own cluster start a single throwaway cluster, so they create the token if it is missing. Today only `ray.init()` creates one: `ray start --head` with no token fails with `AuthenticationError`, and `ray.cluster_utils.Cluster()` builds `Node(head=True)` directly, so its GCS crashes on `Check failed: has_token || ignore_auth_mode` (`authentication_token_loader.cc:115`) and the user only sees `Timed out waiting for file .../gcs_server_port_...`.

Change:

- `ray start --head` keeps `create_token_if_missing=False`. With no token, it fails before starting any process with a head-specific error: run `ray get-auth-token --generate`, then put that token on every node. This is the only auth error that names `--generate`.
- `AuthenticationError.__str__` doesn't append `TOKEN_AUTH_FIX_MESSAGE` (#67051) to the `ray start --head` no-token error, since that text tells the reader to copy a token from the head.
- A bare `ray.init()` that starts a new cluster, and `ray.cluster_utils.Cluster()` before it builds the head, create a missing token.
- C++ and Java drivers that start their own cluster, and `ray.cluster_utils.AutoscalingCluster`, pass a hidden `ray start` option, `--create-auth-token-if-missing`. It isn't documented for users, carries no secret, and applies only to that one call.
- Connecting paths keep `create_token_if_missing=False`.
- Token creators that start at the same time with no token file yet all end up with the same token. An existing token file that holds a token (its first non-blank line, as the token loader reads it) is never overwritten. A leftover file with no token is overwritten in place, as today. A race between creators over such a file is best-effort and out of scope.
- Test: `ray start --head` with an empty HOME exits non-zero before starting any process, names `ray get-auth-token --generate`, and creates no token file. With a token present, it starts normally.
- Test: a bare `ray.init()` with an empty HOME creates `~/.ray/auth_token` with mode 0600.
- Test: `ray.cluster_utils.Cluster()` with an empty HOME starts with auth on.
- Test: several processes creating the token at once in an empty HOME all end up with the token on disk.
- Test: an existing token file that holds a token, including one that starts with a blank line, is left unchanged by every creator.
- Test: a C++ driver (`//cpp:metric_example`) and a Java driver that start their own cluster work with an empty HOME and auth on.
- Test: a `ray.cluster_utils.AutoscalingCluster` with an empty HOME starts with auth on.
- Test: `ray start --address` and `ray.init(address=...)` never create a token file.

No behavior change while the default is still `disabled`.

items.title: [Core] Keep job env_vars values off podman's command line in image_uri and container runtime envs
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

For `image_uri` and `container` runtime envs, `RuntimeEnvContext._exec_container_worker` in `python/ray/_private/runtime_env/context.py` passes the job's `env_vars` to podman as `--env NAME=VALUE`. The values stay in podman's `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` for the worker's whole lifetime, so they show in `ps` and in the dashboard's process view. The dashboard reporter only redacts `--serialized-runtime-env-context=`. `runtime_env={"image_uri": ..., "env_vars": {"DB_PASSWORD": "..."}}` puts `--env DB_PASSWORD=...` on that command line. This predates #66975 (master put the same values in its `bash -c` string), and `.claude/rules/security.md` says `env_vars` values must not go on process command lines.

The proposed fix is to pass the job's values through `--env-file=/dev/fd/N`, where N is an inherited `os.memfd_create` fd holding `NAME=VALUE` lines. The env file goes before the by-name `RAY_*` `--env` flags and `run_options`, so a later `--env` still wins as it does now. An env file can't hold a newline in a value, so runtime env setup should reject such a value with an error that names the variable. We also need to check that rootless podman still reads the fd after it re-execs itself.

### Use case

Follow-up to #66975. Jobs pass credentials through `env_vars`, and other local users and dashboard viewers shouldn't see them on a container worker's command line.

items.title: Illegal memory access in triton kernel and non-determinism codegen
items.author: xw285cornell
items.body_excerpt:
Hi team, we seem to identified an issue that triton is generating non-deterministic codegen results, and in certain cases (small chances) it seems to have illegal memory access due to out of bound access in shared memory. 
The triton code is fairly simple (shown below). We run the code many times (disabled pytorch's codegen cache) and it seems it produced different shared memory: 
Most of times: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 2560, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}
Sometimes: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 544, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}

So sometimes it only asks for 544 bytes for shared memory space which might lead to out of bound access to shared mem. We checked and ttir is the same across the two runs, but llir is different. Wondering if you can shed some lights on this (and whether the codegen is deterministic. Also this is still on llvm IR - not sure if it repros in MLIR. 

```
from torch._inductor.triton_ops.autotune import pointwise

@pointwise(
    size_hints=[262144, 64],
    tile_hint=TileHint.DEFAULT,
    filename="notebook",
    meta={
        "signature": {0: "*bf16", 1: "*fp32", 2: "*bf16", 3: "i32", 4: "i32"},
        "device": 0,
        "constants": {},
        "mutated_arg_names": [],
        "configs": [instance_descriptor(divisible_by_16=(0, 1, 2, 3), equal_to_1=())],
    },
)
@triton.jit
def triton_(
    in_ptr0,
    in_ptr1,
    out_ptr0,
    xnumel,
    ynumel,
    XBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
    YBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
):
    xnumel = 262144
    ynumel = 62
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:, None]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    yoffset = tl.program_id(1) * YBLOCK
    yindex = yoffset + tl.arange(0, YBLOCK)[None, :]
    ymask = yindex < ynumel
    x0 = xindex % 512
    x1 = xindex // 512
    y2 = yindex
    x3 = xindex
    tmp0 = tl.load(
        in_ptr0
        + (
            512
            + x0
            + (1536 * x1)
            + (786432 * y2)
            + (786432 * (((x0 + (512 * x1)) // 262144)))
        ),
        xmask & ymask,
    ).to(tl.float32)
    tmp1 = tl.load(in_ptr1 + (512 + x0), xmask)
    tmp2 = tmp1.to(tl.float32)
    tmp3 = tmp0 + tmp2
    tmp4 = 2.8284271247461903
    tmp5 = tmp3 / tmp4
    tl.store(
        out_ptr0 + (y2 + (62 * x3) + tl.zeros([XBLOCK, YBLOCK], tl.int32)),
        tmp5,
        xmask & ymask,
    )
```

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL: export_to_c fails for a --gpu-arch other than the current GPU's
items.author: hwanseoc
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

`export_to_c` fails on the plain C path (no `--enable-tvm-ffi`) when the function was compiled for a different arch than the current GPU. For example, `--gpu-arch sm_90a` on a B200:

```text
JIT session error: Symbols not found: [ _cuKernelGetAttribute, _cudaDeviceGetAttribute, _cudaFuncSetAttribute, _cudaGetDevice, _cudaKernelSetAttributeForDevice, _cudaLaunchKernelEx, _cudaLibraryGetKernel, _cudaLibraryLoadData ]
error: Error dumping object file: Failed to dump object file with PIC relocation
```

The same export works for the native arch, and it also works if I load the runtime libraries `RTLD_GLOBAL` first. My guess is that no execution engine gets built for an arch the GPU can't run, so `libcute_dsl_runtime.so` never gets loaded before the object dump.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

```python
import ctypes, sys, tempfile

import cuda.bindings.driver as cuda
import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute
from cutlass.cute.runtime import make_fake_stream


@cute.kernel
def noop_kernel(x: cutlass.Int32):
    pass


@cute.jit
def noop(x: cutlass.Int32, stream: cuda.CUstream):
    noop_kernel(x).launch(grid=(1, 1, 1), block=(32, 1, 1), stream=stream)


if "--preload" in sys.argv:
    for lib in cute.runtime.find_runtime_libraries(enable_tvm_ffi=False):
        ctypes.CDLL(lib, mode=ctypes.RTLD_GLOBAL)
fn = cute.compile(noop, cutlass.Int32(0), make_fake_stream(), options="--gpu-arch sm_90a")
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    fn.export_to_c(tmp, "noop", function_prefix="noop")
print(f"cutlass-dsl {cutlass.__version__}: exported", flush=True)
```

```console
$ python repro.py
JIT session error: Symbols not found: [ _cuKernelGetAttribute, ... ]
$ python repro.py --preload
cutlass-dsl 4.8.0: exported
```

**Expected behavior**

`export_to_c` works for any `--gpu-arch` the compiler accepts, with no manual preloading.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
 - Environment location: Bare-metal
 - nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0 and 4.7.0 (cu13), cuda-python 13.4.1
 - B200, driver 580.159.03, Ubuntu 22.04, Python 3.12

**Additional context**

#2859 had the same error on the TVM-FFI path and was fixed in 4.3.3; the TVM-FFI path does export cross-arch now. The plain C path still fails. Workaround: preload `cute.runtime.find_runtime_libraries()` with `RTLD_GLOBAL`.

items.title: [BUG] SM90 TMA GEMM mainloops rely on elect_one_sync() electing lane 0 (TMA issuer vs. PipelineTmaAsync is_leader)
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CUTLASS C++

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

**Summary.** Most SM90 TMA GEMM mainloop collectives work only if `elect.sync` elects lane 0, because two threads are chosen by different rules: the TMA issuer is the elected lane, while the producer's arrival comes from warp-group thread 0. PTX does not say which lane `elect.sync` elects, and if another lane were elected the kernel would hang. We suggest deriving the leader from the election in the mainloop warp, as in-tree code already does elsewhere.

Paths and lines are at main `0b55a2f`.

#### Evidence

**TMA issuer.** These collectives call `producer_acquire` and issue the TMA copies only inside `if (lane_predicate)`, where `lane_predicate = cute::elect_one_sync()`, that is, `elect.sync` with a full mask:

| Collective (`include/cutlass/gemm/collective/`) | elect / `producer_acquire` lines |
|---|---|
| `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp` | 320 / 374 |
| `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized_fp8.hpp` | 318 / 372 |
| `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_rs_warpspecialized.hpp` | 401 / 457 |
| `sm90_sparse_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp` | 415 / 458 |
| `sm90_sparse_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized_fp8.hpp` | 426 / 469 |
| `sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp` | 370 / 425 |
| `sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized_fp8.hpp` | 368 / 422 |
| `sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized_fp8_blockwise_scaling.hpp` | 463 / 543 |

The non-warp-specialized `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss.hpp` (lines 365 and 504) and the SM90 implicit-GEMM conv collective (`conv/collective/sm90_implicit_gemm_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp:558–559, 612`) have the same pattern.

**Producer arrival.** `PipelineTmaAsync::producer_acquire` performs `arrive_and_expect_tx` only when `params_.is_leader` is set (`include/cutlass/pipeline/sm90_pipeline.hpp:533–535`, and 555–557 in the token overload). This arrival is the stage's only producer arrival. The kernels set `is_leader = warp_group_thread_idx == 0`:
- `sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:324`;
- `sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_cooperative.hpp:471`;
- `sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_pingpong.hpp:463`;
- the array cooperative and pingpong kernels, lines 522 and 531;
- `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss.hpp:334`.

The mainloop warp is warp 0 of the producer warp group, so warp-group thread 0 is its lane 0.

#### Cause

PTX ISA 9.4 (§9.7.15.15, `elect.sync`) promises only that the election is deterministic, with the same leader for the same `membermask` every time. It does not say which lane. If another lane were elected:
- that lane would call `producer_acquire` without being the leader, so nothing arrives on the full barrier;
- lane 0 would not enter the `if` at all;
- the TMA's complete-tx would only drive the transaction count negative.

The phase would never complete. Consumers would block in `consumer_wait`, then the producer in `producer_acquire` once every stage is used.

#### Suggested fix

Precedents for deriving the leader from the election:
- on the same `PipelineTmaAsync`, `examples/88_hopper_fmha/kernel/fmha_kernel_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:205, 210` and `sm120_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_cooperative_asymmetric_dma.hpp:443, 448`;
- in the SM100 kernels, e.g. `sm100_gemm_tma_warpspecialized.hpp:465`.

For the SM90 kernels, that would be:

```cpp
mainloop_pipeline_params.is_leader =
    warp_group_role == WarpGroupRole::Producer &&
    producer_warp_role == ProducerWarpRole::Mainloop && lane_predicate;
```

Restrict it to the mainloop warp. The `MainloopAux` warp in the blockwise kernels also has the Producer role and calls `producer_acquire` from all lanes. Giving it a leader would add a second `arrive_and_expect_tx` per stage.

This works because the kernel's `elect_one_sync()` and the collective's later one use the same full mask, and PTX guarantees the same leader for the same mask. Two more changes go with it:
- `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss.hpp` would need `lane_predicate` computed before `is_leader` is set;
- the debug-build `brkpt` checks in `producer_acquire` (`sm90_pipeline.hpp:542–544` and 564–566), which fire when the leader is not lane 0, would need to go. They already assume lane 0 for the FMHA and SM120 kernels above.

The alternative is to gate the TMA issue in each affected collective on lane 0 instead of `elect_one_sync()`.

#### Scope

- Unaffected: some collectives call `producer_acquire` from all 32 lanes and issue TMA only from the elected lane, so lane 0 always arrives:
  - the mixed-input collectives (`sm90_mma_tma_gmma_rs_warpspecialized_mixed_input.hpp:684/694`, and the array variant at 774/784);
  - the non-array FP8 blockwise collective (577/587–588).

  The epilogue's TMA loads are also unaffected, because one elected lane both posts the expect-tx and issues the copy.
- Current hardware: the kernels run today, so current hardware evidently elects lane 0 here. The code also states that intent:
  - `sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss.hpp:356` says "Set predicate for the lowest lane_id in the warp";
  - `sm90_pipeline.hpp:286` says "We have exactly one thread elected in the Producer as the 'leader'";
  - CuTe's fallback without `elect.sync` returns `(threadIdx.x % 32) == 0` (`include/cute/arch/cluster_sm90.hpp:197`).

#### Why there is no PR

The fix can go in the kernels (`is_leader` from the election) or in each affected collective (TMA issue gated on lane 0), so we'd rather follow your preference than guess. Tell us which and we'll write the PR.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

Found by reading the source against the PTX ISA. There is no runtime reproduction.

**Expected behavior**

The lane that issues the TMA loads is the lane that arrives with the expected bytes.

**Environment details**

Source analysis; no runtime environment involved. Hopper (sm_90a).

items.title: [DOC] Dynamic-layout guide example uses incompatible singleton strides
items.author: 0z5a
items.body_excerpt:
## Report incorrect documentation

**Location:** [Framework integration guide, dynamic-layout code example](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/91843b71d90737e0a9b86f7d9df213cff5a3526f/media/docs/pythonDSL/guides/framework_integration.rst), at the v4.8.1 source revision.

**Problem and reproduction:** The example assumes that singleton dimensions of `b` have stride 1, but the shown PyTorch construction retains stride 4:

```python
import torch
from cutlass.cute.runtime import from_dlpack

b = torch.empty(32, 1, 1, 1, 4).permute(3, 4, 1, 0, 2)
print(b.stride())  # (4, 1, 4, 4, 4)
from_dlpack(b).mark_layout_dynamic(leading_dim=0)
# Expected strides[leading_dim] == 1, but got 4
```

The same mismatch affects the later `leading_dim=2` example. The `t1` and `t2` examples also print `t2` and `t3`, respectively, before those variables have been defined.

**Verification:** Ran the six positive examples t0–t5 in a GH200 environment with the main editable core and torch 2.11.0, and an H100 environment with CuTe DSL 4.8.1 and torch 2.13.0. The original and a print-only repair fail at the stride check. Using explicit singleton strides and correcting the print variables makes all six layouts match the documented output in both environments. This checks tensor-layout metadata, not GPU kernel performance; deliberate-error snippets elsewhere in the guide are outside this report.

**Suggested fix:** Construct `b` with `torch.empty_strided((1, 4, 1, 32, 1), (1, 1, 1, 4, 1))`, and print the variables just defined.

items.title: [Store] Does Mooncake store plan to support awareness of layers, chunk ordering, and TP?
items.author: Hadigan
items.body_excerpt:
It looks like the current Mooncake store does not have awareness of layer granularity, chunk order (earlier vs. later chunks), or TP ranks. This can cause problems during cache eviction:

1. The store might evict KVs for only some layers, forcing prefill to recompute all layer KVs for those tokens.
2. The store might evict the KVs corresponding to the earliest chunk(s) of a token sequence, forcing prefill to recompute KVs for all chunks/tokens.
3. The store might evict KVs produced by some TP ranks, forcing all TP ranks to recompute KVs.

I think the Mooncake store should be aware of layers, chunk ordering, and TP. On eviction, it should evict a token’s KV caches for all layers and for all TP ranks together (i.e., keep KV state complete per token). 
From the chunk-order perspective, eviction policies should prefer removing KVs for later chunks first rather than evicting early-chunk KVs that make prefill expensive.

items.title: [train] Soft-failure mode / retries for errors raised during checkpoint uploading via `train.report`
items.author: justinvyu
items.body_excerpt:
Any errors such as AWS file upload rate-limiting errors or transient S3 bucket connectivity issues can result in user code exiting. 

However, these errors should not always cause training to crash immediately. Instead, this should be configurable.

Users can already do something like this by wrapping `train.report` in a try catch:

```python
def train_fn_per_worker():
    num_consecutive_checkpointing_failures = 0
    ...
    try:
        ray.train.report(...)
        num_consecutive_checkpointing_failures = 0
    except Exception as e:
        logger.exception("Checkpoint uploading failed...")
        num_consecutive_checkpointing_failures += 1

    if num_consecutive_checkpointing_failures > MAX_CONSECUTIVE_CKPT_FAILURES:
        raise RuntimeError("Something is wrong. Checkpoints are not being saved, so killing this run.")
```

Ray Train could provide something like this out of the box, or at least show an example of this kind of logic in the docs.

items.title: [Core/Auth] Distribute the auth token to ray up and autoscaler nodes via file_mounts
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
`ray up` clusters need the token on the head and every worker, without putting it on a command line. Passing it as an env var in the start commands puts it in `ps` on both ends of the SSH command and twice in the `ray up` console log.

Change:

- In `_set_up_config_for_head_node` (`autoscaler/_private/commands.py`), before the file mounts are rewritten, add a file mount for `~/.ray/auth_token` unless `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` is set locally or the YAML already mounts that path. The source follows token precedence: `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` written to a 0600 temp file, else `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH`, else `~/.ray/auth_token` (created with `generate_and_save_token` if missing). The autoscaler reuses `file_mounts` for workers.
- `ray up` creates a missing token under the same rules as #67049, and never overwrites a token file that holds a token.
- Opting out: the user sets `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` on the nodes in the cluster YAML. `ray up` never copies the local auth mode to the nodes.
- Existing `ray up` clusters update their worker nodes once after upgrading: the new file mount changes the autoscaler's runtime hash, so each worker reruns its setup commands and restarts Ray. Instances aren't relaunched; in Docker mode the container restarts to pick up the new mount. Call this out in the PR so it reaches the release notes.
- Also cover `--no-monitor-on-head`, which skips `_set_up_config_for_head_node`.
- The fake multi-node docker provider skips worker `file_mounts` (`disable_node_updaters`), and the head's `ray start` runs at container start, before `ray up` syncs files. So add the token file to the shared `node_spec["volumes"]` in `fake_multi_node/node_provider.py`, mounted read-only at `/home/ray/.ray/auth_token`. The fake command runner must then skip `ray up`'s `~/.ray/auth_token` upload, because `docker cp` can't overwrite a read-only single-file mount.
- Test: a fake-provider cluster with `RAY_AUTH_MODE=token` scales up a worker that joins. It runs in the "core: HA integration tests" CI job (tag `ha_integration`).

Checked: `rsync -avz` keeps mode 0600. In Docker mode, file mounts are rsynced to the host and bind-mounted into the container at the expanded `~/.ray/auth_token`; this comes from reading `command_runner.py` and hasn't been run on a real cluster.

items.title: [Core/Auth] Require the auth token on Ray's Prometheus metrics endpoints
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
With token auth on, Ray's Prometheus metrics endpoints (each node's metrics port, the autoscaler and the dashboard head) serve metrics to anyone who can reach them. That discloses job, actor and deployment names, node IPs and resource use.

Change:

- Each metrics endpoint checks the token the way the dashboard does, accepting `Authorization`, `X-Ray-Authorization` or the `ray-authentication-token` cookie. With auth on, a missing token gets 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` and a wrong one gets 403. With auth off, the check is skipped.
- With auth on, `ray metrics launch-prometheus` writes `authorization: {type: Bearer, credentials: <token>}` into its config when `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` is set. `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` takes precedence, so this applies even when a token file exists. Otherwise it writes `authorization: {type: Bearer, credentials_file: …}` pointing at `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` if set, else `~/.ray/auth_token`. The config is `./prometheus-<version>.linux-amd64/ray_prometheus.yml`, in the folder launch-prometheus extracts into the current directory. With an inline token, Ray creates that file atomically with mode 0600 (`O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW`), never at the umask's 0644. With auth off, the config is unchanged.
- Ray reads the token from the first non-blank line of a token file (`AuthenticationTokenLoader::ReadTokenFromFile`), so blank lines around the token are allowed.
- `ray metrics launch-prometheus` exits with an error when auth is on, `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` isn't set, and the token file is missing, unreadable, empty, or holds more than one non-blank line (Prometheus sends the whole file). It also exits with an error, not a traceback, when it can't write its config.
- When `RAY_AUTH_MODE` is unset and launch-prometheus finds no token, it warns that every Ray target returns 401 if the cluster runs token auth.
- The dashboard's `prometheus.yml` in the session folder (`MetricsHead._create_default_prometheus_configs`) never gets an `authorization` block, and no warning is logged about it. No Ray component reads it: it's a template for users who run their own Prometheus, and they add the block themselves.
- Metrics tests send the token when auth is on (`fetch_raw_prometheus`).
- Test: with auth on, each endpoint returns 401 without a token, 403 with a wrong one, and 200 with each accepted form. With auth disabled, it returns 200 without a token.
- Test: with auth on, `ray metrics launch-prometheus` on a multi-node cluster shows every target up.
- Test: with only `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` set, `ray metrics launch-prometheus` shows every target up, and its config holds the token inline with mode 0600.
- Test: with auth on, the dashboard's `prometheus.yml` has no `authorization` block.
- Test: with auth disabled, the generated Prometheus config is unchanged.

Local clusters have run with token auth on by default since 2.59, so their metrics endpoints require the token as soon as this merges.

The token goes inline because without it, `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN`-only users can't use launch-prometheus at all. Writing the token under `/tmp/ray` was rejected. Ray creates `/tmp/ray` and its session folders 0777 without the sticky bit, and they outlive `ray stop`. In testing, another local user can't read a 0600 file there, but can delete it or put their own at the same path. The user's own directory is normally not writable by others. The cost is that the inline token stays on disk after Prometheus stops and doesn't follow token rotation, unlike `credentials_file`, which Prometheus re-reads on every scrape.

items.title: [Data] Filtered read_lance reports incorrect row counts and can produce an empty test set
items.author: jiangxt2
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

`ray.data.read_lance(..., filter=...)` can report the unfiltered row count through `Dataset.count()`. `train_test_split()` also trusts this row-count metadata, so filtering before an 80/20 split can silently put every remaining row in the training set and leave the test set empty.

For a 28-row Lance dataset filtered to seven rows, `count()` returns 28 and `train_test_split(test_size=0.2)` returns train/test sizes of **7/0**, rather than **5/2**. No deleted records are required. The same count and split error occurs when the filter is supplied through `scanner_options["filter"]`.

The following larger cases reproduced the same problem with `test_size=0.2`:

| Dataset | Source rows | Filtered rows | Native `count()` | Actual train/test | Expected train/test |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Tabular data | 1,048,576 | 262,144 | 1,048,576 | 262,144 / 0 | 209,715 / 52,429 |
| JPEG images | 8,192 | 2,048 | 8,192 | 2,048 / 0 | 1,638 / 410 |
| MP4 video clips | 512 | 128 | 512 | 128 / 0 | 102 / 26 |

The media tables contain complete JPEG or H.264/MP4 bytes in a regular Arrow `large_binary` column. Each clip has 24 frames at 12 fps. Both media types were decoded and their payload hashes checked. The filtered output rows are preserved; the failure is in counting and allocating them between the splits. These media cases use S3-compatible storage backed by MinIO; the small and tabular reproductions use local files.

The error can also produce incorrect nonempty splits. Filtering the million-row table to 943,719 rows gives 838,860 training rows and 104,859 test rows: the test fraction is about **11.11%**, although 20% was requested. `shuffle=True` and an integer `test_size` also reproduced the problem in the tabular case.

Expected behavior: `count()` should describe the filtered output, and splitting should use that output's actual row count. Row-count metadata should not claim an exact total that the read does not produce.

**Workaround and comparison:** explicitly materializing the filtered dataset before splitting restores the expected split sizes. In the media cases, that reads about 150.9 MiB for the selected images or 29.6 MiB for the selected videos. The `lance_ray.read_lance` comparison returned correct counts and splits; its filtered counts read about 2.0 MiB per media table. These are single-run local Docker/MinIO S3 response-body measurements, including driver planning and worker reads, not general throughput results.

**Source observation:** [`LanceDatasource.get_read_tasks()`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/e8c5f61d83b29e200eb5a51c34887db1c39e1ca8/python/ray/data/_internal/datasource/lance_datasource.py#L151) sums fragment row counts without applying the scanner filter. [`_try_count_or_materialize()`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/e8c5f61d83b29e200eb5a51c34887db1c39e1ca8/python/ray/data/dataset.py#L3243) trusts the resulting metadata and skips materialization before calculating the split boundary.

**Related work:** #53162 attempted to address filtered Lance counts but was closed without merging. #66472 concerns floating-point rounding and stratified allocation, which are different causes of incorrect split sizes. This report concerns the Lance reader's filtered row-count metadata.

AI assistance was used to prepare this report and run the reproductions.

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray 2.59.0, Python 3.12.14, Linux ARM64.
- PyLance 12.0.0, PyArrow 23.0.1, NumPy 2.2.6, pandas 2.3.3.
- The `lance-ray` comparison uses [main at b4c1a2e](https://github.com/lance-format/lance-ray/tree/b4c1a2e87673976322106dc5b356e55859ab98ce).
- The media cases additionally use Pillow 11.3.0, PyAV 16.0.1 and MinIO RELEASE.2025-09-07T16-13-09Z. Media were derived from Big Buck Bunny, (c) copyright 2008, Blender Foundation / www.bigbuckbunny.org, under [CC BY 3.0](https://peach.blender.org/about/). None of these media assets or services is needed for the minimal reproduction below.

### Reproduction script

This is a reduced version of the executed 28-row reproduction. The reduced script has been checked statically but has not been run verbatim.

```python
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import lance
import pyarrow as pa
import ray

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    path = Path(directory) / "example.lance"
    lance.write_dataset(
        pa.table({"id": range(28)}), str(path), max_rows_per_file=7
    )
    ray.init(num_cpus=2, include_dashboard=False, log_to_driver=False)
    try:
        def read():
            return ray.data.read_lance(
                str(path), filter="id >= 21", override_num_blocks=4
            )

        print("count:", read().count())

        train, test = read().train_test_split(test_size=0.2)
        print("train/test:", train.count(), test.count())

    finally:
        ray.shutdown()
```

Recorded values from the executed 28-row fixture:

```text
count: 28
train/test: 7 0
```

Expected: `count: 7` and `train/test: 5 2` without requiring explicit materialization.

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

items.title: [Feature][Console]: Manage ModelClaims in the AIBrix Console (frontend + backend)
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

ModelClaim attaches a model to a warm GPU runtime pool, several models to a GPU, but today it can only be managed with kubectl and YAML. To create one and call it, a user has to know the CRD fields, the pool labels, which engine flags the runtime owns, and gateway details such as the `routing-strategy` header. The Console already manages LoRA adapters through a Kubernetes-backed BFF and pages; ModelClaim should get the same, so a user can attach a model, watch it come up, and try it without writing YAML.

### Use Case

- Pick a warm pool, declare the model and its per-GPU cost, submit, and follow the claim from Pending to Active, or see why it waits (`NoMatchingPods`, `InvalidPerGPU`, ...).
- See every claim in the namespace, including those applied with kubectl; change `perGPU`; delete a claim.
- Chat with the claimed model in the Playground right after creating it, including a sleeping model that the first request wakes.

### Proposed Solution

Three PRs:

1. **Backend BFF** (`apps/console/api/handler/modelclaim.go`), with Kubernetes as the source of truth like the ModelAdapter BFF:
   - `GET/POST /api/v1/model-claims`, `GET/PATCH/DELETE /api/v1/model-claims/{name}` (PATCH changes `perGPU` only), `GET /api/v1/model-claim-pools`. Writes require admin.
   - Create rejects what the controller would never place: missing or invalid `perGPU`, runtime-owned flags (`--port`, `--served-model-name`, ...), `--gpu-memory-utilization`, DP != 1, TP x PP that does not match the pool's GPUs per Pod, negative priority, and a served name already in use (409).
   - The TP x PP, perGPU and GPU-count helpers move to `pkg/utils`, so the console and the controller share one implementation.
2. **Frontend pages** next to LoRA: list, create (pool picker, required perGPU, placement priority, engine flags with live validation, YAML preview) and detail (conditions in lifecycle order, inline perGPU edit, engine instances with their routes and KV limits).
3. **Playground**: list Active and Sleeping ModelClaims next to Deployments; send a `routing-strategy` for claims, since they have no HTTPRoute; wait out the 503 + `Retry-After` while a model wakes; cap max tokens to the claim's `--max-model-len`.
